## Proposition 9

**I**f from the endpoints of two lines descending from some angle, two lines intersecting each other are reflected <note>The term "reflexe" here refers to transversal lines that cross between the two main legs of the angle.</note> back upon the descending lines: the ratio of the descending line to its upper part will be composed of two ratios: one of which is from the endpoint of this reflected line to its part above the intersection; the other is the ratio of the part below the intersection of the other reflected line to the whole of that same reflected line.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a triangle with vertices a, b, g. Two lines, b-e and g-d, are drawn from the base vertices to the opposite sides, intersecting at point z. An auxiliary line e-h is drawn parallel to g-d.</image-desc>
</margin>

¶ As two lines $a.b$ and $a.g$ descend from angle $a$; and from their endpoints $b$ and $g$, two lines are reflected back across the descending lines, which are $b.e$ and $g.d$, intersecting each other at $z$. I say that the ratio of $g.a$ to $a.e$ is composed of two: namely, the ratio of $g.d$ to $d.z$ and the ratio of $z.b$ to $b.e$. ¶ For, by the 31st [proposition] of the first [book of Euclid], let $e.h$ be drawn parallel to $g.d$. By the 29th of the first, angle $d.g.a$ will become equal to angle $h.e.a$, and angle $g.d.a$ will be equal to angle $e.h.a$; and angle $a$ is common to both triangles. Therefore, by the fourth [proposition] of the sixth [book], the ratio of $g.a$ to $a.e$ will be as $g.d$ to $e.h$. Between $g.d$ and $e.h$, I shall place $d.z$ as a middle term; and thus the ratio of $g.d$ to $e.h$ becomes composed of two: namely $g.d$ to $d.z$ and $d.z$ to $e.h$. But by the 29th of the first and the fourth of the sixth, $d.z$ to $e.h$ is as $z.b$ to $b.e$. Therefore, $g.d$ to $e.h$ is composed of two, namely $g.d$ to $d.z$ and $z.b$ to $b.e$. Wherefore the ratio of $g.a$ to $a.e$ is also composed of two: namely, $g.d$ to $d.z$ and $z.b$ to $b.e$, which was the intent.

## Proposition 10

**L**ikewise, the ratio of the parts of the lower descending line to the upper will be composed of two: one of which is the ratio of the parts from the endpoint of this lower reflected line to the upper; the other is the ratio of the lower part of the other descending line to that whole same descending line.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram similar to the one above, depicting a triangle a-b-g with intersecting internal lines b-e and g-d. An auxiliary line a-h is extended parallel to line e-b.</image-desc>
<gloss>The ratio of two triangles, in which one angle of one is equal to an angle of the other, the sides corresponding to the equal angles are proportional. 7. 6. <note>original: "proportio duoz triāg[u]l[orum] quoz an[gulus] / un̄ alteri sit eq[u]ales lat[er]a equos a[ngulos] / resp[ici]entia sūt p[ro]p[orti]onalia 7. 6." This gloss refers to Euclid's Elements, Book VI, Proposition 7, regarding similar triangles.</note></gloss>
</margin>

¶ Let the descending and reflected lines be as before. I say that the ratio of $g.e$ to $e.a$ is composed of two: namely, the ratio of $g.z$ to $z.d$ and the ratio of $d.b$ to $b.a$. ¶ For, by the 31st of the first, let $a.h$ be drawn parallel to $e.b$, which the continued line $g.d$ meets at $h$. As before, triangles $a.h.d$ and $b.z.d$ become equiangular. Moreover, in triangle $g.a.h$, the line $e.z$ cuts two sides while being parallel to the third. Therefore, by the second [proposition] of the sixth [book], $e.g$ to $e.a$ is as $g.z$ to $z.h$. But between $g.z$ and $z.h$, let us place $z.d$ as a middle term. Therefore, the ratio of $g.z$ to $z.h$ will be composed of two: namely, $g.z$ to $d.z$ and $d.z$ to $z.h$. However, by the fourth of the sixth, combined with the converse of the proportions, $z.d$ to $z.h$ is as $d.b$ to $b.a$. Wherefore the ratio of $g.z$ to $z.h$ is composed of two: namely $g.z$ to $z.d$ and $d.b$ to $b.a$. It is clear, therefore, that the ratio of $g.e$ to $e.a$ is composed of the two: $g.z$ to $z.d$ and $d.b$ to $b.a$, which is the intent.

### Proposition 12

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a semicircle with center d. A chord ag is drawn. A perpendicular dz is dropped from the center d to the midpoint z of the chord ag. A radius db intersects the chord ag at point e. Points a, b, and g are on the circumference.</image-desc>

**I**f a known arc in a semicircle is divided into two: and the ratio of the chord of the double of one to the chord of the double of the other is given: each of those arcs which it divides will be known. ¶ Because the whole arc $a.b.g$ is known, its chord $a.g$ will be given from the table of chords. And because the ratio of the chord of the double arc $a.b$ to the chord of the double arc $b.g$ is given—but this is, by the preceding [proposition], as $a.e$ to $e.g$—therefore the ratio of $a.e$ to $e.g$ is given. And since the whole $a.g$ is given: by the rule of joined proportionality <term>joined proportionality: a method of solving ratios where if a:b and the total a+b are known, the individual parts can be found.</term> and the 15th of the sixth [book], both of the two segments $a.e$ and $e.g$ will be revealed. ¶ Now, let the perpendicular $d.z$ be drawn from the center $d$ to $a.g$. By the third [proposition] of the third [book], $a.z$ will be equal to $z.g$; therefore $e.z$, the difference of the half of $a.g$ over $a.e$, will be known. But since the triangle $a.d.z$ is right-angled <note>original: "orthogonius"</note> and subtends half of the arc $a.g$, it is therefore known. And since the angle $z$ in triangle $a.d.z$ is a right angle: by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], the angle $d.a.z$ will be known, because angle $z.a.d$ and angle $a.d.z$ together make one right angle. Therefore, since triangle $a.d.z$ is right-angled and has known angles, its sides will be known through the table of chords; or, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Refers to the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, $z.d$ will be known from $a.z$ and $a.d$. Likewise, by the same penultimate [proposition] of the first, $e.d$ will be known from the known lengths $e.z$ and $d.z$. Thus, in the right-angled triangle $e.d.z$, with known sides in parts where $a.d$ is 60 <note>The author uses the sexagesimal (base-60) system common in medieval astronomy, where the radius of a circle is divided into 60 parts.</note>, the sides will be known by the 15th [proposition] of the first in parts where $d.e$ is 120. From this, its angles will be known by the table of chords, just as the three angles of a right-angled triangle correspond to the whole circle circumscribed around it—that is, where a right angle is 180 degrees. Therefore, its angles will be known when a right angle is 90 degrees; thus angle $z.d.e$ will be known. But $a.d.z$ was known previously; therefore angle $a.d.e$ will be known, the quantity of which is arc $a.b$, which was sought.

**I**f a line is drawn from one endpoint of an arc smaller than a semicircle, passing away from the center and cutting the arc until it meets the diameter joined through the other endpoint of the same arc: the ratio of the line passing beyond the center to its part outside the circle will be as the ratio of the chord of double the whole arc to the chord of double the part which the extended lines include.

I say that the ratio of $g.e$ to $e.b$ is as the ratio of the chord of double the arc $a.g$ to the chord of double the arc $a.b$. ¶ From points $b$ and $g$, let the perpendiculars $b.z$ and $g.h$ descend upon $l.e$. Wherefore, by the fourth [proposition] of the sixth [book], $g.e$ is to $e.b$ as $g.h$ is to $b.z$. But by the ninth [proposition] of the third and last...

<margin>
If a diameter is drawn so that it is between two parallels with equal angles and a common <unclear>fibi</unclear> <unclear>munis</unclear> similar parts. From which, in a circumference through which a right angle is formed: if a perpendicular is drawn from one point to the base, that perpendicular will be the mean proportional between the two sections of the base. This is established because both sides [of the triangle] are in proportion to the whole base and to the segments they contain.
</margin>

But $b.d$ is equal to $d.g$ by <note>original: "per.28.tertij"</note> Proposition 28 of the third book [of Euclid's *Elements*]. Therefore, triangle $e.d.g$ becomes an isosceles triangle (having two equal sides). Thus, by Proposition 4 of the first book, angle $d.e.g$ is equal to angle $d.g.e$. However, both angles at $a.d.z$ are right angles because $d.z$ is a perpendicular. Therefore, triangle $e.d.z$ is equiangular to triangle $g.d.z$. Hence, by Proposition 4 of the first book, $e.z$ becomes equal to $z.g$. But $e.g$ is the difference <term>excessus<gloss>The "excess" or the remaining length when one segment is subtracted from another.</gloss></term> of $a.g$ over $a.b$; therefore, $z.g$ is half of that difference. Through the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book, from the given chord $b.g$, the chord $a.b$ will become known. Therefore, $e.g$ will be known as the difference; so its half, namely $z.g$, will be given. Furthermore, since in the right-angled triangle $a.d.g$, by Proposition 30 of the third book, the perpendicular $d.z$ descends from the right angle to the base; therefore, by Proposition 8 of the sixth book, $d.g$ is the **mean proportional** between $a.g$ and $g.z$. Thus, by Proposition 16 of the sixth book, the product of $a.g$ and $g.z$ is equal to the square of $d.g$. Since $a.g$ and $g.z$ are given, $d.g$ (which was sought) will become known. By this doctrine, you will find the chords of many arcs: just as the chord of an arc of twelve degrees is known from the above, the chord of an arc of six degrees will now become known; from this, the chord of an arc of three degrees; from this, the chord of an arc of one and a half degrees; from this, the chord of an arc of a half and a quarter [three-quarters]; and so on for others.

## Proposition VI.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a circle with an inscribed quadrilateral labeled b, g, d, e and center z. Handwritten annotations: "note", "to be made", "known", "motion".</image-desc>

**Given the chords of two arcs in a semicircle, the chord of the arc composed of these two will also be known.**
Let there be in circle $a.b.d$ (with center $z$ and diameter $a.z.d$) two arcs $a.b$ and $b.g$ with known chords $a.b$ and $b.g$ given. I say that the chord of the whole arc $a.g$ becomes known. For when the lines $a.g, b.d, g.d$ are drawn, as well as the diameter $b.z.e$ and lines $g.e$ and $d.e$, then by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book, $b.d$ will be known from $a.b$, and $g.e$ will be known from $b.g$. Therefore, in the quadrilateral $b.g.d.e$, the diagonals $b.d$ and $g.e$ are given; and the two sides $b.g$ and $a.b$ are equal to $d.e$. The side $b.e$ is also known because it is the diameter of the circle. Therefore, by the first [proposition] of this book, the square of the side—namely $d.g$—will become known. Hence, from the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book, $a.g$ will be known, which is what was proposed. From these premises, the chords of all arcs in a semicircle increasing by one and a half degrees are made clear.

## Proposition VII.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a circle with complex intersecting lines and arcs labeled b, g, z, d, a, e, t, s.</image-desc>

**For unequal arcs in a semicircle, the ratio of the larger arc to the smaller is greater than the ratio of the chord of the larger to the chord of the smaller.**
In a semicircle, let arc $b.g$ be larger than arc $a.b$. Let the chord of the larger be $b.g$ and the chord of the smaller be $a.b$. I say that the ratio of arc $b.g$ to arc $a.b$ is greater than the ratio of chord $b.g$ to chord $a.b$. For I shall divide angle $a.b.g$ into equal parts by line $b.d$ by Proposition 9 of the first book; and I shall extend $a.g$ intersecting $b.d$ at $e$. Also, $a.d$ and $d.g$ [are drawn], and by Propositions 28 and 25 of the third book, $a.d$ becomes equal to $d.g$. Since, by Proposition 3 of the sixth book, the ratio of chord $b.g$ to chord $a.b$ is as $g.e$ to $e.a$, and $g.b$ is greater than $a.b$, therefore $g.e$ is greater than $e.a$. Thus, point $z$ dividing $a.g$ into equal parts will be within $e.g$, and when $d.z$ is drawn, by Proposition 8 of the first book, both angles at $a.d.z$ will be right angles. Therefore, in triangle $e.z.d$, by Propositions 18 and 32 of the first book, side $d.e$ is greater than side $d.z$; and likewise in triangle $a.e.d$, side $d.a$ is longer than side $d.e$. Therefore, if we set $d$ as the center of a circle whose circumference passes through $e$, it is necessary that this periphery cuts $d.a$ passing below $a$ and does not reach $d.z$ passing above $z$. Let it therefore cut $d.a$ at $b$ and let the continued $d.z$ meet the periphery at $t$. Because, therefore, sector $e.d.t$ is larger than triangle $e.d.z$.

<margin>
You place both [angles] as equal sides, because those which are above the base were equal <unclear>cē nāe d̄ q̄</unclear> if the equal sides are presented directly.
</margin>

-> According to Menelaus, for equals among equals, it is necessary to have both those chords. <- <note>This refers to the Theorem of Menelaus, a fundamental result in spherical geometry and trigonometry used by astronomers like Regiomontanus.</note>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proofs for constructing a table of chords. Having established the geometric relationship between arcs and chords in Proposition 6, the author now applies these principles in Proposition 7 to determine the value of a chord for a single degree—a fundamental unit for astronomical calculations.</meta>

3. According to the eighth [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of sector $e.d.t$ to sector $e.d.b$ will be greater than the ratio of triangle $e.d.z$ to sector $e.d.b$. But also, by the same [proposition], the ratio of triangle $e.d.z$ to sector $e.d.b$ is greater than the ratio of triangle $e.d.z$ to triangle $e.d.a$. Therefore, even more strongly <note>original: "a fortiori"</note>, the ratio of sector $e.d.t$ to sector $e.d.b$ is greater than the ratio of triangle $e.z.d$ to triangle $e.d.a$.

But the ratio of one sector to another in the same circle, according to Archimedes' demonstrations in *On the Measurement of the Circle*, is as the ratio of one arc to the other. Furthermore, according to the last [proposition] of the sixth [book] <note>Refers to Euclid's *Elements*, Book VI, Prop. 33, which states that in equal circles, angles have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand.</note>, one arc is to another as the angle of one (which is at the center) is to the angle of the other. Likewise, the ratio of triangle $e.d.z$ to triangle $e.d.a$, according to the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], is as the line $z.e$ is to $e.a$. Therefore, joined together by the third of the added [propositions], the ratio of the combined angle $z.a.d$ to angle $e.d.a$ is greater than the ratio of $g.e$ to $e.a$.

By the last [proposition] of the sixth [book], however, the ratio of angle $g.d.b$ to angle $b.d.a$ is as arc $b.g$ is to arc $a.b$; and by the third [proposition] of the sixth [book], the ratio of $g.e$ to $e.a$ is as chord $b.g$ is to chord $a.b$. Therefore, the ratio of arc $b.g$ to arc $a.b$ is greater than the ratio of chord $b.g$ to chord $a.b$, which was the thing proposed [to be proved].

## Proposition 7.

To reveal the chord of an arc of one degree without noticeable error.

Let arc $a.b$ be half a degree and a quarter of one <note>This equals three-quarters of a degree, or 45 arc-minutes.</note>. Its chord $a.b$, according to the preceding principles and following the discovery of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman astronomer whose *Almagest* provided the foundation for this trigonometry.</note>, will be 47 minutes and 8 seconds. Likewise, if there is an arc $a.g$ of one degree, its chord is sought. Through the preceding [proposition], it is clear that the ratio of arc $a.g$ to arc $a.b$ is greater than the ratio of chord $a.g$ to chord $a.b$. But since arc $a.g$ contains arc $a.b$ plus its third part, it follows that chord $a.g$ contains chord $a.b$ and *less* than its third part.

Now, a third of chord $a.b$ is 15 minutes, 42 seconds, and two-thirds of a second. When these are added to the 47 minutes and 8 seconds [of the original chord], they make 1 degree, 2 minutes, 50 seconds, and two-thirds of a second. This value is therefore necessarily greater than the chord of one degree.

Next, let arc $a.b$ be one degree, and arc $a.g$ be a degree and a half ($1.5^\circ$). From his earlier work, Ptolemy found the chord of $a.g$ to be 1 degree, 34 minutes, and 15 seconds. From this, the chord $a.b$ is sought. By the preceding [proposition], the ratio of arc $a.g$ to arc $a.b$ is greater than the ratio of chord $a.g$ to chord $a.b$. But since arc $a.g$ contains arc $a.b$ and its half, then chord $a.g$ contains chord $a.b$ and *less* than its half.

Thus, if I subtract a third of arc $a.g$ (namely $b.g$) from arc $a.g$, arc $a.b$ remains. Therefore, if I also subtract a third of the chord of arc $a.g$ (namely 31 minutes and 25 seconds) from the total $a.g$, which is 1 degree, 34 minutes, and 15 seconds, there remains 1 degree, 2 minutes, and 50 seconds. This value must necessarily be less than the chord of an arc of one degree.

Therefore, the chord of an arc of one degree will be more than 1 degree, 2 minutes, and 50 seconds, and less than 1 degree, 2 minutes, 50 seconds, and two-thirds of a second. It was therefore appropriate to set the chord of an arc of one degree at 1 part, 2 minutes, and 50 seconds. From this, no noticeable error would follow in astronomical calculations, because of the small and imperceptible difference between the quantities within which it has now been concluded to stand. From the chord of an arc of one degree, following the teaching of the fourth [proposition] of this [book], the chord of half a degree will be established. From here, following the teachings of the preceding [propositions], you will complete the chords of all arcs increasing by half a degree.

Given one part of an arc—with the lines drawn out as already stated—and the division being known: because the proportion of the chord of the double arc of the whole to the chord of the double arc of its part (which the drawn lines include) is known, the arc included by those lines shall also be known.
¶ Let the proportion of one arc $b.g$ of the arc $a.g$ be known, and let the proportion of the chord of the double arc $a.g$ to the chord of the double arc $a.b$ be given. Therefore, the whole $e.z$ is known. From the known values of $e.z$ and $d.z$, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], $e.d$ will be known. Thus, for the <term>right-angled triangle<note>original: "orthogonij"</note></term> $e.d.z$, with the lengths of the sides known by the method mentioned in the previous sections, all the angles will become known. Thus, angle $a.d.z$ is known; from which, by subtracting the already known angle $b.d.z$, there remains angle $a.d.b$, the quantity of which is the arc $a.b$ that was sought.

## Proposition 15.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram in the right margin illustrating spherical trigonometry. One of these is the proportion of the chord of the double arc of the lower part of the line reflected from the end of that descender to the chord of the double arc of its upper part; the other is the proportion of the chord of the double arc of the lower part of the other descender to the chord of the double arc of the whole of this descender.

...from the ratio of $a$ to $b$, the proportion of $e$ to $f$ will remain, which was what was to be shown. ¶ When, however, one proportion is to be added to another: we multiply the first term of the one by the first term of the other, and we establish the product as the first term of the compound proportion. Likewise, we multiply the second term of the one by the second term of the other, and the product we establish as the second term of the compound proportion made from them. For example, if the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is to be joined to the proportion of $c$ to $d$, I multiply $a$ by $c$ to produce $e$; likewise $b$ by $d$ to produce $g$. </margin>

¶ I call the sine of any arc <note>original: "Sinum alicuius arcus voco"</note> half of the chord of double that same arc. Therefore, whatever Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Almagest" defined the field for over a millennium.</note> showed in his figures—which the Greeks call "sections"—concerning the proportions of the chords of double arcs, is also shown to be true by the 15th proposition of the fifth book concerning the proportions of the sines of such arcs. Therefore, in the figure of this proposition, the proportion of the sine of arc $z.a$ to the sine of arc $a.b$ is aggregated from two proportions: namely, the sine of arc $z.t$ to the sine of arc $t.h$, and the sine of arc $h.e$ to the sine of arc $e.b$. But the three arcs $z.a$, $z.t$, and $e.b$ are equal, because each is a quarter of a great circle, and the sine of each of them is the semi-diameter of the circle, which we call the total sine <term>sinus totus</term> <note>In medieval trigonometry, the "total sine" is the radius of the reference circle, often assigned a value like 60,000 or 100,000 to avoid fractions.</note>. Therefore, the proportion of the total sine to the sine of arc $a.b$ (which is the sine of the maximum declination) will be composed of two: namely, the proportion of the total sine to the sine of $t.h$, and the proportion of the sine of $h.e$ to the total sine. It makes no difference which of these last two you make the first. But two proportions—namely, the proportion of the sine of $h.e$ to the total sine, and the proportion of the total sine to the sine of $t.h$—together produce the proportion of the sine of $h.e$ to the sine of $t.h$, because the total sine is the middle term between them. Therefore, the proportion of the total sine to the sine of the maximum declination is as the proportion of the sine of arc $h.e$ to the sine of arc $t.h$. With the first three thus known, by the 15th proposition of the sixth book <note>Euclid, Book VI, Prop 15 discusses the ratios of sides in triangles of equal area.</note>, the sine of arc $t.h$ will become known; hence, by a table of sines, the arc $t.h$ will be given. And thus the truth and use of the corollary is clear. ¶ From what has been said, it is established: when there are six quantities, and the proportion of the first to the second is composed of the proportions of the third to the fourth and the fifth to the sixth, if five of these quantities are known, the sixth will also become known. For example, let the proportion of $a$ to $b$ be composed of two: namely, $c$ to $d$ and $e$ to $f$. Let one of these be unknown, and the rest be known. I say that it also becomes known. For it is necessary in such six quantities that the multiplication of the first by the fourth and then by the sixth be equal to the multiplication of the second by the third and then by the fifth. For from $a$ times $d$, let $g$ be produced; and from $c$ times $b$, let $h$ be produced. By the stated rule regarding the subtraction of proportions, it is established that $g$ is to $h$ as $e$ is to $f$. Therefore, by the 15th proposition of the sixth book, the product of $g$ and $f$ is as much as the product of $h$ and $e$. If, therefore, $f$ were unknown, since $g$ is to $h$ as $e$ is to $f$, and since $g$, $h$, and $e$ are known, $f$ will become known. If $e$ were unknown, since $g$ is to $h$ as $f$ is to $e$, and the first three of them are given, the fourth will also be given. If, however, any of $c$ or $d$ were unknown, I would put $e$ in the third place and $f$ in the fourth, and I would proceed in the way already stated, and the unknown would be recognized. If instead any of $a$ or $b$ were unknown: from $c$ times $e$, let $k$ be produced; from $d$ times $f$, let $l$ be produced. By the rule of addition of proportions, $k$ to $l$ will be as $a$ to $b$. And since $k$ and $l$ and one of $a$ or $b$ are known, the remaining one will also become known. Thus the proposition is clear.

## Proposition 25.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram located in the right margin. To show the right ascension <note>original: "ascensionem in sphera recta" - The right ascension is the distance measured along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note> of any arc of the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the sun's apparent path across the sky.</note> beginning from the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic.
¶ From this it is manifest: that the ratio of the total sine <term>total sine: In medieval trigonometry, this is the sine of 90 degrees, acting as the radius of the calculation circle.</term> to the sine of the complement of the right ascension is as the ratio of the sine of the complement of the declination <note>Declination is the celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring how far north or south an object is from the celestial equator.</note> of the point terminating the ecliptic arc to the sine of the complement of such an ecliptic arc; specifically, the arc which corresponds to such a right ascension.
¶ The right ascension of any arc of the ecliptic is called the equinoctial arc: which begins and finishes rising together with such an arc of the ecliptic in a right sphere <note>A "right sphere" refers to the celestial sphere as seen from the Earth's equator, where all stars rise and set perpendicular to the horizon.</note>. Therefore, let the figure be that of the previous proposition. In it, the right ascension which corresponds to the ecliptic arc **e. h.** is the arc **e. t.** This is what is sought. Because two arcs descend from angle **a**, namely **a. e.** and **a. z.**, from which two others are reflected, **e. b.** and **z. t.**, intersecting each other at **h**. Therefore, by

Therefore, the chords or sines of these five arcs will be made known through the tables. Therefore, by the rule of six quantities <term>rule of six quantities: A fundamental formula in spherical trigonometry (Menelaus's Theorem) used to find an unknown value when five others are known.</term> the sine of **e. t.** will be known: therefore also the sine of the arc which was sought. However, by this path the corollary does not follow: but it shall proceed thus: because by the 15th [proposition] of this [book] the ratio of the sine of **e. a.** to the sine of **a. t.** is composed of two: namely the ratio of the sine of **e. b.** to the sine of **b. h.** and the ratio of the sine of **h. z.** to the sine of **z. t.** Five indeed are known: because arcs **e. a.**, **e. b.**, and **z. t.** are quadrants of circles. **b. h.** indeed is the complement of the given arc **e. h.** **b. z.** indeed is the complement of the declination of the given point **h**. Therefore, by the rule of six quantities, **a. t.** will be known. Therefore, the remainder of the quadrant is known: which was sought. From this, the corollary is evident: because the ratio of the total sine to the sine of **a. t.** is composed of two: namely the ratio of the total sine to the sine of **b. h.** and the sine of **h. z.** to the total sine. It does not matter which of these latter ratios you place before the other. For it follows that the ratio of the sine of **h. z.** to the sine of **b. h.** is equal to the ratio of the total sine to the sine of **a. t.** But of these quantities three are known: therefore also the fourth will be revealed. Therefore, the truth of the corollary and its use is evident.

# Book Two explains most exactly the variety of regions, the rising of stars, the length of the day, the altitude of the pole, the shadows of the sun, and the oblique ascensions of angles resulting from the various intersections of circles.

## Proposition 1.

In an oblique horizon <note>An "oblique horizon" refers to any location on Earth except the equator or the poles, where the celestial equator meets the horizon at an angle.</note>, to demonstrate the latitude of rising <note>original: "latitudo ortus" - Today called "amplitude," this is the angular distance along the horizon from the true east point to the point where a celestial body rises.</note> of a given point of the ecliptic through the semi-diurnal arc of such a point. From this it is clear: that the ratio of the total sine <term>total sine: The sine of 90 degrees, which served as the radius of the reference circle in medieval trigonometry.</term> to the sine of the semi-diurnal arc of any point of the ecliptic is as the ratio of the sine of the complement of the declination of the same point to the sine of the complement of its latitude of rising.

¶ An oblique or "slanting" horizon is said to be that over which one of the poles of the world is elevated. The latitude of rising of any point of the ecliptic is called the arc of the horizon intercepted between the rising of such a point and the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note>. The semi-diurnal arc of any point of the ecliptic is half of the arc of the parallel circle of such a point that exists above the horizon <note>Essentially, half the time the sun or a star spent above the horizon on a given day.</note>. ¶ In the figure, let the meridian circle be **a.b.g.d.**, the half of the equator **a.e.g.**, and the half of the oblique horizon **b.e.d.**, which cuts the equator at **e**. Let the pole of the world be **z**, either below or above the horizon. Let the given point of the ecliptic rise at **h**; its latitude of rising is the arc **e.h.** Let an arc of a great circle pass from the pole **z** through **h**, which is **z.h.t.** Therefore, from the ends of the two great arcs descending from **a**—namely **a.z.** and **a.e.**—two arcs **z.t.** and **e.b.** are reflected, intersecting at **h**. Therefore, by the 15th proposition of Book One <note>This refers to Menelaus's Theorem, a fundamental rule for spherical trigonometry used throughout this work.</note>, the ratio of the sine of **e.a.** to the sine of **a.t.** is composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine of **e.b.** to the sine of **b.h.** and the ratio of the sine of **h.z.** to the sine of **z.t.** Five of these arcs are known. For **e.a.**, **e.b.**, and **z.t.** are quadrants (quarters) of circles. Arc **a.t.** is the semi-diurnal arc. Arc **h.z.** is the complement of the declination <note>Declination is the distance north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the point of the ecliptic whose rising is at **h**. Therefore, by the "rule of six quantities" <note>Another name for Menelaus's Theorem.</note>, the arc **b.h.** will become known; its complement is **h.e.**, the remainder of the quadrant, which was sought.

A corollary is drawn from these things. For in these six quantities, the first, third, and sixth are equal to each other. Therefore, by the same argument by which the previous corollaries were shown: the ratio of the first to the second becomes as the ratio of the fifth to the fourth. The first is the total sine; the second is the sine of the diurnal arc; the fifth is the sine of the complement of the declination of the point; the fourth is the sine of the complement of the latitude of rising. Therefore, etc.

To know the same through the altitude of the pole. It is manifest, therefore, that the ratio of the sine of the altitude of the equator to the total sine is as the ratio of the sine of the declination of a point of the ecliptic to the sine of the latitude of rising of the same point.

¶ Use the previous figure: because the ratio of the sine of **z.a.** to the sine of **a.b.** is composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine of **z.t.** to the sine of **t.h.** and the ratio of the sine of **h.e.** to the sine of **e.b.**, by the 15th proposition of Book One. But five arcs are known: for **z.a.**, **z.t.**, and **e.b.** are quadrants.

**Vocabulary from the source:**
- **Oblique horizon:** A horizon where the celestial pole is at some height above it (anywhere but the equator).
- **Ecliptic:** The sun's annual path.
- **Semi-diurnal arc:** Half the time the sun is above the horizon.
- **Total sine:** The maximum value of the sine (radius).
- **Declination:** Angular distance from the celestial equator.
- **Latitude of rising:** Distance of sunrise from the east point of the horizon.
- **Equator:** The celestial equator.
- **Pole of the world:** The North or South celestial pole.
- **Rule of six quantities:** Menelaus's Theorem for spherical triangles.

# Proposition 7.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of a celestial sphere on the left of the text. It contains a vertical and horizontal axis with several intersecting arcs. Points are labeled with small letters: 'a' at the top left, 't' and 'e' along the upper interior arcs, 'h' on the left circumference, 'z' on a lower interior arc, 'b' at the bottom left, 'g' on the right interior, and 'd' on the right circumference.</image-desc>

To reduce the discovery of the difference between the equal and the shortest semi-diurnal arc <term>semi-diurnal arc: Half the time the sun is above the horizon, representing half a day's length.</term> in any region to four proportional quantities.
¶ The figure for this fifth part <note>The author refers back to a previous figure or step in the sequence of proofs.</note> had the ratio of the sine of z.b. to the sine of b.a. composed of two others: namely, the ratio of the sine of z.b. to the sine of b.t., and the sine of t.e. to the sine of e.a. But since b. will be the point of the rising of the Tropic of Capricorn <note>The southernmost point of the sun's path, marking the winter solstice.</note>, it follows that z.b., b.t., t.e., and e.a. remain the same quantities in every region. For z.b. is the complement of the maximum declination <term>declination: The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</term>; b.t. is the maximum declination; and e.a. is a quarter of the circle.
¶ Therefore, let the multiplication of the sine of h.t. by the sine of e.a. produce l. Or, if l. is divided by the sine of z.b., let it produce n. I say that the ratio of n. to the sine of t.e. is the same as the ratio of the sine of b.a. to the sine of z.b.
¶ For the multiplication of the sine of z.b. by the sine of t.e. produces m.; by the rule of the addition of ratios, it is established that the ratio of l. to m. is as the ratio of the sine of z.b. to the sine of b.a. But m. to l. (by Proposition 15 of Book Five <note>Likely referring to Euclid’s Elements, a standard mathematical reference of the time.</note>) is as the sine of t.e. to n.; therefore, the ratio of the sine of t.e. to n. is as the ratio of the sine of z.b. to the sine of b.a. And so, conversely, the ratio of the sine of b.a. to the sine of z.b. is as the ratio of n. to the sine of t.e.
¶ This will remain the same in every region because the quantities z.b., b.t., t.e., and e.a., from which n. was produced, remain the same. Therefore, multiply the sine of the altitude of the pole <note>The observer's geographic latitude.</note> in whatever region you wish by n., and divide the product by the sine of the complement of that same altitude of the pole; the result will be the sine of the difference of the equal and the shortest semi-diurnal arc in that region. By this clever method, the construction of a table for the longest day in any region becomes easy.

# Proposition 8.

<image-desc>A more complex circular diagram below the first. It depicts a sphere with intersecting great circles and parallel arcs. Points are labeled: 'a' (top left), 'n' (top), 'l' (top right), 't' (center left), 'k' and 'e' (center), 'f' (center right), 'h' (mid-left circumference), 'b' (bottom left circumference), 'g' (lower right interior), 'm' (bottom), and 'd' (right circumference).</image-desc>

Any two parallels <term>parallels: Circles on the celestial sphere parallel to the equator, representing the daily paths of stars or the sun.</term> passing through points of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: The apparent path of the sun across the sky over the course of a year.</term> at an equal distance from the two tropical points cut equal arcs from the oblique horizon <note>original: "horizonte obliquo" — The horizon as seen from a specific latitude, rather than from the equator.</note> on both sides of the equinoctial; and the arc of the day for one becomes equal to the arc of the night for the other alternately. The same also happens for parallels passing through points of the ecliptic at an equal distance from the two points of the equinoxes.
¶ Let there be two such points of the ecliptic: one toward the north from the equator, and the other toward the south.
¶ Let the southern point rise on the oblique horizon at b., and the northern one at k. Let the portions of the parallels passing through them be n.k. and m.b. Let the quarters of the great circles coming from the poles be z.b.t. and l.k.f. I say that arc b.e. is equal to arc e.k., and alternately the arc of one day is equal to the arc of the night of the other. For since the given points are at an equal distance from the points of the tropics or equinoxes, it is necessary—according to what is held concerning declination—that they have equal declination. Thus, arc b.t. will be equal to arc k.f.; therefore, both parallels will be of equal size, because the sine of arc h.z. is equal to the sine of arc l.k., which are the radii of the parallels. Therefore, by Proposition 6 of the first book of Theodosius <note>Theodosius of Bithynia, a Greek astronomer known for his work on the geometry of the sphere.</note>, the horizon, being a great circle, cuts equal arcs from them alternately. Thus, arc m.b. will be equal to arc n.k. But n.k. is the arc of the semi-day for the point rising at k., while m.b. is the arc of the semi-night for the point rising at b. Likewise, the arcs a.f. and t.g. are similar to these and therefore equal. When the equal arcs a.t. and f.g. are subtracted from them, t.e. and e.f. remain equal. Therefore, the remaining arcs a.t. and f.g. are equal; and the arc of the semi-day for the point rising at b. is equal to the arc of the semi-night for the point rising at k., which is the second point.

b 4

...let t.b. be equal to the two arcs e.f. and l.k., and the angles t.z.f. be right angles: and let the composite angles a.d.e. be equal. It follows by the method of proof according to Euclid’s First Book <note>original: "iuxta primū euclidis"</note> that arc e.b. is equal to e.k., which was the first point. Or you could prove this first point through those things demonstrated in the second [proposition] of this book: because the ratio of the sine of b.a. to the total sine <term>total sine: The radius of the mathematical circle used for calculation, often set at 60,000 or 100,000 in this era.</term> is as the ratio of the sine of h.t. to the sine of h.e. Likewise, the ratio of the sine of d.g. to the total [sine] is as the ratio of the sine of k.f. to f.e. But a.b. is equal to d.g., and h.t. is equal to k.f.; therefore, the sine of t.h. is to the sine of h.e. as the sine of t.h. is to e.k. Wherefore, by the ninth [proposition] of the fifth [book of Euclid], h.e. will be equal to e.k. In a similar way, you will prove the second part by those things said in the preceding proof: because the ratio of n. to the sine of t.e. is as n. to the sine of e.f., and so on.

**Given** the altitude of the sun: to investigate the straight or reversed shadow. But we call the "reversed shadow" <term>reversed shadow: Also known as "umbra versa," this is the vertical shadow cast by a horizontal pole against a wall.</term> the shadow which an object parallel to the horizontal surface produces on a surface perpendicular to the horizon—such as the shadow of a stylus on a hanging cylinder <note>A reference to a "shepherd's dial" or portable cylindrical sundial.</note>. ¶ Let, therefore, the circle of altitude be a.b.g., whose center is e. It will become known from the fourth [proposition] of the sixth [book of Euclid], because the ratio of e.d. to d.c. is as the ratio of e.m. to m.n. Since the first three are given, the fourth, m.n., will become known. From this, that corollary is inferred.

## Proposition XI.

**Under the equator, all days are equal to the nights;**
**and all stars have a rising and a setting; and shadows**
**sometimes turn toward the south, sometimes toward the**
**north, and sometimes they decline nowhere.**
For the horizon of those living under the equator <note>original: "sub eq̃to:re"</note> cuts the equator itself and all its parallels into semicircular portions. And because it passes through the poles of the world, upon which the revolution of the stars occurs, it is necessary that all stars rise and all set. And since the sun at the hour of noon is sometimes to the south of the zenith, sometimes to the north, and sometimes in the zenith itself—which is the pole of the horizon—that which is said concerning the shadows is clearly established.

## Proposition XII.

**From every parallel toward the north from the equator,**
**the day becomes equal to the night only twice in a year;**
**and summer days are longer than winter days, while**
**nights are shorter. And the further they are from the**
**equinoxes, the more summer days are lengthened and winter**
**days shortened. And some stars are always appearing, and**
**some always hidden. And the distance of the zenith from the equinoctial is equal to the altitude of the pole.**
Let the meridian be **a.b.c.d.**, the axis of the world within it be **a.e.c.**, and the two poles be **a.** and **c.** Let the equinoctial <term>equinoctial: The celestial equator, the Great Circle in the sky directly above the Earth's equator.</term> be **b.d.**, and let there be one meridian parallel **h.i.** and another **f.t.** Let the northern ones be **l.m.**, **o.p.**, **s.g.** Thus, **a.e.c.** will be in the place of the horizon in a right sphere <term>right sphere: The view of the heavens for an observer at the equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon and all stars rise and set vertically.</term>. And because in an oblique sphere one of the poles is elevated, let that be **c.**; and let the line designating the oblique horizon be **f.e.g.** It is clear, however, that the horizon **f.e.g.** cuts the equator **m.b.d.** into equal parts. But it is necessary that it cuts the remaining parallels unequally: **r.o.q.** is greater than **l.n.** Likewise, **l.n.** is greater than **b.e.**, and **b.e.** is greater than **h.k.** Likewise, stars between the parallel **g.s.** will always be above the horizon, and those between the parallel **f.t.** will always be below the horizon. Likewise, let the zenith of the heads be **r.**, and arc **b.r.** will become equal to arc **c.g.**, because **b.c.** is a quarter [of a circle], and **r.g.** is a quarter.

## Proposition XIII.

**From a parallel further removed from the equator, the**
**inequality of days and nights is greater; the portion of**
**stars always appearing is greater, and the portion**
**always hidden is also greater.**
As if, in the figure above, you incline the oblique horizon more and designate it by the line **v.e.x.** in the parallel **o.p.**, then the semi-diurnal arc <term>semi-diurnal arc: Half the time a celestial body spends above the horizon; essentially half the length of a day.</term> will be marked by **o.y.** and the nocturnal arc by **y.p.** In the less oblique horizon, however, point **q.** separated these. But the inequality of **o.y.** and **y.p.** is greater than that of **o.q.** and **q.p.** Likewise, the portion of stars always appearing will now be distinguished by the parallel **z.r.** and those not appearing by **v.z.**; but the parallels of **h.i.** include more than the parallels of **f.g.**; therefore, etc.

## Proposition XIV.

**From every parallel between the equinoctial and the Tropic**
**of Cancer, noon shadows sometimes turn toward the north**
**and sometimes toward the south, and twice in the year**
**they turn nowhere.**

### Proposition XV.

<image-desc>A celestial sphere diagram in the right margin, showing intersecting circles and arcs used to calculate solar projections and shadows.</image-desc>

Under the Tropic of Cancer <note>original: "sub tropico cancri"</note>, once a year there is no meridian shadow, nor will there ever be a turning toward the south. 
It lacks a turning indeed when the sun is at the beginning of Cancer <note>This occurs at the Summer Solstice, around June 21st, when the sun is directly overhead at noon on this latitude.</note>. ### Proposition XVI.

For those living between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle, the meridian shadow never lacks a turn: but all are bent toward the north. 
This is evident because the sun never reaches their zenith.

### Proposition XVII.

<image-desc>A second spherical diagram in the right margin, illustrating the horizon and the path of the sun at the Arctic Circle where it touches the horizon without setting.</image-desc>

Under the Arctic Circle, once a year a day of 24 hours is established without night; and the shadow in that place circles around to every part of the horizon; and once a night of 24 hours is produced without day. 
For there, the Tropic of Cancer, by touching the horizon, never sinks [below it], just as the Tropic of Capricorn never rises [above it]. <note>This describes the "Midnight Sun" and "Polar Night" phenomena experienced at the Arctic Circle.</note>

### Proposition XVIII.

Under the pole of the world, half of the sphere is always visible and the rest is always hidden. And for half the year there is continuous light, and for the rest, one single night. 
For there, the equinoctial <note>original: "equinoctialis"; the celestial equator.</note> is on the surface of the horizon; therefore the proposition is clear.

### Proposition XIX.

In an oblique horizon, any two equal arcs of the ecliptic starting from the points of the equinoxes have equal ascensions. Moreover <note>original: "Alm̃," likely an abbreviation for "Almagesto" (the Almagest), Ptolemy's foundational work on astronomy.</note>, it is established that any two equal arcs of the ecliptic, and equally distant from the points of the equinoxes, have equal ascensions.
Let the meridian be **a.b.g.d.**, the half-equator **a.e.g.**, the half of the oblique horizon **b.e.d.**, and two equal arcs of the ecliptic **z.b.** and **t.k.**, such that each of the points **z.** and **t.** is an equinoctial point. It is clear that with arc **z.b.** rises the equatorial arc **z.e.**, and with arc **t.k.** rises the equatorial arc **t.e.** I say that the two arcs **z.e.** and **t.e.** are equal. Let the poles of the world be **l.** and **m.**; let arcs of great circles be drawn: **l.e.**, **m.**, **l.k.**, **l.t.**, **m.h.**, and **m.z.** Because **b.**, **z.**, and **k.** are points of equal distance from the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic: therefore, through those things held concerning declination <term>declination: The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator.</term>: their declinations and the complements of their declinations are equal. Therefore, by the science of spherical triangles, angle **z.m.b.** is equal to angle **t.l.k.** Likewise, by the eighth [proposition] of this [book], **e.k.** is equal to **e.h.** and two [points] **k.l.**

->Proposition XXII.<-

From any given oblique horizon <term>oblique horizon: The horizon as viewed from any location that is not the equator or the poles.</term>, to reduce the aforementioned discovery to four quantities. ¶ From this it is manifest: if the sine of the altitude of the pole in your horizon <note>This "altitude of the pole" corresponds to the observer's latitude.</note> is multiplied by the whole sine <term>whole sine: In medieval trigonometry, the "whole sine" (sinus totus) refers to the radius of the calculating circle, acting as a constant.</term>, and the result is divided by the sine of the complement of that same altitude of the pole: then the ratio of the result of this division to the sine of the difference of right and oblique ascensions being sought will be as the ratio of the sine of the complement of the declination to the sine of that same declination.
¶ For you have from the premise: that the ratio of the sine k.d. to the sine g.d. is composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine k.l. to the sine l.m., and the ratio of the sine m.e. to the sine e.g. Whichever of these you place last, it makes no difference. Multiply sine k.d. by sine e.g. and let it create quantity q. Divide q. by sine d.g. and let r. be produced. I say that the ratio of r. to sine m.e. is the same as the ratio of sine k.l. to sine l.m. For sine k.d. times sine e.g. makes q. Likewise, sine d.g. times r. also makes q. Therefore, by the 15th [proposition] of the sixth [book of Euclid], the ratio of sine k.d. to sine d.g. is as the ratio of r. to sine e.g. Wherefore, the ratio of r. to sine e.g. will also be composed of the same two ratios from which sine k.d. to sine d.g. is composed. It is necessary, therefore, that the ratio of r. to sine m.e. be as the ratio of sine k.l. to sine l.m., which is what was proposed and the intent of the corollary. Therefore, r. will always remain the same in any proposed region, because in it the arcs k.d., d.g., z.e., and g. remain continuously the same, from which r. is produced.

To determine the difference of the right and oblique ascensions of any arc of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: The sun's apparent path across the sky during the year.</term> by means of an arc of a great circle coming from the pole of the world.

Wherefore, such a difference of ascensions will always be determined by the arc of a great circle coming from the pole through the point of intersection of the parallel and the horizon.

¶ Let the horizon, meridian, and equator remain as in the previous figure. Of the quadrants of great circles coming from the pole **z**, let there be **z.h.t.** and **z.k.l.** It is clear from the aforementioned things that **l.e.** is the difference of ascensions that is sought, and **t.e.** is the difference between the minimum and equal half-day arc. Since from the ends of the two arcs **t.z.** and **t.e.** two others are reflected, **z.l.** and **e.h.**, intersecting each other at **k**, the ratio of the sine of **z.h.** to the sine of **h.t.** will be composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine of **z.k.** to the sine of **k.l.** and the ratio of the sine of **l.e.** to the sine of **e.t.** But from the last proposition of the first book <note>original: "ex ultima primi huius"; referring to the concluding theorem of Book I regarding spherical triangles.</note>, it is clear that the ratio of the sine of **z.h.** to the sine of **h.t.** is composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine of **z.k.** to the sine of **k.l.** and the ratio of the sine of the right ascension of such an ecliptic arc (whose endpoint rises at **k**, or whose parallel has the declination **k.l.**) to the whole sine <term>whole sine: In medieval trigonometry, the radius of the circle used for calculation, often 60,000 or 100,000 units.</term>. It is therefore necessary that the ratio of the sine of arc **t.e.** to the sine of arc **e.l.** be as the ratio of the whole sine to the sine of the right ascension of such an ecliptic arc. Thus the proposition is clear.

### Proposition XXV.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of a celestial sphere with labeled points: a (top), b (left), k (top), h, l, m, e (center), d (right), and g (bottom).</image-desc>

**In a region where the pole of the world is elevated by 48 degrees <note>While the text specifies 48 degrees—likely reflecting the author's local latitude—the geometric proof that follows assumes a latitude of 45 degrees, where the altitude of the pole equals its complement.</note>, the ratio of the sine of the complement of the declination of any ecliptic arc to the sine of its declination is as the ratio of the whole sine to the sine of the difference of right and oblique ascensions of such an arc.**

¶ Let the horizon of such a region be **b.e.d.**, the half of the equator **a.e.g.**, and the meridian **a.b.g.d.** Let the pole of the world be **k**. Let the vernal point be **b**. Let the arc of the ecliptic be **b.l.** Let the quadrant of the great circle coming from the pole be **k.l.m.** Therefore, the equinoctial arc **b.m.** will be the right ascension, the ecliptic arc will be **h.l.**, and its oblique ascension <term>oblique ascension: The arc of the celestial equator that rises with a star or a point on the ecliptic in an oblique sphere.</term> will be **b.e.** The difference between these ascensions is **e.m.** I say that the ratio of the sine of **k.l.** to the sine of **l.m.** is as the ratio of the sine of **g.e.** to the sine of **e.m.** For the ratio of the sine of **k.d.** to the sine of **d.g.** is composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine of **k.l.** to the sine of **l.m.** and the ratio of the sine of **m.e.** to the sine of **e.g.** But in this region, **k.d.** is equal to **d.g.** <note>This equality occurs only at 45 degrees latitude.</note>, therefore a ratio of equality is established from the two aforementioned ratios. Therefore, by the rule of the addition of ratios, that which results from the multiplication of **k.l.** by the sine of **m.e.** is equal to that which results from the multiplication of the sine of **l.m.** by the whole sine. Therefore, by the 15th proposition of the sixth book [of Euclid's Elements], the ratio of the sine of **k.l.** to the sine of **l.m.** is as the ratio of the whole sine to the sine of **m.e.**, which was what was intended.

->Proposition 28<-

If upon two points of the <term>ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of a year.</term> equally distant from the vernal or autumnal equinox point, two arcs of great circles come from the pole of the world, they will cause two angles on the same side of the ecliptic, the exterior being equal to the interior opposite to it.
¶ Let the half of the <term>equinoctial: The celestial equator.</term> be **a.b.g.**, the half of the ecliptic **d.b.e.**, and the point of the equinox **b**. Let the two points of the ecliptic be **h** and **t**, equally distant from point **b**. Let two arcs of great circles come from the pole **z** upon those points, which are **z.k.h.** and **t.l.** I say that angle **z.t.e.** is equal to angle **z.h.b.** For **k.h.** is equal to **l.t.** because of the equal declinations, and **b.l.** is equal to **b.k.** because of the equal right ascensions. Therefore, triangles **b.h.k.** and **b.t.l.** have equal sides; thus they also have equal angles through those things drawn from <term>Theodosius: Theodosius of Bithynia, a Greek astronomer and mathematician (c. 160 BC – c. 100 BC) known for his work on the geometry of the sphere.</term> and <term>Mileus: Menelaus of Alexandria (c. 70–140 AD), the mathematician who first proved the theorem of the "six quantities" in spherical trigonometry.</term>. Therefore, angle **b.h.k.** is equal to angle **b.t.l.** But **b.t.l.** is equal to its vertical opposite **z.t.e.**; therefore what was proposed [is proven], etc.

Moreover, two such angles are together equal to two right angles <note>In spherical geometry, two right angles equal 180 degrees.</note>, provided that the points of the <term>ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of a year.</term> are at an equal distance from the <term>tropic point: Either of the two points on the ecliptic where the sun is at its greatest distance from the celestial equator; the solstices.</term>.

The angle formed by the intersection of the <term>meridian: A great circle passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a specific location.</term> and the ecliptic at the tropic point is a right angle.
¶ Let the meridian be **a-b-g-d** and the half of the ecliptic be **a-e-g**, in which **a** is the tropic point. For then the poles of the ecliptic will be in the meridian, namely **d** and **b**; from which **a-d** will be a quarter of a circle <note>90 degrees</note>. Similarly, let us describe **d-g** as a half of a great circle passing through the poles **d** and **b**, of which the poles are **a** and **g**. Let this [circle] intersect **a-e-g** at **e**. It will be established that **a-e** is a quarter [circle], just as **e-g** is. Therefore, since the arcs of great circles—namely **d-a**, **d-e**, and **d-g**—descend from the pole **d** to the circle **a-e-g**, it is necessary that each be a quarter [circle]. Therefore, **d-e** is a quarter. But it is subtended by angle **a**; therefore, angle **d-a-e** is a right angle, which is what was intended.

## Proposition XXXIII.

**T**he ratio of the sine of the complement of the declination of a given point on the <term>ecliptic: The sun's apparent path.</term> to the sine of the complement of the maximum declination <note>Maximum declination refers to the "obliquity of the ecliptic," the tilt of the Earth's axis (approx. 23.5 degrees).</note> is the same as the ratio of the sine of the arc of that ecliptic from the <term>intersection of equality: The equinoctial point where the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator.</term> to the given point, to the sine of its <term>right ascension: The distance of a point measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</term>.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of the celestial sphere with labeled arcs and points: 'b', 'a', 'h', 'e', 't', 'd', 'z', and 's'. The vertical axis connects 'z' at the top and 'd' at the bottom. Point 'h' is located on an arc to the left.</image-desc>

¶ Let the last figure of the first book be repeated: in which the <term>meridian: The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith.</term> **a-b-g-d** takes the place of the <term>solstitial colure: The great circle that passes through the celestial poles and the solstices.</term>. Let **a-e-g** be the half of the equator, and **b-e-d** be the half of the ecliptic. Let **e** be the intersection of equality, and arc **e-h** be given. Let the pole of the world be **z**, from which comes the quadrant of a great circle **z-b-t**. From the previous sections, **t-b** will be the declination of point **b**, **h-z** its complement, and the right ascension of arc **e-h** will be **e-t**. I say that the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of the arc **z-h** (which is the complement of the maximum declination) is as the ratio of the sine of **e-h** to the sine of **e-t**. This is evident because the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **b-a** is composed of two others: namely, the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **h-t**, and the ratio of the sine of **t-e** to the <term>total sine: The radius of the circle used in calculations, often 60,000 or 1 in early trigonometry.</term> (that is, the sine of arc **e-a**). I place the sine of **b-a** in the middle position between the sine of **z-b** and the sine of **z-h**; it will then be established that the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **z-h** is composed of two: the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **b-a**, and the ratio of the sine of **b-a** to the sine of **z-h**. Therefore, the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **z-h** will consist of three: the ratios of the sine of **b-a** to the sine of **z-h**, the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **h-t**, and the sine of **t-e** to the total sine. But the first two produce the ratio of the sine of **b-a** to the sine of **h-t**; therefore, the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **z-h** is composed of two: the ratio of the sine of **b-a** to the sine of **h-t**, and the ratio of the sine of **t-e** to the total sine. Now, the ratio of the sine of **b-a** to the sine of **h-t**—by the corollary of the penultimate proposition of the first book and by permuted proportionality—is as the ratio of the total sine to the sine of **e-h**. Therefore, the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **z-h** is composed of two: the ratio of the total sine to the sine of **e-h**, and the ratio of the sine of **t-e** to the total sine. Whichever of these you place first, it changes nothing. But together they compose the ratio of the sine of **t-e** to the sine of **e-h**; therefore, the ratio of the sine of **z-b** to the sine of **z-h** is as the ratio of the sine of **t-e** to the sine of **e-h**. Thus, by conversion, the proposition is clear.
¶ From this, you again have the method for finding right ascensions reduced to four quantities.

### Proposition XXXV.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of a celestial sphere containing several intersecting arcs. A vertical line serves as a meridian, while other arcs represent the horizon and ecliptic. Points are labeled a (top), g (bottom), b (left), d (right), and internal points include e, z, h, and t. A small number '3' is placed in the upper left quadrant.</image-desc>

**A**ny two angles resulting from the intersection of the ecliptic and the <term>oblique horizon: The horizon as viewed from a location not on the equator, where the celestial equator meets the horizon at an angle.</term> at points on the ecliptic equally distant from the equinoctial points, coming from the same side—namely, an exterior angle and its opposite interior angle—are equal.

¶ Let the <term>meridian: The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith.</term> be **a.b.g.d.**, the half of the oblique horizon **b.e.d.**, and the half of the <term>equator: The celestial equator, the projection of Earth's equator into space.</term> **a.e.g.** Let there be two equal arcs of the ecliptic, **z.h.** and **k.l.**, so that both **z.** and **k.** represent the <term>autumnal point: The location on the ecliptic where the sun crosses the equator moving south, marking the start of autumn.</term>. I say that angle **e.h.t.** is equal to angle **d.l.k.** For the triangles **z.h.e.** and **k.l.e.** have equal sides. This is because **z.h.** is equal to **k.l.**, and **h.e.** is equal to **l.e.**, as can be shown from the second [proposition] of this book. The base **e.z.** is equal to the base **e.k.** because of their equal right ascensions, as is drawn from the 33rd [proposition] of this book. Therefore, the angles contained by the equal sides will be equal. Thus, angle **e.h.z.** is equal to angle **e.l.k.**, whereby the remaining angle **e.k.t.** is equal to the remaining angle **d.l.k.**, which is what was intended.

### Proposition XXXVI.

<image-desc>A similar circular diagram to the first, but with a different configuration of intersecting arcs. The internal labels include points m, l, k, e, h, and z. The number '3' is again present in the upper left quadrant.</image-desc>

**S**uch two angles—one of which is in the east and the other in the west—one being exterior and the other interior on the same side of the ecliptic opposite it, are together equal to two right angles <note>In geometry, "two right angles" equals 180 degrees.</note>.

¶ Let the circle of the horizon be **a.b.g.d.** and the circle of the ecliptic be **a.e.g.**, intersecting at points **a.** and **g.**. I say that the two angles **d.g.z.** and **d.a.e.** are together equal to two right angles. For the two angles **z.a.d.** are equal to the angle **z.g.d.** because the arc of the maximum declination of these circles (such as the arc **d.z.** passing through the points of their maximum declination) is one and the same. Wherefore, the two angles **d.g.z.** and **d.a.e.** are together equal to two right angles; which is the proposition. ¶ From this it is manifest:

Two such angles which are formed at points of the ecliptic equally distant from the <term>tropic point: The points of the summer or winter solstice.</term>—one being oriental [rising] and the other occidental [setting]—are together equal to two right angles.

<image-desc>A diagram showing two circles overlapping like a Venn diagram. The horizontal axis passes through points b, e, d, and z. Vertical points on the intersection are labeled a and g. The circles represent the intersection of two celestial coordinate systems.</image-desc>

¶ Since at points of the ecliptic equally distant from the equinoctial points, the two oriental angles are both equal (as in the previous proposition, angle **m.h.** is equal to angle **m.l.**), therefore the occidental angles of the two points opposite to points **h.** and **l.** are equal to one another. But the oriental angle of point **h.** together with the occidental angle of the opposite point **l.** belong to points equally distant from the <term>solstice: The points where the sun reaches its highest or lowest excursion relative to the celestial equator.</term> point; but they themselves are together equal to two right angles; thus [it is proved]. Therefore, once the oriental angles from Aries to Libra are known, the oriental angles of the other half will become known, and from these, the occidental angles of both halves will be made clear.

## Proposition XXXVII.

To reveal the angles formed <note>original: "victos"; likely a transcription error for "factos" (made/formed) or "visos" (seen)</note> at the points of the equinoxes.
Let the **meridian** be **a.b.g.d.**, the **oblique horizon** **a.e.d.**, a quadrant of the **equinoctial** <note>The celestial equator</note> **z.e.z.**, the vernal point of the quadrant of the **ecliptic** **e.g.** Likewise, let **e.** be the autumnal point of the quadrant of the ecliptic **e.b.**; **g.** is the point of the summer solstice, and **b.** the winter solstice. I say that the angles **d.e.g.** and **d.e.b.** are made known: from the reasoning of the sphere by Proposition 3, **z.** and **b.** and **z.** and **g.** are the maximum <term>declinations: The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator.</term> of the ecliptic. And **d.** is the complement of the altitude of the pole <note>The co-latitude of the observer’s location</note>. If you subtract **z.g.** from this, or add **z.b.** to it, the arcs **d.g.** and **d.b.** will become known: namely the quantities of the angles **d.e.g.** However, **d.e.b.** is the oriental <note>Eastern</note> angle which occurs at the vernal point. The remainder of the two right angles is the occidental <note>Western</note> angle, which occurs at that same point **d.e.b.**; or it is the oriental angle which occurs at the autumnal point. The remainder of the two right angles is the occidental angle, which occurs at that same point.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a celestial sphere. The outer circle is marked with points a, b, g, and d. A central point e is the intersection of several internal arcs representing the horizon and celestial circles. Points z, s, and a numerical 3 are marked along these internal curves.</image-desc>

## Proposition XXXVIII.

To investigate the oriental angle <note>original: "Angulũ oriẽtalẽ"</note> which is formed from the intersection of the **ecliptic** and the **oblique horizon** at any point of the ecliptic, through the <term>midheaven: The point of the ecliptic that is highest in the sky at a given time.</term> of the sky and its declination.
Let the meridian be **a.b.g.d.** and the half of the ecliptic be **a.e.g.**, of which two points **a.** and **e.** are given. Let the half of the oblique horizon be **e.d.** Furthermore, for the sake of example, let **e.** be the first point of **Taurus**. Therefore, through the <term>ascensions: The rising times of zodiacal signs.</term>, the point **a.** in the midheaven will be known, as well as its opposite point **g.**; hence the arc **e.g.** will be given. But in northern regions, this itself is less than a quadrant of a circle. Therefore, let the quadrant be **e.g.h.** Let a great circle pass through **h.**, whose pole is **e.**, cutting the horizon at **t.** and the meridian at **z.** Therefore, because the angles at **d.** and **t.** are right angles, it is necessary that **z.** be the pole of the horizon. Thus, **z.d.** and **z.t.** are quadrants. Likewise, through the declination of the degree of the midheaven and the latitude of the region, the meridian altitude of the degree of the midheaven becomes known: namely the arc **a.b.**, to which the arc **d.g.** is equal. But the ratio of the <term>sine: A trigonometric function representing the ratio of the side opposite an angle to the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle.</term> of **z.t.** to the sine of **t.h.** is composed of two others: namely the ratio of the sine of **z.d.** to the sine of **d.g.** and the ratio of the sine of **e.g.** to the sine of **e.h.** Five of these arcs are known. For **z.t.**, **z.d.**, and **e.h.** are quadrants. **d.g.** is the meridian altitude of the point in the midheaven. **g.e.** is the distance of the ascending degree from the degree of midnight. Therefore, the arc **t.h.** will become known, which is the quantity of the angle **d.e.g.** that was sought. From these things, this corollary is drawn:

<image-desc>A second circular diagram showing the intersection of the ecliptic and the horizon at point e. Labeled points include a, b, g, d on the perimeter and internal points z, s, t, d, and e, with additional arcs and a numerical 3 indicating geometric relationships.</image-desc>

### The ratio of the total sine to the sine of the angle being sought is as the ratio of the sine of the ecliptic arc between the ascending and midheaven points to the sine of the altitude of the ecliptic point in the midheaven.

It is clear: for the two ratios which compose the first make the ratio of the sine of **g.e.** to the sine of **g.d.** But the sine of **g.e.** is the same as the sine of **a.e.**, because **a.e.g.** is a semicircle; therefore, etc.

And the two angles which are formed from the meetings of the circles of altitudes and the ecliptic at those points—the exterior with the interior opposite to it on the same side—are together equal to two right angles.

## Proposition XL.

<margin>Diagram 2: Intersecting arcs of the ecliptic and horizon labeled a, b, c, d, e, g, s, t, showing how great circles meet at the observer's horizon.</margin> When the same point of the ecliptic is equally distant from the meridian on either side through the arcs of its parallel circle, its distance from the pole of the horizon <note>The Zenith, the point directly above the observer</note> will be equal. And the angles from the intersections of the circles of altitude with the ecliptic at that point—the exterior with the interior opposite to it on the same side—will together be equal to double the angle formed by the meridian and the ecliptic at the same point of the ecliptic; whether the points of the ecliptic then <term>mediating the sky: Culminating, or reaching the highest point on the meridian.</term> are southerly from the pole of the horizon, or northerly.

Let a portion of the meridian be **a.b.d.**, in which **g.** is the pole of the horizon and **d.** the arctic pole. Let there be two portions of the ecliptic **a.e.z.** and **b.h.t.**, in which **h.** and **e.** represent the same point of the ecliptic, when they are equally distant from the meridian on either side through arcs of its parallel circle: **e.** being toward the east and **h.** toward the west. Let the various points of the ecliptic then mediating the sky be **a.** and **b.**, and let them first be distant from the pole of the horizon **g.** toward the southern part by arcs of great circles **g.e.**, **g.h.**, **d.e.**, and **d.b.** being drawn. 

I say that arc **g.h.** is equal to arc **g.e.**, and the two angles **g.h.b.** and **g.e.z.** are together equal to double the angle **d.h.b.** or **d.e.z.** Just as in the previous proposition, because the arcs of the parallel through which the point is distant from the meridian are equal, it follows that angle **g.d.h.** is equal to angle **g.d.e.**, and because of the same declination, arc **d.h.** must be equal to arc **d.e.** Then, by making side **g.d.** common to both triangles **g.d.h.** and **g.d.e.**, the base **g.h.** will be equal to base **g.e.**, which is the first part. And angle **g.d.h.** is equal to angle **g.d.e.** But **d.h.b.** is equal to **d.e.z.** since **h.** and **e.** represent the same point. And the two angles **g.h.b.** and **g.b.d.** constitute the angle **d.h.b.** just as it equals **d.e.z.** Therefore, the two angles **g.h.b.** and **g.e.d.** constitute an angle equal to angle **d.h.b.** or **d.e.z.** Thus, the three angles **g.h.b.**, **g.e.d.**, and **d.e.z.** are double the angle **d.e.z.**, whereby the two angles **g.h.b.** and **g.e.z.** are equal to double the angle **d.e.z.**, which is the second part. 

<margin>Diagram 3: Spherical geometry with arcs a, b, d, e, g, s, z, k, specifically illustrating the case for points in the northern part of the horizon.</margin> Furthermore, let points **a.** and **b.** be northerly from the pole of the horizon **g.** Let arc **g.h.** be continued to **l.** and **g.e.** to **k.** I say that angles **l.h.b.** and **k.e.z.** are together equal to double the angle **d.e.z.** For **g.h.** is shown to be equal to **g.e.** as before, and angle **d.h.g.** equal to angle **d.e.g.** Therefore, the remaining angle **d.h.l.** is equal to the remaining **d.e.k.** But because **d.h.b.** is equal to angle **d.e.z.** since **b.** represents the same point, therefore the total **l.h.b.** is equal to the two angles **d.e.z.** and **d.e.k.** By adding **k.e.z.** to both sides, the two **l.h.b.** and **k.e.z.** will be together equal to double the angle **d.e.z.**, which is what was proposed.

For angle **d.h.g.** is equal to angle **d.e.g.**. These two, **d.e.k.** and **d.h.g.**, are equal to two right angles, because **d.h.g.** is equal to **d.e.g.**; therefore, the two angles **k.e.z.** and **g.h.b.** together are less than the two angles **d.e.z.** and **d.h.b.** by the quantity of two right angles. ### Corollary

->The ratio of the sine of the arc of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic; the apparent path of the sun across the celestial sphere</term> between the points of the rising and the midheaven to the sine of the meridian altitude of the midheaven point is as the ratio of the sine of the arc of the ecliptic between the rising point and the given point of the ecliptic to the sine of the altitude of that same point.<-

¶ For let **m.** be produced from the <term>whole sine; the radius of the circle used in calculations, often set to 60,000 or 1.0 in this period</term> multiplied by the sine of **e.h.**. Likewise, let **n.** be produced from the whole sine multiplied by the sine of **b.z.** From the rule of subtraction, it is established that **m.** to **n.** is the ratio of the sine of **h.t.** to the sine of **t.z.**. But **m.** to **n.** (by the 15th [proposition] of the fifth [book of Euclid’s Elements]) is as the ratio of the sine of **e.h.** to the sine of **b.z.**; therefore the ratio of the sine of **h.t.** to the sine of **t.z.** is as the sine of **e.h.** to the sine of **b.z.** By permutation, therefore, conclude the corollary.

### Proposition 44.
->To investigate the same thing in another way.<-

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a celestial sphere with various arcs. Points are labeled: a (top), b (left), z (top-left), e (center), t (right), and d (far right).</image-desc>

I establish **t.** as the pole of a great circle passing through the maximum declination of the ecliptic from the horizon: let its quadrant be **a.n.o.**; therefore **t.n.** will be a quadrant and **t.o.** will be a quadrant. Because the angles at **n.** and **o.** are right angles, it must necessarily go through the poles of the horizon and the ecliptic. The quantity of angle **h.t.e.** is known through the 38th [proposition] of this [book], and it is the arc **n.o.**. Because the ratio of the sine of **a.o.** to the sine of **o.n.** is composed of two: namely the ratio of the sine of **a.e.** to the sine of **e.h.** and the ratio of the sine of **h.t.** to the sine of **t.n.**. But **a.o.**, **a.e.**, and **t.n.** are quadrants of circles; therefore, since **n.o.** and **b.t.** are also known, **h.e.** will be known. From this, its complement **a.h.**, which was sought, is found.

It is clear, therefore, from this that the ratio of the whole sine to the sine of the altitude of a point of the ecliptic at a quadrant's distance from the ascendant <note>original: *ascendente*</note> is as the ratio of the sine of the distance of a given point of the ecliptic from the ascendant to the sine of its own altitude.

<image-desc>A celestial sphere diagram showing complex intersecting arcs. Points are labeled: a (top), z (mid-left), n (upper-left), h (mid-left below n), b (far left), o (near center), e (center), t (right), and d (far right).</image-desc>

¶ For the last two ratios from which the first is composed, together they form the ratio of the sine of **h.t.** to the sine of **e.h.**.

### Proposition 45.
->At any other point of the ecliptic, to investigate the angle arising from the coincidence of the circle of altitude and the ecliptic.<-

Let the figure of the one before the previous be resumed. We seek the angle **a.h.t.** by establishing **h.** as the pole of a great circle, of which a portion is **k.l.m.**. The poles of the two great circles **h.e.d.** and **k.l.m.** are in the circle **a.e.g.**; therefore **e.k.** will be their maximum declination. Thus **e.z.h.** are distant by quadrants from the intersection **m.**, and **h.k.** and **h.l.** will be quadrants. Because the ratio of the sine of **h.e.** to the sine of **e.k.** is composed of two: namely the ratio of the sine of **h.t.** to the sine of **t.l.** and the ratio of the sine of **l.m.** to the sine of **m.k.**. Furthermore, the arcs **h.e.**, **e.k.**, **h.t.**, **t.l.**, and **m.k.** are known. For **h.e.** is the altitude of the given point, known through one of the previous [propositions]. **e.k.** is its complement. **h.t.** is the distance of the given point from the ascendant. **t.l.** is its complement. **m.k.** is a quadrant of the circle. Therefore **l.m.** will become known. Thus the remainder of the quadrant, namely arc **l.k.**, will be known, which is the quantity of the angle **k.b.l.**; therefore the remainder of the two right angles, namely angle **a.h.t.**, will become known, which was sought.
