# Book Three

The Third Book teaches in a logical sequence the timing of the **Solstices** and **Equinoxes**: the quantity of the **Year**: the entry of the Sun into those same points: as well as its **Mean motion**: the difference between the **Equal** and **Apparent Motion** of the Luminaries and Planets: the establishment of the **Root** <note>The "root" or *radix* is the starting position of a celestial body at a specific epoch or point in time used for calculations.</note> of any motion: the discrepancy of the **Equal** or **Astronomical Natural Day**, as well as the **Diverse** or **Apparent [Day]**: by indicating their Causes and Methods.

---

## Proposition One.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram of an astronomical quadrant instrument. The quadrant is labeled with letters 'a' at the sight, 'b' at the top of the arc, 'c' at the vertex/pivot point, and 'e' at the bottom of the vertical radius. A sighting line or alidade is positioned on the arc, which is marked with a scale. Behind the main diagram are faint geometric construction lines showing intersecting circles and a triangle.</image-desc>

To determine the entry of the sun into the point of the equinox with the help of an instrument. ¶ Let the quadrant **a.b.c.** be placed in the meridian plane <note>original: *superficie meridiana*; aligned exactly north-south to catch the sun at its highest point</note>: just as was shown in the 16th proposition of the first book of this work: and with it, near the time of the equinox—which you will easily estimate from the meridian altitudes—make your observation. For indeed, you must first know through your own observations the altitude of your region <note>The latitude of the observer</note>: the maximum declination of the sun: and even the declinations themselves for the individual points of the <term>ecliptic; the sun's apparent path throughout the year</term>. Therefore, if on any day the meridian altitude is precisely the complement of the altitude of the pole <note>The "complement of the altitude of the pole" is 90 degrees minus the latitude, which equals the altitude of the celestial equator</note> in your region: know that on that day at noon it is the equinox. ¶ However, using the meridian altitudes closest to—both greater and less than—the complement of the altitude of the pole: if no meridian altitude is precisely equal to the complement of the altitude of the pole: you will find the hour of the entry of the sun into the point of the equinox thus: If it is near the **vernal equinox** <note>Spring</note>: for every minute of difference between the lesser meridian altitude and the complement of the altitude of the pole, take one hour: and the entry occurs at that number of hours counted from the noon preceding the equinox. If, however, it is near the **autumnal equinox** <note>Fall</note>: by counting as many hours from the noon preceding the equinox as there are minutes of difference between the greater meridian altitude and the complement of the altitude of the pole: the entry into the equinox will occur. Such observation is more suitable in the autumn, however, because the air then becomes clearer. ¶ Moreover, entries into the <term>tropical points; the solstices, where the sun appears to "turn" back toward the equator</term> are of more difficult observation: because then the declination of the sun varies so little it is almost imperceptible. For this reason, the meridian altitude of the sun remains nearly the same for about four days. But entries into the points of the equinox are more convenient for this purpose: because then the declination of the sun varies greatly: such that the meridian altitude increases or decreases by 24 minutes of one degree in a single day.

## Proposition 2.

To derive the quantity of the year by observation. ¶ Different people have held different views regarding the quantity of the year. For the most ancient of the **Egyptians** said the solar year was the return of the sun to one of the fixed stars. They found that this occurred in 365 days, a quarter of a day, and a 130th part of a day. Truly, this definition of the year is not suitable: because the fixed stars have a motion separate from the motion of the whole <note>referring to the precession of the equinoxes</note>: and by the same reasoning, the return of the sun to Jupiter or Saturn would have to be called a year. Therefore, **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy** said the year...

It compares the observations of classical astronomers like Hipparchus and Ptolemy with the medieval Islamic astronomer Albategni (al-Battani) to account for discrepancies in the "true" length of the year.</meta>

### Book

<margin>
<image-desc>A partial geometric diagram showing a large circle intersected by chords and a smaller arc, representing celestial spheres or paths of motion.</image-desc>
</margin>

...to be the return of the sun to a specific point of the equinox or solstice. Therefore, the amount of time from the sun's entry into the point of the autumnal equinox until its next entry into that same point is the length the year is said to have. However, because of the "fallacy" <note>Meaning the inherent inaccuracy or margin of error in physical measurement</note> of the instruments with which such entries are detected, the true quantity of the year can hardly be found except through a span of many years. The greater the time that passes between two observations, the more truthfully we will be able to find this quantity of the year.

From this, **Hipparchus** found the year to be 365 days and one quarter. **Ptolemy**, however, found it to be 365 days and one quarter minus a 300th part of a day. Proceeding in this way, he takes the observation of Hipparchus, who carefully—as he says—considered the autumnal equinox in the 32nd year of the third revolution <note>original: *reuolutionis tertie*; referring to the Calippic cycle, a period used to synchronize solar and lunar calendars</note>. This was the 178th Egyptian year <note>The Egyptian year was a "wandering" year of exactly 365 days, used by astronomers because of its mathematical simplicity</note> from the death of Alexander [the Great]. He says it occurred on the third day of the added days <note>original: *supraddita*; these are the five "epagomenal" days added to the end of the 12-month Egyptian calendar to make 365 days</note> at midnight in Alexandria, the following day of which was the fourth of the added days.

He then takes his own observation, by which he considered the autumnal equinox in the 463rd Egyptian year from the death of Alexander. He says it was on the ninth day of the month of **Athyr** (which is the third Egyptian month), about one hour after sunrise. The interval between both observations was 285 Egyptian years, 70 days, and 1/4 plus 1/20 of a day.

Because there were 285 revolutions of the sun in this interval, if the year had consisted of 365 days and a quarter, the interval would have had to be 285 Egyptian years, 71 days, and one quarter. But the interval was only 285 years, 70 days, 7 hours, and one fifth [of an hour]. Therefore, the quantity of the year is less than 365 days and six hours. The difference between these intervals is 23 hours and four fifths, which is 19/20ths of a day. The proportion of 19 to 20 is the same as 285 years to 300 years; wherefore Ptolemy concluded that in 300 solar years, one day is missing from the number of days that 300 years would make if the year consisted of 365 days and a quarter. Therefore, he said the true quantity of the year consists of 365 days and a quarter, minus a 300th part of a day.

He found this same quantity through several similar observations. Later, **Albategni** <note>Also known as al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a major Arab astronomer who refined many of Ptolemy's values</note>, in the year 1206 from the death of Alexander (that is, 743 years after Ptolemy), observing and comparing his own consideration with those of Ptolemy, found that one day was missing in 106 years from the number of days that 106 years [of 365.25 days] constitute. Thus, each year is 365 days and a quarter, minus a 106th part of a day—which is 13 minutes of an hour and three fifths of one minute.

For the observation of Albategni was 743 Egyptian years, 178 days, and 1/2 plus 1/4 of a day, minus two fifths of an hour, after the aforementioned autumn. Ptolemy observed in **Alexandria**, but Albategni observed in **Aracta** <note>Ar-Raqqah, in modern Syria</note>, which is 10 degrees further East. And the equality <note>The calculated time of the event</note> of Albategni was nearly 4 hours and three quarters before sunrise with respect to his own meridian; whereas Ptolemy's, with respect to the meridian of Albategni, was one hour and two thirds after sunrise. Thus, beyond the whole days in the interval, there are nearly 15 hours and three fifths.

However, 743 solar years, with each year consisting of 365 days and a quarter, are 743 Egyptian years, 185 days, and 18 hours. These exceed the actual interval by 7 days and 25 minutes of an hour. If these are divided by 743 solar years, it results in 13 minutes of an hour and three fifths of a minute for each year. He therefore established the solar year as 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, and two fifths [of a minute].

Because of this diversity in the quantity of the year found by various people—though sought with similar instruments and methods—**Thebit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 826–901 AD)</note>, inquiring into the cause of this diversity, was moved to propose the motion of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>, which we call **trepidation** <note>A theory in medieval astronomy that the equinoxes do not move at a constant rate but "wobble" or oscillate back and forth on small circles</note>, upon two small circles in which the heads of **Aries** and **Libra** revolve. By this position, the variations of the declinations...

...the ecliptic <note>The path the sun appears to follow across the sky</note>: which strives to preserve the various lengths of the years, as is clear to one contemplating the nature of this motion. He said that the length of the year is not the time from one equinox to a similar equinox, nor from one solstice to a similar solstice, but rather the return of the sun from any point on the moving ecliptic back to the same point; or the return of the sun from any fixed star back to that same star. He stated that this occurs in 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, 7 seconds, and 12 thirds <note>This is a measurement of the "sidereal year," which is slightly longer than the seasonal "tropical year."</note>.

### Proposition 3.
#### To tabulate the mean motion of the sun.

<margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut diagram in the right margin illustrating the eccentric orbit model. It features a large circle with points labeled a, b, g, and d on the circumference. Point 'e' is the center of the orbit, while point 'z' (the center of the world) is placed lower on the vertical diameter 'ad'. Lines connect 'z' and 'e' to points 'b' and 'g' to demonstrate differences in angular motion.</image-desc>
</margin>

From the preceding, it is known in what time the sun completes a circle—that is, 360 degrees—by its **mean motion** <note>The "mean motion" is the theoretical average speed of the sun, assuming it moved in a perfect, unchanging circle.</note>. Therefore, if you divide 360 degrees by that total of days and their fractions, you will have the mean motion of the sun in a single day. **Ptolemy** set this at 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 17 thirds, 13 fourths, 12 fifths, and 31 sixths. From this, you may easily compose tables.

### Proposition 4.
#### That there are two ways by which the equal motion of a planet in its own orbit may appear varied in the circle of the signs.

<image-desc>A second woodcut diagram below the first, illustrating the epicycle model. A large circle centered at 'e' has a smaller circle (epicycle) centered at point 'a' on its circumference. Lines from 'e' extend through the epicycle's center and its sides, labeled with points z, h, t, k. Points b, d, and g are marked on the main deferent circle.</image-desc>

One way is by an **eccentric orbit** <note>A circle whose center is not the Earth</note> alone; the other is by a **concentric orbit with an epicycle** <note>A small circle (epicycle) that carries the planet, while the center of that small circle moves along a larger circle (concentric)</note>. For let there be an eccentric orbit **a.b.g.d.**, whose center **e** is outside the center of the world **z**. Let its diameter passing through the farthest distance <term>apogee <gloss>original: longitudo longior</gloss></term> **a** and the nearest distance <term>perigee <gloss>original: longitudo propior</gloss></term> **d**, and through both centers, be **a.e.z.d.** I say that if a planet is moved equally in the orbit **a.b.g.d.**, then its motion will appear varied relative to the center of the world **z**. 

For let **a.b.** and **g.d.** be equal arcs; having drawn lines **e.b.**, **e.g.**, **z.b.**, and **z.g.**, it will be established by the last proposition of the sixth book <note>Referring to Euclid's Elements</note> that the angles **a.e.b.** and **d.e.g.** are equal. But by the 21st proposition of the first book, angle **a.e.b.** is greater than angle **a.z.b.**, and **g.e.d.** is smaller than angle **g.z.d.** Therefore, angle **g.z.d.** is greater than angle **a.z.b.** This holds because whatever is greater than the greater is certainly greater than the lesser. But in equal time, the planet cuts these angles because arc **a.b.** is equal to arc **g.d.**; therefore, the equal motion with respect to center **e** will become varied with respect to center **z**. 

Likewise, let there be a concentric orbit of a planet **a.b.g.d.** around the center of the world **e**, and on the circumference of this concentric circle let there be the center of an epicycle orbit **a**, with the circumference of the epicycle being **z.h.t.k.** Let the diameter passing through the center of the world, the center of the epicycle, and the farthest distance of the epicycle **z** and the nearest **t** be **z.a.t.e.g.** I say that if the center of the epicycle **a** is moved equally in the concentric circle **a.b.g.d.** and the planet is moved equally in the circumference **z.h.t.k.**, its equal motion in these will appear varied relative to the center **e**. 

For once the lines **e.h.** and **e.k.** are drawn, if the planet has moved through the arc of the epicycle **z.h.**, its motion in the epicycle will add the arc of angle **a.e.h.** to the motion of the epicycle’s center in the concentric circle. And if the motion is through the arc **t.k.**, its motion in the epicycle will subtract the arc of angle **a.e.k.** from the motion of the epicycle’s center in the concentric circle. Thus, it will add to the equal motion through one half of the epicycle, namely **z.h.t.**, and subtract from it through the other half, namely **t.k.z.** So, in one half of the epicycle, the appearance is greater than the mean, and in the other, it is less. 

From this it is clear that according to the way of the eccentric, the apparent motion is greater at the nearest distance <note>perigee</note> than at the farthest distance <note>apogee</note>. However, according to the way of the concentric with an epicycle, a greater motion can occur both at the farthest distance and at the nearest distance. For in the figure of the eccentric, angle **g.z.d.** is greater than angle **a.z.b.** But in the figure of the epicycle, let it be moved from **a** toward **b**; if the motion of the planet is from **a** toward **h**, the motion is greater at the farthest distance. But if the motion of the planet were then from **z** toward **k**, the motion would be less at the farthest distance and greater at the nearest distance.

->Proposition 5.<-

<image-desc>A circular diagram in the left margin illustrating an eccentric orbit. The circle has its center at point e. Point z, representing the Earth, is located off-center within the circle. Lines radiate from z to various points on the circumference (t, h, l, d, k, b). Arcs th and bk are marked. Points a, g, and p are on the main diameter passing through e and z.</image-desc>

If two equal arcs are taken in the half of an **eccentric circle** <note>An "eccentric" is a circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center. This was a standard way for ancient astronomers to explain why the seasons have different lengths.</note>, the arc that is closer to the **perigee** <note>original: "longitudini propiori"; the point where the planet is closest to the Earth.</note> subtends a larger angle at the center of the Earth. From this, it is established that the closer a planet is to its perigee, the greater its **apparent motion** will appear to be.

In the eccentric circle *a.b.g.d.*, let the center be *e*. Let the diameter passing through the **apogee** <note>The point furthest from Earth.</note> and the perigee be *a.e.z.g.*, in which *z* is the center of the Earth. Let two arcs, *t.h.* and *b.k.*, be equal. From this, the angle *h.e.t.* will be equal to the angle *k.e.b.* <note>These are the angles as seen from the center of the circle, *e*.</note>. I say that the angle *k.z.b.* is greater than the angle *h.z.t.* because the arc *k.b.* is closer to the perigee. If lines *t.z.* and *b.z.* are extended to meet the circumference of the eccentric at *l* and *d*, and if the lines *h.l.* and *k.d.* are drawn perpendicular to *e.a.z.p.* and *z.q.*, then the angle *h.l.t.* is equal to the angle *k.d.b.* by the 25th proposition of the third book <note>This refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of the time.</note>. And since the angle *z.p.l.* is equal to the angle *z.q.d.*, then by the 4th proposition of the sixth book, the proportion of *z.d.* to *z.l.* is as *z.k.* to *z.p.* But *z.d.* is greater than *z.l.* by the seventh proposition of the third book; therefore, *z.q.* is greater than *z.p.* Moreover, the line *h.z.* is greater than the line *k.z.* by that same seventh proposition of the third book. Therefore, by the eighth proposition of the fifth book, the proportion of *h.z.* to *z.p.* is greater than the proportion of *k.z.* to *z.q.* And by the same reasoning, *h.z.* to *z.p.* is greater than *h.z.* to *z.q.* Thus, the proportion of *h.z.* to *z.p.* is greater than the proportion of *k.z.* to *z.q.* Wherefore, by the ratio of **sines or chords** <note>Early trigonometric functions used to calculate the sides and angles of triangles.</note>, angle *z.k.q.* is greater than angle *z.h.p.* Therefore, the two angles *z.k.q.* and *z.d.q.* together are greater than the two angles *z.h.p.* and *z.l.p.* Consequently, by the 32nd proposition of the first book, angle *k.z.b.* is greater than angle *h.z.t.*, which was to be shown. The corollary is thus manifest.

->Proposition 6.<-

<image-desc>A circular diagram in the left margin illustrating an epicycle system. A smaller circle (the epicycle) has its center at point e. Far below it, point z represents the Earth. Lines are drawn from z to points on the epicycle (h, t, k, b, m, l). Points a and g are on the vertical diameter of the epicycle. Perpendicular lines are dropped from various points to meet at p and q near the base of the diagram.</image-desc>

If two equal arcs are taken in the upper half of an **epicycle** <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle. This was another model used to explain varying planetary speeds and retrograde motion.</note>, the one closer to the apogee subtends a larger angle at the center of the Earth.

Let there be an epicycle *a.b.g.* around the center *e*, with the diameter *a.e.g.* passing through the apogee *a*, the perigee *g*, and the center of the Earth *z*. Let two equal arcs, *h.t.* and *b.k.*, be taken in the upper part, with *h.t.* being closer to the apogee. I say that the angle *h.z.t.* is greater than the angle *b.z.k.* For let the lines *t.z.* and *k.z.* intersect the lower part of the epicycle at *l* and *m*, and let perpendiculars *z.p.* and *z.q.* fall upon the extended lines *h.l.* and *b.m.* Thus, angles *h.l.t.* and *b.m.k.* are equal by the 25th proposition of the third book. Because their opposite angles *z.l.p.* and *z.m.q.* are equal, and *p* and *q* are right angles, then by the 4th proposition of the sixth book, the proportion of *m.z.* to *l.z.* is as *z.q.* to *z.p.* But *m.z.* is greater than *l.z.* by the eighth proposition of the third book; therefore, *z.q.* is greater than *z.p.* But *z.h.* is greater than *z.b.* by that same eighth proposition of the third book. Wherefore, by the eighth proposition of the fifth book, the proportion of *h.z.* to *z.q.* is greater than the proportion of *b.z.* to *z.q.* Since *h.z.* to *z.p.* is greater than *h.z.* to *z.q.* by the same reasoning, then *h.z.* to *z.p.* is greater than *b.z.* to *z.q.* Therefore, by the ratio of sines, the angle *z.b.q.* is greater than the angle *z.h.p.* But their external angles *b.m.k.* and *h.l.t.* are equal; therefore, the two remaining internal angles are unequal: namely, the angle *h.z.t.* is greater than the angle *b.z.k.*, which was the intent. From these things, it is clear that whether by the eccentric or the epicycle model, a star describes unequal arcs in the **zodiac** <note>original: "orbe signorum"; the circle of the signs of the zodiac.</note> during equal intervals of time.

->Proposition 7.<-

<term>eccentric</term> <note>A circle whose center is shifted away from the Earth.</note>, <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle moving on the circumference of a larger one.</note>, <term>planet</term> <note>In this context, including the Sun and Moon.</note>, <term>angle</term>, <term>center of the earth</term>, <term>distance</term>, <term>proposition</term>, <term>arc</term>, <term>circumference</term>

<header>Book Three</header>

<image-desc>
Three geometrical diagrams are positioned in the right margin.
1. Top diagram: A circle representing an eccentric orbit with a vertical diameter labeled a-g. A point 'e' (geometric center) and a point '3' (center of the world) are marked on the vertical line. Point 'b' lies on the circumference such that line 3-b is perpendicular to the diameter. Lines connect 'e' and '3' to points 'b', 't', and 'k' on the arc.
2. Middle diagram: A similar eccentric circle with center 'e' and point '3'. It illustrates the geometric proof of the maximum difference (prosthaphairesis) by drawing lines from '3' and 'e' to various points (b, t, l) on the upper-left quadrant of the circle.
3. Bottom diagram: An epicyclic model. A large concentric circle with center 'e' is labeled a-g-d-s. Several smaller circles (epicycles) are drawn at different points along the circumference (a, k, l, b, n). Lines from the center 'e' extend to the planet's positions on the epicycles to demonstrate the varying angles of apparent motion.
</image-desc>

According to the **eccentric model** <note>A model where the planet moves in a perfect circle, but the Earth is slightly off-center.</note>, the maximum difference between **mean motion** <note>The steady, average speed a planet would have if its orbit were perfectly uniform.</note> and **apparent motion** <note>The speed the planet appears to have when viewed from Earth.</note> occurs at the point of **mean transit**. This point is determined by the line of apparent motion standing perpendicularly to the diameter that passes through both centers.

¶ Let there be an eccentric circle *a.b.g.d.* whose center is *e*. Let the diameter *a.g.* pass through *e* and through the center of the world *z* <note>The OCR uses the numeral '3' to represent the letter 'z', a common practice in early typography for the Earth's center.</note>, as well as through the **apogee** *a* <note>original: "longitudinem longiorem"; the point furthest from Earth.</note> and the **perigee** *g* <note>original: "propiorem"; the point closest to Earth.</note>. Let the line of apparent motion *z.b* stand orthogonally (at a right angle) upon *a.g*. Once the line *b.e* is drawn, the angle of **diversity** <note>Also called the "equation of center"; the angular difference between where the planet is and where it appears to be.</note> between the mean and apparent motion is angle *e.b.z*. For the mean motion at that time is angle *a.e.b*, but the apparent motion is angle *a.z.b*. Let two other angles of diversity also be formed at two points *t* and *k*, which are *e.t.z* and *e.k.z*. I say that angle *b* is the greatest of these. For *b.z* is contained within *d* <note>referring to the geometric construction in the diagram</note>, and let lines *t.d*, *e.d*, and *k.d* be drawn. Because, by the **seventh [proposition] of the third [book of Euclid]** <note>Euclid’s Elements III.7 deals with lines radiating from a point inside a circle that is not the center.</note>, *t.z* is longer than *z.d*, therefore by the **19th [proposition] of the first [book]**, angle *t.z.d* will be greater than angle *t.d.z*. But *e.d.t* is equal to angle *e.t.d* by the definition of a circle and the **fifth [proposition] of the first [book]** <note>Elements I.5: the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.</note>; therefore the remaining angle *z.d.e* is greater than the remaining angle *e.t.z*. But *e.d.z* is equal to angle *e.b.z*; therefore angle *e.b.z* is greater than angle *e.t.z*. In the same way, it will be proven that *e.b.z* is greater than *e.k.z*.

¶ Or demonstrate it this way: Let *b* and *t* be points on the arc *a.b*. Once the lines *e.k* and *e.l* are drawn perpendicular to *b.z* and *t.z*, it is clear by the penultimate [proposition] of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Elements I.47.</note> that *e.z* is longer than *e.k*, and *e.k* is longer than *e.l*. But *e.b* and *e.t* are equal; therefore by the **eighth [proposition] of the fifth [book]**, the ratio of *e.t* to *e.l* is greater than the ratio of *b.e* to *e.k*, and the ratio of *b.e* to *e.k* is greater than the ratio of *b.e* to *e.z*. Therefore, by the reasoning of the **sine** <note>original: "sinus"; early use of trigonometry to compare angles via the ratios of sides in right triangles.</note>, angle *b* is greater than angle *b* <note>The author is comparing the angles of diversity at different points.</note> and angle *b* is greater than angle *t*, and so on.

From this it is inferred: the closer the line of apparent motion is to the point of mean transit, the greater the difference between the apparent and mean motion is.
¶ You can show the same regarding the points between *b* and *g*.

From this it is also established that the arc from the apogee (that is, the point of slowest motion) to the point of mean transit is larger than the arc from the point of mean transit to the perigee (the point of fastest motion) by **double the maximum diversity**.
¶ For however much angle *a.e.b* is greater than angle *a.z.b*, by that much also is angle *g.z.b* greater than angle *g.e.b*. Therefore angle *a.e.b* is greater than angle *g.e.b* by twice the angle *e.b.z*, which is what was intended.

### Proposition VII.

According to the **epicycle model** <note>A model where the planet moves in a small circle (epicycle), and the center of that small circle moves along a larger circle (concentric).</note>, while the center of the epicycle is on the concentric and the planet revolves at an equal speed in the epicycle, and the slowest motion occurs at the apogee: the maximum difference between the mean and apparent motion will occur when the line of apparent motion is distant from the apogee by a quarter of a circle.

¶ Let the concentric be *a.b.g.d.* around center *e*, and let *a* be the location of the center of the epicycle while the planet is at the apogee of the epicycle. Let *z* be the point of the center of the epicycle while the line *e.n* of apparent motion is distant from *a* by a quarter of a circle, or...

...a right angle *a.e.n.* I say that angle *z.e.n.*, which is the <term>difference<note>original: "diuersitas"; the difference between where a planet is expected to be based on average speed versus where it is actually seen.</note></term> between the **uniform** and **apparent motion**, is the greatest of all. Let *h* be the <term>apogee<note>original: "longitudo longior"; the point in the orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note></term> of the epicycle. Because the motions are proportional, it is necessary that angle *h.z.n.* be equal to angle *z.e.a.* Therefore, by the 28th proposition of the first book <note>Referring to Euclid’s Elements.</note>, *z.n.* is parallel to *a.e.* Thus, by the 29th proposition, the alternate angles *a.e.n.* and *z.n.e.* are equal. Therefore, *z.n.e.* will also be a right angle. Wherefore, by the 15th corollary of the third book, the line *e.n.* is tangent to the epicycle. Because of this, angle *z.e.n.* will be at its maximum. Likewise, let the center of the epicycle be at two other points, namely *t* and *k*. It will similarly be necessary for angle *h.t.l.* to be equal to angle *t.e.a.*, and *b.k.m.* to be equal to angle *k.e.a.*, because of the positioning of the uniform motions. Thus, angle *h.t.l.* will become greater than angle *b.k.m.*, and therefore, by the 8th proposition of the third book, *e.m.* will become longer than *e.l.*, because the arc *b.m.* is smaller than arc *h.l.*, and from this, angle *t.e.l.* will be greater than angle *k.e.m.*

¶ It is therefore clear: the closer the line of apparent motion is to the point of <term>mean transit<note>The middle point between the planet's fastest and slowest points in its orbit.</note></term>, the greater the difference between the uniform and apparent motion.
¶ However, the point of mean transit *b* is located on the <term>concentric circle<note>A circle that shares the same center as the Earth or the observer.</note></term> indicated by the line *e.n.*, which stands perpendicularly upon *a.g.* ¶ The same could be shown if points *t* and *k* were between *z* and *g*.

¶ Again, it is clear: the time from the point of <term>slowest motion<note>original: "motus minoris"; the planet moves slowest at its furthest point (apogee).</note></term> to the point of mean transit is greater than the time from the point of mean transit to the point of <term>fastest motion<note>original: "motus maioris"; the planet moves fastest at its closest point (perigee).</note></term> by double the time of the maximum difference.
¶ For just as angle *a.e.z.* is greater than angle *z.e.g.*, so also angle *h.z.n.* is greater than angle *n.z.e.* Furthermore, *a.e.z.* is greater than angle *z.e.g.* by double the angle *z.e.n.* Therefore.

## Proposition IX.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram in the left margin showing two large intersecting circles, one concentric around point 'd' and one eccentric around point 't'. An epicycle is centered at point 'b' on the circumference of the concentric circle. Lines connect the various centers and points on the circumferences, including points 'a', 'e', 'z', 'h', and 'g'.</image-desc>

If there are three uniform motions: namely, of the star in an <term>eccentric<note>A circle whose center is shifted away from the Earth.</note></term>, of the <term>epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle.</note></term> in a concentric, and of the star in the epicycle; provided, however, that its motion at the apogee is smaller. If the eccentric and the concentric are of the same size, and the radius of the epicycle is equal to the distance between the centers: whatever difference occurs according to one of these models will also happen according to the other.

¶ Let there be a concentric circle *a.b.g.* around center *d*, and let there be an equal eccentric *e.z.h.* around center *t*. Let the common diameter passing through the apogee and perigee and both centers be *e.g.* Let there be an arbitrary arc of the concentric *a.b.*, and let an epicycle be described around *b* as its center. Let the size of the epicycle’s radius *b.k.* be equal to the line *d.t.* Let the intersection of this epicycle with the eccentric be *z*. I say that the position of the star according to both models will be at such an intersection. For on account of the equality of the motions, the three arcs *a.b.*, *k.z.*, and *e.z.* are always similar. Also, the quadrilateral *b.z.t.d.* has equal opposite sides; therefore, it is always a parallelogram as long as the center of the epicycle is outside *a* and *g*. Wherefore, the angles *k.b.z.*, *b.d.a.*, and *z.t.e.* are always equal. Because of this, the apparent motion will always be determined by the line *d.z.*, and thus according to either model, the apparent position of the star is at point *z*. For the difference between uniform and apparent motion—which according to the eccentric model is angle *t.z.d.*, but according to the epicycle model is angle *b.d.z.*—these are alternate angles, and therefore equal. It is clear, then, that according to the epicycle model, the star describes an eccentric circle and never departs from it.

## Proposition 10

The same also occurs if the <term>eccentric circle<note>original: "ecentricus"; a circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth.</note></term> and the <term>concentric circle<note>original: "concentricus"; a circle whose center is exactly at the center of the Earth/world.</note></term> are of unequal size: provided that the ratio of the radii of the eccentric and concentric is at least the same as the ratio of the distance between the centers to the radius of the <term>epicycle<note>original: "epicyclus"; a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one.</note></term>.

¶ Let the eccentric be *a.b.g.* upon center *d*, with diameter *a.g.*, in which the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note> is *e*. Let the <term>apogee<note>original: "longitudo longior"; the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth.</note></term> be *a*, and the <term>perigee<note>original: "longitudo propior"; the point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note></term> be *g*. Let the star be at point *b* of the eccentric. It is clear that its apparent position is upon line *e.b.* and the angle of the <term>diversity of motion<note>original: "diuersitas motus"; the mathematical difference between where a planet is expected to be based on average speed and where it is actually observed.</note></term> between the uniform and apparent is *d.b.e.* Next, let *e.h.* be parallel to *d.b.* and let a concentric be imagined according to the quantity of the radius *e.k.* taken at will. Thus, according to the epicycle model, when the star is at *b* on the concentric, the center of the epicycle will be at *k* because of the equality of motions, and the angles *a.d.b.* and *a.e.k.* are equal. Therefore, let the radius of the epicycle *k.h.* be of such a size that the ratio of *a.d.* to *e.k.* is as the ratio of *d.e.* to *k.h.* Likewise, let *d.z.* be parallel to *e.h.*: thus, according to the epicycle model, the position of the star will be at *z*. I say that *z* is directly on the line *e.b.*, so that *e.b.z.* forms a single line. For let *e.z.* be drawn. Because *z.d.* and *e.h.* are parallel, the angle *d.z.e.* will be equal to its alternate angle *h.e.z.* Likewise, because *k.e.* is parallel to *d.b.* and *z.k.* is parallel to *e.d.*, therefore by the 34th proposition of the first book <note>Referring to Euclid’s Elements.</note> the opposite angles must be equal, namely *b.d.e.* and *e.k.z.* But also the ratio of the sides is the same: because *b.d.* to *e.k.* is as *d.e.* to *k.z.*, wherefore by the 6th proposition of the sixth book <note>Euclid VI.6 regarding similar triangles.</note> triangle *b.d.e.* is equiangular to triangle *e.k.z.* Therefore, angle *k.z.e.* is equal to angle *d.e.b.* But angle *k.z.e.* was already equal to angle *a.e.z.*, therefore angle *d.e.b.* is equal to angle *a.e.z.*, which is why *e.b.* and *e.z.* are a single line: which was to be shown. From which also angle *z.e.k.* is equal to its alternate, namely angle *e.b.d.*, which is the angle of diversity according to the epicycle model and the angle of diversity according to the eccentric model. It is therefore clear that according to either of the two foundations <note>The eccentric model or the epicycle model.</note> the apparent position of the star is always determined by the line *e.b.*, and the diversity in each is the same, whether the eccentric is larger or smaller than the concentric.

## Proposition 11

Under the eccentric model, the diversities of the uniform and apparent motions are the same whenever the line of the apparent position in the <term>zodiac<note>original: "orbe signorum"; the "circle of signs" or the path of the sun and planets through the constellations.</note></term> stands at an equal distance from the apogee and the perigee.

¶ Let the eccentric be *a.b.g.d.* upon center *e*. Let the center of the zodiac be *z*. Let the diameter through the apogee and perigee be *a.e.z.g.*, and let angles *a.z.b.*, *d.z.g.*, and *h.z.g.* be equal. I say the three angles of diversity, namely at *b*, *h*, and *d*, are equal. For by the 5th proposition of the first book, angle *b* is equal to angle *d*. But also the two triangles *e.h.z.* and *e.d.z.* have equal sides. For *e.h.* is equal to *e.d.* by the definition of a circle, and *z.h.* is equal to *z.d.* by the 7th proposition of the third book. At points *a* and *g*, however, there will be no diversity of motions. The converse of this is also clear. Let angles *b* and *h* be equal. I say that angles *a.z.b.* and *g.z.h.* are equal. For if one of them were larger, by reducing it to equality with the other, it would follow from this 11th proposition, contrary to the corollary of the 7th proposition, that the closer the line of apparent motion is to the point of mean transit, the difference of diversity would not be greater, which is impossible. ¶ It is also clear that the line of mean transit always divides in half the angle of apparent motion between the points of those same diversities.

->Proposition 12<-

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram illustrating planetary motion using the epicycle model. It features a large main circle representing the concentric path, centered at point d (the center of the world). On this circle, three smaller circles (epicycles) are drawn at different points (a, l, and o). Lines (radii) extend from the central point d to various points on the epicycles, labeled with letters like z, h, m, n, p, and q. These lines represent the lines of apparent motion. The vertical axis connects points f (apogee) and g (perigee). Additional points k, r, and s are marked on the far left edge of the larger system.</image-desc>

The same also occurs according to the <term>epicycle model<note>original: "modum epicycli"; a model where a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle) which itself moves along a larger circle (deferent).</note></term>.
<margin>¶</margin> Let there be a <term>concentric circle<note>original: "concentricus"; a circle whose center is at the center of the world/Earth.</note></term> *a.g.f.* upon the center of the world *d*. Let point *f* be the location of the center of the epicycle when the star is at its <term>apogee<note>original: "longitudine longiori"; the point furthest from Earth.</note></term>, and point *g* when it is at its <term>perigee<note>original: "propiori"; the point closest to Earth.</note></term>. Likewise, let there be three points and locations for the center of the epicycle: *a*, *l*, and *o*, situated such that the lines of <term>apparent motion<note>original: "motuum apparentium"; the planet's position as seen by an observer on Earth.</note></term> stand at equal distances from the apogee and perigee in the <term>zodiac<note>original: "orbe signorum"; the circle of signs.</note></term>; so that the lines of apparent motion are *d.z*, *d.n*, and *d.q*, and the three angles *z.d.f*, *n.d.g*, and *q.d.g* are equal. I say that the angles of <term>diversity<note>original: "diuersitatũ"; the difference between where a planet is expected to be (mean motion) and where it is observed (apparent motion).</note></term>—namely *a.z.l*, *d.n*, and *o.d.q*—are equal. From the arrangement of <term>uniform motions<note>original: "motuum equalium"; motion at a constant speed.</note></term>, it follows that *a.z.l.n* and *o.q* must be parallel to the diameter *f.g*. Therefore, the three angles *a.z.h*, *m.n.l*, and *o.q.p* are equal, because their alternate and interior angles are equal <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 29, regarding parallel lines.</note>. From this, the three triangles *z.a.h*, *n.l.m*, and *q.o.p* are equiangular according to the fifth part of the 32nd proposition of the First Book <note>Euclid, Elements I.32, which deals with the sum of angles in a triangle.</note>. But the sides *z.a*, *n.l*, and *q.o* are equal <note>Because they are radii of the same epicycle.</note>. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of the Sixth Book <note>Euclid, Elements VI.4, regarding similar triangles.</note>, the lines *z.h*, *n.m*, and *q.p* are equal. Furthermore, the products of *z.d* times *d.h*, *m.d* times *d.n*, and *p.d* times *d.q* are equal, because each of these is equal to the product of *d.i* times *d.t*, as is clear from the 35th proposition of the Third Book <note>Euclid, Elements III.35, the "Power of a Point" theorem regarding intersecting chords.</note>. Wherefore, if *z.h*, *m.n*, and *q.p* are divided equally, then by the 6th proposition of the Second Book and common knowledge, you will prove that the three lines *z.d*, *m.d*, and *p.d* are mutually equal. Therefore, the triangles *z.a.d*, *m.l.d*, and *p.o.d* have equal sides (each relative to its counterpart). By the 4th proposition of the First Book <note>Euclid, Elements I.4, the Side-Angle-Side theorem.</note>, you may conclude the proposal: namely, that the angles *a.d.z*, *l.d.m*, and *o.d.p* are equal. You can also show the converse of this: if the angles *a.d.z*, *l.d.m*, and *o.d.p* are equal, then the angles *f.d.z*, *g.d.n*, and *g.d.q* are also equal. For if one were larger, by adjusting it to match the other using this 12th proposition, an impossibility would follow against the corollary of the 8th proposition of this book.

<margin>¶</margin> From this, it is clear that the uniform motion (which is the angle *a.d.l* in this arrangement) is equal to the apparent motion (which is the angle *z.d.n*) which equally divides the line going to the two middle points of passage. Likewise, when a line from the center of the world cuts the epicycle, a star placed at the two points of intersection will have equal diversities of uniform and apparent motion—as when line *z.d* cuts the epicycle at *z* and *h*. Whether the star is at *z* or *h*, the angle of diversity is *a.d.z*; however, it will be at *h* when the center of the epicycle is located at *l*. For then *h* and *n* will be one point; and the angle of uniform motion from the apogee (namely *e.a.z*) is greater than the angle of apparent motion (which is *a.z.d* or *z.d.f*) by the angle *a.d.z*, which is the diversity.

<margin>¶</margin> Furthermore, the angle of uniform motion from the perigee (which is *l.d.g* or *d.l.n*) is smaller than the angle of apparent motion from that same perigee (namely angle *m.n.l* or *m.d.g*) by the angle *n.d.l*, which is of the same quantity as angle *a.d.z*. Thus, by as much as one exceeds the other in position *a*, it will be exceeded by the other in position *l* when the calculation is made from the closer distance (the perigee).

<margin>¶</margin> From the premises, it is clear that it is possible for the diversity of apparent motion in any star to be caused by one model alone—such as by the eccentric model, or by an epicycle on a concentric circle. In some cases, it might be caused by both. In the case of the Sun, however, only one type of diversity is found: namely, that the time from its slowest motion to its mean motion is always greater than the time from its mean motion to its fastest. Therefore, it is sufficient to assign to it only one of these models. But because the eccentric model is simpler and easier, and is completed by only one motion, whereas the epicycle model requires two motions, it is more appropriate to assign the eccentric model to the Sun.

# To investigate the ratio of the radius of the Sun's eccentric to the distance of its center, and the location of the apogee of the eccentric.

<margin>¶</margin> **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Albatachis"; a 9th-century Arab astronomer whose observations corrected many of Ptolemy's earlier findings.</note> found the time from the entry of the Sun into the point of the **spring equinox** until the **summer solstice** to be 94 days and a half. From the summer solstice to the **autumnal equinox**, he found it to be 92 days and a half. **Ptolemy** states that he found similar values. From these, he found the **eccentricity** <note>The distance between the center of the Earth and the center of the Sun's circular orbit.</note> and the location of the **apogee** <note>original: "augis"; the point where the Sun is furthest from the Earth.</note> in this manner: Let the <term>zodiac<note>original: "orbis signorum"; the circle of the signs.</note></term> be *a. b. g. d.* around the center *e*. Let *a* be the spring equinox, *b* the summer solstice, *g* the autumn equinox, and *d* the winter solstice. Because the time from the spring equinox to the autumn was more than half a year, it was clear from this that the apogee of the eccentric was in the half of the <term>ecliptic<note>original: "eclyptice"; the Sun's apparent path.</note></term> marked *a. b. g.* Likewise, because the time from the spring equinox to the summer solstice was greater than the time from the summer solstice to the autumn equinox, it was known from this that the apogee of the Sun’s eccentric was in the <term>quadrant<note>original: "quarta"; one-quarter of the circle.</note></term> of the zodiac *a. b.*

Therefore, let the center of the eccentric be at point *3* in this part, and upon it the <term>eccentric circle<note>original: "ecentricus"; a circle whose center is offset from the Earth's center.</note></term> *t. k. l. m.* Let there be two lines parallel to the two lines *a. g.* and *b. d.*, intersecting each other at point *3*. Let *n. q.* be parallel to *a. g.*, and *f. r.* be parallel to *b. d.* Let the line *e. 3.* be drawn so that it meets the zodiac at point *h*. We seek the length of the line *e. 3.* and the <term>arc<note>original: "arcus"; a segment of a circle's circumference.</note></term> *b. h.* From what has been said, it is established that the Sun traverses the arc *t. k.* in 94 and a half days, and the arc *k. l.* in 92 and a half days. Therefore, from the table of the Sun's <term>mean motion<note>original: "medij motus"; the average speed of the Sun if its orbit were a perfect, centered circle.</note></term>, each of these arcs will be known.

But since *f. t.* is equal to *f. l.*, therefore *f. t.* is known, and since *f. n.* is a quarter of a circle, *n. t.* will become known. Also, from the known values of *t. f.* and *t. k.*, *f. k.* will be known. Therefore, the <term>sines<note>original: "sinus"; a trigonometric function used to calculate lengths within a circle.</note></term> of arcs *t. n.* and *f. k.* are known, which are equal to the lines *3. c.* and *c. e.* Because of the right angle at *c*, the **hypotenuse** *e. 3.* will be known in such units where *3. f.* is the <term>total sine<note>original: "sinus totus"; the radius of the reference circle used in calculations, typically 60 units.</note></term>. Ptolemy found this eccentricity to be nearly 2 parts and 29 and a half minutes, where the radius *3. f.* is 60. Thus, the ratio of the radius to the eccentricity is nearly 24 to 1. Therefore, he set the **maximum equation** <note>The greatest difference between the Sun's observed position and its calculated average position.</note> at 2 degrees and 23 minutes. From the sides of the triangle *e. c. 3.*, the angle *3. e. d.* will be known, whose arc *a. h.* is the distance of the Sun's apogee from the beginning of **Aries**; Ptolemy found this to be 65 and a half degrees, just as Al-Battani also found. From this, Ptolemy concluded that the Sun’s apogee was immobile and fixed with respect to the points of the spring and autumn equinoxes.

**Al-Battani** <note>original: "Albategni"; another spelling of Al-Battani.</note> found the eccentricity to be 2 parts, 4 minutes, and 45 seconds, and the arc *b. h.* to be 7 degrees and 43 minutes. **Al-Zarqali** <note>original: "Arzacel"; an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer.</note>, although he varied the mean motion, found the same eccentricity as Al-Battani. However, he found the arc *b. h.* to be 12 degrees and 10 minutes. This certainly appears strange, since Al-Zarqali lived after Al-Battani. Therefore, consider whose observation you might trust: Al-Battani found the time from the spring equinox to the summer solstice to be nearly 93 days and 14 hours. But from the spring equinox to the autumn, 186 days, 14 hours, and 45 minutes. Therefore, he set the maximum equation of the Sun at 1 degree, 59 minutes, and 10 seconds. Al-Zarqali, 195 years after Al-Battani, made 402 observations regarding the four points midway between the equinoxes and solstices, and found *b. h.* to be 12 parts and 10 minutes. Therefore, he was forced to say that the center of the Sun's eccentric moved in a certain small circle, just as is held in the case of **Mercury**.

# **To find the same thing in another way.**

# Proposition XV.

To reveal how great the maximum diversity <note>term: "diversity" (Latin: *diversitas*). In historical astronomy, this refers to the 'equation of center,' or the difference between the planet's mean (average) position and its true (apparent) position.</note> is between equal and apparent motion, and at what distance from the furthest length <note>term: "furthest length" (Latin: *longitudo longior*). This is the 'apogee,' the point in the orbit where the Sun is furthest from the Earth.</note> it happens to occur.

Let the diameter of the eccentric circle **a.b.g.** be **a.d.e.g.**, the center [of the orbit] be **d**, and the center of the zodiac <note>The Earth, located at the center of the observer's universe.</note> be **e**. Let **e.b.** stand perpendicularly upon **a.b.**, and let **d.b.** be drawn. From the seventh [proposition] of this book, it is clear that the angle **d.b.e.** is the one we seek. Since the ratio of **b.d.** to **d.e.** is known from the two preceding [propositions], and the triangle is right-angled, the angle **d.b.e.** which is sought will be known. From this, the exterior angle **a.d.b.** will also be revealed. Various observers have found this maximum diversity to be different, as was said above, which happens because of the different ratio of **b.d.** to **d.e.** found by them.

# Proposition XVI.

According to the method of the eccentric, to find the angle of diversity given the angle of equal motion <note>The 'mean motion,' or the position the Sun would have if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle centered on the Earth.</note> from the furthest length.

Let the circle of the signs <note>The zodiac.</note> be **a.b.g.** upon center **d**, and the eccentric be **e.z.h.** upon center **t**. Let the line passing through the furthest and nearest lengths <note>The line of apsides, connecting apogee and perigee.</note> and through both centers be **e.a.t.d.h.g.** Let the given angle of equal motion be **e.t.z.**, which is the quantity of the arc **e.z.** Draw lines **z.t.k.** and **z.d.**, and draw the perpendicular **d.k.** upon **z.k.** The angle of apparent motion will be **e.d.z.** Its diversity from the equal motion is the angle **d.z.k.**, which we seek. In the right-angled triangle **d.t.k.**, the angles **t.** and **d.** are known; therefore the ratio of the sides **d.t.**, **t.k.**, and **k.d.** is known. But the ratio of **z.t.** to **t.d.** is also known from the 13th [proposition] of this book. Therefore the ratio of **z.k.** to **k.d.** is known. Thus the angle **d.z.k.** is known, which was sought; and it is the difference between arc **e.z.** and arc **a.b.** Conversely, if **e.d.z.** of the apparent motion is given, the angle **e.t.z.** will be known from this. For let **t.l.** be the perpendicular upon **z.d.** Because the angle **d.** of the right-angled triangle **d.l.t.** is known, the ratio of **d.t.** to **d.l.** and **l.t.** will be known. Therefore the ratio of **z.t.** to **l.t.** is given. Thus the angle **t.z.l.** is known. Hence the exterior angle **e.t.z.** which was sought will be known. Furthermore, from the given angle of diversity **t.z.l.**, we can find the angle **e.t.z.** of equal motion. For because of the given angle **z.**, the ratio of **z.t.** to **t.l.** will be known. But the ratio of **z.t.** to **t.d.** was known before; therefore the ratio of **d.t.** to **t.l.** will be known, whereby [angle] **l.d.t.** and the exterior [angle] **e.t.z.** are known.

### Corollary.

Given any of the three angles—namely, of equal motion, apparent motion, and diversity—the remaining two will also be known.

# Proposition XVII.
-> To show the same thing by way of an epicycle. <-

Let the eccentric orbit <note>The path the Sun appears to follow.</note> be upon center **d** of the zodiac <note>term: "zodiac" (Latin: *orbis signorum*). Here referring to the celestial sphere or the observer's reference frame.</note>. Let **f** be the point of the center of the epicycle <note>term: "epicycle." A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note> while the Sun is at the apogee <note>term: "apogee" (Latin: *auge*). The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> of the epicycle. Let the arc of mean motion <note>term: "mean motion" (Latin: *motus medius*). The theoretical uniform movement of a celestial body.</note> be **f. a.**, to which the arc of the epicycle **e. 3.** is similar; thus **a. 3.** will be equally distant from **f. d.** <note>original: "eque distabit," meaning they are parallel.</note>. We seek the angle **a. d. 3.** and the arc **b. f.** Because the angle **k. a. 3.** of the right-angled triangle is given, the ratio of **d. a.** to **a. 3.** is known. Therefore, the ratio of **d. k.** to **k. 3.** will become known, and from this, **d. 3.** to **3. k.**, whereby the angle **a. d. 3.** is known, etc. Conversely, given the angle **f. d. b.** or **b. 3. a.** of the apparent motion <note>term: "apparent motion" (Latin: *motus apparens*). The observed movement of the Sun as seen from Earth, which varies in speed.</note>, we shall also know the two remaining angles. For in the right-angled triangle **3. a. l.**, the ratio of **3. a.** to **a. l.** will be known; wherefore the ratio of **d. a.** to **a. l.** will also be known, and thus the angle **a. d. 3.** is known. From this, the external angle **3. a. e.**, which was sought, is found. Furthermore, from the angle of diversity <note>term: "diversity" (Latin: *diversitas*). Also known as the 'equation of center,' the difference between mean and apparent positions.</note>—namely **a. d. 3.**—the remaining two angles will become known. For the ratio of **d. a.** to **a. l.** will be known, and therefore the ratio of **3. a.** to **a. l.** will become known. Hence the angle **a. 3. l.** is known, which is equal to angle **f. d. b.** of the apparent motion; therefore, the external angle **e. a. 3.** is also known, which is the equal [mean] motion.

# Proposition XVIII.
-> By way of the eccentric, given the angle of mean motion from <-
-> the first distance, to know the angle of diversity. <-

Let the eccentric be **e. 3. h.** upon center **t**, and the zodiac be **a. b. g.** upon center **d**. Let the angle **b. t. 3.** be given. We seek the angle **d. 3. t.** and similarly the angle **3. g. b.** By making **d. k.** perpendicular to **t. 3.**, the ratio of the sides of triangle **d. t. k.** will be known. Wherefore, also the ratio of **3. k.** to **k. d.**, and from this, **3. d.** to **d. k.** Therefore, angle **3** is known, and the external angle **3. d. b.**, which was sought. Conversely, from a given angle **3. d. b.**, we shall know the others. By making **t. l.** perpendicular to **b. d.**, the ratio of **d. t.** to **t. l.** will become known. From this, **3. t.** to **t. l.**; by this, angle **3** and the internal angle **t** will become known. Furthermore, given the angle of diversity **3**, the rest will also be known. For the ratio of **3. t.** to **t. l.** will become known, and therefore also **d. t.** to **t. l.** is given. From this, angle **d. t. l.** or **d. g. b.** is known, and the remaining one from this—namely **b. t. 3.**—will be known.

# Proposition XIX.
-> To find the same thing by way of an epicycle. <-

Let the concentric circle be **f. a. g.** upon the center of the world **d**, and let **g** be the point upon which the center of the epicycle is located while the Sun is at the first distance <note>The apogee.</note>. Let the center of the epicycle be distant [from] **a. g.** by the arc **g. a.**, or let the angle **g. d. a.** of mean motion be given. Let **b. t.** be an arc similar to arc **a. g.** because of the equality of motion, and angle **b. a. k.** be equal to angle **g. d. a.** Therefore, the ratio of **a. h.** to **b. k.** and **k. a.** is known. But **d. a.** to **a. h.** was previously known; therefore **d. k.** to **k. b.** will be known. Thus, the angle of diversity **b. d. k.** will be known; and from this, **b. d. g.** of the apparent motion. Conversely, from the angle **b. d. g.** of the apparent motion, we shall know the others in the right-angled triangle **b. l. a.**; from the given angle **b**, the ratio of **b. a.** to **a. l.** will become known, wherefore **d. a.** to **a. l.** is given. From this, the angles **l. d. a.** and **a. d. g.** are known. Furthermore, given angle **b. d. k.**, the ratio of **d. a.** to **a. l.** will become known, and therefore **b. a.** to **a. l.** is known. Wherefore angle **l. b. a.**, which is equal to angle **l. d. g.**, will become known, and the remaining angle **a. d. g.** which was sought.

-> Given the angle of apparent motion equal to the angle of mean motion: to find the angle of difference for both and the distance from the furthest or nearest distance. <-

<image-desc>
A circular geometric diagram labeled with points. A vertical diameter is marked 'a' at the top and 'd' at the bottom. The center of the circle is 'm'. An offset center point 'e' is located on the diameter 'ad' below 'm'. Point 'b' is on the upper-left circumference, point 'c' on the lower-left, and point 'f' on the lower-right. Let the eccentric orbit <note>A circular path where the Earth is not at the exact center.</note> be **a.g.d.** upon center **e**, and let **f** be the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note>. Let **a** be the furthest distance <note>term: "apogee" (Latin: *longitudo longior*). The point in orbit furthest from Earth.</note> and **d** be the nearest. Let the angle **b.e.c** of mean motion <note>term: "mean motion." The idealized, perfectly uniform speed of the Sun.</note> be equal to another angle **b.f.c** of apparent motion <note>term: "apparent motion." The Sun's speed as it actually appears to an observer on Earth.</note>. The goal is to find the angle **e.b.f** <note>The angle of difference, often called the "equation of center."</note> and the angle **a.f.b**. When the line **b.c** is drawn, since angle **b.e.c** is equal to angle **b.f.c** and the opposite angles at **a.d.m** are equal, the two angles of difference **b** and **c** will be equal. Because of this, the quadrilateral **b.e.f.c** can be inscribed in a circle; otherwise, according to the 26th proposition of the third book [of Euclid], an impossibility would follow against the 16th proposition of the first book, if the circle passing through the three points **b.e.f** did not also pass through **c** but instead cut through **f.c** or went above it. Therefore, since angle **b.e.c** is given, each of the remaining equal angles **e.b.c** and **e.c.b** will also be given. Thus, angle **e.f.b**, being equal to **e.c.b**, is known. From this, the arcs subtended in the circle circumscribing triangle **e.b.c** are known. Therefore, the chord **b.e** subtending angle **e.c.b** (or **e.f.b**) is known. But the ratio of **b.e** to **e.f** is also known through the 13th proposition of this book; clearly, arc **e.f** will be known. Consequently, angle **e.b.f** will become known, and the exterior angle **a.e.b** will clearly be given. Moreover, the converse of the 11th proposition of this book proved that angle **e.f.b** is equal to angle **d.f.c**, since angles **f.c.e** and **f.b.e** are equal; and so on.

### Proposition XXI.

### To establish the "root" of any motion for the beginning of any time period through observation.
<note>term: "root" (Latin: *radix*). In astronomy, this refers to the "epoch"—the specific position of a celestial body at a specific starting date and time.</note>

Through the third proposition of this book, you have the mean motion in tables; through the 13th, you have the ratio of the eccentric's semi-diameter to the distance between centers; through the 16th and 18th, you have the mean motion derived from observation and apparent motion. From these, you will now be able to establish the root of the mean motion for the beginning of any time period, whether it precedes or follows the moment of your observation. 

Following the example of Ptolemy: he assumed the apogee <note>The furthest point.</note> or the furthest distance of the eccentric to be immobile. He found the distance of the point of the autumnal equinox <note>The moment in autumn when day and night are equal.</note> from the apogee to be 116 degrees and 40 minutes according to mean motion, as shown in the figure for the 18th proposition. If **b** were the beginning of Libra <note>The zodiac sign marking the start of autumn.</note>, then from angle **b.d.g**, which he calculated as 65 degrees and 30 minutes (because he placed the opposite of the apogee at 5 degrees and 30 minutes of Sagittarius), he found angle **z.t.b** to be 63 degrees and 20 minutes. 

Wishing to establish the root of the uniform motion at the beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar <note>Latin: *Nabuchodonosar*. A Babylonian king whose reign was used as a standard chronological era by ancient astronomers.</note>, he took his most precise and true observation of the autumnal equinox in the 17th year of Hadrian, on the 7th day of the Egyptian month Athyr, nearly two equal hours after midday. The years from the beginning of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar until the death of Alexander [the Great] were 424 Egyptian years. From then to the beginning of the first year of Augustus were 294 years; and this beginning was on the first day of the month of Thoth <note>Latin: *Thus*. The first month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> at midday. From then until the said observation were 161 years, 66 days, and two hours. Therefore, from the beginning of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar—which was at the beginning of the month of Thoth at the preceding midday—until the hour of this observation, there were 879 Egyptian years, 66 days, and two hours. The mean motion of the Sun in this time (after full revolutions) was, according to his calculation, 211 degrees and 25 minutes. If you subtract this from the position of the uniform Sun in the said observation, there will remain the position of the uniform Sun at 45 minutes of the first part of Pisces <note>The zodiac sign.</note> at the beginning of the first of the years of Nebuchadnezzar. Do likewise in other cases according to this example. However, the said observation of Ptolemy was after the beginning of the years...

...of Christ. 131 Egyptian years, 301 days, 2 hours, and 25 minutes. <note>original: "christi.131.annis egyptijs.301.diebus.2.ꝛ.horis.25." This is part of a calculation determining the interval between astronomical epochs.</note> For from the beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar <note>Nebuchadnezzar refers here to the Era of Nabonassar, starting in 747 BCE, which was the standard chronological reference for Ptolemy and later astronomers.</note> to the beginning of the years of Christ, 747 Egyptian years and 130 days passed.

# Proposition XXII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial D with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>
**Natural days are unequal for two reasons.**
¶ A natural day is defined as the time of one revolution of the Sun by the motion of the "prime mover" <note>The *primum mobile*, or the outermost celestial sphere that carries the stars and planets around the Earth once a day.</note> from the horizon or meridian until it returns to that same spot. Thus, however much time passes from the point of noon until the next point of noon: that is a natural day. This is the time in which the entire equinoctial <note>term: "equinoctial" (Latin: *equinoctialis*). The celestial equator, the Great Circle in the sky directly above the Earth's equator.</note> revolves, plus an additional portion of the equinoctial that corresponds to the arc of the ecliptic <note>term: "ecliptic" (Latin: *eclyptice*). The apparent path the Sun follows through the constellations of the Zodiac over the course of a year.</note> which the Sun travels during that time. However, this addition varies for two reasons. One reason is that the Sun cuts off unequal arcs of the circle of signs <note>The Zodiac.</note> in equal amounts of time <note>Because the Sun appears to move faster when it is closer to the Earth and slower when further away.</note>. The other reason is that equal arcs of the ecliptic have unequal ascensions, both "right" and "oblique" <note>This refers to the tilt of the Earth’s axis; because the Sun's path is angled relative to the equator, some degrees of the Sun's path take longer to cross the horizon than others.</note>. Therefore, because these additions are varied by this double cause, it is necessary for natural days to be unequal—which is what was proposed. From this, it is clear that these natural days (which are called "varying" days) are not a suitable measure for other motions, since they are unequal. It was therefore necessary to adopt other days for such measurement that would be equal. By this reasoning, one solar year is the time in which the equinoctial revolves as many times as there are units in the number of days found in a year (according to the teaching of the second [book] of this work), with the addition of one revolution which is completed along with the true motion of the sun over the course of one year. Thus, by dividing this number of revolutions by the number of days in the year, the quantity of the "mean day" <note>term: "mean day" (Latin: *diei mediocris*). The 24-hour average day used for modern timekeeping.</note> is produced: namely, one revolution of the equinoctial plus an addition of 59 minutes and eight seconds <note>These are "arc minutes" and "arc seconds" measuring the rotation of the sky.</note> of the equinoctial, corresponding to the quantity of the mean motion of the Sun in a day. Since these additions are equal to one another, it is established that the "mean" days are equal to one another. It is evident, therefore, that the "varying" natural days differ from one another and also differ from the "mean" days. And although a single varying day differs only slightly and imperceptibly from a mean day, when this diversity is collected over many days, it creates a quantity that must be reckoned with, as will be shown below.

# Proposition XXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C with foliate patterns.</image-desc>
**The cause of the inequality of days resulting from the variation of the Sun's motion begins from one of the middle distances and ends at the opposite; the maximum difference collected from this is double the maximum variation of the equal and varying motions in the Sun.**
¶ It begins from either "middle distance" <note>The points halfway between the Sun's furthest point (apogee) and nearest point (perigee).</note> because at those points, the apparent motion is equal to the mean motion for one day. However, in proceeding through the upper half of the circle of signs (in which the "further distance" <note>apogee</note> of the eccentric is located), it is clear that the mean motion is greater than the varying motion by double the angle of the maximum variation. But in proceeding through the lower half (in which the "nearer distance" <note>perigee</note> is located), the mean motion is less than the apparent or varying motion by double that same angle. Ptolemy found the double of this angle to be 4 degrees and 45 minutes. Thus, through the upper half, the varying motion is less than the mean by 4 and three-quarter parts; through the lower half, the same amount occurs [in the opposite direction]. Therefore, the total that arises from the addition and subtraction while proceeding through both halves is nine and a half degrees; the "varying" days that are longer exceed the "varying" days that are shorter by this much due to this specific cause.

### Proposition XXIV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a central floral motif surrounded by leafy flourishes in a square frame.</image-desc>
**T**o show at what place the cause of the inequality of days—arising from the inequality of ascensions <note>term: "ascension" (Latin: *ascensio*). The arc of the celestial equator that rises above the horizon at the same time as a given arc of the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> at an oblique horizon—begins or ends, and how great the total difference collected from this is.

¶ That location varies according to the variety of horizons; however, in every region, it is found before the summer tropic <note>The Summer Solstice, when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky.</note> and after the winter tropic <note>The Winter Solstice, when the Sun is at its lowest.</note>.
¶ For the beginning of the inception is where one degree of the ecliptic <note>term: "ecliptic" (Latin: *eclyptica*). The apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year.</note> rises together with one degree of the equinoctial <note>term: "equinoctial" (Latin: *equinoctialis*). The celestial equator.</note>. You should, therefore, determine this through the table of "oblique ascensions" for your specific horizon. Observe, then, the portion of the ecliptic between these two locations and how great the oblique ascension of this portion is; the difference between these is what you seek. Now, as much as "mean days" <note>term: "mean days" (Latin: *dies mediocres*). Days of an exactly equal length (24 hours), as measured by a perfect clock rather than the shifting position of the Sun.</note> add over "varying days" <note>term: "varying days" (Latin: *dies differentes*). Apparent solar days, which fluctuate in length throughout the year.</note> through the portion of the ecliptic in which Aries is located, by that same amount do the varying days add over the mean days through the remaining portion of the ecliptic. ¶ From this it is established that the greater varying days add twice the collected difference over the smaller varying days, as much as arises by reason of this cause. It is now clear that the difference found in this way exceeds the increase of the solstitial day over the equinoctial day, because one of the places in which this inequality begins and ends is before the summer tropic, and the other is after the winter tropic. ¶ Therefore, this cause varies according to the variety of horizons. But the cause of the diversity of days which is due to the inequality of "right ascensions"—which occur with respect to the meridian circle—is the same in every region. It is therefore more convenient for days to take their beginning from the instant when the Sun is at the meridian <note>The "meridian" is the imaginary line running north-south through the zenith; this passage argues for using "Solar Noon" as the reference point for calculations.</note>.

### Proposition XXVI.

<image-desc>A second spherical triangle diagram, similar to the first but with different configurations of arcs. **T**he arc of the ecliptic <note>term: "ecliptic" (Latin: *eclyptice*). The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky over the course of a year.</note> that differs the most from its right ascension, when combined with its right ascension, completes a quadrant of a circle <note>A quadrant is 90 degrees.</note> when it takes its beginning from the point of equality <note>term: "point of equality" (Latin: *puncto equalitatis*). The equinox, where the ecliptic intersects the celestial equator.</note>.
¶ Let arc $b.e.$ in the figure be the arc of the ecliptic that differs most from its right ascension, which is $b.l.$ I say that the sum of $e.b.$ and $b.l.$ makes a quadrant of a circle. This is drawn from the demonstrations of Menelaus <note>original: "Mileus". Referring to Menelaus of Alexandria (c. 70–140 AD), a Greek mathematician who wrote "Sphaerica" on the geometry of the sphere.</note>. ¶ Let $g.d.k.$ be on the solstitial colure <note>term: "solstitial colure" (Latin: *coluro solstitiali*). The great circle on the celestial sphere that passes through the celestial poles and the two solstices.</note>, $d$ be the midpoint between $g$ and $a$, and let $k.z.$ be a quadrant of the circle. Then $d.z.$ will be half of the maximum declination <note>The maximum tilt of the Earth's axis, roughly 23.5 degrees.</note>, because it is drawn from Menelaus: that the ratio of the square of the sine of $z.d.$ to the square of the sine of $d.k.$ is as the ratio of the sine of the excess of $e.b.$ over $b.l.$ (which is $e.m.$) to the sine of the sum of $e.b.$ and $b.l.$ Therefore, as much as the sine of the sum of $e.b.$ and $b.l.$ is greater, so much greater is the sine of $e.m.$ But it cannot be greater than the total sine <note>The "total sine" is the sine of 90 degrees, or 1.</note>. Therefore, when $e.b.$ and $b.l.$ complete a quadrant of the circle, $e.m.$ will be at its maximum, which is what was proposed. ¶ Or thus: In the figure above, the sine of $e.b.$ is to the sine of $b.l.$ as the sine of $e.d.$ is to the sine of $d.a.$ However, the sine of $e.d.$ to the sine of $d.a.$ is set forth as the sine of $l.d.$ to the sine of $d.e.$ But the sine of $l.d.$ to the sine of $d.e.$ is as the sine of $l.g.$ to the sine of $e.a.$; therefore, the product of the sine of $b.e.$ and the sine of $e.a.$ is equal to the product of the sine of $b.l.$ and the sine of $l.g.$ But this cannot be unless $b.e.$ is equal to $l.g.$ and $b.l.$ is equal to $e.a.$ For in two equal right-angled triangles <note>original: "trigonis orthogonis"</note> constructed upon one base, it is necessary that two sides of one be equal to two sides of the other. For they are inscribable in the same circle; otherwise, an impossibility would follow by the 30th [proposition] of the Third [Book] against the 16th of the First. And since they are equal by the 39th of the First, they will be between parallel lines; hence from the alternate angles of the 25th and 28th of the Third, the proposition will be clear.
