## Proposition XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
**T**o determine at what point the beginning of the addition of the varying days over the mean days <note>term: "mean days" (Latin: *dies mediocres*). A day of exactly 24 hours, based on the average motion of the Sun, as opposed to the "varying" or "true" solar day which fluctuates in length.</note> occurs, and how great the total difference is when both causes are combined.
¶ From the above, collect for each day the differences arising from both causes. And when both are adding to or subtracting from the mean days, join them into one. But when one is adding and the other is subtracting, take the smaller from the larger. But when one subtracts as much as the other adds, at that point the varying day is equal to the mean day. If after this both add together, or one adds more than the other subtracts, let that be the beginning of addition. But if after this both subtract together, or one subtracts more than the other adds, let that be the beginning of subtraction. The maximum of this kind of aggregated difference regarding addition has been found in the portion which is from the beginning of Scorpio to the middle of the sign of Aquarius. But regarding subtraction, it is in the portion from the middle of Aquarius to the end of Libra. For in the first, each difference is adding; in the other, each is subtracting. And in these, the difference by reason of the inequality of the Sun <note>term: "inequality of the Sun" (Latin: *inequalitatis solis*). The variation in the Sun's apparent speed caused by the elliptical (or eccentric) shape of its orbit.</note> is 3 degrees and two-thirds. The difference by reason of the inequality of right ascensions <note>term: "right ascensions" (Latin: *ascensionum rectarum*). The measurement of a star or planet's position along the celestial equator; the "inequality" refers to how equal steps along the Sun's path (the ecliptic) do not result in equal steps along the equator due to the Earth's tilt.</note> is 4 degrees and two-thirds; which together make eight degrees and a third of one: namely, the difference collected from both causes. This makes nearly half an hour and an eighteenth part of an hour <note>Totaling approximately 33 minutes and 20 seconds.</note>. Although we may not neglect this in the Sun or in other planets of slow motion, for no perceptible error would occur; in the case of the Moon, however, if it is neglected, a perceptible error occurs because of the speed of its motion, as it reaches nearly three-fifths of one degree.

## Proposition XXIX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
**T**o convert varying days into mean days, and vice versa.
¶ In a given time, calculate both the true and the mean course of the Sun. For the true course, take the corresponding elevation in the right sphere, and note its difference from the mean motion of the Sun. For that will be the equation of days, of which every degree represents four minutes of one hour. Therefore, add the time of this equation to the varying days if the right elevation exceeds the mean course. Or you shall subtract it if it is the opposite; and the mean days will result. If you wish to reduce mean or equal days to varying days in time, similarly calculate the true and equal course. For the true course, take the corresponding right ascension; its difference from the mean motion will be the equation of days. Add the time of this to the mean or equal days if the mean motion is greater than the ascension. Or subtract it if the opposite is true; and the diverse or varying days will come forth. By this way you will more certainly grasp what the previous points explained. ¶ It should be noted, however, that if the root of time <note>term: "root of time" (Latin: *radix temporis*). The starting point or reference epoch used for astronomical calculations.</note> is placed at the beginning of addition, this difference must always be added to the varying days so that they become mean days, and always subtracted from the mean days so that...

### Proposition XXX.

<image-desc>An astronomical diagram is positioned in the left margin. It features several concentric and intersecting arcs representing the celestial sphere. Radial lines originate from a point 'd' at the bottom (labeled 'polus mundi' in text) and extend to points labeled on outer and inner arcs: 's', 'r', 'q', 'p', 'a', 'n', 'm', 'o', 'b' on the outer ecliptic/equator arcs, and 'h', 'k', 'l', 'c' on an inner arc likely representing the eccentric. **T**o investigate in another way the beginning of the decrease of varying days from the mean, and to compose a table of the equation of days.

¶ Such a beginning has already been shown to be around the middle of Aquarius. But it was supposed that the Sun's apogee <note>term: "apogee" (Latin: *aux*). The point in the Sun's orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> was immobile; now, however, since the Sun's apogee is found to move, this principle must be sought more precisely. And that principle will be in that place around the middle of Aquarius: where the equal motion of the Sun corresponding to one degree of true motion shall be precisely equal to the right ascension <note>term: "right ascension" (Latin: *ascensio recta*). The distance measured along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note> corresponding to one degree of the Sun's true motion. And before such a point of beginning, it is necessary for the varying day to be greater than the mean; and after such a point of beginning, it is necessary for the mean day to be greater than the varying one. 

Let there be, therefore, in the figure a portion of the ecliptic from the vernal intersection <note>The vernal equinox, the starting point of the zodiac.</note> toward the beginning of Capricorn: *b. a.*; a portion of the equator coterminous with it: *p. q.*; and the pole of the world: *d*. Likewise, let the surface of the Sun's eccentric [orbit] in the surface of the ecliptic be *h. c.*, the center of which is *e.*, and the center of the world [Earth] be *f.* The perigee <note>term: "perigee" (Latin: *longitudo propior*). The point in the Sun's orbit closest to the Earth.</note> is established from the things said above to be under the beginning of our Capricorn in this time: namely under *a.* 

Therefore, the beginning of the decrease of the varying days from the mean will be in the portion *a. b.*; let that point be *n.* Having made *m. n.* one degree and *n. o.* one degree, and having drawn the lines and circles as in the figure: let the right ascension *q. p.* and the mean motion *k. h.* correspond to the true motion *m. n.* Similarly, the right ascension *r. q.* and the mean motion *l. k.* correspond to the true motion *o. n.* It is necessary, if *n.* is the point of the beginning of the decrease of varying days from the mean, that arc *r. q.* be greater than arc *l. k.* and arc *k. h.* be greater than arc *p. q.* For while the varying day is greater than the mean, it is necessary that the true addition <note>term: "addition" (Latin: *additamentum*). The small amount of extra rotation the Earth must do to complete a solar day beyond a 360-degree turn.</note> be greater than the mean addition. But when the mean day is greater than the varying one, it is necessary that the mean addition be greater than the true addition. 

The mean addition, however, is nothing other than the mean motion of the Sun in a given time. The true addition is the right ascension which corresponds to the true motion of the Sun in a given time, as is clear from the logic of varying and mean days. Therefore, it is necessary that before the point of the beginning of the decrease of varying days from the mean, the right ascension which corresponds to the true motion of the Sun in a given time be greater than the mean motion of the Sun in the same time. And after such a point, let it be the reverse. 

To find the point *n.* and to compose the table of the equation of days: first, compose a table which, from a given true motion of the Sun from its apogee, extracts the mean motion corresponding to it. Do this according to the teaching given in the 16th [proposition] of this [book]; with the help of that table, you will easily have what is proposed. Place *n.* at the end of the 21st degree of Aquarius; and *n. m.* one degree; similarly *n. o.* one degree; and let the apogee be in the beginning of Cancer. Therefore, *a.* will be the beginning of Capricorn. From the table of the distance of the mean motion from the true, *l. k.* becomes 58 minutes 33 seconds; *k. h.* 58 minutes 35 seconds. From the table of right ascension, *r. q.* will be 58 minutes 49 seconds...

## Book Four: Concerning the motion of the Moon, determined both through eclipses and by means of instruments, demonstrating its diverse variations.

### Proposition I.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial V containing a nude male figure standing amidst scrolling vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>

The true location of the Moon on the ecliptic <note>The "ecliptic" is the sun's apparent path across the sky; the "true location" is the Moon's actual coordinate on this path.</note> is determined more certainly through lunar eclipses than through instruments or observations relative to the fixed stars or solar eclipses. 
¶ This is evident because the radius of the Earth's size is of a significant magnitude relative to the distance of the Moon from the Earth. Therefore, a parallax <note>term: "parallax" (Latin: *diversitas aspectus*). The displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> occurs in the Moon which acts as an impediment; thus, its true location cannot always be certainly determined through instruments or observations relative to the positions of the fixed stars or solar eclipses. In lunar eclipses, however, since one may easily know the middle of the eclipse through its beginning and end—and in the middle, the Moon is diametrically opposite the Sun—you will have a certain location for the Moon derived from the location of the Sun, which was known from previous sections.

### Proposition II.

<image-desc>Large ornate woodcut initial R decorated with dense foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

The cycles of the Moon in the circle of its diversity, in the circle of the signs, and in latitude appear to be diverse.
¶ For we see it under one and the same part of the zodiac moving now slowly, now quickly, and now with a mean motion; nor does it always maintain the same latitude <note>In astronomy, "latitude" refers to the distance north or south of the ecliptic line.</note> under the same part of the zodiac. This is sufficient for us...

## Proposition 3

### By what path our ancestors discovered the returns of the moon in the circle of diversity and in the zodiacal circle.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring a central rose-like flower and foliage within a double-lined square border.</image-desc>
Because they saw that the apparent motion of the moon was diverse—at times fast, at times slow, and at times middling—it was necessary that there be four points in its circle of diversity. At one of these points, the fastest motion of the moon occurs; at the opposite point, the slowest; and at the two middle points, a middling motion. Indeed, these points divide the circle into four portions. In the first portion, the moon’s motion goes from its fastest speed toward the first middle point, and it is "fast-decreasing." In the second, it is "middling-decreasing." In the third, it is "slow-increasing." In the fourth, it is "middling-increasing." By observing the moon’s motion daily, they were able to know in which portion of its circle the moon was moving.

They chose, therefore, two lunar eclipses in each of which the moon was moving with the same velocity in the same portion of its circle of diversity. From this, they conjectured that by the time of the second eclipse, the moon had returned to the exact point of its circle where it had been during the first eclipse. Thus, the interval of time between both eclipses would contain a whole number of revolutions in its circle of diversity. To ensure such a span of time was verified with the utmost certainty, they also considered two other lunar eclipses in which the moon was again moving at an equal speed, but in the portion of its circle of diversity opposite to the first pair. They found the interval between these two eclipses to be equal to the interval between the first two, and the true motion of the moon in the first interval was equal to its true motion in the second.

**Hipparchus** <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who is often called the "father of astronomy" for his discovery of precession and his detailed star catalogs.</note>, however, found the length of this interval to be 126,007 days and one hour. Within this interval, there were 4,267 lunar months, which he was easily able to calculate by counting the number of **new moons** <note>original: "nouiluniorum".</note>. The returns in the circle of diversity were 4,573, which he also discovered through the categorized motions of the moon (slow, middling, fast, and middling). The returns in the zodiacal circle, however, were 4,612, minus almost seven and a half degrees. For the sun decreases by this much in the 347 revolutions <note>This refers to solar years.</note> of this time, because these returns were calculated in relation to the fixed stars.

Therefore, the said interval divided by the number of months reveals the length of a single lunar month. Likewise, because in every lunar month the moon completes its circle and adds an amount equal to the motion of the sun during that month, the whole of this divided by the span of a lunar month will reveal the mean motion of the moon in a single day. The full circle (360 degrees) divided by this daily motion will show the time required for one revolution of the moon's mean motion. Alternatively, from the number of returns in the zodiacal circle and the interval itself, you can determine a single revolution in the zodiac and the daily motion. You would do the same for the number of returns in the circle of diversity: by multiplying the number of returns by the full circle and dividing the product by the days in the interval, the result will be the motion in the circle of diversity for one day. Likewise, the aforementioned numbers—namely 4,267 months and 4,573 returns of diversity—exist in a ratio of 251 to 269. Therefore, in 251 lunar months, the diversity of similar motion returns, and in that same amount of time, 269 revolutions of diversity occur.

# Fourth [Book]

If the interval between the first two eclipses is equal to the interval between the two later eclipses; and if in the second eclipse the motion of the moon was in the same portion of the **circle of diversity** <note>term: "circle of diversity" (Latin: *circulus diuersitatis*). This is the lunar epicycle, the smaller circle the Moon moves around to explain its changing speed.</note> and of the same velocity as it was in the first; and likewise in the fourth [eclipse] in the same portion and of the same velocity as in the third; and if the true motion of the moon in the first interval is equal to the true motion of the moon in the second interval: it is necessary that both intervals contain complete returns <note>original: "reditiones"; complete orbital revolutions.</note> of the moon in the circle of diversity.

Let the moon have an epicycle **a, b, g, d**, whose center is **e**, and the center of the world is **z**. The **apogee** <note>term: "apogee" (Latin: *aux*). The point in the orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> is **a**, and the opposite point is **g**. The line through the apogee is **a-e-g-z**. Two tangent lines, **z-b** and **z-d**, will mark the two points **b** and **d**, which are the **middling transits** <note>term: "middling transit" (Latin: *transitus mediocris*). These are the specific points on the epicycle where the Moon’s apparent speed matches its average speed.</note>. Let the moon be at point **b** in the first eclipse and at point **p** in the third, so that its two movements are diverse: one with an increase and the other with a decrease. However, let its motion in the second eclipse be of the same velocity as in the first, and in portion **a-d**. In the fourth, let it also be of the same velocity as in the third, and in portion **g-b**. Let the intervals be equal, and let the true motions of the moon in both intervals be equal. I say that in the second eclipse, it must necessarily have returned to point **b**, and in the fourth, it must have returned to point **p**. For if not: let it be at **t** in the second and at **q** in the fourth. Because the intervals are equal, the distance **t-b** must be equal to **q-p**, and the mean motion of the moon in the first interval equal to the mean motion in the second. And because the movements at **t** and **b** are different from the movements at **q** and **p** (since one is with an increase and the other with a decrease), it is necessary that the true motion of the moon in the first interval differs from its true motion in the second by the quantity of the two angles of the **equations of diversity** <note>The "equation of diversity" is the mathematical adjustment needed to find the Moon's actual position relative to its average position.</note> corresponding to arcs **t-b** and **q-p**. But this contradicts our hypothesis. Therefore [the proposition is proven].

### Proposition 5

**In the investigation of the time of the moon's returns in its diversity, one must be careful regarding eclipses in which the moon is near the points of middling transit.**

The most suitable eclipses for this work are those in which the true motion of the moon differs most from the **mean** <note>Average.</note> motion. This happens near the points of the **greatest and least distance** <note>term: "greatest and least distance" (Latin: *longitudo longior et propior*). These are known today as apogee and perigee.</note>. However, those in which the moon is near the middling transits are less suitable and deceptive. For if in the first eclipse the moon was near **d**, namely at **m**, because of the proximity of these points and the minimal variation of apparent motion, it is possible that in the second eclipse it is above **d** at **n**, where its apparent motion does not have a perceptible variation from its motion at **m**. And if in the third eclipse it is at point **k** near **b**, so that arc **b-k** is equal to arc **d-n**, it is possible in the fourth eclipse for it to be at **l** below **b**, so that arc **b-l** is equal to arc **d-m**. We might therefore think the moon in the second eclipse had returned to the same place where it was in the first, and in the fourth had returned to the place where it was in the third. And although it may be that the true motion of the first interval is equal to the true motion of the second interval—because the angle of diversity corresponding to arc **k-l** is equal to the angle of diversity corresponding to arc **n-m**, and both angles are of one degree (namely, as to the increase or decrease in true motion)—and the intervals of time are also equal because arcs **n-m** and **l-k** are equal; nevertheless, in neither interval have complete returns in diversity been made. Similarly...

### Proposition VI.
#### To determine the return of the moon in latitude.

Observers have reconsidered the interval between two eclipses in which: the magnitude of the eclipsed portion of the diameter was the same; the moon stood at the same point of its **diversity** <note>term: "diversity" (Latin: *diuersitas*). In medieval astronomy, this refers to the "anomaly" or the change in the moon's speed as it moves around its epicycle.</note> in both; and the eclipsed part in both was toward the north, or in both toward the south in the same manner. For from these conditions, the following position will result: that the distance of the moon from the **node** <note>term: "node" (Latin: *nodus*). The two points where the moon's tilted orbit crosses the path of the sun (the ecliptic).</note> in the first of these eclipses is equal to its distance from the node in the second, and in the same direction. Therefore, this interval will contain complete **returns** <note>original: "reditiones"; meaning full orbits or cycles.</note> of the moon in latitude, and of the center of its revolution-circle on the inclined orbit. Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who is often called the father of trigonometry; he produced the first known star catalog.</note> found that this interval contains 5,458 months, in which there were 5,923 returns in latitude. Thus, by dividing the interval of time by the number of returns, the time of one return will be produced. And by dividing the circle by the time of one return, the motion of the moon in latitude for one day will be produced.

### Proposition VII.

If the motion of the moon in the **eccentric** <note>term: "eccentric" (Latin: *ecentricus*). A circular orbit whose center is offset from the center of the Earth.</note> is equal or similar to the motion of the moon in the **epicycle** <note>term: "epicycle" (Latin: *epicyclus*). A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note>; and if the eccentric is moved in the direction of the **succession of the signs** <note>Moving forward through the zodiac (e.g., from Aries to Taurus).</note> by the amount of the excess of the mean motion in longitude over the mean motion of diversity; and if the eccentric and the **concentric** <note>term: "concentric" (Latin: *concentricus*). A circle centered exactly on the Earth.</note> are of the same size, and the eccentricity is equal to the radius of the epicycle: then whatever diversity occurs according to one of these models will also happen according to the other.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram demonstrating Proposition VII. It consists of a large main circle with center d and a vertical diameter labeled a-d-k. ¶ Let there be a concentric circle **a.b.g** centered on the center of the world **d**, with diameter **a.d.k**. Let the epicycle be **e.z** on center **g**. Let the arc of the concentric circle **a.g** be the mean motion of longitude from point **a** (at which time, while the center of the epicycle was there, the moon stood at the apogee of its epicycle). Meanwhile, as the center of the epicycle completes arc **a.g**, let the moon in the epicycle complete arc **e.z**. And because arc **a.g** is a larger portion of its circle than **e.z** is of its own, let arc **b.g** be similar to arc **e.z**. Therefore, according to the hypothesis, the center of the eccentric must be on the drawn line **d.b**. And the motion of the eccentric in that same time will become angle **a.d.b**, which is the excess of angle **a.d.g** over angle **e.g.z**. Therefore, let **d.b** be equal to **g.z**, and when line **b.z** is drawn, it will be equal to line **g.d** by the 34th proposition of the first book [of Euclid's Elements]. On center **b**, let an eccentric be made of the same size as the concentric, which shall be **t.z**, whose apogee is **t**. I say, therefore, whether we suppose the moon to move in an epicycle such that the center of the epicycle revolves on the concentric according to the amount of the mean motion in longitude, and the moon in the epicycle according to the amount of the motion of diversity; or whether we suppose the moon to move in an eccentric according to the amount of the motion of diversity, and with this the apogee of the eccentric (or the eccentric itself) moves in the same direction according to the amount of the excess of the mean motion in longitude over the motion in diversity: the same thing always appears regarding its apparent motion. For the quadrilateral **g.z.b.d** always has parallel sides; therefore angle **e.g.z** is equal to angle **g.d.b**. But **g.d.b** is also equal to angle **z.b.t**; therefore arc **e.z** is similar [to the corresponding arc in the eccentric model].

### Proposition VIII.

#### The same result occurs if the eccentric and concentric circles are unequal. However, the proportion of the radii of the eccentric and concentric should be the same as the proportion of the distance between the centers to the radius of the epicycle: the ratio of motion being preserved as before.

->Let there be in different figures a **concentric circle** <note>A circle centered exactly on the Earth.</note> **a-b-g** on the **center of the world** <note>term: "center of the world" (Latin: *centrum mundi*). ->Likewise, in the other figure **h-t-k**, let there be an **eccentric circle** <note>A circle whose center is offset from the Earth.</note> of a different size on its own center **l**, with the center of the world at **m**, and the diameter **t-l-p**. In the time that the center of the epicycle moves through the angle **a-d-g**, let the eccentric motion be through the angle **h-m-t**, to which angle **a-d-b** is equal in the first figure. In that same time, the moon in the epicycle describes the angle **e-g-z**, which is equal to the angle **t-l-k** that the moon describes from the apogee in the second figure.<-

I say that according to both methods, the moon appears in the same place in the heavens. This will be clear if we prove that the angle **a-d-z** is equal to the angle **h-m-k**. Because the angle **e-g-z** is equal to the angle **t-l-k**, therefore the remaining angle **z-g-d** is equal to the remaining angle **m-l-k**. And since the two sides **z-g** and **g-d** are proportional to the two sides **m-l** and **l-k**, then by the **sixth [proposition] of the sixth [book]** <note>A reference to Euclid's *Elements*, which was the standard textbook for geometry.</note>, the angle **g-z-d** will be equal to the angle **l-m-k**. Therefore, the angle **l-m-k** is equal to the angle **b-d-z**. Since, therefore, the same thing happens according to both methods—and as we shall say later, a **second diversity** <note>The "evection," a solar perturbation of the moon's orbit discovered by Ptolemy.</note> has also been found in the moon, which arises from the different relationship of the moon to the sun—it is more convenient that we preserve this first diversity of the moon through an epicycle and an eccentric, and [then] preserve the second diversity.

### Proposition X.

#### To reveal the proportion of the radius of the epicycle to the line between the center of the Earth and the center of the epicycle through three known eclipses.

Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the most influential astronomer of antiquity.</note> takes three ancient eclipses. The first was in the first year of **Mardokempad** <note>original: "Mardochei"; referring to the Babylonian King Mardokempad, whose reign provided the earliest reliable eclipse records used in the Almagest.</note>, after 29 days of the Egyptian month **Thoth** had passed. The morning of this eclipse was the 30th day, with the Sun being at 24 degrees and 30 minutes of **Pisces**, 3 hours and one-third of an hour before midnight in **Alexandria**. The second was in the second year of Mardokempad, after 18 days of the month Thoth had passed. Its morning was the 19th day, in which three **digits** <note>A "digit" represents 1/12th of the diameter of the celestial body.</note> were eclipsed on the southern side; this was at midnight in **Babylon**, but in Alexandria it was half and one-third of an hour <note>i.e., 50 minutes.</note> before midnight, by which the meridian of Alexandria precedes the meridian of Babylon. The Sun was then at 13 degrees and a half and a quarter of a degree <note>13° 45'</note> of Pisces. ### Proposition 10

->To derive the distance of the moon from the apogee <term>apogee: the point in the orbit farthest from the center</term> of the epicycle in any of the three stated eclipses: and the location of the moon according to its mean course.<-

**L**et the epicycle be $l. b. m.$ in the figure above, with center $k$, and the line from the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note> be $d. m. k. l.$ and $d. e. b$. Indeed, let the location of the moon in the second eclipse be $k. n. s.$ perpendicular to $b. e.$ and $b. k.$ is drawn. Because in the previous proposition the ratio of $d. c.$ to $e. b.$ was known, and $e. n.$ is half of $e. b.$ Also, the ratio of $d. e.$ to $d. k.$ was given. Therefore, the ratio of $d. k.$ to $d. n.$ will be known, by which the angle $d. k. n.$ will be known, and as a result the remaining angle $k. d. n.$, which is the angle of **diversity** <term>diversity: also called "anomaly," the difference between the moon's average (mean) position and its actual appearance due to its movement on the epicycle</term> of the mean position of the moon from the true position in the second eclipse. Therefore, the mean position of the moon in that case will be known. But the angle $d. k. n.$ makes known the arc $m. s.$, therefore the remainder of the semicircle, namely $l. b. s.$, is known. But $b. s.$ is half of the arc $b. e.$; therefore it is known. And because of this, the remaining distance $l. b. s.$ — the distance of the moon from the apogee of the epicycle in the second eclipse — is known. He found it to be 12 degrees and 24 minutes, and the angle $k. d. n.$ to be 59 minutes. From these you will draw the mean position of the moon as 14 degrees and 44 minutes of Virgo; and from these you may easily seek the other roots <note>original: "radices," astronomical reference points or starting values for calculations.</note>.

# Book Four

...not from *a* to *b* and *a* to *b* into *g* as the position of the epicycle requires. And the arc *a-b* will be 110 degrees, 21 minutes, subtracting 7 degrees and 42 minutes from the mean motion <note>The "mean motion" is the average speed of a planet, assuming a perfectly circular orbit; the subtraction accounts for the moon's specific position on its smaller epicycle</note>. And the arc *b-g* is 81 degrees and 36 minutes, adding one degree and 21 minutes to the mean motion. Therefore, the arc *g-a*, the remainder of the circle—namely 168 degrees and 3 minutes—will be adding 6 degrees and 21 minutes to the mean course in longitude. Therefore, it is necessary that the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth, here called the 'longitudo longior'</term> of the epicycle be within the arc *a-b*, because it cannot be in the arc *b-g* nor in the arc *g-a*, because both of those are smaller than a semicircle and are additive. For it is necessary that in an arc smaller than a semicircle in which the apogee is located, the moon must move against the succession of the signs <note>original: "contra successionem signorum"—this refers to retrograde motion on the epicycle, moving westward rather than the standard eastward direction of the zodiac</note>.

Therefore, let a figure be made according to this, with *d* as the center of the circle of signs <note>The zodiac</note>. Lines *d-e-a*, *d-b*, *d-g*, *b-g*, *e-b*, *e-g* are drawn, and *e-h* is perpendicular to *d-g*, *e-z* is perpendicular to *d-b*, and *g-t* is perpendicular to *e-b*. Because, therefore, in the right-angled triangle *e-d-z*, angle *d* is known, the ratio of *d-e* to *e-z* is known. Similarly, in triangle *b-e-z*, angle *b* is known because the exterior angle *a-e-b* and interior angle *e-d-b* are known. Therefore, the ratio of *b-e* to *e-z* is known. But since the ratio of *d-e* to *e-z* was already given, the ratio of *d-e* to *e-b* will therefore become known. Similarly, in the right-angled triangle *e-d-h*, because angle *d* is known, the ratio of *d-e* to *e-h* will become known. And in triangle *g-e-h*, angle *g* will be known because the exterior angle *a-e-g* and interior angle *e-d-g* are known; therefore the ratio of *g-e* to *e-h* will be known. But the ratio of *d-e* to *e-h* was already known, so the ratio of *d-e* to *e-g* will be known. Likewise, because of the known angle *b-e-g* in triangle *e-g-t*, it will be known in the parts in which *d-e* was known. Therefore the remainder *t-b* is also known. And from *g-t* and *t-b*, the line *b-g* will be given as known. But from the arc *b-g*, the chord *b-g* will become known with respect to the parts of the radius of the epicycle; therefore, in that same respect, *e-g* will become known, and thus arc *e-g* is given. From this, the whole *b-g-e* is known, and consequently the remainder *e-a* will become known: which he found to be ninety-five degrees, sixteen minutes, and fifty seconds.

From this it was manifest that the center of the epicycle fell in the portion *a-b-c*. Therefore, let *k* be the center of the epicycle. The line *d-m-k-l* is drawn through *m*, the perigee <term>perigee: the point in the orbit closest to the Earth, here called 'longitudo propior'</term>, and *l*, the apogee. Now, by means of the chord *e-g* or *b-g*, the ratio of *d-e* to *e-a* will be known; therefore the whole *d-e-a* will be known in parts of the radius of the epicycle, and also *d-e* in the same. But that which is formed from *a-d* times *d-e* with the square of the radius of the epicycle is equal to the square of *k-d*. Therefore, the ratio of *l-k* to *k-d* will be known, which is what was proposed. Thus he found *l-k* to be five parts and fourteen minutes while *d-k* is sixty, which is close to the findings and the ancient eclipses.

Furthermore, he similarly found the distance of the moon from the apogee of the epicycle and the root of the mean motion of the moon in the aforesaid things in a form similar to the previous one, by drawing the line *k-n*, namely perpendicular to *d-e-a*, and drawing line *a-k*. Because the ratio of *d-e* to *d-k* was already known, the angle *d-k-n* and its arc *m-e-s* will be known, and thus the whole *m-s-a* will be known. Therefore, the remainder *a-l* is also known, which is the distance of the moon from the apogee of the epicycle in the middle of the first eclipse; from which are recognized forty-three minutes; and *l-b* is sixty-four degrees and thirty-eight minutes; and *l-g* is one hundred forty-six degrees and fourteen minutes. Likewise, from the known angle *d-k-n*, the remaining angle was known, namely *n-d-k*, which he found to be three degrees and twenty minutes. Through this, he recognized the mean location of the moon to be nine degrees and fifty-five minutes of **Scorpio** in the first eclipse. In the second, however, it was twenty-nine degrees and thirty minutes of **Aries**. In the third, it was seventeen degrees and four minutes of **Virgo**.

# Book Four

### Proposition 12

**To verify the quantity of the mean motions of the moon in longitude and anomaly from the aforementioned eclipses.**

<margin>An image illustrates the circular path of the moon. A large circle contains a smaller eccentric point, with lines demonstrating how astronomers calculate the "mean motion" (average speed) versus the "true motion" (actual observed position) by accounting for the moon's epicycle.</margin>

¶ In the second of the three ancient eclipses, the mean position of the moon was 14 degrees and 44 minutes of Virgo. The mean position in anomaly <term>anomaly: here called 'diversity,' this refers to the moon's position on its smaller epicycle, which causes it to appear to speed up or slow down</term> was 12 degrees and 24 minutes from the apogee of the epicycle. However, in the second of the three later eclipses, the mean position of the moon was 29 degrees and 30 minutes of Aries, and the mean position in anomaly was 64 degrees and 38 minutes from the apogee of the epicycle. The interval between these two eclipses contains 854 Egyptian years <note>An Egyptian year is exactly 365 days, used by ancient astronomers for its simplicity in calculation</note>, 73 days, 23 hours, and a half of one hour according to "apparent time" <note>original: "tempore differente"—time as measured by a sundial</note>; but according to "equal time" <note>original: "de equali"—mean solar time, which flows at a constant rate</note> it was 23 hours and one-third of an hour. In this period, beyond the completed full revolutions, the mean motion of the moon in longitude was 224 degrees and 46 minutes, and the mean motion in anomaly was 52 degrees and 24 minutes. 

But according to calculations for that same time, the mean motion in longitude beyond the full revolutions was 224 degrees and 46 minutes, while in anomaly it was 52 degrees and 51 minutes. Therefore, the motion in longitude according to calculation agrees with the motion in longitude according to observation. However, in anomaly they differ by 27 minutes. Therefore, these 27 minutes, divided by the days of the interval, show how much should be subtracted from the motion of anomaly for one day as previously tabulated, so that a corrected daily motion of anomaly may be obtained. 

¶ Following a similar path, Albategni <note>Albategni is the Latinized name of Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a famous Muslim astronomer who refined Ptolemy's measurements</note> in his own time found that the mean motion of anomaly set down by Ptolemy was greater than the mean motion of anomaly which he himself found through eclipses. He divided the difference by the number of days falling between Ptolemy’s observation and his own, and subtracted the result from the daily motion of anomaly given in Ptolemy’s tables. He found the motion of longitude to be the same as Ptolemy’s, except for what he added to it because of what he had added to the motion of the sun, for he had taken the time of that equal lunation.

### Proposition 13

**To establish the "roots" of the mean motion of the moon in longitude and anomaly for a given starting point from the eclipses.**

<margin>A secondary geometric diagram shows a circle with internal chords and a triangle. This represents the calculation of "radices" or roots—the specific starting coordinates of a planet at a fixed moment in history, such as the beginning of a king's reign.</margin>

¶ Just as Ptolemy, wishing to fix these roots <term>roots: also called 'radices,' these are the base positions of celestial bodies at a specific epoch or starting date</term> to the beginning of the years of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabucho donosaris"—Ptolemy used the Era of Nabonassar (747 BC), though the text here uses a Latin form of Nebuchadnezzar</note>, he considered the interval between this beginning and the middle of the second eclipse of the three ancient eclipses: namely, that which occurred in the second year of Mardokempad <note>original: "Mardochei"—this refers to the Babylonian king Mardok-empad</note> when 18 days of the Egyptian month of Thoth had passed, half an hour and a third of an hour before midnight. The interval was 27 Egyptian years, 17 days, 11 hours and one-sixth of an hour, in both apparent and mean time. In this mean time, the mean motion of the moon in longitude according to calculation is 123 degrees and 22 minutes, and in anomaly it is 103 degrees and 35 minutes. When these are subtracted from the position of the mean motion of the moon in longitude and anomaly at the hour of the second eclipse, they leave the mean "roots" of the moon for the beginning of the years of Nabonassar: in longitude, 11 degrees and 22 minutes of Taurus, and in anomaly, 268 degrees and 49 minutes. Therefore, the mean distance between the sun and the moon then was 70 degrees and 37 minutes, as is held from the root of the mean motion of the sun in the 21st proposition of the third book of this work.

# Book Four

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram at the top left representing an eccentric lunar orbit. It features a center point 'k' and an offset "center of the world" 'd'. A horizontal diameter 'p-q' and vertical 'l-m' are shown. Points 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'g' on the circumference indicate the moon's positions, connected by lines to points 'd', 'e', and 'h' to illustrate trigonometric relationships and the calculation of eccentricity.</image-desc>

¶ A position was established in the seventh proposition of this book, and also expressed in the eighth: that the motion of the moon in the eccentric would be according to the proportion of the motion of the moon in the epicycle. In such a way, however, that the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the center; here called 'aux'</term> of the eccentric would move in [zodiacal] succession according to the proportion of the amount by which the mean motion of the moon in longitude exceeds its mean motion in diversity <term>diversity: a term used by ancient astronomers for 'anomaly,' or the motion of the moon along its smaller epicycle</term>. Let this now be our position. We wish to find the eccentricity of the moon through the three ancient eclipses which were mentioned in the ninth proposition. Therefore, let the eccentric of the moon be **b.a.g.e.** upon its center **k**, in which **d** is the center of the world. We seek the distance **k.d.**

Let the position of the moon in the eccentric during the first eclipse be **a**, in the second **b**, and in the third **g**. Lines are drawn from **b**, **d**, and **e** to **g**, **d**, **a**, **g**, and **g**, **e**, with perpendiculars **e.z** falling upon **a.d**, **e.h** upon **g.d**, and **g.t** upon **a.e**. Since in the first interval the true motion according to longitude <note>original: "verus motus sm longitudine"</note> is 349 degrees and 15 minutes, while the mean motion is 345 degrees and 51 minutes, and the mean motion in diversity is 306 degrees and 25 minutes. In the second interval, however, the true motion in longitude is 169 degrees and 30 minutes, the mean is 170 degrees and 7 minutes, and the mean in diversity is 150 degrees and 26 minutes. Therefore, the motion of the apogee of the eccentric in the first interval was 39 degrees and 26 minutes—namely, the excess of the mean motion in longitude over the mean motion in diversity.

But in the second interval, it was 19 degrees and 41 minutes. And so the "diverse motion" <note>the motion relative to the eccentric center</note> in the eccentric during the first interval was 309 degrees and 49 minutes. For the true motion of the moon in longitude, according to our position, exceeds the diverse motion in the eccentric by as much as the mean motion of longitude exceeds the mean motion of diversity, as is clear from the figure of the seventh proposition of this book. And the diverse motion in the eccentric in the second interval was 149 degrees and 49 minutes, by similar reasoning. Therefore, the arc **a.b.g** is 308 degrees and 25 minutes. But the arc of diverse motion corresponding to it—namely **q.s.p** of the eccentric above **d**—will be 306 degrees and 49 minutes. Therefore, the remainder of the circle is 50 degrees and 11 minutes, which is the angle **b.d.a**. Likewise, the arc **b.a.g** is 150 degrees and 26 minutes. But the arc of diverse motion corresponding to it will be 149 degrees and 49 minutes, which is the angle **b.d.g**. Now the process is similar to that which was stated in the 14th proposition of the third book of this work. From the known angle **b.d.a**, the proportion of **d.e** to **e.z** will be known. Likewise, from arc **b.a** and its angle **a.e.b**, and the external angle **b.d.a**, the proportion of **a.e** to **e.z** will be known. But since the proportion of **d.e** to **e.z** was already known, the proportion of **a.e** to **e.d** will now be known. Likewise, from the known angle **b.d.g**, the proportion of **d.e** to **e.h** will be known. But from arc **b.g** and its angle **g.e.b** and the external angle **b.d.g**, the proportion of **g.e** to **e.h** will be known. Since **d.e** to **e.h** was already known, the proportion of **g.e** to **e.d** will be known; wherefore the ratio of **g.e** to **a.e** will be given. ¶ Furthermore,

<image-desc>A circular diagram at the bottom left, similar to the first, detailing the geometric constructions for the lunar eclipses. It shows various chords and internal lines labeled with letters such as 'a', 'b', 'g', 'e', 't', 'v', 'n', and 'm'. A specific perpendicular line 'e-n' is shown meeting the line 'b-d'. from arc **a.g** and its angle **g.e.a**, the proportion of **e.g** to **g.t** will be known, and also to **t.e**, and therefore to the remainder **t.a**. Hence, from the known **g.t** and **t.a**, the proportion of **e.g** to **g.a** will be known. Thus triangle **a.g.e** is known: one of its sides with respect to the known parts of **d.e**. But arc **a.g** is also known, because it is the excess of **b.g** over **b.a**; therefore, from the known chord **a.g**, the lengths of **d.e** and **a.e** (or **g.e**) will be expressed in the parts in which **k.m** is the known total sine <term>total sine: the radius of the reference circle used in trigonometric tables, often set to 60 or 100,000 units</term>. Therefore, the arc **a.g.e** is known, and likewise **b.a.e** is known; hence its chord **b.d.e**. And since its proportion to **d.e** in those same parts was already known, the remainder—namely **b.d**—will be known in those same units. But the product of **e.d** times **d.b** added to the square of **d.k** is equal to the square of **k.m** <note>This is a geometric theorem regarding the power of a point relative to a circle</note>. Therefore, the square of **k.d** will be known, and thus the proportion of **d.k** to **k.l** will be known, which was what we sought. If you then wish to find arc **l.b**, you will do so from the known sides of triangle **b.d.k**. For if a perpendicular is drawn upon **d.b**, **e.n** will be equal to **n.b**. Therefore, **d.n** is known. Thus from **k.d** and **d.n**, the angle **n.k.d** is recognized, and the remaining angle to the complement of a right angle, **n.d.k**, is known.

### Proposition xv.

**To rectify the quantity of the mean motion of the moon in latitude.**

¶ To achieve this, two lunar eclipses must be selected that meet specific conditions: first, that the amount of the diameter eclipsed is the same in both; second, that they occur at the same node <term>node: the two points where the moon's tilted orbit crosses the path of the sun (the ecliptic)</term>; third, that they occur on the same side, namely either both in the north or both in the south; and finally, that the moon is in nearly the same position on its epicycle. For in this way, the distance of the moon from the node will be the same in both instances, and they will have occurred within an interval of complete revolutions.

¶ Ptolemy selected two such eclipses. The first was in the 21st year of the reign of Darius I; after three days of the Egyptian month of Tybi had passed, on the morning of the fourth day, one hour and one-third before midnight in Alexandria. Two "digits" <term>digit: a measurement of an eclipse where the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 parts</term> of the moon were eclipsed on the southern side. The second was in the ninth year of Hadrian, on the 17th day of the Egyptian month of Mechir; on the morning of the 18th day, three hours and one-third and one-fifth <note>This equates to 3 hours and 32 minutes</note> before midnight in Alexandria. In this case, one-sixth of the diameter was also eclipsed on the southern side. Furthermore, both occurred near the descending node <note>original: "nodũ caude," literally 'node of the tail,' referring to the Dragon's Tail or descending node</note>, and in both, the moon was near the mean distances of its epicycle. This was determined through the tables of motion regarding "diversity" <term>diversity: another term for anomaly, or the moon's position on its smaller epicycle circle</term> already established, using the "root" <term>root: the starting value or 'epoch' for astronomical calculations</term> from the beginning of the era of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosaris"</note> and the time difference between the two eclipses.

The first eclipse occurred 256 Egyptian years, 122 days, and 10 hours and two-thirds of an hour (of apparent time) from the beginning of the era of Nebuchadnezzar; but in mean time, it was 10 hours and a quarter. The second was 871 Egyptian years, 256 days, 8 hours, and two-fifths of an hour (of apparent time) from the start of the era; but in mean time, it was 8 hours and one-half of a sixth of an hour <note>8 hours and 5 minutes</note>. Thus, in the first eclipse, the moon was 100 degrees and 19 minutes away from the apogee <term>apogee: the point in the orbit furthest from the center</term> of the epicycle. In the second, it was 251 degrees and 6 minutes away. Therefore, in the first, the true course was 5 degrees less than the mean; in the second, the true course was 4 degrees and 53 minutes more than the mean.

Consequently, in the interval between the two eclipses—which is 615 Egyptian years, 133 days, 21 hours, and 50 minutes—the true motion of the moon in latitude will consist of complete revolutions. However, the mean motion was one full revolution less than the true motion, combined with the sum of the two differences, namely 9 degrees and 53 minutes. But according to the calculations set down by Hipparchus <note>original: "Abrachis"</note> for the aforementioned interval, the mean motion in latitude was 10 degrees and 2 minutes less than the true motion. Therefore, the mean motion in latitude in this interval is actually 9 minutes greater than what Hipparchus assigned. When these 9 minutes are divided by the days of the interval—approximately 224,609 days—they show what must be added to the mean motion of latitude for a single day as established by Hipparchus, so that a rectified course may be produced.

### Proposition xvi.

**To investigate the distance of the moon from the node according to the mean and true course of latitude through eclipses; and to fix the root of the mean motion in latitude for a given starting point.**

¶ For this purpose, Ptolemy assumed two eclipses should be known. One of them is the one we mentioned as the second of the three ancient eclipses: namely, that which occurred in the second year of Mardokempad <note>original: "Mardochei," referring to the Babylonian king Mardok-empad</note>, after 18 days of the month of Thoth had passed, half an hour and one-third before midnight in Alexandria. In this eclipse, three digits were eclipsed on the southern side. It took place 27 Egyptian years, 17 days, 11 hours, and one-sixth of an hour from the beginning of the era of Nebuchadnezzar (the time being the same for both apparent and mean). The distance of the moon from the apogee of its epicycle was 12 degrees and 24 minutes, which was 59 minutes less than the mean course. He assumed another eclipse: which was in the 20th year of Darius, who reigned after Philip, on the 28th day of the Egyptian month of Thoth; on the morning of the 29th, before midnight...

This occurred 245 years, 327 days, 10 hours, and a half and a quarter <note>This equals 10 hours and 45 minutes</note> from the beginning of the years of Nabonassar <term>Nabonassar: an era beginning in 747 BCE used by ancient astronomers as a baseline for calculations</term> according to apparent time, but 10 hours and a quarter-hour according to mean time. Therefore, the interval between both eclipses was 218 years, 309 days, and nearly 23 hours and 12 minutes. In this time, the mean motion of latitude, according to calculation, has 160 degrees and 4 minutes beyond its complete revolutions.

Let the inclined circle of the moon be **a. b. g.** upon the diameter **a. g.** Let **a** be the Dragon’s Head <term>Dragon’s Head: the ascending node where the moon crosses the ecliptic moving north</term> and **g** be the Dragon’s Tail <term>Dragon’s Tail: the descending node where the moon crosses the ecliptic moving south</term>, and let **b** be the maximum declination of this inclined circle from the ecliptic. Let **d. z.** be the distance of the mean position of the moon from its true position in the first eclipse; and in the second, let it be **e. h.** Thus, arc **z. b.** will become 160 degrees and 4 minutes. But **z. d.** is 59 minutes; therefore, **h. d.** is 161 degrees and 3 minutes. However, **h. e.** is 13 minutes, which makes **d. e.** 160 degrees and 50 minutes. Therefore, the remainder of the semicircle was 19 degrees and 10 minutes, of which the half—**a. d.** or **g. e.**—was 9 degrees and 35 minutes, representing the true motion of the moon in latitude from the node. Therefore, **a. z.** was 10 degrees and 34 minutes, the distance of the moon from the node according to the mean motion of latitude in the first eclipse; and **b. g. a. z.** <note>The full arc from the northern point</note> was 280 degrees and 34 minutes, the distance of the moon in latitude according to uniform motion from the point of maximum northern latitude. From this and the interval from the beginning of the years of Nabonassar, the radix <term>radix: the "root" or foundational value for a specific point in time</term> of this motion was established. For the mean motion in latitude during the aforementioned interval—namely 27 Egyptian years, 17 days, 11 hours and a sixth—was 286 degrees and 19 minutes. If we subtract this from 280 degrees and 34 minutes, there remains 354 degrees and 15 minutes: the radix of the mean motion in latitude, counting from the northern point of maximum latitude at the beginning of the years of Nabonassar.

### Proposition xvii.

->To determine the quantity of the mean motion of the node against the succession of the signs.<-

**B**ecause the mean motion in longitude for one day is less than the mean motion of latitude for one day, it is necessary that this happens because of the motion of the node: namely, against the succession of the signs <note>original: "contra successionem signorum," meaning the nodes move in retrograde, or backwards through the zodiac</note>. Therefore, subtract the mean motion in longitude of one day from the mean motion in latitude of one day; the remainder will be the mean motion of the Dragon's Head for one day, which is always against the succession of the signs.

---

### Proposition xviii.

->To compose the table of the first diversity.<-

**T**his is always sufficient for equating the positions of the moon at the hour of true conjunction or opposition. It is composed with the same skill as that held in the 17th and 19th [propositions] of the third book of this [work] concerning the sun, following the path of the epicycle; except that here, the proportion of **d. a.** to **a. e.**—that is, the distance of the moon from the center of the earth to the center of the epicycle—is held to the line which is the semi-diameter, which is 60 to five parts and a quarter <note>A ratio of 60:5.25</note>.

### Proposition xix.

**T**hat the proportion of the semi-diameter of the epicycle to the line between the center of the earth and the center of the epicycle was found to be different from the proportion of the distance of the center of the eccentric from the center of the world to the semi-diameter of the eccentric happened due to an error in the calculation of Arzachel <note>original: "Abzachis," referring to the 11th-century Andalusian astronomer Arzachel</note>, and not from a diversity of these modes of the epicycle and eccentric.

### Book Four
c 4

For it has already been demonstrated in the eighth <note>original: "8."</note> chapter of this work that the same result follows from both methods. **Hipparchus** <note>original: "Abrachis"</note>, however, found that according to the method of the eccentric <term>eccentric: a model where the planet moves in a circle whose center is offset from the Earth</term>, the ratio of the radius of the eccentric to the distance between the centers was 3144 to 327 and one-third of a part—which is roughly the same as a ratio of 60 to 6 and one-fourth. But according to the method of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term>, he said he found the ratio of the line from the center of the world to the center of the epicycle at conjunction or opposition to the radius of the epicycle to be 3122 to 347 and a half—which is roughly the same as a ratio of 60 to 4 and 45 minutes.

A ratio of 60 to 6 and one-fourth produces an angle of maximum diversity <term>diversity: also known as the "equation" or "prosthaphairesis," the difference between the mean and true positions of a planet</term> of the true motion from the mean in eclipses of 5 degrees and 59 minutes. But the ratio of 60 to 4 and three-fourths produces an angle of 4 degrees and 34 minutes. However, the ratio which **Ptolemy** found—namely 60 to 5 and one-fourth—produces an angle of 5 degrees and 1 minute. Because of the varying ratios that Hipparchus found, he believed that the method of the epicycle gave a different diversity than the method of the eccentric. But since that is impossible, it follows that he must have erred in the calculation of the eclipses.

We shall therefore describe the three eclipses he used in his first method. The first was a small part of the moon eclipsed in the 365th year of **Nabonassar** <note>original: "Nabuchodonosaris"; here referring to the Era of Nabonassar starting in 747 BCE</note>, on the 25th day, at 18 hours and 30 minutes of apparent time <term>apparent time: time measured by the actual position of the sun, which varies slightly throughout the year</term>, but at 18 hours and 15 minutes of mean time <term>mean time: time measured at a constant rate, used for astronomical calculations</term> in Alexandria. In this eclipse, the sun was found by calculation to be at 28 degrees and 18 minutes of **Sagittarius**. The Moon, meanwhile, was at 28 degrees and 17 minutes of **Gemini**. But the mean motion of the moon at that time was at 24 degrees and 20 minutes of Gemini; the argument <term>argument: the position of the moon on its epicycle</term> of the moon was at 22 degrees and 43 minutes.

The second eclipse was in the 365th year of Nabonassar, on the 203rd day, at 8 hours and 15 minutes of apparent time, but 7 hours and 50 minutes of mean time. In this one, the sun was found by calculation to be at 21 degrees and 46 minutes of Gemini; the moon was at 21 degrees and 46 minutes of Sagittarius. But according to the mean motion, the moon was at 23 degrees and 55 minutes of Sagittarius; the argument of the moon was 27 degrees and 57 minutes.

The third eclipse was a universal one <note>A total eclipse covering the entire lunar disk</note> in the 366th year of Nabonassar, on the 15th day, at 10 hours and 10 minutes of apparent time, but 9 hours and 50 minutes of mean time. In this, the sun was found by calculation to be at 17 degrees and 29 minutes of Sagittarius; the moon was at 17 degrees and 29 minutes of Gemini. But according to the mean motion, the moon was in the 22nd degree and 28th minute of Gemini; the argument of the moon was 81 degrees and 12 minutes.

The first interval, therefore, was 177 days, 13 hours, and 35 minutes of mean time, and the true motion of the sun during it was 173 degrees and 28 minutes. The second interval was 177 days and 2 hours of mean time, and the true motion of the sun during it was 175 degrees and 43 minutes. Hipparchus, however, said the first interval was 177 days and 13 and three-quarters hours, and the true course of the sun in it was 172 degrees and 53 minutes. And he said the second interval was 177 days, 1 hour, and 40 minutes, and the true course of the sun in it was 175 degrees and 7 minutes. He therefore erred in the time of the interval by nearly a third of an hour, and in the sun’s course by nearly three-fifths of a degree.

He also used three other eclipses. The first was in the 546th year of Nabonassar, on the 345th day, at 7 hours of apparent time, but 6 minutes and 30 seconds of mean time <note>The text likely implies 6 hours and 30 minutes, or a very specific correction</note>. The sun, according to calculation, was at 26 degrees and 6 minutes of **Virgo**, and the moon was at 26 degrees and 7 minutes of **Pisces**. But according to the mean motion, the moon was in the 22nd degree of Pisces; the argument of the moon was 13 degrees and 13 minutes.

The second was a universal eclipse in the 547th year of Nabonassar, on the 158th day, at 13 hours and a third for both times <note>meaning apparent and mean time were calculated as equal</note>. The sun, according to calculation, was at 26 degrees and 17 minutes of Pisces; the moon was at 26 degrees and 17 minutes of Virgo. But the mean motion of the moon was at 1 degree and 7 minutes of **Libra**; the argument of the moon was 109 degrees and 24 minutes.

The third was also a universal eclipse in the 547th year of Nabonassar, on the 334th day, at 14 hours and a quarter of apparent time, but 13 hours and three-quarters of mean time. The sun, by calculation, was at 15 degrees and 12 minutes of Virgo; the moon was at 15 degrees and 13 minutes of Pisces. But the mean motion of the moon was at 10 degrees and 24 minutes of Pisces; the argument of the moon was 249 degrees and 9 minutes.

The first interval, therefore, was 178 days, 6 hours, and 50 minutes of mean time, and the true motion of the sun in this was 180 degrees and 11 minutes. The second was 176 days, 0 hours, and 25 minutes of mean time; the true course of the sun in it was 168 degrees and 55 minutes. Hipparchus, however, said the first interval was 178 days and 6 hours, and the true course of the sun in it was 180 degrees and 11 minutes.

# Book Five proceeds with the investigation of the motion of the Moon in both longitude and latitude using several astronomical instruments: and most clearly declares its varying relation in its different parts to the sun and earth, etc., with the parallax <note>original: "diversitate aspectus," literally "diversity of aspect," the standard medieval term for parallax</note>.

## First Proposition.

<image-desc>Large woodcut initial 'I' decorated with floral and leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>
To construct an armillary instrument <term>armillary instrument: a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings, centered on Earth, representing lines of celestial longitude and latitude</term>.
Two rings, fittingly made and of the same size with smooth surfaces: let them first be joined to one another in such a way that one takes the place of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the sun's apparent path across the sky</term> and the other the place of the solstitial colure <term>solstitial colure: one of the two great circles that intersect at the celestial poles, passing through the solstices</term>. In the poles of the ecliptic—namely, on the colure—let two small round pins of equal size be fixed, so that they project both outward and inward. To these we shall add two other rings. One indeed fixed on the inside, so that it may be turned on the aforementioned pins above the poles of the zodiac: so that with an easy motion its outer surface touches the inner surface of the ecliptic. The other fixed to the same pins on the outside, so that it can be turned on the same poles of the ecliptic with an easy motion on the aforementioned pins, touching the outer surface of the ecliptic with its inner surface. Now the ring that takes the place of the ecliptic should have divisions of 360 degrees, and of hours as far as can be done through subdivisions. Similarly, the ring which is fixed to the pins on the inside—which takes the place of the circle of latitude of the moon or stars—should have 360 <note>The OCR reads "306," but a circle requires 360 degrees.</note> divisions of degrees. To this inner ring, which is for latitudes, we will adapt another ring which can move within it, and it should have two sighting vanes <term>pinnulae: small plates with holes used to align the instrument with a star or planet</term> diametrically opposite each other. But it will come to the same thing if you fit a ruler <note>original: "regula"</note> with sighting vanes to the center of this inner ring, along with a fiducial line <term>fiducial line: a precise line used as a fixed standard of reference for measurement</term> as is done on an astrolabe; for it can take the place of the ring. This is done for the purpose of taking the latitudes of the moon and stars. Furthermore, on the ring which takes the place of the solstitial colure, according to the amount of the maximum declination <note>This refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis, or the obliquity of the ecliptic.</note>, you will take points from the poles of the ecliptic where the axes of the poles of the world are to be fixed, so that this entire instrument can be turned upon them. Finally, a base is to be prepared for it, which should be a ring: square on the outside but an immovable circle on the inside, having the pins of the poles of the world fixed into it, so that the whole instrument can be turned on them according to the motion of the "first mobile" <term>primum mobile: in the geocentric model, the outermost sphere that carries all other spheres in a daily rotation around the Earth</term>, having the poles elevated according to the latitude of the region in which you are located.

### Proposition 2.

->To find the position of a star in longitude and latitude with the help of this instrument.<-

<image-desc>A marginal diagram consisting of a larger circle representing an orbit (the deferent) with a smaller circle (an epicycle) centered on its circumference. A radial line extends from the center of the larger circle through the center of the smaller circle.</image-desc>

To find the position of a star in longitude and latitude with the help of this instrument. 
Having situated the instrument in your region as is required—so that the fixed ring <term>fixed ring: the "armilla immobilis," representing the local meridian</term> fulfills the role of its meridian, and the poles of the instrument correspond to the poles of the world—observe when you see both the sun and the moon above the earth, and you wish to know the position of the moon in longitude and latitude by means of the sun's known position. Place the outer rotating ring on the poles of the zodiac <term>poles of the zodiac: the two points around which the ecliptic or zodiac path rotates</term> over the known position of the sun on the ecliptic. Turn it, fixed in its place, with the whole instrument toward the sun until both rings shade each other; specifically, the ecliptic ring and the outer ring passing over the position of the sun. In this way, the position of the ecliptic on the instrument will correspond to the position of the ecliptic in the heavens. 

Then, with the instrument fixed, quickly turn the inner ring (which is divided into parts) with its ruler—or the ring that moves within it—toward the moon until you see the moon in the sky through the sight-holes or the edges of the sight vanes <term>sight vanes: small plates with holes or slits used to align the instrument with a celestial body</term>. At the same time, ensure the ecliptic and the outer ring shade each other. Then, the intersection of the inner ring with the ecliptic ring will show the moon's position in longitude, and the arc of the inner ring between the ecliptic and the ruler of the sight vanes will show the latitude of the moon from the ecliptic. In a similar way, through a known position of the moon, you may verify the positions of other stars in longitude and latitude. Take note, however, that in the case of the moon, this observation can fail because of its parallax <note>original: "diversitatem aspectus," literally "diversity of aspect," the medieval term for the shift in apparent position depending on the observer's location</note>, as will be made clear.

### Proposition 3.

->To declare by what indications the second variation of the moon was discovered.<-

<image-desc>A marginal diagram showing a large circle with a central point. Four lines intersect at the center, dividing the circle into quadrants. Small circles are placed at the four cardinal points of the large circle, representing the positions of a celestial body (likely the moon) at conjunction, opposition, and quadratures.</image-desc>

Ptolemy frequently verified the position of the moon using the armillary instrument. To exclude the effect of parallax, he observed it when it was in the middle of the sky <note>The meridian, where parallax has the least effect on longitude</note>. He found that the position of the moon found through observation was sometimes in agreement with the position given by calculations from the models described earlier, and sometimes in disagreement. Sometimes the difference was small, and sometimes it was great. However, the closer the observation was to conjunction <note>New Moon</note> or opposition <note>Full Moon</note>, the smaller the difference was. The closer it was to quadrature <note>the quarter moons, when the moon is 90 degrees from the sun</note>, the greater the difference. 

Furthermore, no difference was found while it was at the apogee <term>apogee: the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth; "auge" in the original Latin</term> of the epicycle or at the opposite point of the apogee <note>perigee</note>. But he discovered the greatest difference when the moon was a quarter distance from the apogee of the epicycle while in quadrature with the sun. And then, if the variation needed to be subtracted, he found the position of the moon through observation to be more diminished than the calculation gave. If it needed to be added, he found it more increased than the calculation required. From these things it was clear: that the moon, besides its first variation, also had a second variation. And that this maximum can occur in its quadratures to the sun, but is nothing in conjunctions or oppositions. Thus, twice in a lunar month, this second variation <term>second variation: known in modern astronomy as evection, a major perturbation in the moon's orbit</term> is completed.

### Proposition 4.

->To provide the cause of this second variation.<-

Therefore, since in the quadratures of the moon to the sun the greatest variation of the moon's true motion from its mean motion is greater than the greatest variation found through calculation, it is necessary that the center of the moon's epicycle in the quadratures be closer to the center of the world...

on the days when it is in conjunction or opposition. Because of its approach to the earth, it happens that the angles of the **first diversity** <term>first diversity: also known as the "equation of center," this is the variation in the Moon's speed caused by its motion on a simple epicycle</term> are found to be larger. It is necessary, therefore, for the center of the orbit to approach and recede from the center of the earth, so that in a lunar month it reaches its maximum approach twice and its maximum distance from the center of the world twice. Indeed, the maximum approach occurs in both **quadratures** <term>quadratures: the points where the Moon is 90 degrees away from the Sun, such as the first and third quarters</term>, and the maximum distance occurs in conjunctions and oppositions. This happens if the center of the eccentric orbit moves around the center of the world in a direction contrary to the succession of the signs <note>original: "contrarium successionis," meaning a retrograde motion</note>: so that while the center of the moon's epicycle makes one revolution according to the succession of the signs—returning to the line of the sun's mean motion—the center of the eccentric also makes one revolution against the succession, also returning to the line of the sun's mean motion. For when this motion is added to the previous motions we mentioned—namely, the motion of the center of the epicycle in longitude, the mean motion in latitude, and the motion in the diversity of the epicycle—the appearance mentioned above concerning the first diversity will remain, and the circumstances already described regarding the **second diversity** <term>second diversity: known today as evection, a major inequality in the Moon's orbit discovered by Ptolemy</term> will occur.

As shown in the figure: let us imagine a circle on the surface of the sloping orbit <note>original: "orbis decliuis," the inclined plane of the Moon's path</note>, whose center is the center of the world at **e**, with a radius **a.e.**. For the sake of example, let the **apogee** <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the center; here the Latin uses "aux"</term> of the eccentric, the center of the epicycle, and the point of the sloping circle most declined toward the north—which is the mean position of the sun and the beginning of Aries—all be together upon the line **e.l.**, so that we understand three mobile lines, namely **e.a.**, **e.b.**, and **e.c.d.**, to lie upon the line **e.l.** as if it were immobile. I say that in one day, the said point of the sloping circle most declined will move according to the motion of the **ascending node** <note>original: "nodi capitis," the "Head of the Dragon" where the Moon crosses the ecliptic</note> against the succession of the signs by nearly three minutes, until it is at 29 degrees and 57 minutes of Pisces; this is designated by the motion of the moon **e.a.** separated from the immobile **e.l.**. And the center of the epicycle will move on that same day according to the succession by 13 degrees and 11 minutes of Aries, the motion of which is designated by the motion of the moon **e.b.** separated from **e**. Thus, the motion in latitude on that day will become the arc **b.a.**, composed of the motion of longitude with the succession and the motion of the node against it, totaling 13 degrees and 14 minutes. And the apogee of the eccentric will move against the succession by the amount of the remainder of the **double mean longitude** between the sun and the moon: that is, 11 degrees and 12 minutes, namely through the arc **l.d.**. Thus, the whole arc **b.a.d.** is 24 degrees and 23 minutes, which is the sum of arc **b.a.** (the motion of latitude) and arc **a.d.** (the motion of the eccentric's apogee against the succession). And let that sum—namely the motion of the eccentric's epicycle from the eccentric's apogee—be equal to the double mean longitude <note>original: "duplo longitudinis medie"</note> between the sun and the moon; for this reason, it is called the **double longitude**. Thus, the line of the sun's mean motion is always in the middle between the center of the moon's epicycle and the apogee of the eccentric, provided the center of the epicycle is not at the apogee of the eccentric. From this it happens that in the middle quadratures, the lines **b.e.** and **e.d.** are opposite each other. Therefore, the moon is then at the opposite of the eccentric's apogee, and it will always return to the eccentric's apogee in every mean conjunction or opposition. It is clear, therefore, that from this the appearance arises which agrees with this discovered second diversity. For when the center of the epicycle is in conjunction with the sun or in opposition to it, no such second diversity occurs, but everything happens according to the first diversity.
