**To reveal how great the maximum second diversity is.**
In the observation of this matter, three things are necessary: namely, that the Moon be in **mean quadrature** <term>mean quadrature: the point where the Moon is exactly 90 degrees away from the Sun’s average position</term> with the Sun. For at that time, the center of its epicycle is at the opposite point of the eccentric's highest point <note>original: "augis," referring to the apogee</note>. Second, that it be distant from the apogee of its own epicycle by about a quarter of a circle [90 degrees], because then the largest possible angle of diversity occurs between the mean and true place of the Moon. And third, that it be a quarter [90 degrees] from the **ascending degree** <term>ascending degree: the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> or near it; for then there is no **parallax** <term>parallax: the apparent shift in position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth</term> <note>original: "diuersitas aspectus"</note> in longitude which could hinder us. In this way, its true place grasped through observation would differ from its mean place (found through true calculation) by the maximum angle of diversity being sought.

Accordingly, Ptolemy observed the place of the Moon in the second year of the reign of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor</note>, on the 25th day of the month of Phamenoth <note>the seventh month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, at five and a quarter hours before noon. The Sun was seen through observation at 18 degrees, one half, and one third of Aquarius [18° 50' Aquarius]. The **Midheaven** <term>Midheaven: the point of the zodiac that is highest in the sky at a given moment</term> at the hour of observation was 4 degrees of Sagittarius. The Moon was seen at 9 degrees and two-thirds of Scorpio [9° 40' Scorpio], and that was its true place, because at that time there was no parallax in longitude for it. Indeed, the distance of the Moon from the meridian of Alexandria was about one and a half hours.

The time from the beginning of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosoris," referring to the Nabonassar era used by ancient astronomers</note> until this observation was 885 years, 203 days, and 18 and three-quarters hours. For this time, the Sun was found according to its mean course to be at 16 degrees and 27 minutes of Aquarius, but according to its true course at 18 degrees and 50 minutes, which agrees with the observation made by instrument. The Moon, however, was found by its mean motion in longitude to be at 17 degrees and 20 minutes of Scorpio. Its mean elongation <term>elongation: the angular distance between two celestial bodies as seen from Earth</term> from the Sun was about a quarter of a circle [90 degrees], and its distance from the apogee of the epicycle was 87 degrees and 19 minutes, which usually produces the maximum angle of diversity. Thus, the true course of the Moon found through observation was less than the mean course found by calculation by 7 degrees and two-thirds [7° 40'], instead of the 5 degrees which constitutes the angle of the **first diversity**.

Likewise, Hipparchus <note>original: "Abhachis," a medieval corruption of the name Hipparchus</note>, in the 50th year of the third revolution of the years of Philip <note>Philip Arrhidaeus</note>, on the 16th day of the month of Achit <note>likely Epiphi</note>—namely 619 Egyptian years, 314 days, and 17 hours and five-sixths from the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar—saw the Sun by observation at 8 degrees, one half, and half of a sixth of Leo [8° 40' Leo]. He saw the Moon at 12 degrees and one third of Taurus [12° 20' Taurus] without sensible parallax. The distance between the Moon and the Sun was therefore 86 degrees and 15 minutes. By Ptolemy's calculation, the Sun is found by its mean course to have been at 10 degrees and 27 minutes of Leo, and by its true course at 8 degrees and 20 minutes. The Moon, in longitude according to its mean motion, was at 4 degrees and 25 minutes of Taurus. Thus, the mean distance between the Sun and Moon was about a quarter of a circle, and the distance from the apogee of the epicycle was 257 degrees and 47 minutes. At this point also, the maximum angle of diversity between the mean and true motion nearly occurs. So the distance between the true place of the Sun and the mean place of the Moon is 93 degrees and 55 minutes, while between the true places of both it is 86 degrees and 15 minutes. Therefore, the place of the Moon according to observation adds to its mean place (found by calculation) 7 degrees and two-thirds, instead of the 5 degrees which are the angle of the first diversity. Since, therefore, Ptolemy's observation decreased the first diversity by 2 degrees and two-thirds, and this observation...

### Proposition 6

<image-desc>A circular diagram illustrating a lunar astronomical model. A large circle (the eccentric) contains a vertical diameter with points labeled 'a' at the top, 'd', 'e', and 'g'. **To determine the distance of the center of the Moon’s eccentric from the center of the Earth.**
¶ Let the center of the epicycle be at the perigee <note>original: "longitudine propiori," the point on the orbit closest to Earth</note> of the eccentric. Let **g** be the center of the eccentric, **d** the center of the world <note>the Earth</note>, and **e** the observer's position. Let the line **e-f** be tangent to the epicycle **h-b-z**. Having drawn the line **f-g**, we seek the quantity of **d-e**. Since the angle **f-e-g** has already been found to be 7 degrees and 40 minutes, and the angle **f-g-e** is a right angle, the proportion of **f-g** to **g-e** is therefore known. But already from the second proposition of the fourth book, the ratio of **f-g** to **e-a** was known; therefore, the ratio of **g-e** to **e-a** will be known. Ptolemy found **g-e** to be 39 parts and 22 minutes, where **e-a** is 60 parts. Therefore, the total **a-g** is 99 parts and 22 minutes. Its half, which is **d-a**, becomes 49 parts and 41 minutes. Thus, **d-e** was 10 parts and 19 minutes, where **e-a** is 60, which is what was sought.

### Proposition 7

**Given the elongation of the center of the epicycle from the apogee, to find the maximum angle of diversity of the true motion from the mean motion that occurs at that point.**

Therefore, because the angle **a-e-b** is known, the proportion of **d-e** to **e-p** and **p-d** will be known from **d-b**. Thus, with **d-p** known, **b-p** becomes known, and from this, the whole length **b-e**. Thus, from the known values of **e-b** and **b-f**, the angle **b-e-f** which was sought will be determined.

# Book Five

It was shown to him by the significance of the matter that the diameter of the epicycle passing through the mean apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> of the epicycle and its opposite does not always look directly toward the center of the world <note>the Earth</note>, but toward another point opposite to it. To prove how great the distance of that opposite point was from the center of the Earth, he took two observations of Hipparchus <note>original: "Abrachis"</note> for this purpose. 

In the first of these, the Moon was near the sextile aspect <term>sextile: an angular distance of 60 degrees</term> of the Sun and near the opposite of its epicycle's apogee. The observation was made in Rhodes in the year 197 after the death of Alexander, on the 11th day of the eighth Egyptian month, Pharmuthi <note>original: "formiche"</note>. At the beginning of the second seasonal hour of the day, he saw the Sun at 7 and one-half and one-quarter degrees of Taurus <note>7° 45' Taurus</note>. He saw the Moon at 21 degrees and two-thirds of Pisces by appearance; but with the difference of aspect <term>difference of aspect: parallax, the displacement in apparent position when viewed from different points</term> removed, it was at 21 degrees and one-third and one-eighth of one degree of Pisces <note>21° 27' 30" Pisces</note>. Therefore, the distance from the true Sun to the true Moon was approximately 313 degrees and 42 minutes. 

The beginning of the second seasonal hour was 5 and two-thirds equal hours <term>equal hours: hours of 60 minutes, as opposed to seasonal hours which varied in length</term> distant from noon. Therefore, from the beginning of the era of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabuchodo."</note> to the hour of this consideration, there were 620 Egyptian years, 219 days, and 18 and one-third hours of solar time, but only 18 mean hours. According to this calculation, the mean course of the Sun was 6 degrees and 41 minutes of Taurus; the true Sun was at 7 degrees and 45 minutes. The mean Moon was at 22 degrees and 13 minutes of Pisces, and its elongation <term>elongation: the angular distance between two celestial bodies</term> from the mean apogee of the epicycle was 185 degrees and 30 minutes. The distance of the mean place of the Moon from the true Sun was 314 degrees and 28 minutes. 

Let, therefore, the eccentric of the Moon be **a-b-g** on center **d** and diameter **a-d-g**. Let the center of the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note> be **e**. Let the epicycle be **z-h-t** on center **b**. Because the mean distance between the Sun and Moon is 315 degrees and 32 minutes, doubled it makes 271 degrees and 4 minutes, which is the distance of the center of the epicycle from the apogee in the order of the signs. Therefore, the angle **a-e-b** was 88 degrees and 16 minutes <note>original: "76 m̄," likely a transcription error for 16</note>. Let **d-k** be perpendicular to **e-b**. Because the angle **d-e-k** is known, the proportion of **d-e** to **d-k** and **k-e** will be known. Therefore, in the parts where **e-d** is 10 parts and 19 minutes, **d-k** and **k-e** become known. 

But in those same parts, the semi-diameter of the eccentric **t-b** was already known to be 49 parts and 41 minutes; therefore **b-k** will be known, and from this **b-e**. And because the elongation of the mean place of the Moon from the true Sun was 314 degrees and 28 minutes, but the elongation by observation of the true place of the Moon from the true Sun was 313 degrees and 42 minutes, their difference is 46 minutes, by which the mean elongation is greater. But **e-b** is the line of the mean place of the Moon; therefore let angle **b-e-h** be 46 minutes. Thus the observed place of the Moon will be at **h**, near the opposite apogee of the epicycle **t**, since its elongation from the mean apogee of the epicycle is 185 degrees and 30 minutes. Let **b-l** be perpendicular upon **e-h**, and having drawn **b-h**, because angle **b-e-l** is known, the proportion of **e-b** to **b-l** will be known. But the proportion of **e-b** to the semi-diameter of the epicycle was already known; while the semi-diameter is 5 parts and 15 minutes, the proportion of **b-h** to **b-l** will thus be known. Therefore angle **b-h-l** is known, and consequently the remaining interior angle **t-b-h** is given, the quantity of which is the arc **t-h**, found to be 6 degrees and 21 minutes; this is the distance of the Moon from the true opposite apogee of the epicycle. 

But because its distance from the mean apogee of the epicycle was 185 degrees and 30 minutes, it is necessary that the Moon be 5 degrees and 30 minutes beyond the mean opposite apogee. Therefore, let the mean opposite apogee of the epicycle be point **m**, and let the perpendicular **e-s** be drawn to **b-m-n**. Thus angle **e-b-s** will be 11 degrees and 51 minutes; therefore the proportion of **b-e** to **e-s** is known. From the exterior angle **a-e-b**, the remaining interior angle **e-n-b** will be known, from which the proportion of **n-e** to **e-s** will be known. Therefore the proportion of **b-e** to **e-n** will be given. Thus **e-n** is found to be 10 parts and 18 minutes, where **e-a** is 60. In those same units, **d-e** was 10 parts and 19 minutes. Wherefore it is established that the point which the epicycle's diameter (passing through the mean apogee and its opposite) looks toward is as far from the center of the Earth as the center of the eccentric is from the same.

The second consideration of Hipparchus was in the same year: namely 197 from the death of Alexander, in Rhodes, on the 17th day of the month Payni <note>original: "Leguz"</note>, the tenth month of the Egyptians, after 9 and one-third hours of the day had passed. He saw the Sun at 11 degrees of Cancer minus 1/10th of a degree, and the Moon at 29 degrees of Leo without any difference in aspect <note>parallax</note>. Therefore, the distance of the observed place of the Moon from the true Sun was 48 degrees and 6 minutes. Those 9 and one-third seasonal hours were 4 equal hours after noon. The interval from the beginning of Nabonassar was therefore 620 Egyptian years, 286 days, and 4 hours of solar time, but 3 and two-thirds mean hours. By this, the mean course of the Sun is calculated at 12 degrees and 5 minutes of Cancer; the true Sun at 10 degrees and 40 minutes. The mean place of the Moon at 27 degrees and 20 minutes of Leo. Therefore, the distance of the mean Moon from the true Sun was 46 degrees and 40 minutes...

...of the moon from the mean apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion</term> of the epicycle was 333 degrees, 15 minutes. ¶ Therefore, according to these values, let the eccentric <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth</term> of the moon $a, b, g$ be described upon center $d$ and diameter $a-d-g$, in which the center of the earth is $e$, and the epicycle $z, h, t$ is upon center $b$, with lines $d-b$ and $e-t-b-z$ drawn. The remaining angle from two right angles <note>meaning the supplementary angle to reach 180 degrees</note>, namely $d-e-k$, will then be known. From this, the proportions of $e-d$ to the lines $d-k$ and $k-e$ will become known. Therefore, in the units where $d-e$ <note>the eccentricity</note> is 10 parts and 19 minutes, those lines themselves will become known; and in those same units, the semi-diameter of the eccentric $d-b$ was already 49 parts and 41 minutes. From these, $b-e$ will become known. And because the distance of the true place of the moon from the true sun by observation was 48 degrees, 6 minutes, but the distance of the mean place of the moon from the true sun by calculation was 46 parts, 40 minutes, the true motion is therefore greater than the mean by 1 degree, 26 minutes. But the line $e-b$ represents the mean motion; therefore, let the angle $b-e-h$ be 1 degree, 26 minutes. Point $h$ will be the location of the moon on the epicycle near the apogee of the epicycle. With $b-h$ and the line $b-l$ drawn perpendicular to $e-h$, the proportion of $e-b$ to $b-l$ will be known; but the proportion of $e-b$ to $b-h$ was also known. Wherefore, the proportion of $b-h$ to $b-l$ is known, and thus angle $b-h-l$ is known. But the external angle $z-b-h$ is equal to the two angles $b-h-l$ and $b-l-e$, and is therefore known. Thus, the arc $z-h$, which is the distance of the moon from the true apogee of the epicycle, is known, and it was 14 degrees, 43 minutes. But the distance of the moon from the mean apogee of the epicycle was 26 degrees, 48 minutes according to the motion in the epicycle <note>that is, the remainder beyond 333 degrees, 12 minutes</note>. Therefore, let $m$ be the mean apogee of the epicycle; $m-z$, the distance of the mean apogee from the true one, will be 12 degrees, 5 minutes. Furthermore, with $e-s$ drawn perpendicular to $b-n$, from the known angle $e-b-s$, the proportion of $b-e$ to $e-s$ will become known. Likewise, from angle $e-b-s$, by the exterior angle $a-e-b$, the other interior angle $e-n-s$ will be known; wherefore the proportion of $n-e$ to $e-s$ will become known. Therefore, the proportion of $b-e$ to $e-n$ is given, and thus $e-n$ is found to be 10 parts, 20 minutes, in units where $e-a$ is 60. Wherefore it is truly shown that the center of the world <note>the Earth</note> lies exactly midway between the center of the eccentric and the point which the diameter of the epicycle—passing through the farther and nearer distances of the epicycle—looks toward.

# Proposition IX.

Given the elongation <term>elongation: the angular distance between two celestial bodies</term> of the center of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric: to find how great the arc of the epicycle is between both of its apogees.
¶ In the preceding figure, let the angle $a-e-b$ be given. From this, we seek the arc of the epicycle $m-z$. With $d-k$ and $n-s$ drawn perpendicular to $e-b$, because the angle is given, the angle $d-e-k$ will be known. Therefore, the proportion of $d-e$ to $e-k$ and $k-d$ is known. Thus, from $b$ and $d-k$, $b-k$ will be known, from which $k-s$ (which is double $k-e$) is subtracted, and $b-s$ will be known. But $s-n$ is equal to $d-k$; therefore from $b-s$ and $s-n$, $b-n$ will become known. And thus the angle $n-b-s$ is known, which is opposite the sought arc $m-z$. In this way, the equation of the center in the moon <term>equation of the center: a correction to account for the non-circularity or non-uniformity of an orbit</term> is made by adding to the mean argument <term>argument: the angle used as the input for astronomical tables</term> when the center of the epicycle is in the half of the eccentric $a-b-g$, or by subtracting from it in the other half; from this arises the distance of the moon from the true apogee of the epicycle, which is called the "true argument."

# Proposition X.

Given the mean motions of the moon in longitude and diversity <note>original: "diuersitate," likely referring to anomaly</note> and its mean distance from the sun: to demonstrate its true place.
¶ In the figure, let the place of the moon $e-b$ be given. Let the doubled mean distance of the moon from the sun be the given angle $a-e-b$. Likewise, let the arc of the epicycle $m-h$ be given. From these, we seek the place shown by line $e-h$. By the preceding proof, line $e-b$ will be known in the parts where $b-h$ is given. Likewise, arc $m-z$ is known, wherefore arc $z-h$ will be known. Therefore, the proportion of $b-h$ to $b-l$ is given, as well as $b-h$ and $l-b$; wherefore $e-l$ will become known, from which and $l-b$, $e-h$ will be recognized. Hence, angle $h-e-l$ is found, and thus the place shown by $e-h$ will be given. From this is derived how the equations of the true arguments are made for the apogee of the eccentric and its opposite; however, by taking $e-a$ and $e-g$ in place of $e-b$, these can be made for any position of the center of the epicycle in the eccentric.

# Proposition 11.
## To complete the tables of lunar equations.

From the 9th proposition of this book, you will have the prescribed equations of the center <note>The "equation of the center" is the correction required due to the orbit being an eccentric circle rather than centered exactly on the Earth</note>. Therefore, seek the equations of the argument <term>argument: the position of a planet or the moon within its epicycle</term> of the moon in mean conjunction or opposition with the sun. From the same, find the equations of the argument of the moon when the center of the epicycle is located at the opposite of the apogee <term>apogee: the point in the orbit furthest from the Earth; its "opposite" is the perigee, the closest point</term> of the eccentric. However, the proportion of the moon from the center of the earth to the center of the epicycle, compared to the line which is the semi-diameter of the epicycle, should now be as 60 to 8. From this, the diversity <note>original: *diuersitas*; here referring to the variation in the apparent size or motion</note> of the small circle of the diameter is known. It remains only to calculate the proportional minutes, which are done as follows. <margin>41</margin> You are assisted by the 7th proposition of this book to find the maximum equation of the argument through individual degrees of the center (or of the double distance) to the semicircle. Then, establish the difference between those values that occur at the apogee and at the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric as 60 minutes. According to this proportion, you should calculate the remaining differences—specifically those occurring between the apogee of the eccentric and other locations—and the work is done. <margin>Note</margin> For example, let the double distance be 120 degrees. This corresponds to 43 parts and 43 minutes, according to the quantity where the semi-diameter of the eccentric is 49 parts and 41 minutes. Therefore, the angle $b-e-m$ of maximum diversity at that time is 6 degrees and 54 minutes. But the maximum diversity at the apogee of the eccentric was 5 degrees and 1 minute, and at the opposite of the apogee it was 7 degrees and 40 minutes. The difference, therefore, between the value at the apogee and the value at the opposite of the apogee is 2 degrees and 39 minutes. But the difference between the value at the apogee and the value at a distance of 120 degrees from the apogee is 1 degree and 53 minutes. When, therefore, 2 degrees and 39 minutes are set to represent 60 minutes <note>This is a scaling technique to make the tables easier to use</note>, then 1 degree and 53 minutes become 42 minutes and 36 seconds.

# Proposition 12.
## That the equation of a given argument at the hour of the true application of the luminaries differs little from the equation of the same at the hour of the mean application.

<image-desc>The right margin contains three astronomical diagrams. The top diagram shows a circle (epicycle) with labeled points k, s, b, m, e, d, featuring a tangent line and internal geometric constructions. The middle diagram depicts a circle with points d, e, m, b, n, z, illustrating the geometric relationship between the observer/center and the lunar epicycle. The bottom diagram is a more complex multi-point construction with labels g, s, z, h, b, e, m, d, showing intersecting arcs and lines used to calculate precise lunar positions.</image-desc>

For it is possible that the distance of the true conjunction <term>conjunction: when the sun and moon appear in the same place in the sky (New Moon)</term> or opposition <term>opposition: when the sun and moon are on opposite sides of the Earth (Full Moon)</term> from the mean position is almost 14 hours. This happens when, at the hour of the mean application <note>original: *applicatio*; a general term for conjunctions or oppositions</note> of the luminaries, the moon has the maximum diversity of its true motion from its mean motion, and the diversity of one must be added while the other is subtracted. This occurs such that the distance between the mean locations of both becomes 5 degrees and 24 minutes—the sum of the maximum diversity of the moon. In such a true application, the distance of the center of the lunar epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric must be 14 degrees and 48 minutes. Because of this, there will be a difference between the equations of the same argument that occur in this position of the epicycle's center and those in the apogee of the eccentric. Such a maximum difference occurs when the moon is in the mean longitudes of the epicycle, namely on the line tangent to the epicycle. This difference, however, does not exceed 2 minutes. <margin>Note</margin> For let the angle $a-e-b$ be 14 degrees and 48 minutes, and $b$ be the center of the epicycle. Let the line tangent to the epicycle be $e-t$; therefore $b-t$, being drawn, will be perpendicular to $e-t$. Let $d-m$ also be perpendicular to $b-e$. From the given angle $d-e-m$, the proportion of $d-e$ to $e-m$ and $m-d$ will be known. From $b-d$ and $d-m$, the line $b-m$ will be known; hence the whole $b-e$ is known. From $e-b$ and $b-t$, the angle $b-e-t$ will be known, which Ptolemy found to be 5 degrees and 3 minutes. But when the center of the epicycle was in the apogee of the eccentric, it was found to be 5 degrees and 1 minute. The difference between these is therefore only 2 minutes, which is what was proposed. <margin>Note</margin> Furthermore, when the moon in true conjunction or opposition is at the apogee of the epicycle or at the opposite of the mean apogee, it is possible that the distance of the mean place of the sun from the mean place of the moon is almost the maximum diversity of the sun, which is 2 degrees and 23 minutes. The center of the epicycle will then be distant from the apogee of the eccentric by almost 4 degrees and 46 minutes. Therefore, let the moon be upon the opposite of the mean apogee of the epicycle. With $l-m$ and $z-s$ drawn perpendicular to $e-b$ as before, from the angle $d-e-m$, the lines $b-e$, $d-m$, and $m-e$ will become known; $z-s$ and $s-e$ are equal to these. Therefore, from $b-s$ and $z-s$, $b-z$ will become known, and thus the angle $z-b-s$ is known. But as $b-z$ is to $z-s$, so is $b-l$ to $l-m$. Likewise, as $b-z$ is to $b-l$, so is $b-s$ to $b-m$. Therefore, $l-m$ and $b-m$ will be known in the parts in which $b-e$ was known. From $l-m$ and $m-e$, $e-l$ was known, and therefore the angle $l-e-m$, which Ptolemy represents as 4 minutes. Thus, in the true application, the distance of the true place of the moon from the mean will be 4 minutes, which in the mean application would have been zero. Ptolemy did not account for this kind of difference, not because finding it was difficult, but because neglecting it induces very little perceptible error. For at most, these 4 minutes, if neglected, can only amount to about an eighth of an hour. However, errors of this kind are often detected during eclipses, which happens both because of the parallax <term>parallax: the difference in the apparent position of the moon when viewed from the surface of the Earth versus its center</term> of the moon being omitted in observations, and because of the variability of its motion, and because instruments are not always verified with enough certainty. One should note, however, that if you always use the mean argument in calculations of the application, it is possible to sometimes fall into a greater error; for instance, if in the true application the equation of the moon were 3 degrees to be subtracted from the mean motion, and the sun's were 2 degrees to be added; at such a distance of the center of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric it would become 10 degrees. From the angle $a-e-b$ of 10 degrees, you will find the arc $k-b$ to be 1 degree...

## Proposition 13.
### How to construct Ptolemy's Rules.

**F**ind flat rules with parallelogram surfaces 4 cubits long <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–22 inches</note>, of sufficient thickness so that they can remain without warping. In the middle of the width of each, let a straight line be drawn; I will mark these lines present in the margin as a-b, a-d, and c-d-e. Of these, the stronger and thicker one, a-b, is to be fixed perpendicularly to a base f-g, which is parallel to the horizon, so that it can be rotated in hole b. In another rule, which is a-d, let two plates be attached with holes <term>pinnules: sighting vanes with small holes used to align the instrument with a star or planet</term> in the manner of a rule on an astrolabe. Let a-b and a-d now be joined together so that a-d can be rotated on an axis fixed at a, like the leg of a compass. And let the length of a-c be equal to the length of a-d. The length of the third rule, namely c-d-e, should be equal to the side of a square inscribed in a circle whose semi-diameter is a-d. Let c-d-e be joined to rule a-b at c, so that c-d-e can be rotated on an axis fixed at c. And let the portion e-d of rule c-e be equal to line a-c, divided into 60 equal parts, of which the whole rule c-e will have 84 [parts], 7 [minutes], and 51 [seconds]. <note>The geometry of the triquetrum relies on the properties of an isosceles triangle; the diagonal of a square with side 60 is approximately 84.85, or 84 parts and 51 minutes</note>. Moreover, let rule c-e be hollowed out as far as line c-e, so that the end of the [sighting] rule can be moved equally along line c-e. Line a-b must be orthogonal <note>perpendicular</note> to the surface of the horizon, and it will perform the office of a plumb line.

## Proposition 14.
### To determine the maximum latitude of the moon.

**P**tolemy, in Alexandria—the latitude of which from the equinoctial <note>the equator</note> is 30 degrees 58 minutes <note>The OCR reads 31. 30. 58, but the later text and historical records for Ptolemy's Alexandria use 30;58</note>—observed the moon with the rules when it was at the beginning of Cancer at the extreme of its northern latitude. He found the distance of the moon from the pole of the horizon <note>the Zenith</note> to be 2 degrees and one-eighth of a degree by observation with the rules. For he raised the rule d-a with its pinnules until he saw the moon through the holes of the pinnules, and to the end d he applied the line c-e, and through the chord c-d he found the arc to be 2 degrees and one-eighth. And because it had such a small distance from the zenith, and the pole of the ecliptic was then in the surface of the meridian (because it was the circle of altitude), the diversity of aspect <term>diversity of aspect: parallax, or the difference in the apparent position of an object seen from the Earth's surface versus its center</term> of the moon in the circle of altitude was itself insensible. Therefore, if 2 degrees and an eighth are taken away from 30 degrees 28 minutes, 28 degrees 51 minutes and a half remain, which exceed the maximum declination <note>The angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</note>—namely 23 degrees 51 minutes and a third of a degree—by almost five degrees. Therefore he concluded the maximum latitude of the moon to be 5 degrees. Once the maximum latitude of the moon is known, the other latitudes at any given distance from the node are produced through it by the way the tables of ecliptic declination were perfectly made in the first [proposition] of this book.

## Proposition 15.
### To conclude the diversity of aspect of the moon in the circle of altitude.

**P**tolemy observed in the 20th year of Hadrian, on the 13th day of the month of Athyr <note>The third month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, which is the third of the Egyptians, at 5 and 5/6 hours <note>original: "medietate ⁊ tertia hoꝛe" (a half and a third)</note> equal hours from midday. The moon was then seen through the instrument of rules to be distant from the pole of the horizon by 50 degrees 55 minutes. This observation was 882 Egyptian years, 72 days, and 5 and 1/3 hours after the beginning of the years of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabucho"; the Era of Nabonassar began in 747 BCE and was the standard for Babylonian and Greek astronomers</note>. With this time, he verified the locations of the luminaries: he found the sun by mean motion at 17 degrees 51 minutes of Libra, but by true motion at 15 degrees 24 minutes of Libra. The moon, according to its mean motion, was at 25 degrees 43 minutes of Sagittarius. The mean elongation <note>The angular distance between the sun and moon</note> of the moon from the sun was 78 degrees 13 minutes. The mean argument was 262 degrees 20 minutes. The mean argument of latitude from the northern point of maximum latitude was 354 degrees 40 minutes. The equation of the moon to be added was 7 degrees 26 minutes. Therefore the true place of the moon according to calculation was 3 degrees 9 minutes of Capricorn, and the true argument of latitude was 2 degrees 6 minutes. Therefore the true northern latitude was 4 degrees 59 minutes. The declination of the true place of the moon was 23 degrees 49 minutes, and the latitude of the region was 30 degrees 58 minutes. Therefore, the true elongation of the moon from the pole of the horizon was 49 degrees 48 minutes. But as it was seen, as was said, it was 50 degrees 55 minutes. Therefore, the diversity of aspect <note>parallax</note> in the circle of altitude was 1 degree and 7 minutes.

# To reveal how great the distance of the center of the moon is from the center of the Earth, in units where the Earth's radius is one, at the hour of the said observation.

Let circle **a-b** in the figure designate the Earth, centered at **k**, and upon that same center let the circle passing through the line and the pole of the horizon be **q-d**. Also, let the circle of altitude—with respect to which the body of the Earth is merely a point—be **e-t**. And let **d** be the center of the moon. Let line **k-a-g-e** proceed from the center of the Earth through the observer's pole **a**, and **g** and **e** in the axis of the horizon <note>The "axis of the horizon" here refers to the vertical line passing through the zenith and the center of the Earth</note>. When lines **a-d-t** and **k-d-b** are drawn, **b** will be the true position of the moon, while **t** is the visible position. The interval **b-t** is the difference of appearance <term>difference of appearance: an early term for parallax, the shift in a celestial body's position when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center</term>. Further, **e-b** is the true distance of the moon from the zenith <note>The zenith is the point in the sky directly above the observer</note>, and **e-t** is its distance seen through the instrument. From the arcs **e-b** and **e-t**, we seek the proportion of line **d-k** to line **a-k**. 

Let **a-z** be parallel to line **k-b**, and **a-l** be perpendicular to **k-b**. Because **a-k** is of a negligible quantity <note>original: "insensibilis quantitatis"</note> compared to **a-t**, the arc **z-t** differs negligibly from arc **b-t**. For the same reason, the arc **z-a-t** differs negligibly from the quantity **e-k** as explained. Therefore, it is necessary that **z-b** be of a negligible quantity with respect to circle **e-t**; thus, arc **z-t** differs negligibly from arc **b-t**. By similar reasoning, angle **z-a-t** differs negligibly from the size of the angle formed at center **k**, which is subtended by arc **z-t**. 

From the previous [proposition], **z-t** was 1 degree 7 minutes, while arc **e-b** was 49 degrees 48 minutes. Therefore, angle **z-a-t** then was 1 degree 7 minutes. Angle **a-d-l** is also equal to this; therefore, the proportion of **d-a** to **a-l**, and also **d-a** to **l-d**, is given. But **d-l** is negligibly shorter than **d-a**, so no error follows if you assume **d-l** to be the same quantity as **d-a**. However, angle **a-k-l** is 49 degrees 48 minutes. Therefore, the proportion of **k-a** to **a-l** and to **l-k** will be known. Thus **a-l** and **l-k** will be known, assuming **a-k** is one part; in these same units, **l-t** will become known. Therefore, the whole **d-k** was 59 parts 45 minutes, in units where **a-k** <note>The Earth's radius</note> is one. This will be shown more easily thus: Because angle **e-a-t** is known by observation—it differs negligibly from angle **e-k-t** if **k-t** were extended—but angle **a-k-d** is known by calculation, therefore the triangle **a-d-k** will have known angles; thus the proportion of the sides is known, which was what was sought.

# To infer from the said observation the proportion of the radii of the moon's eccentric and epicycle, as well as the eccentricity to the radius of the Earth.

At the hour of the said observation, let the eccentric <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth</term> be **a-b-g** on the diameter **a-g** passing through the center of the eccentric **d**, the center of the world **e**, and the point opposite **d**. Also, let the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent)</term> be **b-l** on center **b**, so that angle **a-e-b** is double the mean elongation <note>The angular distance between the sun and the moon</note> between the sun and the moon: namely, 156 degrees 26 minutes. Let the position of the moon in the epicycle be **l**. With lines drawn as you see in the figure: let the opposite of the mean apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth</note> of the epicycle be **k**, and the true [apogee] be **t**. 

Therefore, since in the said observation the mean argument <note>The moon's position within its epicycle</note> of the moon was 262 degrees 20 minutes, the arc **k-l** becomes 82 degrees 20 minutes. Since angle **a-e-b** is known, the proportion of **e-d** to **d-m** and **m-e** will be known. But the proportion of **b-d** to **d-e** was already known; therefore the proportion of **b-d** to **d-m** and **m-e** is known. From the two, **b-d** and **d-m**, **b-m** will become known; hence from **b-m** and **n-z**, **b-z** becomes known, and angle **z-b-n** is known. Also, arc **t-k** is that which Ptolemy found to be 7 degrees 40 minutes. But **k-l** was already 52 degrees 20 minutes, and therefore arc **t-l** was 90 degrees. Thus angle **e-b-l** is known. 

Line **b-d** was 49 parts 41 minutes, while **b-l** was 5 parts 7 [minutes] 15 [seconds], and in those same units **e-b** was 40 parts 4 minutes. Thus from **e-b** and **b-l**, **e-l** is found to be 40 parts 25 minutes. But it has already been shown in the previous [proposition] that **e-l** was 59 parts 45 minutes, in units where the radius of the Earth is one. Therefore, from the said proportion of lines, **d-b** becomes 48 parts 51 minutes, **b-l** becomes 5 parts 10 minutes, and **d-e** becomes 10 parts 9 minutes, which were sought. Therefore, **e-a** is almost 59 parts, and **e-g** is 38 parts 43 minutes. From these...

...they will now easily know the distance of the moon from the center of the earth in units where the earth's radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> is one part, at the hours of the conjunctions <note>original: "applicationum"</note> of the sun and moon. Similarly in their quadratures <term>quadrature: a position where the moon is 90 degrees away from the sun, such as a half-moon</term>. However, I advise in this work: that you hold the lines already drawn—namely, **a. e.**, **e. d.**, **d. b.**, and **b. l.**—in these numerical values: namely, **a. e.** 60,000; **e. d.** 10,317; **d. b.** or **d. a.** 49,683; and **b. l.** 5,250. Work with these values to avoid a multitude of fractions, until you find the value of **e. l.** in those quantities. The square of **d. a.** will always remain the same: namely, 2,468,400,489. Once **e. l.** is found in these units, you will also find **e. l.** in parts where **e. a.** is 59, and the calculation will be complete.

->## Proposition xviii.<-

<image-desc>A horizontal diagram showing three circles. The two largest circles overlap and share a common center 'c'. To the right, a smaller circle is connected. Labels include 'a', 'f', 'b', 'e', 'c', 'd', 'g', 'k'.</image-desc>

**T**o declare the quantities of the visual diameters of the sun and moon, and also of the shadow in the place of the moon’s transit at various distances.
Because this cannot be found precisely enough through water clocks <note>original: "instrumenta aquarum," referring to clepsydras</note> nor through elevations of the equatorial circle, Ptolemy chose two lunar eclipses for this purpose. The first was on the 12th day of the Egyptian month of June <note>original: "Iunii egypitoꝝ," likely referring to the month of Payni in the Nabonassar era</note>. The time from the beginning of the years of Nabonassar <term>Nabonassar: an era starting in 747 BCE used by ancient astronomers for calculations</term> was 126 years, 86 days, and 17 hours of "different" time, but 16 and 3/4 hours of "equalized" time <term>equalized time: mean solar time, adjusted for the Earth's varying orbital speed</term>. The mean position of the moon was 25 degrees and 22 minutes of Libra; its true position was 27 degrees and 5 minutes of Libra. The mean argument of the moon <term>argument: an angular measurement used to locate a planet or the moon in its orbit</term> was 340 degrees and 5 minutes, and the moon's distance from one of the nodes <note>The nodes are the two points where the moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note> was 9 and 1/3 degrees. Therefore, the northern latitude of the moon was 48 and 1/2 minutes, and nearly a quarter of the moon's diameter was eclipsed from the southern side.

The second eclipse was in the year of Nabonassar 224, 196 days, at 10 and 1/6 hours of "different" time, but 9 and 5/6 equalized hours. The Sun was at 18 degrees and 12 minutes of Cancer. The Moon according to its mean position was at 20 degrees and 20 minutes of Capricorn, and according to its true position at 18 degrees and 12 minutes. The argument of the moon was 28 degrees and 54 minutes. The distance of the moon from the node was 7 and 4/5 parts. Therefore, the southern latitude of the moon was 40 and 2/3 minutes. And half of the diameter was eclipsed from the northern side.

Let us therefore place in the figure the circle of the shadow at the place of the moon's transit—noting that in both eclipses it was nearly at the same distance from the center of the world—as circle **a. f. b. e.** upon center **c.**, and let **a. c. b.** represent the ecliptic. In the first eclipse, let the moon be at center **d.**; in the second, at **e.** Thus, **f. g.** will be a quarter of the lunar diameter, and **e. k.** half of it. It follows that **c. d.** is 48 and 1/2 minutes, and **c. e.** is 40 and 2/3 minutes. But **c. e.** is equal to **c. f.**, therefore **f. d.** will be 7 and 5/6 minutes. But since **d. f.** is a quarter of the lunar diameter, the entire visible visual diameter of the moon becomes 31 and 1/3 minutes, and the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> of the shadow **c. e.** is 40 and 2/3 minutes. Moreover, when we calculate the proportion of **k. e.** to **c. e.**, we find that **c. e.** contains **k. e.** twice and three-fifths times. And since we have found this same proportion to remain constant in many other instances, it follows that we shall work according to this. Regarding the visual diameter of the sun, Ptolemy says he found it through his rules to be equal to the visual diameter of the moon just discovered—specifically, when the moon is at its greatest distance from the earth.

->## Proposition xix.<-

<image-desc>Two diagrams on the left margin. The top one shows Earth (circle 'n') and the Moon (circle 't') with tangent lines 'r-n-h' and 'z-t' illustrating the geometry of the solar shadow cone. The bottom diagram depicts a long, narrow cone representing the Earth's shadow, with the Moon shown inside the narrowing cone.</image-desc>

**T**o show the proportion of the Earth’s radius to the radius of the moon’s body and the radius of the shadow.
Let the circle on **n.** designate the Earth, and the circle on center **t.** designate the moon at its greatest distance from the earth. With line **n. t.** drawn, and **r. n. h.** being a tangent, and **t. h.** perpendicular to **n. h.**, the angle **n. t. h.** is known from the premises to be 15 and 2/3 minutes. Therefore, the proportion of **n. t.** to **t. h.** is given. But **n. t.** is 64 parts and 10 minutes, where **m. n.** (the radius of the earth) is one, as was shown in the preceding premises. Therefore, **t. h.** will be known in those same units. Similarly, from the known proportion of **h. t.** to **t. z.**, the radius of the shadow **t. z.** will be known in the same units. Thus, **t. h.** is found to be 17 minutes and 33 seconds, and **t. z.** is 45 minutes and 38 seconds.

<header>The Fifth [Book]</header>

# To reveal the diameter of the Sun, its distance from the center of the Earth, and the length of the axis of the Earth's shadow, in units where the Earth's radius is one part.

**T**he diameter of the Sun, its distance from the center of the Earth, and the length of the axis of the Earth's shadow are to be made manifest in parts where the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> of the Earth is one part.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram on the right side of the page illustrates the celestial geometry of the Sun, Earth, and Moon. At the top is a large circle labeled "sol." (Sun) with points a, d, g and b. Below it is a smaller circle (Moon) with center t and points e, h. Further down is a third circle labeled "tra" (terra/Earth) with center n and points k, l, m. Tangent lines from the edges of the Sun pass by the edges of the Earth to converge at a point 's' at the bottom, representing the cone of the Earth's shadow. Various horizontal chords (e.g., e-h, k-m) and vertical lines (the axis d-n-s) are drawn with supplementary points labeled f, c, and z.</image-desc>

¶ Ptolemy says it is discovered that the moon at its greatest distance <note>apogee</note> covers the entire sun without delay. This fact was a sign that the radius of the sun subtends the same angle at the eye as the radius of the moon then subtends.
¶ Therefore, let circle **a.b.g.** on center **d** represent the sun; circle **e.h** on **t** represent the moon at its greatest distance; and circle **k.l.m.** represent the earth on center **n**. Let **n**, **t**, and **d** be on a straight line. Let the lines touching the sun and the earth be **a.k.** and **g.m.**, meeting at the cone of the shadow **s**. The axis of the shadow will be **n.s.**. Let the chords of the arcs included by the contacts on the sun be **a.d.g.**, on the earth **k.n.m.**, and on the moon **e.t.h.**, while **n.e.** and **n.h.**, when extended, also touch the sun. It is established, however, because of the great distances of the sun and moon from the earth, that such chords differ imperceptibly from the diameters of their circles. Likewise, let **n.f.** be equal to **n.t.**, and **g.f.e.** be the diameter of the shadow in the place of the moon's transit at its greatest distance. The goal is to find the proportion of **d.g.** to **n.m.**; likewise **d.n.** to **n.m.** and **n.s.** to **n.m.** Let **e.h.** extend to **z**. Because it was said that angle **t.n.h.** is known, therefore by the previous [proposition], the proportion of **n.t.** to **e.t.** and **t.h.** to **n.m.** is known. And **t.h.** was found to be 17 minutes and 33 seconds <note>17' 33''</note> where **n.m.** is one part.
But the proportion of **t.h.** to **f.e.** was as one to two and three-fifths; therefore **f.e.** is known and was 45 minutes and 38 seconds in the same units. But because **n.t.** is equal to **n.f.**, the two lines **f.e.** and **t.z.** taken together will become double **n.m.**, which would easily be clear if a line **c.f.** were drawn through **n** parallel and equal [to the radius]. Therefore **f.c.** and **t.z.** are likewise two parts. Wherefore, after subtracting **f.e.** and **t.h.**, there will remain **h.z.**, 6 minutes and 49 seconds. But the proportion of **n.m.** to **h.z.** is as **n.g.** to **g.h.**, and **n.g.** to **g.h.** is as **n.d.** to **d.t.**; wherefore **n.m.** to **h.z.** is as **n.d.** to **d.t.** Therefore, if line **n.d.** were one part, **d.t.** would be 56 minutes and 49 seconds, and **t.n.** the remainder, 3 minutes and 11 seconds. Therefore the proportion of **t.n.** to **n.d.** is known. Thus if **n.t.** is 64 parts and 10 minutes <note>64;10 Earth radii</note> of such units where **n.m.** is one, **n.d.** will become almost 1210 parts. Likewise, **n.t.** is to **t.h.** as **n.d.** is to **d.g.**; therefore **d.g.** <note>the sun's radius</note> will become almost 5 parts and 30 minutes of such units. From this, the proportion of **d.g.** to **t.h.** is also known. Likewise, **n.m.** is to **f.e.** as **n.s.** is to **s.f.**; therefore the ratio of **f.n.** to **n.s.** is known. Thus **n.s.** <note>the length of the shadow</note> is found to be 265 parts of such units where **n.m.** is one. But **n.f.** is 64 parts and 10 minutes.

### Proposition xxi.

### To assign the proportions of the three bodies—Sun, Earth, and Moon—to one another.

**T**o assign the proportions of the three bodies—Sun, Earth, and Moon—to one another.
¶ From the preceding, you have the proportions of their radii <note>original: "semidiametrorum"</note>; therefore, by tripling the proportions <term>tripling the proportions: in geometry, the volume of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius</term>, the proportions of the bodies will arise thus: Let the Sun's radius **d.g.** be four and a half <note>this seems to refer to a specific calculation step</note> of such units where **n.m.** is one. The cubes of these are 166, one fourth, and one eighth <note>166 3/8</note>, and one [for the Earth]. Wherefore the sun is one hundred sixty-six times larger than the whole earth, and contains three-eighths of it besides. ¶ Furthermore, since **d.g.** contains **d.h.** eighteen times and four quarters <note>18.75 times</note>, the cube of this is almost 6644 and a half. Therefore the sun is six thousand six hundred forty-four times larger than the moon, and contains a half besides. Likewise, **n.m.** <note>Earth</note> contains **t.h.** <note>Moon</note> three times and almost two quarters <note>3.5 times</note>; the cube of this is almost 39 and a quarter. Therefore the earth is thirty-nine times <note>original: "trigesichonies", likely a typo for "trigesiesnonies"</note> larger than the moon, and contains almost a quarter besides. These, therefore, are the proportions of the three bodies as found by Ptolemy. But he...

<header>The Book</header>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram on the left margin illustrating astronomical observations. It features a central vertical axis intersecting several circles and arcs of varying radii. Lines radiate from two distinct points on the central axis toward the circumferences of the circles, representing the geometry of sightlines, parallax, or eclipse paths relative to the observer and celestial bodies.</image-desc>

[Ptolemy] established that the diameters of the sun and moon, as seen by the eye, subtend the same angle when the moon is at its greatest distance <note>apogee</note> from the earth. However, he posited no variation in the diameter of the sun due to the small eccentricity <note>the off-center nature of an orbit</note> of its path relative to its maximum distance. But Albategni <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer whose work refined Ptolemaic models</note> found the eclipses he observed to be different in magnitude and timing from those shown by Ptolemy’s calculations. Indeed, he says that he studied two solar eclipses. The first was in the year 1202 of the era of Dhu'l-Qarnayn <note>original: "Iulcarnam," referring to the Seleucid era</note>, which is the year 1214 from the death of Alexander. The true conjunction <note>alignment of the sun and moon</note> occurred after the middle of the eighteenth month in the city of Aracta <note>Raqqa, in modern-day Syria</note> by the space of one seasonal hour. According to sight, more than two-thirds of the sun was eclipsed. According to calculation, the sun's mean motion <note>average position</note> was at 20 degrees and 54 minutes of Leo; its true position was at 19 degrees and 14 minutes of the same sign. The moon's mean motion was at 17 degrees and 50 minutes of Leo, and its true position was at the same place as the sun. The adjusted anomaly <note>original: "argumentum... equatum," a value used to determine the moon's irregular movement</note> of the moon was 332 degrees and 57 minutes. The mean argument of latitude was 174 degrees and 43 minutes, and the adjusted version was 167 degrees and 41 minutes. The middle of the eclipse—that is, the visible conjunction—followed the true conjunction by almost one-eighth of an hour. At that time, therefore, the adjusted argument of latitude was 177 degrees and 11 minutes; the true latitude was 16 minutes north, but the visible latitude was 6 minutes south. According to Ptolemy’s calculation, however, the eclipse should have covered more than a half plus a quarter <note>three-quarters</note> of the sun, and the middle of the eclipse, as seen through an instrument, should have occurred one hour earlier.

¶ The second solar eclipse was in the aforementioned year, three and two-thirds equal hours before noon on the 23rd day of the month of Elul <note>original: "Lalbat"</note> in Antioch. According to sight, a little more than half of the sun was eclipsed. In Aracta, however, the middle of the eclipse occurred three and a half equal hours before noon. There, a little less than two-thirds of the sun appeared eclipsed according to sight. According to his calculations, the sun was at a mean motion of 7 degrees and 9 minutes of Aquarius, and at a true position of 8 degrees and 37 minutes. The moon's mean course was 12 degrees and 49 minutes of Aquarius. The adjusted anomaly of the moon was 126 degrees and 22 minutes. The mean argument of latitude was 173 degrees and 25 minutes, but the adjusted version was 169 degrees and 41 minutes. The visible conjunction preceded the true conjunction by half an hour; at that time, the adjusted argument of latitude was 168 degrees and 45 minutes. The true latitude was 79 minutes, while the visible latitude was 10 minutes. According to Ptolemy’s calculation, however, the sun should have been totally eclipsed, and the middle of the eclipse should have occurred almost two hours after we observed it. 

He also studied two lunar eclipses. The first was in the year 1206 from the death of Alexander, on the 23rd day of the month of Tammuz <note>original: "kemir"</note>. Its middle in Aracta was a little more than 8 equal hours after noon, and a little more than a half and a third <note>five-sixths</note> of the moon's diameter was eclipsed. By calculation, the sun’s mean motion was at 5 degrees and 21 minutes of Leo; its true position at 4 degrees and 2 minutes. The moon's mean position was at 8 degrees and 45 minutes of Aquarius. The mean anomaly was 93 degrees, but the adjusted version was 94 degrees and 10 minutes. The mean argument of latitude was 100 degrees and 49 minutes, while the adjusted version was 186 degrees and 51 minutes. The southern latitude of the moon was almost 32 minutes. But according to Ptolemy’s calculation, a half, a third, and an eighth part of the diameter should have been eclipsed. And the time of the middle of the eclipse should have preceded the observed time by a half and a quarter <note>three-quarters</note> of an equal hour. 

¶ The second was in the year 1224 from the death of Alexander, after noon on the second day of the month of Ab: nearly 15 and one-third hours in Antioch. But in Aracta, it was nearly 15 and a third plus a quarter hours. A little less than the diameter of the moon was eclipsed. According to calculation, the sun's mean motion was 16 degrees and 10 minutes of Leo; its true course, however, was 14 degrees and 36 minutes. The moon’s mean position was 19 degrees and 24 minutes of Aquarius. Its adjusted anomaly was 91 degrees and 5 minutes. The adjusted argument of latitude was 185 degrees and 21 minutes. The latitude of the moon was 28 minutes. But according to Ptolemy’s calculation, only a half and a third <note>five-sixths</note> should have been eclipsed, and the time of the middle of the eclipse should have preceded the observed time by nearly a half and a third <note>five-sixths</note> of an hour. He says that in many other lunar and solar eclipses, he found a discrepancy from the values calculated according to Ptolemy’s tables. He wished these two examples already explained to be sufficient to investigate the cause of this diversity.

<header>Fifth</header>

...because in both of them the sun was near the apogee <note>the highest point in an orbit, furthest from Earth; original: "augem"</note> of its eccentric <note>a circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center</note>; and the moon was at the middle distance of its epicycle <note>a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle</note>. And the latitude <note>celestial latitude, or distance north or south of the ecliptic</note> of the moon was nearly the same in both directions. However, the difference in latitudes was 3 minutes and 50 seconds. But the difference of the eclipsed parts was one-eighth of the diameter and half of one-eighth of a fourth. He thus found the diameter of the moon at that time to be 33 minutes and 20 seconds, and the semidiameter of the shadow to be nearly 45 minutes and 30 seconds. Furthermore, he considered the proportions of the true motion of the moon in one hour relative to the quantity of the visible diameter of the moon already found. According to that same proportion, from the true motion of the moon in an hour—with the moon being at the apogee of its epicycle during the alignments—he found the diameter of the moon at the apogee of the epicycle to be 29 and a half minutes. Similarly, following the same proportion from the true motion of the moon in an hour, at the opposite of the apogee <note>perigee, the point closest to Earth</note> of the epicycle, he found the diameter of the moon to be nearly 35 minutes and one second. For he estimated the proportion of the moon's varying motion in an hour to its visible diameter to be as 6 is to 6 minus one-eighth; that is, 48 to 47. Based on this, he established the diameter of the moon everywhere from its varying motion in an hour.

The proportion of the semidiameter of the moon to the semidiameter of the shadow which Ptolemy established, however, he preserved: namely, 5 to 13, which is 1 to 2 and three-fifths. Thus, he found the semidiameter of the shadow at the moon's furthest point of passage to be smaller than what Ptolemy established by nearly 2 minutes and one-third of a minute. He also posits a variation in the diameter of the sun. For at its furthest distance <note>apogee</note>, he says it is 31 minutes and one-third, just as Ptolemy did. Therefore, he concludes that the entire sun cannot be obscured by the moon when both are at their furthest distance <note>resulting in an "annular" eclipse where a ring of light remains visible</note>. He also considered the proportions of the true motion of the sun in an hour while it was at its furthest distance relative to this diameter of its own; and through this, he found the diameter of the sun in other locations from its true motion in an hour, holding that the motion of the sun in an hour is to the diameter of the sun as 5 is to 66; that is, as 1 is to 13 and one-fifth. Therefore, the sun's diameter at its closer distance <note>perigee</note> would be 33 minutes and two-thirds of a minute. Thus, the sun's diameter varies between its furthest and closest distances by 2 minutes and one-third of a minute.

Finally, it happens that the diameters of the shadow vary on account of the sun’s approach and withdrawal. For at the moon's most remote point of passage, with the sun being at the apogee of its eccentric, he found it to be 1 degree and 17 minutes. But with the sun at apogee and the moon at its closer distance, it was 1 degree and 32 minutes. It is also agreed that the diameter of the shadow, when the sun is at its closer distance, is smaller than the diameter of the shadow when the sun is at its furthest distance by 1 minute and 40 seconds. From these things, therefore, Albategni <note>Al-Battani</note> found the distance of the center of the sun from the center of the earth and the length of the axis of the shadow by other means. For according to the aforementioned things, when the sun and moon are at their maximum distance, the diameter of the moon is smaller than the diameter of the sun, according to sight, by 1 minute and 50 seconds. The variation of the diameter of the moon from the apogee of the epicycle to its opposite is 5 minutes and 50 seconds. 

He took, therefore, from the 10 and one-third parts by which the distance of the moon from the earth varies from the apogee of the epicycle to its opposite, a proportional part according to the ratios of 5 minutes 50 seconds to 1 minute 50 seconds, which was 3 and a quarter parts. When these were subtracted from 64 parts and 10 minutes—namely, the maximum distance of the moon—60 parts and 55 minutes remain. This will be the distance of the moon from the earth when its visible diameter is 31 minutes and one-third; and then the semidiameter of the shadow, according to the assigned proportion, becomes 40 minutes and 4 seconds. From these things, following the path of the premise, there was found "n.d." <note>likely *numerus distantiae*, distance value</note>, namely the distance of the sun at its apogee, to be 1146 parts, of which the semidiameter of the earth is one; and "n.s." <note>likely *numerus sphaerae* or *shadow*</note>, namely the length of the axis of the shadow then, to be 254 parts of the same. Likewise, from the proportion of the semidiameter of the sun's eccentric to the distance of the centers of the sun's eccentric and the earth, he found that the eccentricity <note>the distance between the center of the orbit and the center of the Earth</note> of the sun contains 38 parts, of which the semidiameter of the earth is one. Therefore, the minimum distance of the sun becomes 1070 and a half parts, and the mean distance 1108 of such parts. And he found that the moon hides the whole sun when the distance between both their centers—namely line *t.d.*—contains 1085 times the semidiameter of the earth; and by these proportions of the quantities of the diameters and distances in an eclipse...

<header>Book</header>

...correspond to what is seen in solar [eclipses], as Albategni <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a famous Arab astronomer whose work refined Ptolemy’s values</note> stated. By this argument, he concludes that the said proportions are certain.

### Proposition 22.

## To investigate the visual semidiameters of the Sun, Moon, and the shadow by a geometric method.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle representing an eccentric orbit with points labeled a, b, g, e, z, k, s. The center of the circle is e, and the center of the Earth is z, offset from e. Lines are drawn from the Earth to various points on the orbit to show how distance changes.</image-desc>
</margin>

The quantities of the distances of the sun and moon, and of the semidiameters <note>radii; original: "semidiametrorum"</note> that occur at their greatest distances, must be presupposed. First, then, concerning the semidiameter of the sun: Let the maximum distance of the sun be *n d*, and the semidiameter of the sun be the drawn line *d g*. Let the line *g n* be drawn. Let the maximum distance *n d* be as Albategni sets it: 1146 parts, where the semidiameter of the earth *n* is one part. And let the angle *d n g* be 15 minutes, 40 seconds, 2 thirds, and 7 fourths <note>these are sexagesimal subdivisions of a degree used for extreme precision</note>. Since angle *g* is a right angle, the proportion of *n d* to *d g* is therefore known; it follows that *d g* is 5 parts and 13 minutes in those units where *n d* is 1146, or where the semidiameter of the earth is one. Later, let the sun be nearer; we wish to find the quantity of its visual semidiameter. This will be done after you have learned its distance from the earth in parts where the semidiameter of the earth is one. Therefore, let there be an eccentric circle <note>an orbit where the Earth is not at the exact center</note> *a b g* on center *e*, and let the center of the earth be *z*. The given angle *a e b* will make *z e* 38 parts, where the semidiameter of the earth is one; and in those same units, *a e* or *b e* is 1108. Therefore, from the known proportion of *e z* to *z k* and *k e*, *z b* will be known in parts where the semidiameter of the earth is one—namely, the distance of the sun from the earth, which was sought.

<margin>
<image-desc>A small geometric diagram featuring a very narrow triangle or wedge with vertices labeled g, v, r, and n, representing the visual radius of the sun as seen from the Earth.</image-desc>
</margin>

Let such a distance be *n v* in the figure, and upon *v* let the semidiameter of the sun *v r* be equal to the line *d g*. Let the line *r n* be drawn so that angle *v r n* is a right angle. Therefore, the proportion of *n v* to *v r* will be known, where *n v* is the distance of the sun already given and *v r* is 5 parts and 13 minutes. Thus, the angle *v n r*—which is subtended <note>the angle formed by the edges of an object as seen by an observer</note> by the visual semidiameter of the sun—is known, which is what was proposed.

<margin>
<image-desc>A diagram illustrating the geometry of the Earth's shadow. It shows a long tapering cone (the umbra) with the vertex at point s and labels including g, m, d, n, f, and c. This is used to calculate the width of the shadow during a lunar eclipse.</image-desc>
</margin>

Now, concerning the semidiameter of the shadow at the point of the moon's crossing: let *n* be the center of the earth, as before. Let the semidiameter of the earth be *n m*, and the semidiameter of the sun be *d g*. Let the line *g m* be continued until it meets the axis of the shadow *m s*, and the cone of the shadow *s* will be formed—provided that angles *d g m* and *m n s* are right angles, as occurs at the contact points of the shadow’s sides. Likewise, let *n f* be the distance of the moon from the earth, known from previous calculations, and at its crossing let the semidiameter of the shadow *f c* be drawn perpendicular to *n s*. By drawing line *n c*, we seek the size of the angle *c n f*, which the semidiameter of the shadow subtends at the place of the moon's crossing, based on the given distance of the sun *n d* and the moon's distance *n f*. For let *l m* be parallel to *n d*; *d l* will be equal to *n m*, and therefore *l g* will be 4 parts and 13 minutes, where the semidiameter of the earth is one. But since *g l* is to *l m* as *m n* is to *n s*, the axis of the shadow *n s* becomes known, and therefore *f s* is known. Also, from *m n* and *n s*, *s m* becomes known. In truth, because of the negligible error, you can use *n s* in place of *s m*. But as *s m* is to *m n*, so *s f* is to *f c*; therefore *f c* is known. Similarly, because of the negligible error, you can take *n f* in place of *n c*; hence from *n c* and *c f*, find the size of the angle *c n f* which was sought.

Thus, when the sun and moon are at their greatest distances, the semidiameter of the shadow at the moon's crossing will be 40 minutes and 54 seconds, and the axis of the shadow will be 271 parts and 47 minutes, where the earth's semidiameter is one. However, with the sun at the apogee <note>the furthest point; original: "auge"</note> of its eccentric and the moon at the opposite of the apogee <note>perigee, the closest point</note> of its epicycle during alignment <note>syzygy</note> with the sun, the semidiameter of the shadow will be 51 minutes and 12 seconds. With the sun at the apogee and the moon at the middle distance of its epicycle during alignment with the sun, the semidiameter of the shadow is 45 minutes and 37 seconds. Likewise, with the sun at the opposite of the apogee of its eccentric and the moon at the apogee of its epicycle during alignment with the sun, the semidiameter of the shadow is 40 minutes and 2 seconds. Therefore, the variation of the shadow due to the sun’s descent from the apogee to the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric—insofar as it affects the shadow at the point of the moon's crossing when the moon is at its eccentric apogee and the opposite of the epicycle's apogee—is 52 seconds. But with the sun at the opposite of the eccentric's apogee and the moon at the opposite of the [epicycle's] apogee...

**From the given distance of the sun or moon from the center of the earth, and its elongation from the pole of the horizon: to investigate the parallax in the circle of altitude.**
Let the figure from the 16th [proposition] of this book be repeated. From the angle *g k d* and the distance *k d*, we seek the arc *h t*. For the proportion of *a k* to *a l* and *l k* will be known, and therefore *d l* will become known. If this were taken in place of *d a*, no sensible error would occur. Hence, from *a d* and *a l*, the angle *l d a* will be known, which is equal to the angle *d a z*. But this differs by an imperceptible amount from the angle which *z t* subtends at the center *k*; therefore, the arc *z t* will be known. And because of the imperceptible quantity of *a k* with respect to *e k*, *z t* exceeds *h t* by an imperceptible amount. Therefore, *h t*, which was sought, is known. <note>The author is demonstrating how to calculate "parallax"—the shift in a body's apparent position caused by the observer being on the Earth's surface rather than at its center.</note>

## Proposition 23.

**To construct tables of parallaxes in the circle of altitude.**
Ptolemy, in constructing tables of this kind, first assumed the same distance from the earth for the sun: namely, 1210 parts, where the semidiameter of the earth is one. He placed *d k* at this quantity everywhere, and found that when angle *g k d* is 90 degrees, arc *h t* is 2 minutes, 51 seconds. Then he calculated the parallaxes <note>original: "diuersitates aspectus"</note> in the circle of altitude for the moon at four limits. The **first limits** are when the moon is at the apogee of the eccentric and the epicycle; then he found the maximum [parallax] to be 53 minutes, 34 seconds. But the **second limits** are when the moon is at the apogee of the eccentric and the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle; then he found the maximum to be 1 degree, 3 minutes, 51 seconds. The **third limits** are when the moon is at the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric and at the apogee of the epicycle; then the maximum was 1 degree, 19 minutes. The **fourth limits** are when the moon is at the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric and the epicycle; and then it was the greatest of all: 1 degree, 43 minutes. *K d* in the first limit was 64 parts, 10 minutes. In the second, it has 53 parts, 50 minutes. In the third, 43 parts, 53 minutes. In the fourth, 33 parts, 33 minutes. Then also, so that the parallax in the circle of altitude might be known from these when the moon exists outside these four limits, he proceeded by a subtle shortcut. And first, when the center of the moon's epicycle is at the apogee of the eccentric: as in figure *e 3*, let it be 60 parts, where *e a*, the semidiameter of the epicycle, is 5 parts and 15 minutes. Let the distance of the moon from the apogee of the epicycle—namely *a b*—be 60 degrees, or another arc; therefore the proportion of *e b*...

...to [line] 3.b. and 3.e. <note>These alphanumeric codes refer to points and lines in the accompanying geometric diagrams</note> are known because the angle *b* is a right angle; and the arc *a.b.* is known from 3.h. and 3.b. is known, thus 3.b. will be determined. Knowing the difference between these, you will enter the table with the mean elongation of the sun and moon, and take the final proportional minutes. According to their ratio to 60, take the proportional part of the noted difference, which you add to the parallax calculated from the first and second limits; thus will come the sought-after parallax of the moon in the circle of altitude for the moon's position in the eccentric and epicycle.

### Proposition .26.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram showing a sphere with intersecting arcs labeled with letters: a, b, d, e, g, h, k, t, z, and s. A vertical arc b-d represents a meridian or altitude circle, and a horizontal arc a-g represents the ecliptic.</image-desc>

Distinguishing the parallax <note>original: "diversitatem aspectus"; literally "diversity of aspect," the standard term for parallax in Renaissance astronomy</note> of the moon or sun in longitude and latitude when the moon is on the ecliptic.
Let the middle of the ecliptic <note><term>ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere as seen from Earth</term></note> be *a.c.g*, in which the position of the moon or sun is *e*, such that *e.a* is a quadrant <note>a quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees</note>. Similarly, let *e.g* be a quadrant. Let the middle of the complete altitude circle <note><term>altitude circle: a vertical circle passing through the zenith and the celestial object</term></note> be *b.e.d*, also such that *c.b* is a quadrant and *e.d* is a quadrant. Let the circle passing through the poles of both of these be *a.b.g.d*, in which the pole of the ecliptic is *z*. Let the parallax of the moon or sun in the altitude circle be *e.h*. Through *h*, let a great circle *z.h.t.k* come from the pole of the ecliptic. The goal is to distinguish from the arc *e.h* and the size of angle *b.e.t* the arc *h.t*—the parallax in latitude—and the arc *e.t*—the parallax in longitude. From the angle *b.e.t*, the remainder will be known: specifically *a.e.b*, the size of which is arc *a.b*. Therefore, *a.b* is known. Indeed, the ratio of the sine of *a.b* to the sine of *a.z* is composed of two ratios: namely, the ratio of the sine of *b.e* to the sine of *e.h*, and the ratio of the sine of *h.t* to the sine of *t.z*. However, *a.z*, *b.e*, and *t.z* are quadrants; and *b.a* and *e.h* are given. Therefore, *b.t* will become known.

The ratio of the total sine <note><term>total sine: the maximum value of the sine in a given system, often representing the radius of the calculation circle</term></note> to the sine of the angle formed by the intersection of the altitude circle and the ecliptic is the same as the ratio of the sine of the parallax in the altitude circle to the sine of the parallax in latitude.
I then establish *h* as the pole of a great circle, whose ratio becomes *k.n.m*, and thus *b.k* and *b.n* will be quadrants. Therefore, its pole is *m*, and from this, *k.m* and *t.m* become quadrants. We first seek the quantity of the arc *k.n*, which is the size of the angle *t.b.e*, if you like, because the ratio of the sine of *h.t* to the sine of *t.k* is composed of two: namely the ratio of the sine of *h.e* to the sine of *e.n*, and the ratio of the sine of *n.m* to the sine of *m.k*. But *h.t*, *k*, *b.e*, *e.n*, and *m.k* are known. Now, therefore, *m.n* will be known, and for that reason its complement *n.k* will become known, which was what was sought. Note, however, that if the angle *a.e.b* is subtracted from a right angle, there will remain an angle nearly equal to angle *e.h.t*; if you take this in place of angle *e.h.t*, no noticeable difference will arise in [calculating] eclipses. Now let us seek the quantity of arc *e.t*, because the ratio of the sine of *m.k* to the sine of *k.n* is composed of two: namely the ratio of the sine of *m.t* to the sine of *t.e*, and the ratio of the sine of *e.h* to the sine of *h.n*.

### Proposition 27.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin consisting of intersecting arcs and lines representing a spherical triangle. Key points are labeled g, z, a, b, k, t, and d. A vertical axis is visible on the far left with markings.</image-desc>

What investigation must precede the inquiry: when the moon has latitude from the ecliptic.
¶ Let the portion of the ecliptic <note><term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path, used as a reference line for planetary positions.</term></note> be *a.b.g.* and the portion of the moon’s inclined circle <note>The "inclined circle" refers to the moon's actual orbital path, which is tilted relative to the ecliptic.</note> be *a.d.*, such that *a* is the node <note><term>node: the point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</term></note> and *d* is the location of the moon on the inclined circle. From point *d*, let *d.b* be perpendicular to the ecliptic. From the pole of the horizon <note>The zenith, the point directly overhead.</note> *e*, let the portions of the altitude circles *e.b*, *e.d*, and *e.h.z* be drawn. Let *d.h* be the parallax of the moon in the altitude circle, so that its seen <note>The "seen" or "apparent" position as opposed to the "true" calculated position.</note> location in that same circle is *h*. From *h*, let two portions fall: *h.k* perpendicular to *a.b*, and *h.t* perpendicular to *d.b*. Thus, the true longitude of the moon from the node will be *a.b*, the seen longitude will be *a.k*, the parallax in latitude will be arc *d.t*, and in longitude it will be *h.t* according to *k.b*. Therefore, the arcs *d.h*, *h.t*, and *d.t* must be sought. However, from the previous premises, arc *e.d* is not established for us, but arc *e.b* is known. Therefore, if we wish to know arc *d.h*, it is necessary first to know arc *e.d* instead of arc *e.b*. Likewise, if we desire to know arcs *h.t* and *t.d* from arc *d.h*, it is necessary to know angle *e.z.g*, which without perceptible difference <note>A common phrase in Renaissance astronomy indicating that the margin of error is too small to affect observations.</note> is equal to angle *d.h.t*; yet this was not yet known from the previous premises, but only angle *e.b.g* was known. Therefore, for the knowledge of arcs *d.h*, *h.t*, and *t.d*, it is necessary to first know arc *e.d* and angle *e.z.g*, which is what was intended.

### Proposition 28.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin showing a vertical line crossing a primary axis with radiating lines. Points are labeled g, z, a, b, d, and e.</image-desc>

When the altitude circle stands orthogonally <note>At a right angle (90 degrees).</note> to the ecliptic: to show the arc between the pole of the horizon and the moon, and likewise the angle from the meeting of this altitude circle and the ecliptic.
¶ Let the portion of the ecliptic be *a.b.g*, and the portion of the altitude circle be *z.d.b.e* falling upon the ecliptic at right angles. Then the same will also become the circle of longitude of the moon’s position. Let *d* or *e* be the location of the moon. It is then clear that there is no parallax in longitude, because the altitude circle passes through the poles of the zodiac. Now let *z* be the pole of the horizon: since arc *z.b* is now known from the previous premises, and the latitude of the moon *b.d* or *b.e* is given, therefore arcs *z.d* or *z.e* will become known, which are sought. It is also clear that the angles at points *d* and *e* resulting from the altitude circle and the inclined circle of the moon differ imperceptibly from right angles, because of the small latitude [of the moon] during eclipses. Therefore, no discrepancy would follow if right angles were assumed for them.

<header>Fifth [Book]</header>

...having drawn arcs *a.d.* and *a.e.*, we seek the quantity of the arcs *a.d.* and *a.e.* and of the angles *b.a.d.* and *b.a.e.* In these calculations, Ptolemy <note>original: "Ptol."</note> uses arcs as if they were straight lines, because the difference between them is so small <note>In small-scale spherical geometry, astronomers often treated arcs as straight lines to simplify calculations without losing significant accuracy.</note>. Thus, since the angles *a.d.b.* are right angles, from the given arcs *a.b.*, *b.d.*, and *b.e.*, he finds the quantity of arcs *a.d.* and *a.e.* through the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>original: "per penultimā p:imi"; this refers to Proposition 47 of Book I of Euclid's *Elements*, better known as the Pythagorean theorem.</note>. From here, as if in right-angled rectilinear triangles, he finds the quantities of the angles *b.a.d.* and *b.a.e.* which were sought.
