## Proposition XXX.

**W**hen the circle of altitude falls obliquely upon the ecliptic: to verify the aforementioned arcs and angles.
¶ Let the portion of the ecliptic be *a.b.f.*, upon which the arc of altitude *z.b.k.* falls obliquely. Let *z* be the pole of the horizon <note>The zenith, or the point directly overhead.</note>. Let the circle of longitude of the moon's position be *d.b.e.*, which must intersect the ecliptic at a right angle. Let the moon be at *d* or *e*. Having drawn arcs *z.g.d.* and *z.e.t.*, from the arc *z.b.*, the angle *z.b.a.*, and the latitude of the moon *b.d.* or *b.e.*, we seek the arc *z.d.* or *z.e.* and the angle *z.g.a.* or *z.t.a.* Let us draw *d.k.* and *e.l.* as perpendicular arcs upon *z.b.k.* Once again, he uses the arcs as if they were straight lines because the difference is imperceptible. From the given angle *z.b.a.* and the right angle *e.b.a.*, the angle *e.b.l.* or *d.b.k.* will be known. Therefore, the ratio of *e.b.* to *e.l.* and *l.b.* is given. Similarly, the ratio of *b.d.* to *d.k.* and *k.d.* is given. And since the latitudes *b.e.* and *b.d.* are given, the arcs *d.k.*, *k.b.*, *e.l.*, and *l.b.* are also given. Thus, from *z.k.* and *k.d.*, the arc *z.d.* will be known as if in straight lines. Similarly, from *z.l.* and *l.e.*, he will know *z.e.* Wherefore, from the ratio of the sides of the triangles, the angles *d.z.k.* and *e.z.l.* will become known. But *d.z.k.* is the difference of the angles, and *z.t.b.* is smaller than angle *a.b.z.* Therefore, the angles *a.g.z.* and *a.t.z.* will become known, which were sought. 

Thus, Ptolemy, having set the arc *z.b.* at 45 degrees and the angle *a.b.z.* at 30 degrees—and likewise for the latitudes of the moon, namely *b.e.* at 5 degrees and similarly *b.d.* at 5 degrees—found the angle *b.z.t.* to be 5 degrees and four-fifths of one [degree]. And angle *b.z.d.* to be 5 degrees and one-sixth of one [degree]. Thus, angle *a.t.z.* is 24 degrees and one-fifth of one. And angle *a.g.z.* is 35 degrees and one-sixth of one. Furthermore, the arc *z.e.* was found by him to be 42 parts and 54 minutes, and arc *z.d.* to be 47 degrees and 54 minutes. Likewise, the greatest difference that can exist in the parallax <note>original: "diuersitate aspectus"; literally "diversity of aspect."</note> in latitude on account of the moon's latitude occurs when the moon is placed 90 degrees from the ascendant; because then there will be no parallax in longitude. And when the moon has a latitude of 5 degrees, the greatest difference of parallaxes that can happen because of this is almost 10 minutes. But when the latitude of the moon is at its maximum during a solar eclipse, which is almost one and a half degrees, the greatest difference of parallax that occurs because of it is one and a half minutes—which, however, happens very rarely.

# The Sixth Book most clearly explains the <term>conjunction<note>The meeting of the Sun and Moon in the same celestial longitude; a New Moon.</note></term> and <term>opposition<note>When the Sun and Moon are on opposite sides of the Earth; a Full Moon.</note></term> of the <term>two lights<note>original: "duorum luminarium"; referring to the Sun and the Moon.</note></term>: likewise the eclipse of each, along with the modes of their variations.

## Proposition I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc> **H**ow the time and place of the <term>mean conjunction<note>The calculated "average" alignment of the Sun and Moon, before accounting for the irregularities in their individual orbits.</note></term> of the lights may be found.
¶ **The example of Ptolemy:** in which he extracted the first mean conjunction in the years of <term>Nabonassar<note>original: "Nabuchodonosaris"; Ptolemy used the reign of the Babylonian King Nabonassar (beginning 747 BCE) as the starting epoch for his chronological calculations.</note></term>. From those things which were set forth in the previous books, he held that at noon on the first day of the month of <term>Thoth<note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar used by ancient astronomers because it had a fixed length of 30 days and no leap days, making it ideal for calculations.</note></term>, which was the beginning of the years of Nabonassar: the mean position of the sun was 45 minutes into the sign of <term>Pisces<note>original: "piscium"</note></term>. The mean <term>elongation<note>The angular distance between the Sun and the Moon as seen from Earth.</note></term> of the moon from the sun was 70 degrees and 37 minutes. The <term>argument of the sun<note>The "argument" (or anomaly) is the angular distance used to determine a celestial body's position in its orbit.</note></term>—which he called the distance of the mean position of the sun from its <term>apogee<note>original: "auge"; the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth.</note></term>—was 265 degrees and 15 minutes. The mean argument of the moon was 268 degrees and 49 minutes. And the distance of the mean position of the moon from the most northerly point of the <term>oblique circle<note>original: "circuli decliuis"; referring to the moon's tilted orbit relative to the ecliptic.</note></term> (which we call the mean <term>argument of latitude<note>The angle used to determine how far north or south the moon is from the ecliptic, essential for predicting if an eclipse will occur.</note></term> of the moon) was 354 degrees and 15 minutes. He therefore divided the mean elongation from the sun by the [daily] elongation of this kind—which occurs in one day—and there resulted 5 days, 47 minutes, and 33 seconds of one day. Therefore, the mean conjunction of the lights occurred 5 days and these [minutes/seconds] before the noon of the first day of the month of Thoth, with the one that immediately preceded it. But the lunar month—that is, the time from one mean conjunction to the next—comprises 29 days, 31 minutes, and 50 seconds of one day. Therefore, at 23 days, 44 minutes, and 17 seconds of one day from the noon of the first day of the month of Thoth, there was the next following mean conjunction of the lights. ¶ And so he established it to have been on the twenty-fourth day of the month of Thoth, at 44 minutes and 17 seconds after noon. ¶ Furthermore, he added the mean motions of the sun, the argument of the moon, and the argument of the moon's latitude for the 23 days, 44 minutes, and 17 seconds to the aforementioned <term>roots<note>The "roots" (radices) are the starting values or positions at the beginning of an era used for all subsequent calculations.</note></term>, and they resulted in the following for the predicted mean conjunction: the mean position of the lights was 24 degrees, 8 minutes, and 50 seconds of Pisces. The argument of the sun was 288 degrees, 38 minutes, and 50 seconds. The mean argument of the moon was 218 degrees, 57 minutes, and 15 seconds. The mean argument of the latitude of the moon, calculating from the most northerly point, was 308 degrees, 17 minutes, and 21 seconds. You may act in a similar manner to this example in other cases.

of **Nabonassar** <note>original: "Nabuchodonosaris"; while this is the Latin name for Nebuchadnezzar, in an astronomical context it refers to the Era of Nabonassar, beginning in 747 BCE.</note>. And in the line corresponding to it is the time of the first mean conjunction, namely: the 24th day of the month of **Thoth**, 44 minutes, 17 seconds. Likewise, the <term>arguments<note>An "argument" in astronomy is a value used to determine the position of a celestial body along its orbit.</note></term> of the Sun, the Moon, and the mean latitude of the Moon were recorded as found in the preceding section. In the second line, he placed the twenty-sixth year of Nabonassar. Across from this number, he considered the time—namely the days and minutes of the month of Thoth—in which the first mean conjunction occurred. He calculated the arguments for the Sun, Moon, and the Moon's latitude using this method: that in every twenty-five Egyptian years, the mean conjunctions would occur earlier by 2 minutes, 47 seconds, and 7 thirds of a day. Therefore, by subtracting this number, he completed the table of time for the first conjunction up to the 1101st year of Nabonassar. During this time, the mean motion of the Sun, beyond full revolutions, was 353 degrees, 52 minutes, 34 seconds, and 13 thirds. The mean argument of the Moon was 57 degrees, 21 minutes, 44 seconds, and 1 third; and the mean argument of the Moon's latitude was 117 degrees, 12 minutes, 49 seconds, and 54 thirds. By adding these movements to the first roots, he completed the entire "first difference," which is the table of mean conjunctions in **collected years** <note>A table showing data for groups of years, typically in 25-year increments.</note>.

In a similar fashion, he established the "second difference," which is for mean <term>oppositions<note>A Full Moon, when the Sun and Moon are 180 degrees apart.</note></term>. For he stated that a mean lunar month is 14 days, 45 minutes, and 55 seconds. The mean motion of the Sun in this time is 14 degrees, 33 minutes, and 12 seconds. The mean argument of the Moon is 192 degrees, 54 minutes, and 30 seconds. The mean argument of latitude is 195 degrees, 20 minutes, and 6 seconds. When these are subtracted from the roots of the first conjunction of the first year of Nabonassar, there remain the roots of the first mean opposition for that same year of Nabonassar. Having obtained these, he continued them just as he did the roots of the conjunctions, up to the 1101st year of Nabonassar.

Then he completed the "third difference," which is for conjunctions and oppositions in **expanded years** <note>A table showing data for each individual year within a cycle.</note>. He considered the excess of 13 <term>lunations<note>The time between two successive new moons.</note></term> over 365 days, which was 18 days, 53 minutes, 51 seconds, and 48 thirds. Likewise, in the time of these 13 lunations, the mean motion of the Sun was 18 degrees, 22 minutes, 59 seconds, and 14 thirds. The mean argument of the Moon was 335 degrees, 37 minutes, 12 seconds, and 51 thirds. He also considered the span of twelve lunations, which was 354 days, 24 minutes, 1 second, and 40 thirds. In this time, the motion of the Sun was 349 degrees, 16 minutes, 36 seconds, and 16 thirds. The argument of the Moon was 309 degrees, 48 minutes, 1 second, and 53 thirds. The mean argument of latitude was 8 degrees, 2 minutes, 49 seconds, and 42 thirds. From these, he completed the table of expanded years up to 25 years. Sometimes he did this by adding twelve lunations with their motions to the numbers placed in the first line and then subtracting 365 days; sometimes he added the aforementioned excess of thirteen lunations with its motions—specifically when he saw that if he had added the excess for twelve lunations, it would have resulted in more than one additional lunation.

Finally, he set down the table of months, which he extended to 12. For one lunation was 29 days, 31 minutes, 50 seconds, 4 thirds, and 20 fourths. In this time, the mean motion of the Sun is 29 degrees, 6 minutes, 23 seconds, and 1 third. The argument of the Moon is 25 degrees, 49 minutes, 0 seconds, and 8 thirds. The argument of latitude is 30 degrees, 40 minutes, 14 seconds, and 9 thirds. From these, he completes the table of months by way of addition.

### Proposition 4.

->To consider the true motion of the Moon in an hour.<-

It is necessary to first know the true motions of the Sun and Moon in an hour. This is a common requirement, and the most certain way is to find the **equation** <note>In historical astronomy, an "equation" is a correction added to or subtracted from the "mean" (average) position to find the "true" position, accounting for the body's varying speed in its elliptical or eccentric orbit.</note> of the Sun and the Moon at the start of that hour, and likewise at its end. The difference between these two positions will be the hourly motion you seek. 

There is an easier way, which provides the method for building a table of true hourly motion: Consider the equation of the **Sun's argument** <note>The "argument" is the specific angle or position used as the input to look up a correction in a table.</note> for the time you wish to find the Sun's true hourly motion. Note the difference between this equation and the equation for an argument that is exactly one degree larger. From this difference, take a proportional part based on the ratio of 2 minutes and 28 seconds to 60 minutes. Subtract this from 2 minutes and 28 seconds if the Sun's argument is less than 93 degrees; add it if it is more, up to 180 degrees. The result will be the true motion of the Sun in an hour. This is how you construct the table for a semicircle. The reason for this is that the Sun's argument increases by 2 minutes and 28 seconds every hour.

Likewise, do the same for the Moon. Consider the equation of the given Moon’s argument, and the equation for an argument one degree larger. From their difference, take the proportional part based on the ratio of 41 minutes and 49 seconds to 60 minutes. Subtract this from 32 minutes and 56 seconds if the argument was less than 45 degrees, or add it if it was greater than 45 degrees up to 180. This is how you construct the table for the semicircle. 

**The Reason:** because the true argument of the Moon one hour after or before a mean conjunction differs from the mean argument at the hour of the mean conjunction by the mean motion of the argument in an hour, and the equation of the center which corresponds to one hour is 41 minutes and 49 seconds. Furthermore, the Moon's equations increase up to 35 degrees of the argument, and after that, they decrease toward the semicircle. Once you have the true hourly motions of the Sun and Moon, subtract the Sun's motion from the Moon's motion, and the result will be the **excess** <note>original: "superatio"; this refers to the difference in speed between the faster Moon and the slower Sun.</note> you seek.

### Proposition 5.

To calculate the true application of the **luminaries** <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note> and their position. 

From the previous instructions, first learn the mean **application** <note>An "application" is the moment two celestial bodies reach the same longitude (conjunction) or opposite longitudes (opposition).</note> using the arguments of the Sun and Moon. From these, according to the higher teachings, you may determine the true positions of the luminaries. If the positions match, the time of the mean application is the time of the true application. If they differ, note their difference. 

To this difference—following the method of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Almagest" was the foundation of this science.</note>—add its twelfth part, because the Sun moves approximately that much in the intervening time. Divide the total by the true hourly motion of the Moon found in the previous proposition. 

Or, even better: divide their simple difference by the true **hourly excess** of the Moon. The time resulting from this division is the interval between the true and mean application. The true application will follow the mean if the Sun’s position was ahead of the Moon’s position. If, however, the Moon's position was ahead of the Sun, then the mean followed the true according to the time calculated from the division. From this, the Sun's hourly motion multiplied by the time interval between the true and mean application will produce the Sun's true motion during that time; this reveals the exact place of the true application. Truly, because this calculation is sometimes insufficient—though it is close to the truth—it will be necessary to apply an equation to the time found in this way...

## Proposition 6.

To derive the semidiameters of the shadow and the moon from two eclipses in which the moon was near its closer distance <note>In historical astronomy, "closer longitude" or "closer distance" refers to the perigee—the point in the moon's orbit where it is nearest to the Earth.</note> on the epicycle.

The first [eclipse] was in the eighth year of the era of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabon:" – An astronomical era beginning in 747 BCE, famously used by the astronomer Ptolemy.</note>, which was 574 years after the beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosaris"</note>. It occurred after 27 days of the month of Phamenoth <note>original: "phumemt" – the seventh month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> had passed; the morning of which was the 28th day. It lasted from the beginning of the eighth hour to the end of the tenth hour. The greatest part of the eclipsed portion was from the north side and measured 7 digits <note>A "digit" is a traditional measure of an eclipse, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body.</note>. The mean time <note>The time calculated based on average motion rather than specific orbital fluctuations.</note> was two and a half temporal hours after midnight, with the sun at 7 degrees of Taurus. The time from the beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar was 573 years, 206 days, 14 hours, and one-third of a time-unit of difference; but of mean time, it was exactly 14 hours until the middle of this eclipse. The mean location of the moon was 7 degrees and 49 minutes of Scorpio; the true location was 6 degrees and 19 minutes of the same. The argument <note>An "argument" is the mathematical value or angle used to find a specific position in astronomical tables.</note> was 160 degrees and 40 minutes, and the argument of latitude from the northernmost point was 98 degrees and 20 minutes.

The second [eclipse] was in the year 607 of the years of Nebuchadnezzar, after two days of the month of Tybi <note>original: "Tobi" – the fifth month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> had passed; the morning of which was the third day, one and five-sixths equal hours <note>original: "ho:a vna eqli: medietate & tertia" (one hour, a half, and a third).</note> before midnight. The eclipsed portion on the southern side was 3 digits, with the sun at 5 and one-eighth degrees of Aquarius. The time from the beginning of the years of Nebuchadnezzar was 606 Egyptian years, 91 days, 10 hours, and one-sixth of an hour of both times. The Moon, according to its mean motion, was at 5 degrees and 15 minutes of Leo; according to its true motion, 5 degrees and 8 minutes of the same. The argument was 178 degrees and 46 minutes. The argument of latitude from the northernmost point was 80 degrees and 36 minutes.

Because the distance of the moon from the node <note>The "node" is the point where the moon's orbit crosses the path of the sun (the ecliptic).</note> in the first eclipse was 8 degrees and 20 minutes, its southern latitude was 43 minutes and 3 seconds. And in the second, the distance from the node was 10 degrees and 3 minutes; its southern latitude was 54 minutes and five-sixths <note>original: "medietas & tertia" (a half and a third).</note>. The difference of the eclipsed parts was one-third of the moon's diameter. And the difference of the latitudes was 11 minutes and 47 seconds. It is necessary, therefore, that the entire diameter of the moon was 35 minutes and one-third. A quarter of this is 8 minutes and five-sixths; namely, the eclipsed part in the second eclipse is equal to the part of the diameter from the edge of the shadow to the center of the moon. When that is subtracted from the latitude of the moon in the second eclipse, there remain 46 minutes for the semidiameter of the shadow at the location of the moon's crossing, while the moon is near the opposite of the apogee <note>The "opposite of the apogee" is the perigee, the closest point to Earth.</note> of the epicycle. Thus, the same ratio of the moon’s semidiameter to the shadow’s semidiameter was found again as before, and so he confirmed it.

Some find the semidiameters of the moon and shadow during conjunctions—when the moon is between the apogee of the epicycle and its opposite—from those values found at the apogee and the opposite in this way: Let the epicycle be **a**, **b**, **g** around center **d**. In the conjunctions, **a** is the apogee, **b** is the opposite of the apogee [perigee], and **e** is the center of the world [Earth]. Let the moon be at **g**. The semidiameter of the moon at **a** is the smallest; at **b** it is the largest that can be in conjunctions. The difference is known from what was said: let it be **l**, **m**, **g**, **z**. Let the sine of the argument be **a**, **g**; therefore, **g**, **z** will be a known sine, and similarly **z**, **g** a used sine. But **a**, **b** is known in those parts where **d**, **e** is 60; therefore, in those same parts **a**, **z**, **g**, **z**, and **z**, **d** will become known. Hence **e**, **z** is known; from this **e**, **g** is known, which is equal to **e**, **h**; therefore **a**, **h** is given. Without a sensible difference, the ratio of **b**, **a** to **a**, **b** is as **l**, **m** is to the increase by which the semidiameter of the moon existing at **g** exceeds its semidiameter existing at **a**. Therefore, that increase will be known. From this, the semidiameter of the shadow will become known. However, a more certain way of finding this is given in [Proposition] 22 of the fifth book. Having shown the quantities of the semidiameters of the moon and shadow at their greatest approach to the earth at the time of an eclipse, the boundaries of the eclipses are defined as follows.

## Proposition 7.

**To determine the limits of solar eclipses.**

From the preceding [proposition], it is clear that the maximum semidiameter of the moon in eclipses is 17 minutes and 40 seconds. The semidiameter of the sun, however, is found from earlier sections to be 15 minutes and 40 seconds. Although this value is variable due to the eccentricity of the sun’s orbit <note>Eccentricity refers to the sun's path being slightly off-center from the Earth, causing its apparent size to change slightly as it gets closer or further away.</note>, it is not considered here, as the difference is almost imperceptible. Therefore, at the moment of contact in a solar eclipse, the distance between the centers of both <term>luminaries<note>A traditional term for the sun and the moon.</note></term> becomes 33 minutes and 20 seconds. 

Furthermore, the maximum <term>parallax<note>original: "diuersitas aspectus" — the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note></term> in latitude that can occur across the <term>seven climates<note>Historical geographic zones categorized by the length of their longest day, used by ancient and medieval astronomers to organize observations.</note></term> commonly listed is 58 minutes toward the south; at that time, the greatest possible parallax in longitude is 15 minutes. But toward the north, the parallax in latitude is 8 minutes, and the parallax in longitude is 30 minutes. 

Additionally, the greatest difference that can occur between the "true place of true conjunction" and the "mean place of mean conjunction" <note>The "mean" position is based on average circular motion, while the "true" position accounts for the actual, irregular speeds of the planets.</note> is 3 degrees. This is found if the maximum equations <note>The "equation" is the correction added to the mean motion to find the true motion.</note> of the luminaries are joined together, and a thirteenth part of the total is taken, and then a thirteenth part of that again. This is because while the moon travels through the sum of the maximum equations, the sun meanwhile travels through a thirteenth part of this distance. And while the moon crosses this thirteenth part, the sun also moves through a thirteenth of that. Therefore, what the sun covers in the time the moon passes the sum of the maximum equations is roughly the twelfth part of that sum. If this twelfth part is joined with the maximum equation of the sun, the result is the greatest possible gap between the mean place of mean conjunction and the true place of true conjunction. According to the calculations of <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose "Almagest" defined astronomy for over a millennium.</note></term>, this is 3 degrees, and it is almost equal to the difference between the mean <term>argument of latitude<note>The angular distance of the moon from its "node," the point where its path crosses the ecliptic.</note></term> at the hour of mean conjunction and the true argument of latitude at the hour of true conjunction. For the latter does not differ from the former except by the movement of the <term>head<note>The "Head of the Dragon," or the Ascending Node of the moon’s orbit.</note></term> during this time.

<margin>
[Diagram showing the intersection of the ecliptic and the lunar orbit, illustrating the angles and points (a, b, d, e, g, k) used to calculate the eclipse limits.]
</margin>

Let the <term>ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the sun across the sky.</note></term> therefore be *a-b*, and the lunar orbit be *b-d*. Let *d* be the true place of the moon, but let its visible place at the time of visible conjunction be *e*. Let the arc *a-e-g* be perpendicular to the ecliptic, where *a* is the place of the sun. Therefore, *e* will be the seen place of the moon on its path. Let *a-3* be the semidiameter of the sun, and *c-3* be the semidiameter of the moon. Let *d-e* be the parallax in the circle of altitude. Then *d-g* will be roughly the parallax in longitude, and *e-g* the parallax in latitude. 

Therefore, when the parallax in latitude is toward the south—which always happens when the moon is south of the pole of the horizon—*e-g* is 58 minutes. Since *a-e* <note>The combined semidiameters.</note> is 33 minutes and 20 seconds, the total distance *a-g* becomes 1 degree, 31 minutes, and 20 seconds. The ratio of *a-g* to *g-b* is nearly 1 to 11 and a half. This is clear from the maximum latitude of the moon and the method given earlier for tabulating the ecliptic's declination and the moon’s latitude. Thus, the arc *b-g* will be roughly 17 degrees and 30 minutes. 

However, since *g* is the place of the visible conjunction, let us assume the true conjunction is yet to happen. While the moon travels the arc *g-d* (which is 15 minutes), the sun meanwhile travels a twelfth part of this distance, which we call arc *g-k*. Therefore, *k* will be the place of the true conjunction. Thus, the arc *b-k* will be roughly 17 degrees and 31 minutes. Let us also assume the mean conjunction is still to come. But between the true place of the true conjunction and the mean place of the mean conjunction—as touched upon above—there can be a gap of 3 degrees. Therefore, the center of the <term>epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent), used to explain planetary retrograde motion.</note></term> at the mean conjunction will be distant from the node by roughly 20 and a half degrees. 

But when the parallax in latitude *e-g* is toward the north (the maximum being 8 minutes), with the moon still in southern latitude, understand *b-g* to be the southern portion of the lunar path from the ecliptic; *a-g* will then be 41 minutes. From this, according to the stated ratio, *b-g* will be nearly 7 degrees and 52 minutes. The value of *g-d* is 30, a twelfth of which is roughly 3 minutes. Thus, *k-b* will be 7 degrees and 55 minutes; to which *k-b*, namely 3 degrees [is added...].

<header>Book Six</header>

...added together make almost 10 degrees and 55 minutes. Ptolemy, however, added those three degrees to the aggregate of the distance of the moon’s visible place at the time of visible conjunction and the <term>parallax<note>original: "diuersitate aspectus"</note></term> in longitude. These degrees represent the maximum difference between the "mean place of mean conjunction" and the "true place of true conjunction" <note>Medieval astronomers distinguished between "mean" motion (calculated as a perfectly uniform circle) and "true" motion (the actual observed position, which varies due to the elliptical-like nature of orbits).</note>. It is necessary that these be added to the distance of the true place of the moon at the hour of true conjunction, so that the distance of the center of the moon's <term>epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent), used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain the varying speeds and directions of planets.</note></term> from the <term>node<note>The point where the moon's path crosses the ecliptic (the sun's path). Eclipses can only happen near these points.</note></term> at the hour of mean conjunction is produced. This is because it is possible for the moon to appear to touch the sun to the eye. Therefore, its eclipse limits are slightly larger. 

We have, therefore, for all seven <term>climates<note>Geographic zones of the known world.</note></term>, these solar eclipse limits: specifically, the mean argument of latitude <note>The "argument of latitude" is the angular distance of the moon from its node.</note> is 10 degrees and 55 minutes south of the node, and the argument of latitude is almost 20 degrees north of the node. Outside of these limits, there is no possibility of a solar eclipse in the said climates; but when the center of the moon’s epicycle is within these limits during a mean conjunction, a solar eclipse is possible. However, <term>Albategni<note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a renowned Arab astronomer whose precise observations corrected several of Ptolemy's earlier findings.</note></term>, because he uses different quantities for the semidiameters or the maximum equations, states these limits are 10 degrees and 40 minutes in the south, and 20 degrees and 12 minutes in the north.

### Proposition 8.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin showing a large circle (the ecliptic) intersected by an arc representing the moon's path. Two smaller circles, labeled 'g' and 'a', are shown touching at point 's', representing the lunar disk and the earth's shadow at the first point of contact.</image-desc>

->**To determine the limits of a lunar eclipse.**<-

Let **a.b.** be the ecliptic and **b.g.** the inclined circle of the moon. Let **a** be the center of the shadow and **g** the center of the moon. When the visual circles of the shadow and the moon first touch at point **s**, the distance **g.s.** <note>The moon's radius.</note> will be 17 minutes and 40 seconds, and **s.a.** <note>The shadow's radius.</note> will be 45 minutes and 56 seconds. Therefore, the total distance **a.g.** becomes 1 degree, 3 minutes, and 36 seconds. Consequently, according to the stated proportion, the distance **g.b.** <note>The distance along the ecliptic from the node to the moon's center.</note> becomes almost 12 degrees and 12 minutes. If the mean opposition follows the true opposition by the maximum possible distance, the 3 degrees previously mentioned must be added, resulting in 15 degrees and 12 minutes as the maximum distance of the center of the moon’s epicycle from the node during opposition at which the moon can touch the circle of the shadow without an eclipse. Outside of this limit, it is not possible for the moon to be eclipsed. Albategni, however, states this limit to be 14 degrees and 45 minutes.

### Proposition 9.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin consisting of two concentric circles representing the celestial sphere and the moon's orbit. Multiple points (a, e, b, f, g, l, d, k) are marked along the circles to demonstrate the calculation of eclipse limits over a six-month period.</image-desc>

->**It is possible for either the sun or the moon to suffer an eclipse twice within six months.**<-

Let us understand **a.b.g.d.** to be the inclined circle of the moon, which intersects the ecliptic at the nodes **a** and **g** (the <term>Head and Tail<note>The ascending and descending nodes, historically called the Dragon's Head and Tail.</note></term>). Let the northern half be **a.b.g.** and the southern half **g.d.a.** Let the eclipse limits on the northern side be **e.f.** and on the southern side be **k.l.** Thus, in solar eclipses, **a.e.** and **f.g.** will each be 20 degrees, and the mean values **f.e.**, **d.g.**, **l.**, and **a.k.** will be 10 degrees and 55 minutes. Therefore, the arc **e.b.f.** contains 139 degrees. Now, the mean motion of the argument of latitude in six equal lunar months is 184 degrees and 1 minute (once full revolutions are removed). Therefore, the motion of the argument of latitude in six months is greater than arc **e.b.f.** and smaller than arc **f.d.e.** 

It is possible, therefore, that if the motion of latitude is currently within the eclipse limit, it may fall within the eclipse limit again after six months, and thus the sun may be eclipsed twice in six months. Likewise, in lunar eclipses, the arcs of the limits will be 15 degrees and 12 minutes; therefore both **e.b.f.** and **l.d.k.** will be 149 degrees and 36 minutes. The stated motion of the argument of latitude will be greater than both of these, yet smaller than arc **k.b.l.** or **f.d.e.** It will thus be evident that what the proposition states is true.

<header>Book Six</header>

It is possible for the moon to be eclipsed twice within a period of **five months**. Whenever this happens, it is necessary that the darkness <note>original: "tenebre"; referring to the Earth's shadow covering the moon</note> extends toward the same side in both eclipses.
¶ For let it be that in these five months the sun moves from the <term>mean distance<note>The point in the orbit between the closest and farthest points from the center of motion.</note></term> of its <term>eccentric orbit<note>original: "ecentrici"; an orbital path where the Earth is not at the exact center, used to explain why the sun appears to move at different speeds.</note></term> through its <term>perigee<note>original: "propior"; the point where the sun is closest to the Earth.</note></term> toward the other mean distance. The sun's motion will then be at its fastest. Meanwhile, the moon on its <term>epicycle<note>A smaller circle carrying the moon, which itself moves along a larger orbital circle.</note></term> completes its motion through the upper part of the epicycle, beyond its full revolutions, where its speed is slowest. Thus, these five months will be longer <note>That is, the time taken for these five "synodic" months (from full moon to full moon) is greater than average.</note>, during which the sun moves with its greater motion and the moon with its lesser. The **mean motion** of the sun and moon in five average months, after subtracting full revolutions, will be **145 degrees and 32 minutes**.
And so that the sun's closest distance <note>perigee</note> divides this motion equally, the <term>solar equation<note>original: "equatio solis"; a correction factor added or subtracted to account for the difference between mean and actual observed position.</note></term> taken from both sides will add **4 degrees and 38 minutes** to the mean course. However, the motion of the moon on its epicycle in five months is **129 degrees and 15 minutes**. Let the farthest distance <note>apogee</note> of the epicycle also divide this equally; thus, the equation taken from both sides will subtract **8 degrees and 40 minutes** from the mean course. Therefore, in the time of those five months when the sun is fast and the moon is slow in its course, the sun will precede the moon by **13 degrees and 18 minutes**. That is to say, the true motion of the sun is greater than the true motion of the moon by this amount. But while the moon travels this distance until it catches up with the sun, the sun moves a twelfth part of this, which is **1 degree and 6 minutes**. If this twelfth is added to the 4 degrees and 38 minutes which was the difference between the sun's true and mean motion, the result is **5 degrees and 44 minutes**; this is the amount by which five "long" months exceed five "mean" months. In such arrangements, the first of these true <term>oppositions<note>Full moons, when the Earth is between the sun and moon.</note></term> must have preceded the mean opposition by as much time as the last one follows the mean. It is established that the difference in the positions of the <term>conjunctions<note>original: "applicationum"</note></term>—the true compared to the true, and the mean compared to the mean—is nearly equal to the difference in the <term>argument of latitude<note>The angular distance of the moon from the point where its path crosses the sun's path.</note></term> between the true and the mean. Therefore, the difference in the arguments of latitude between the true and mean in the aforesaid five months will be nearly **5 degrees and 44 minutes**.
But the mean argument of latitude in five average months is **153 degrees and 21 minutes**. Therefore, the true argument of latitude in five true lunar months is **159 degrees and 5 minutes**. Finally, the lunar eclipse limits when the moon is at the mean distance of its epicycle are **11 degrees and 30 minutes**. For then the combined <term>semidiameters<note>Half the width of the moon and the Earth's shadow.</note></term> of the moon and the shadow is one degree; this is because when the moon is at the <term>apogee<note>original: "auge"; the farthest point</note></term> of its epicycle during these conjunctions, such a total is **56 minutes and 24 seconds**, but at its perigee <note>original: "propiori longitudine"</note> it becomes **1 degree, 3 minutes, and 36 seconds**. Look now at the figure provided: each of the arcs **e-f** and **l-k** will be **157 degrees**. This is less than the true argument of latitude in the longer five-month period by **2 degrees and 5 minutes**. If, therefore, this motion of latitude **a-b-e** began at one degree in arc **a-e** and ended in arc **f-g** at nearly one degree **a-b-f**, it is possible for a lunar eclipse to occur in both. This is also shown through the arc **l-d-k**. And while this motion is through arc **e-b-f**, the southern part of the moon will be obscured in both eclipses; but through arc **l-d-k**, the northern part will be obscured. However, such eclipses are almost imperceptible.

A horizontal line passes through the middle. Several points are labeled with lowercase letters: 'b' at the very top of the outer circle, 'd' at the bottom. ## Proposition xi.

It is **not possible** for a lunar eclipse to be repeated in the **seventh month**.
¶ The demonstration is similar to the preceding one. Let us take seven minimum months for this purpose; they are possible, and it is necessary that in these the sun moves at its slowest course and the moon at its fastest, compared to seven equal months. The mean motion of the luminaries <note>The sun and the moon</note> is **205 degrees and 45 minutes**. The argument...

<summary>This page uses geometry and motion calculations to prove that two lunar eclipses can occur five months apart under specific conditions, while a seven-month interval between eclipses is physically impossible.</summary>

...argument of the moon is 180 degrees and 45 minutes. Let it be that the sun's farthest distance <note>apogee; the point where the sun is furthest from Earth</note> divides the sun's mean motion equally, and the moon's closest distance <note>perigee; the point where the moon is closest to Earth</note> divides this argument equally. Therefore, let the solar <term>equation<note>A correction factor used to account for the difference between the average (mean) position of a planet and its actual observed position.</note></term> taken from both sides subtract 4 degrees and 42 minutes from the mean motion, and the lunar equation add 9 degrees and 58 minutes to the mean motion. Thus, in this time of 7 months, the mean motion of the sun will be less than the true motion of the moon by 14 degrees and 40 minutes. One-twelfth of this is 1 degree and 13 minutes, which when added to the solar equation makes 5 degrees and 55 minutes—this is the quantity by which the true sun in seven "shorter" months <note>months where the orbital speeds make the time between full moons shorter than average</note> falls short of the sun's mean course in seven equal months. But the true <term>argument of latitude<note>The moon's position along its orbit relative to the nodes, where it crosses the sun's path.</note></term> in seven shorter months also differs by this same amount from the mean argument of latitude in seven mean months. The mean argument of latitude in seven mean months is 214 degrees and 42 minutes; therefore, the true argument of latitude in seven shorter months will be 208 degrees and 47 minutes. However, the entire arc in Figure *k b l* or *f d e* is only 203 degrees, while the moon is at the mean distance of its <term>epicycle<note>A smaller circle on which a planet moves, while the center of that circle moves around a larger orbit.</note></term>. Therefore, it is not possible that if the moon is eclipsed at the first <term>opposition<note>A full moon, when the sun and moon are on opposite sides of the Earth.</note></term> of seven shorter months, it would also be eclipsed at the last of them, which was what was proposed.

->Proposition 12<-

<margin>
<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram showing geometric constructions of arcs and intersecting lines. Points are labeled with lowercase letters: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m, n, o, p, q. The diagram illustrates calculations for the conditions under which solar eclipses occur over a five-month cycle.</image-desc>
</margin>

For the sun to be eclipsed twice in five months across many inhabited regions of the Earth is not entirely impossible.

To demonstrate this, let us assume five "long" months <note>synodic months that last longer than the average of 29.5 days due to the varying speeds of the sun and moon</note>, as was shown in the previous section. The true motion of the moon's latitude in these is 159 degrees and 5 minutes. The sum of the two <term>semidiameters<note>The radius of the visible disks of the sun and moon.</note></term> of the sun and the moon, when they are at their mean distances, is 32 minutes and 20 seconds. This is the average between the sum at the <term>apogee<note>original: "auge"; the point in the orbit furthest from Earth</note></term> and the sum at the <term>perigee<note>original: "opposito augis"; the point opposite the apogee, where the body is closest to Earth</note></term>. Therefore, if the moon's <term>latitude<note>The moon's angular distance north or south of the ecliptic (the sun's path).</note></term> is 32 minutes and 20 seconds, the moon's distance from the <term>node<note>The point where the moon's path crosses the sun's path.</note></term> will be 6 degrees and 12 minutes. Thus, the arc *e b f* (or *l d k*), within which an eclipse does not occur, becomes 167 degrees and 36 minutes. It is clear, then, that if the moon has no <term>parallax<note>original: "diversitatem aspectus"; the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth.</note></term> in latitude, it is not possible for there to be two solar eclipses in five long months, because the arc *e b f* (or *l d k*) is larger than the true motion of latitude in five long months—larger, I say, by nearly 8 degrees and 31 minutes. 

And if we arrange the true motion of latitude so that it is divided equally by point *b* (the point of maximum <term>declination<note>Distance from the celestial equator.</note></term>), each of its ends will be about 10 degrees and 28 minutes from the node. The latitude at these points is 54 minutes. When the sum of the semidiameters of the sun and moon is subtracted from this, there remains about 22 minutes of excess latitude at the boundaries of the true motion of latitude over that sum. When taken twice—that is, on either side of point *b*—this makes 45 minutes, which is also the latitude of 8 degrees and 31 minutes of the argument of latitude, as shown by the frequently mentioned ratio of 1 to 11.5. For this ratio is preserved everywhere around the eclipse limits: just as *g f* is to *f o*, so is *g n* to *n p*; and so also is *f n* to *n m*, while *n p* is equal to *f o*. Thus, when *f n* is 8 degrees and 31 minutes, the difference *m n* (that is, the excess of *n p* over *f o*) will be 45 minutes. To know at what hours and places these eclipses might happen, we must look at the duration of five long months, which is determined as follows: five equal months contain 147 days, 15 hours, and three-quarters of an hour. In this time—as has been shown—when the moon is slow in its course and the sun is fast, the true motion of the sun is greater than the true motion of the moon by 13 degrees and 18 minutes. While the moon travels through this space in the middle of its path to catch up with the sun, the sun meanwhile travels one-twelfth of this distance. Let the total therefore be 14 degrees and 24 minutes. If this is divided by the mean daily course of the moon, the result is one day and two hours...

and a quarter of one hour. For the moon in such conjunctions moves at nearly its <term>mean motion<note>The average speed of a celestial body, assuming a perfectly circular orbit.</note></term>. Therefore, the difference between five "longer" months <note>months where the orbital speeds are slower than average due to the bodies being near their apogees</note> and five mean months is one day, two hours, and a quarter; wherefore the total time of five longer months becomes approximately 148 days and 18 hours. Also, the true motion of the sun in the predicted time of five longer months, as gathered from the previous premise, is approximately 151 degrees. In such conjunctions at the said hours and places, while the combined parallaxes in latitude do not reach 45 minutes <note>at the equator</note>, starting from the second climate and moving toward the north, they exceed 45 minutes. Therefore, in these northern regions, it is possible to see a solar eclipse twice in five months. The further north the region, the greater the possibility, because the parallax in latitude increases. Nor does this happen unless the moon has moved once in northern latitude from the <term>head<note>The ascending node, or "Dragon's Head," where the moon crosses the sun's path going north.</note></term> toward the <term>tail<note>The descending node, or "Dragon's Tail," where the moon crosses the sun's path going south.</note></term>, such that in the first eclipse it was near point *e* and in the second near point *f*.

### Proposition 13.

<sig>r.iii.</sig>

->A solar eclipse can occur twice in seven months for the same region of the earth.<-

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram depicting astronomical orbits or eclipse paths. It consists of a large main circle and an overlapping or eccentric inner circle. On the left side, several points 'f', 'e', 'n', and 'p' are marked on the arc, with lines connecting them towards the center and intersecting at points 'c' and 'o'. Let there be seven "shorter" months. In these, it has been shown that the true <term>argument of latitude<note>The distance of the moon from its nodes, which determines how far it is from the sun's path.</note></term> is 208 degrees and 47 minutes. But the arc *f d e* from the previous premise is 192 degrees and 24 minutes, which is the distance from the eclipse limit approaching the tail to the eclipse limit receding from the head. It is clear, therefore, that if the moon has no parallax in latitude, it is not possible for the sun to be eclipsed twice in these seven months; namely, in the first of these conjunctions and the last, because 208 degrees and 47 minutes exceeds the arc *f d e* by 16 degrees and 23 minutes. Moreover, if the arc of the true place of latitude is arranged so that point *d* (which is the maximum southern latitude) divides it equally, each of its limits will be 14 degrees and 23 minutes from the node. From the latitude corresponding twice to these points, once the sum of the <term>semidiameters<note>Half the width of the sun and moon disks.</note></term> of the luminaries is subtracted, the doubled excess makes approximately 1 degree and 25 minutes. And such is also the latitude for an argument of latitude of 16 degrees and 23 minutes, as is evident from the ratio of 1 to 11 and a half <note>A geometric ratio used to calculate the moon's latitudinal deviation from the ecliptic.</note>. Thus, if you begin to calculate the true argument of latitude from *b f*, proceeding through *d*, it exceeds the arc *f d e* by the said degrees, which are *e n*. However, its latitude (namely *n p*) will exceed the latitude of point *e* (which is *c o*, i.e., the sum of the semidiameters of the luminaries) in the proportional part to 16 degrees 23 minutes, according to the ratio of 1 to 11 and a half; and that is *n m*, which is 1 degree 25 minutes. It is clear then: if a solar eclipse is to return in the seventh month, it is necessary for the moon to have a parallax in one of these conjunctions, or a combined parallax from both, which is greater than 1 degree and 25 minutes. It must be seen, however, in which hours and in which places this can happen. The time of seven equal months contains approximately 206 days and 17 hours, in which the sun moves at a slower pace and the moon moves at a faster one. And the mean motion of the sun is less than the true motion of the moon by 14 degrees and 40 minutes; an arc which the moon, along with its twelfth part, traverses at mean motion in one day.

five hours. Therefore, seven minor months <note>Months shorter than the average lunar cycle due to the speed of the celestial bodies in their orbits.</note>, which are the shortest possible, contain 205 days and 12 hours. ## ->Proposition XIV.<-

<margin>
<image-desc>
A circular astronomical diagram consisting of several concentric rings and overlapping circular paths. Various points on the circles are labeled with minuscule letters: a, b, d, e, f, g, k, l, m, n, o, p, q, r, s, t. It is entirely impossible for a solar eclipse to occur twice
in a single month for people of the same climate.
Although the agreement of all causes for this is impossible,
let us nevertheless assume for the sake of imagination that the causes are gathered together:
namely, that the moon is at its <term>perigee<note>original: "longitudine propiori"; the point where the moon is closest to Earth.</note></term> during the conjunctions, and thus has the greatest parallax in latitude; that the <term>lunation<note>The time from one new moon to the next.</note></term> is the shortest possible, and thus the true motion of the <term>argument of latitude<note>The distance of the moon from its node.</note></term> in a month is minimized, adding as little as possible to the arc of the inclined circle contained between the two solar eclipse limits; and that those conjunctions occur at the hours and places where the greatest parallaxes occur. Because, therefore, in one equal month the mean motion of the <term>luminaries<note>The Sun and the Moon.</note></term> is 29 degrees and 6 minutes, and the argument of the moon is 25 degrees and 49 minutes.
Suppose that the solar apogee divides this arc of the mean sun equally, and the lunar perigee also divides the lunar argument equally. Let it be that the solar <term>equation<note>The correction applied to mean motion to account for the elliptical nature of the orbit.</note></term> taken from both sides subtracts 1 degree and 8 minutes from the mean sun, and the lunar argument adds 2 degrees and 28 minutes. These combined equations make 3 degrees and 36 minutes. The twelfth part of this—namely 18 minutes—if added to the solar equation, produces 1 degree and 26 minutes; this is the difference by which the true motion of the sun in a minimum month falls short of the mean motion of the sun in an equal month. But the true argument of latitude in a minimum month also differs by nearly the same amount from the mean argument of latitude in an equal month. The mean argument of latitude in a month is 30 degrees and 40 minutes.
Therefore, the true course of latitude in a minimum month is 29 degrees and 14 minutes. Let us assume that a <term>node<note>The intersection of the lunar and solar orbits.</note></term> divides this equally; each of its limits will have a latitude of 1 degree 16 and a half minutes, which when doubled makes nearly 2 degrees and 33 minutes—that is, the latitude of the argument of 29 degrees and 14 minutes according to the often-mentioned proportion. But the sum of the <term>semidiameters<note>Half the apparent width of the celestial discs.</note></term> of the luminaries while the moon is at perigee is 33 minutes. When these are subtracted from 1 degree 16 and a half minutes, they leave 43 minutes, which when taken from both sides of the node (that is, taken twice) make nearly 1 degree and 27 minutes.
It is therefore not possible for the sun to be eclipsed twice in one month, unless the moon has zero parallax in latitude in one of the conjunctions, and in the other has a parallax greater than 1 degree and 27 minutes. Or if, in both conjunctions, its parallax is in the same direction and the difference between them is greater than 1 degree 27 minutes. Or if, in both conjunctions, its parallax is in opposite directions and their sum is greater than 1 degree 27 minutes. For in eclipses, it is necessary that the <term>apparent latitude<note>The latitude of the moon as seen by an observer on Earth, including the effect of parallax.</note></term> in each conjunction be less than the sum of the semidiameters...

...which cannot happen in these conjunctions unless the aforementioned conditions are observed. It is also necessary that the true latitude of the moon in the first conjunction, combined with the true latitude of the moon in the second, equals 2 degrees and 33 minutes, which is the latitude of the true argument of latitude <note>The "argument of latitude" is the distance of the moon from its node, which determines how far north or south of the ecliptic it is.</note> in a minor month. Truly, there is no place on Earth where the <term>parallax<note>original: "diversitas aspectus"; the apparent shift in a celestial body's position when viewed from different points on Earth.</note></term> of the moon relative to the sun in latitude is greater than 1 degree and 27 minutes. Nor is there a place where, in both conjunctions, the difference of the parallaxes in latitude in the same direction is greater than 1 degree and 27 minutes. 

If, therefore, the sun is to be eclipsed twice in one month, it is necessary that the parallax in each conjunction be in opposite directions, and that their sum be greater than 1 degree and 27 minutes. Under the <term>equator<note>original: "equinoctiali"</note></term>, however, the maximum parallax in latitude is not more than 25 minutes in either direction. Nor in any of the <term>seven climates<note>The traditional seven latitudinal zones of the inhabitable world used by ancient and medieval geographers.</note></term>, proceeding toward the north, is the parallax in latitude greater than one degree. Therefore, it is not possible for the sun to be eclipsed twice in one month for a single region of the earth. 

Nevertheless, nothing prevents people of one habitable region from seeing an eclipse of the sun, and in the following conjunction, people of another region also having an eclipse; for both parallaxes occurring to them in opposite directions can together be greater than 1 degree and 27 minutes—as if one region were south of the equator and the other to the north. It is clear, therefore, that it is not possible for the sun to be eclipsed twice in one month for people of the same climate, or even of different climates, as long as they are on the same side of the equator. It is, however, possible in places of opposite positions relative to the equator.

### Proposition XV.

**The passage of the moon on the inclined circle cuts unequal arcs on the ecliptic, but the difference in longitude in both circles is quite small.**

¶ From the node **a**, let two arcs be taken: **a. g.** on the ecliptic, and **a. b.** on the inclined circle <note>The "inclined circle" refers to the moon's orbital path, which is tilted relative to the Earth's orbital plane (the ecliptic).</note> of the moon. Let the moon be at **b**. Let there proceed from point **b** an arc of a great circle perpendicular to the ecliptic, which shall be **b. g.** It is clear that the true location of the moon on the ecliptic is at point **g**. Given arc **a. b.**, through the known science of <term>right ascensions<note>The method of mapping coordinates from one slanted circle onto a primary reference circle, usually the celestial equator or, here, the ecliptic.</note></term>, the arc **a. g.** will be known, which will always be smaller than arc **a. b.** By the science of the 24th [proposition] of the third book of this work, the maximum difference that can exist between these is found to be 6 minutes, and this occurs when arc **a. b.** is approximately 45 degrees, and the maximum latitude of the moon is assumed to be 5 degrees. 

Within the <term>eclipse limits<note>original: "terminis eclypticis"; the specific range near the nodes where an eclipse is physically possible.</note></term>, the maximum difference of arcs **a. b.** and **a. g.** can be 4 minutes; for instance, if arc **a. b.** is 20 degrees, you will find **a. g.** to be 19 degrees and 56 minutes. For the proportion of the sine of **b. d.** to the sine of **d. f.** is as the proportion of the sine of **b. a.** to the sine of **a. g.**, provided **d.** is the pole of the ecliptic, and **a. f.** and **a. l.** are quadrants. **b. d.** and **d. f.** and **b. a.** are known. For **l. f.** is 5 degrees, and the proportion of the sine of **a. f.** to the sine of **f. l.** is as the proportion of the sine of **a. b.** to the sine of **b. g.**; thus when **a. b.** is 20 degrees, **b. g.** is 1 degree and 42 minutes. 

Likewise, let a perpendicular fall from point **g** upon **a. b.**, which shall be **d. g.** Because the proportion of the sine of **a. l.** to the sine of **l. f.** is as the proportion of the sine of **a. g.** to the sine of **g. d.**, you will find that **g. d.** differs imperceptibly from **g. b.** For while **a. b.** is 20 degrees, you will find **g. d.** to be approximately 1 degree and 42 minutes. No sensible error will follow if, in [calculating] eclipses, arc **g. b.** is taken in place of arc **g. d.**, or if arc **a. b.** is taken in place of arc **a. d.**; for if **g** is the center of the sun or the shadow, **b** becomes the true place of the moon in the true application. However, **d** is the moon's true [place] in the middle of the eclipse; yet the knowledge of arcs **g. d.** and **a. d.** is possible, as has already been shown regarding arc **g. d.** You will find arc **a. d.** by the same way the right ascensions were found from arc **a. g.**, which is already known: or because the proportion of the sine of the complement of **d. g.** to the sine of the complement of **g. a.** is as the sine of the whole to the sine of the complement of **d. a.** If, however, anyone...

### Proposition 16.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing three circles of varying sizes representing the moon's path relative to the Earth's shadow. Points are labeled to show the distances between the centers of the moon and the shadow (latitude) and the resulting overlap.</image-desc>

**T**o foreknow the **eclipse digits** from the latitude of the moon at the middle of the eclipse and the sum of the semidiameters of the moon and the shadow. <note>An "eclipse digit" is a unit of measurement equal to one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body being eclipsed.</note>

¶ Let there be a circle designating the shadow at the location of the moon's passage, *b. f.* Let its semidiameter be *a. b.* and let the semidiameter of the moon be line *b. c.*, so that the sum of both semidiameters is *a. b. c.* Let the portion of the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; lunar eclipses occur when the moon crosses this path while opposite the Sun.</note></term> be *a. d.* and the inclined circle of the moon be *d. e.*, in which the location of the moon at the middle of the eclipse is *e.* If, therefore, the latitude of the moon *a. e.* is equal to the sum of the semidiameters, namely *a. c.*, it is established that the moon will touch the circle of the shadow and none of it will be eclipsed. ¶ But if the latitude of the moon *a. e.* is less than line *a. c.*, yet still greater than line *a. b.*, a partial eclipse of the moon will occur. Therefore, by subtracting the latitude *a. e.* from the sum of the semidiameters *a. c.*, there will remain *e. b.*, which is equal to *f. g.*, the part of the moon's diameter that is eclipsed. Since the total diameter of the moon is known—being set at 12 digits—it will be clear how many digits *f. g.* represents. This is done if you multiply *f. g.* by 12 and divide the product by the diameter of the moon. ¶ If, however, the latitude of the moon were less than the semidiameter of the shadow by the amount of the moon's semidiameter, it would become a total eclipse without **delay** <note>original: "sine mora"; a "total eclipse without delay" means the moon is fully covered for only an instant before it begins to emerge.</note>; and thus it would be 12 digits. When the semidiameter of the shadow exceeds the latitude of the moon by more than the semidiameter of the moon, then a total eclipse occurs **with delay** <note>original: "cum mora"; this means the moon stays entirely within the shadow for a period of time.</note>. When the moon lacks latitude <note>i.e., its latitude is zero.</note>, then at the middle of the eclipse its center would be the center of the shadow, and the greatest possible eclipse of the moon would occur, especially if its motion were slow. Therefore, when you wish to find the eclipse digits: subtract the latitude of the moon from the sum of the semidiameters. Multiply the remainder by 12 and divide by the diameter of the moon: if the resulting points are fewer than 12, the eclipse will be partial. If exactly 12, it will be universal <note>total</note> but without delay. If more than 12, it will be universal with delay. The inverse of this is also known: when you wish to know the latitude of the moon at the middle of the eclipse from the eclipse digits and the semidiameters of the moon and shadow, multiply the digits by the visual diameter of the moon and divide by 12. Subtract that result from the sum of the semidiameters, and the sought latitude will remain. You will find the argument for this—that is, the distance from the **node** <note>The "node" is the point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note>—either through the tables of the moon's latitude, or by the proportion of one to eleven and a half. Or more precisely, if you wish, through the **spherical triangle** *a. e. d.*: from angle *d.* and side *a. e.* and angle *e.*, you will find side *a. d.*, and from this *e. d.*, which is sought. Truly, in the preceding it was shown that these differ by an imperceptible amount.

### Proposition 17.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a larger circle (the shadow) and a diagonal line (the moon's path) with points g, e, and f marking the moon's progression into and out of the shadow.</image-desc>

**T**o determine the **minutes of incidence** and the **minutes of delay**—when it has a delay—in a lunar eclipse. <note>"Minutes of incidence" (minuta casus) refers to the time/arc spent entering the shadow; "minutes of delay" (minuta more) is the duration of totality.</note>

And *a. e.* is the latitude of the moon at the middle of the eclipse—or an arc differing very little from *e. a.*—known from the previous proposition. If with three arcs...

...of the triangle *a.e.g.*, you may use the arcs as if they were straight lines: no erroneous difference will follow because of their extreme smallness. Therefore, subtract the square of *a.e.* from the square of *a.g.*, and there will remain the square of *e.g.*, from which *e.g.* becomes known; this is what was being sought. Similarly, if the moon will be eclipsed with a delay <note>original: "cum mora" — referring to a period of totality where the moon remains completely within the Earth's shadow.</note>: let *m* be the center of the moon at the beginning of total obscuration, and *n* be its center at the end of total obscuration. Truly, if it pleases you to follow even greater precision: you can find the quantity of arc *e.g.* from the knowledge of the spherical triangle *e.a.g.*, of which two sides *e.a.* and *a.g.* and the right angle *e* are known. For the ratio of the **cosine** <note>original: "sinus complementi" — the sine of the complement, which we call the cosine.</note> of *a.g.* to the cosine of *e.g.* is as the ratio of the cosine of *e.a.* to the **total sine** <note>original: "sinum totum" — the radius of the trigonometric circle, usually 60,000 or 100,000 in this era, representing the sine of 90 degrees.</note>. ¶ Certain people render the minutes of incidence and totality—which they found by way of straight lines—more precisely in this way. Let the ecliptic be *a.b.*, in which *a* is the center of the shadow. Let the sum of the semidiameters of the shadow and the moon be *a.m.*, and the oblique path of the moon be *b.m.z.t.* Let *m* be the center of the moon at the first contact with the shadow, *z* the center of the moon at true opposition, and *t* the center of the moon at the contact with the shadow after it has been freed from the eclipse. Let *a.d.* be perpendicular to *a.b.*; this will be the latitude of the moon *a.z.* at true opposition. Therefore, from the minutes of incidence found previously, while you add a twelfth part to them <note>The "twelfth part" is a standard correction in medieval astronomy to account for the fact that the Sun moves slightly while the Moon is traveling through the shadow.</note>, you may learn the argument of latitude at the beginning and end of the eclipse: namely, by subtracting the minutes of incidence (with their twelfth part) from the argument of latitude *a.z.*, and adding the same to it. From these, you will have the latitudes of the moon at the beginning and end of the eclipse. Let the latitude at the beginning be *a.e.*, and at the end *a.d.* From *e.a.* and *a.m.*, because of the right angle *e*, *e.m.* will become known; and from the known *m.e.* and *e.z.*, *z.m.* will become known, which are the minutes of incidence from the beginning of the eclipse to true opposition. Similarly, from *t.a.* and *a.d.*, because of the right angle *d*, *t.d.* will become known; from which and the known *d.z.*, *z.t.* will be known, namely the minutes of incidence from true opposition to the end of the eclipse. They proceed in a similar way regarding the minutes of totality. Truly, as has often been shown in the preceding section: this work offers little utility. If, however, you truly love precision: perform the work according to the way of the preceding section, so that you may know the arc between the true place of opposition and the place of the middle of the eclipse; and then you will find everything more precisely defined.

### Proposition 18.

**To define the three times in a partial lunar eclipse, or five in a total one.**

<image-desc>Two geometric diagrams positioned in the right margin. The upper diagram shows a circle with center 'a' representing the Earth's shadow (umbra), with a vertical line 'a-b' and points 'e', 'g', 'm', 'n', and 'd' illustrating the geometric relationships of the moon's position relative to the shadow's center. If it has no delay <note>Meaning a partial eclipse, which has no period of totality.</note>: you will find three times: namely the beginning, the middle, and the end. You have the true opposition from what has been said, which differs little or not at all from the middle of the eclipse. If, however, it does differ, and you wish to define it more precisely: you will recognize the middle itself from the teaching given in the 15th proposition of this book, and the arc *b.d.* in the figure of the same; divide it (with its twelfth part) by the hourly motion of the moon: or divide that arc alone by the **hourly gain of the moon** <term>superationem lune in hora<note>The difference between the moon's hourly speed and the sun's hourly speed.</note></term>; and the result will be the time between true opposition and the middle of the eclipse. From this, you will know the middle of the eclipse. Likewise, divide the minutes of incidence by the hourly gain of the moon: and the result will be the time from the beginning to the middle. The time from the middle to the end is the same. ¶ If it has a delay <note>a total eclipse</note>: it will have five times: namely, the beginning of contact with the shadow; the beginning of total obscuration; the middle; the end of total obscuration; and the end of the eclipse. You will find the beginning and the end as before. Then divide the minutes of totality by the hourly gain of the moon: and the result will be the time that is...

...from the beginning of total obscuration to the middle of the eclipse; and it is the same amount from the middle to the end of total obscuration. From these, the position of the moon at these specific points in time will be easily obtained: namely, by adding the **minutes of incidence** <term>minuta casus<note>The time or angular distance the moon travels from the first moment it touches the Earth's shadow until it is fully immersed.</note></term> with their twelfth part to the position of the moon at the middle of the eclipse, and then dividing. Likewise, the **minutes of totality** <term>minuta moræ<note>The time or distance the moon remains entirely within the Earth's shadow.</note></term> with their twelfth part may be added to the moon's position at the middle of the eclipse, or subtracted from it. From these, you will also easily learn the latitudes of the moon at the start and the end points.

### Proposition 19.

**To show the visible position of the moon in the ecliptic, given its true position.**

¶ For a given moment, collect the **parallax** <term>diversitatem aspectus<note>Literally "diversity of aspect." Parallax is the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note></term> of the moon in longitude according to the preceding books, specifically the fifth part of this work. If the moon is between the **ascendant** <note>The point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon.</note> and the **nonagesimal** <term>nonagesimum gradum<note>The 90th degree from the ascendant, which is the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon.</note></term>, add the parallax of the moon in longitude to its true position at the given moment, and its visible position will result. But if the moon is between the western degree <note>the descendant</note> and the nonagesimal degree, subtract the said parallax from the true position of the moon, and you will arrive at what you seek.

---

### Proposition 20.

**To determine the visible latitude of the moon.**

¶ From the previous sections, obtain the true latitude of the moon at a given moment and its parallax in latitude. If both are in the same direction from the **ecliptic** <note>The sun's apparent path; the "equator" of the zodiac.</note>, join one to the other. If they are in different directions, subtract the smaller from the larger, and the remainder will be the visible latitude of the moon, belonging to the direction of whichever part was larger.

---

### Proposition 21.

**To determine the visible motion of the moon in an assigned hour.**

<image-desc>To the left of the text column are very faint geometric diagrams consisting of circles, chords, and intersecting lines, likely representing astronomical projections or eclipse calculations.</image-desc>

¶ Through the preceding principles, find the visible position of the moon at the beginning of the assigned hour. And through the same, find the visible position of the moon at the end of the given hour. The difference between these is what you desire. Alternatively, consider the longitude parallax for the beginning and similarly for the end of the hour using the aforementioned methods. If the parallax at the beginning of the hour is greater than the parallax at the end of the hour, subtract the difference between them from the true motion of the moon in that hour. If, however, the parallax at the beginning is less than the parallax at the end, add the difference to the true motion of the moon in that hour; the visible motion of the moon in the hour will then result. This applies if the moon is between the ascendant and the 90th degree. When the moon is between the 90th degree from the ascendant and the western degree: if the parallax at the beginning of the hour is greater than the parallax at the end, add the difference to the true motion of the moon in that hour. If the parallax at the beginning is less than at the end, subtract the difference from the true motion of the moon in the hour; the visible motion of the moon in the hour will be found. Similarly, you will find the visible **hourly elongation** <note>original: "superationem... in hora" — the amount by which the moon's motion exceeds the sun's motion.</note> of the moon, by taking the true elongation in the hour in place of the true motion.

# Book Six

**b 2**

At the horizon it is greater: the **parallax** <term>diversitas aspectus<note>Literally "diversity of aspect." This is the shift in the apparent position of a celestial body (like the moon) when viewed from the Earth's surface compared to an ideal view from the Earth's center.</note></term> in longitude occurs; the parallax itself will be greater at the hour of the visible conjunction than at the hour of the true conjunction. If, however, it should be against the **succession of the signs** <note>original: "successionem signorum" — the standard order of the zodiac (Aries to Taurus, etc.). "Against the succession" means moving in the opposite direction relative to the stars.</note>, this occurs when the place of conjunction is between the western degree and the **ninetieth degree from the ascendant** <term>nonagesimum gradum ab ascendente<note>Also called the nonagesimal; the highest point of the ecliptic currently above the horizon.</note></term>: the true conjunction precedes the visible one. And when it is again greater at the horizon and the parallax in longitude occurs, the parallax itself at the hour of visible conjunction will again be greater than at the hour of true conjunction. If, however, there were no parallax in longitude—which only happens when the place of conjunction is at the ninetieth degree from the ascendant—then the visible and true conjunctions will occur at the same time.

¶ Let us therefore understand a quadrant of the ecliptic from the horizon to the ninetieth degree from the ascendant as **g.v.**, such that **g.** is at the horizon and **v.** is at the ninetieth degree. In this quadrant, let the place of the true conjunction be **l.**, and let the parallax in longitude then be the arc **l.m.**; let the visible place of the sun be **r.**, and the visible place of the moon be **m.** Our goal is to find the point on the ecliptic where, when the moon is truly there, its visible position is exactly at **r.** 

The parallax of the moon relative to the sun will be the arc **r.m.**; let **l.c.** be equal to this on the opposite side. Therefore, when the moon was at **c.**, if its parallax were equal to the arc **l.m.** (or **c.r.**), then **c.** would be the point sought. But because the moon is nearer to the horizon when it is at **c.**, its parallax in longitude was greater than when it was at **l.** Let the parallax of the moon while at **c.** be **c.p.**, which is greater than the former by the arc **e.p.**; let **c.q.** be equal to this, against the succession of signs. If, therefore, the moon existing at **q.** had a parallax in longitude of the arc **q.c.**, it would be the point sought. But since it is nearer to the horizon while at **q.**, its parallax will be greater than the arc **c.p.** or **q.r.** 

Let it then be **q.s.**, exceeding **q.r.** by the arc **r.s.**; hence let **r.f.** be equal to **q.s.** against the succession of signs. I say that **s.** is the point sought. For if the moon is at **s.** according to its true place, its visible place will be at **r.**, or will differ from it by an imperceptible amount. You will have it more precisely, however, if you make **q.s.** equal to **r.f.**, and by as much a part of **r.f.** as **r.f.** is a part of **r.p.** 

A similar path should be followed in the remaining quadrant of the ecliptic. The work is thus: Divide the parallax in longitude of the moon relative to the sun—namely the arc **r.m.**—by the true hourly motion of the moon; subtract the resulting time from the hour of the true conjunction if it occurs before the ninetieth degree from the ascendant, or add it if after. For the resulting time, seek the parallax in longitude, which is the arc **c.p.** Divide its difference from the first parallax—which was **c.r.**, namely the arc **r.p.**—by the hourly motion of the moon. Again, add or subtract the resulting time as before from the time with which you sought the second parallax. 

For the time now resulting, seek the parallax in longitude a third time, which is the arc **q.s.** Its difference from the second parallax—which was **q.r.**—is **r.s.** Above **r.s.**, if it is a perceptible quantity, let us join as much a part of **r.f.** as **r.f.** is a part of **r.p.**, so that **r.f.** with its part is equal to **q.s.** Thus **s.r.** will be roughly the parallax of the moon in longitude at the hour of visible conjunction. Divide the arc **s.r.** by the hourly motion of the moon, and subtract or add the time to the time of true conjunction, as was said before; and the desired visible conjunction will result. 

Or you may act thus, and more easily: At the hour of true conjunction, seek the parallax of the moon in longitude and its visible hourly motion. Do this by using the hour preceding the true conjunction if it is before the ninetieth degree, or the following hour if it is after the ninetieth degree. Divide the parallax in longitude by the visible hourly motion of the moon; the result will be the time of the distance of the visible conjunction from the true. Add or subtract this, as said before, to the time of the visible conjunction.
