The difference in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from the Earth's surface versus the Earth's center.</note></term> of the moon relative to the sun. If the distance between the true locations of the luminaries is equal to the parallax of the moon relative to the sun in longitude, the work is certain. If they differ, repeat the process until it is so. For it is necessary in a visible conjunction that the two aforementioned values correspond, as shown in the figure.

¶ Let the moon be truly at **o.** and visibly at **n.** on the circle of altitude. ### Proposition 23.

**Foreknowing the digits of a solar eclipse.**

¶ At the hour of the visible conjunction, find the visible latitude of the moon; likewise, find the visible parallax in latitude of the sun. From these you will know the distance between the centers according to sight. Also, find the values of the visual **semi-diameters** <note>The radius of the celestial disk.</note>. If, therefore, the sum of the visual semi-diameters is equal to the distance between the centers according to sight, no eclipse will occur in your region, although the sun would touch the moon as far as the eye can see. If the sum of the semi-diameters is greater, subtract the distance of the centers from it; the remainder will be the part of the sun's diameter that is eclipsed. This part, multiplied by twelve and divided by the sun's visual diameter, shows the **digits** <term>digitos<note>A standard unit for measuring eclipses; the diameter of the sun or moon is divided into 12 "digits."</note></term> sought. And if there were no visual distance between the centers, the center of the moon would, according to sight, become the center of the sun, and the greatest eclipse would occur—especially if the sun were at the **apogee** <term>auge<note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth.</note></term> of its eccentric and the moon near the opposite of the apogee of its **epicycle** <term>epicycli<note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle, used in pre-Copernican astronomy to explain planetary motions.</note></term>. For then the whole moon would darken the whole sun and would cause a delay in the darkness. The logic of the work is in the figures: let circle **a. c.** of the sun be on center **b.**, and **d. f.** of the moon on center **e.** The sum of the semi-diameters is **e. d.** and **b. c.**, from which if **b. e.** is subtracted, **c. d.** will remain as the eclipsed part of the sun's semi-diameter. But if **e.** coincides with **b.**, it will eclipse as much of the sun's diameter as the diameter of the moon occupies. You can also convert this, as in the 16th [proposition] of this [book], from the given digits and the sum of the semi-diameters by extracting the distance of the centers.

### Proposition 24.

**Extracting the minutes of incidence in a solar eclipse.**

¶ Subtract the square of the distance between the centers at the middle of the eclipse from the square of the sum of the semi-diameters. The square root of the remainder shows the **minutes** <note>original: "minuta casus" — also known as the "minutes of incidence," representing the time from the start of the eclipse to the moment of maximum obscuration.</note> sought. The logic is the same as in the seventeenth [proposition] of this [book]. And if the labor of precision pleases you, you may use the science of the **spherical triangle** <term>trianguli spheralis<note>A triangle drawn on the surface of a sphere, used for complex astronomical calculations.</note></term>. For side **g. a.** is the sum of the semi-diameters of the moon and sun; **a. e.** is the distance of the centers at the middle of the eclipse; and angle **e.** is a right angle. Therefore [the calculation follows].

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for calculating solar eclipses from Book Six. Having previously established how to find the moment of visible conjunction and the magnitude of the eclipse, the author now focuses on the "three times": the start, the middle, and the end of the event. It specifically addresses how the moon's parallax—the shift in its apparent position due to the observer's location on Earth—causes the duration of the first half of the eclipse to differ from the second half.</meta>

<header>Six</header>

# To extract the three times of a solar eclipse.

Divide the minutes of incidence <note>original: "minuta casus"; the distance the moon travels from the first contact of the eclipse until the moment of greatest obscuration.</note> by the moon's excess speed per hour <note>original: "superatione lune in ho:a"; the speed by which the moon outpaces the sun.</note> and the result will be the time from the beginning to the middle. It is often assumed that the time from the middle to the end is the same. Alternatively, add one-twelfth to the minutes of incidence, and you will have the visible motion of the moon from the beginning to the middle, and from the middle to the end. Convert this motion into time by dividing it by the visible hourly motion of the moon.

## Proposition 26.

# To render the times more precise here.

Because the parallax <term>diversitas aspectus<note>The difference in the apparent position of the moon when viewed from the surface of the Earth compared to its theoretical position viewed from the Earth's center.</note></term> of the moon in longitude varies at the beginning, the middle, and the end of an eclipse, the times will differ. Even though the arc of visible motion from the beginning to the middle may be equal to the arc of visible motion from the middle to the end, a difference arises in how these arcs are described according to sight. Thus, even if the arcs are equal, they appear to be traveled in different amounts of time. So, the time from the beginning to the middle will be different from the time from the middle to the end.

Therefore, let the arc of the moon’s true motion from the beginning to the end of the eclipse be **a.b.c.**, so that in truth it is at **a.** at the start, at **b.** in the middle, and at **c.** at the end. But according to sight, let it be at **g.** at the beginning, at **e.** in the middle, and at **f.** at the end. The visible motion from the beginning to the end will be **g.f.** However, the segment **g.e.** will differ imperceptibly from **e.f.** because the sum of the radii at the beginning and end varies only slightly. If the parallaxes in longitude follow the succession of the signs <note>The standard west-to-east order of the Zodiac signs.</note>—which happens before the 90th degree from the ascendant <term>90. gradum ab ascendente<note>Also known as the nonagesimal, the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon. Parallax behaves differently depending on whether the moon is east or west of this point.</note></term>—then it is necessary that **a.g.** be greater than **c.b.** Thus, the true motion from the beginning to the middle is greater than the visible motion in that same time, by as much as **a.g.** exceeds **b.e.** Therefore, subtract the parallax **e.b.** from the parallax **g.a.** and add the remainder to **e.g.**; the result will be **a.b.** Divide this by the true hourly motion of the moon, and it will give the time in which the moon, according to sight, passes from **a.g.** to **e.** Similarly, from the parallaxes **f.c.** and **e.b.**, you will find the arc **b.c.** and its time.

But if the parallaxes in longitude are contrary to the succession of the signs—which happens after the 90th degree—then **a.g.** will be less than **b.e.**, and **b.e.** less than **c.f.** In this case, the true motion of the moon from the beginning to the middle is again greater than the visible motion of the moon in the same time, by the difference between the parallaxes **b.e.** and **a.g.** Therefore, subtract **a.g.** from **b.e.**, add the remainder to **g.e.**, and **a.b.** will be produced. Divide this by the true hourly motion of the moon, and the result will be the time in which the moon, according to sight, moves from the beginning of the eclipse to the middle. Similarly, from the difference of the parallaxes **c.f.** and **b.e.** and the arc **c.f.**, you will find the time in which the moon moves from the middle of the eclipse to the end.

From this it is clear: if the difference in parallax in longitude between the beginning and the middle is equal to the difference between the middle and the end, the time of incidence <note>The first half of the eclipse.</note> is equal to the time of emergence <note>The second half of the eclipse.</note>. This happens if the middle of the eclipse occurs exactly at the 90th degree from the ascendant. When, however, the difference in parallax between the beginning and middle is less than the difference between the middle and end—which happens before the 90th degree—the time of incidence is less than the time of emergence. But when the difference in parallax between the beginning and middle is greater than the difference between the middle and end—which happens after the 90th degree—the time of incidence is greater than the time of emergence. Furthermore, the fact that differences in parallax in longitude are greater toward the 90th degree than toward the ascendant or descendant is derived from the science of angles in the second book of this work and its tables. To summarize these points briefly: divide the minutes of incidence by the visible excess of the moon per hour found for the beginning of the eclipse, and you will get the time of incidence. Likewise, divide them by the visible excess found for the middle of the eclipse, and you will get the time of emergence.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of eclipses from Book Six. It provides a method for calculating the actual surface area of the sun or moon that is covered during a partial eclipse, moving beyond simple linear measurements of the diameter to the area of the resulting "lune" or lens-shaped intersection.</meta>

<header>Book Six</header>

### Proposition 27.

<image-desc>Two circular geometric diagrams on the left margin illustrating the intersection of two circles representing a partial eclipse. The top diagram shows circles intersecting along a chord marked with points a and g; points b, d, e, and t are labeled along the vertical diameters. The bottom diagram shows a more complex construction with triangles and arcs within the overlapping region, adding labels z and k to the geometry. Lines connect the centers and intersection points to form triangular regions used for calculation.</image-desc>

->**In a partial eclipse, to measure the quantity of the eclipsed surface based on the digits of the eclipsed diameter.**<-

Let there be a circle $a.b.g.d$ representing the Sun in a solar eclipse, or the Earth's shadow in a lunar eclipse. Let the circle $a.h.g.z$ be the Moon. Let the center of the Sun or the shadow be $e$, and the center of the Moon be $t$. Let points $z$ and $d$ on the diameter of the Sun or Moon be given. The objective is to find the quantity of the area of the oval figure <note>The "oval figure" refers to the lens-shaped area of intersection between the two circles, technically called a circular vesica or lune.</note> $a.d.g.z$ in a solar eclipse, or $a.b.g.z$ in a lunar eclipse.

Because the line $e.t$—which is the distance between the two centers at the middle of the eclipse—is known from what was previously established (specifically from the given points and the radii), once the lines $e.a$, $a.t$, $g.e$, $g.t$, and $a.g$ (intersecting $e.t$ at $k$) are drawn, $e.a$ and $a.t$ will be known. These are the visual radii of the Sun (or shadow) and the Moon. In the triangle $a.e.t$, the difference between the squares of $a.e$ and $a.t$ divided by $e.t$ will yield the difference between the lines $e.k$ and $k.t$. Therefore, $e.k$ and $k.t$ become known. And since the angles at $a, d, k$ are right angles, $a.k$ will be known, which is equal to $k.g$. Thus, both triangles $e.a.g$ and $t.a.g$ are known, as is the common measure of the small squares of one part, such as those of which $e.a$, $a.t$, and $t.e$ are known parts.

Next, from the ratio of $e.a$ to $a.k$, the arc $a.d.g$ will be known by the table of sines. Similarly, from the ratio of $t.a$ to $a.k$, the arc $a.z.g$ will be known, assuming the circumference of the circle is 360 degrees. Finally, the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter—as **Archimedes** demonstrated—is less than triple and one-seventh <note>original: "tripla sexquieptima"; this refers to the fraction 22/7, approximately 3.1428.</note> and greater than triple and ten-seventy-firsts <note>original: "tripla superpartiens 10 septuagesimaprimas"; this refers to the fraction 223/71, approximately 3.1408.</note>. Between these, the mean ratio is 3 parts, 8 minutes, and 30 seconds to 1 part <note>The author is using a sexagesimal (base-60) approximation for Pi: $3 + 8/60 + 30/3600 \approx 3.1416$.</note>.

From this ratio and the known radii $e.a$ and $a.t$, the circumferences of circles $a.b.g$ and $a.b.g.z$ will be known. From the ratio of the arc $a.d.g$ (or $a.z.g$) to the whole circumference, the arcs $a.d.g$ and $a.z.g$ will be known in the same units in which $e.a$ and $a.t$ were known. By multiplying $e.a$ by the arc $a.d$, the sector $e.a.d.g$ is produced. Similarly, by multiplying $t.a$ by the arc $a.z$, the sector $t.a.z.g$ is produced. Therefore, the sectors will be known in the same units as the triangles $e.a.g$ and $t.a.g$ were already known.

But if triangle $e.a.g$ is subtracted from sector $e.a.d.g$, the portion <term>portion<note>In this context, a "portion" refers to a circular segment—the area between a chord and its arc.</note></term> contained by arc $a.d.g$ and chord $a.g$ remains; thus, it becomes known. Similarly, the portion contained by arc $a.z.g$ and chord $a.g$ will become known. Therefore, the whole oval figure $a.z.d$ will be known. Since the surface of circle $a.b.g$ is also known in the same units (because it is produced by multiplying the radius $e.b$ by the semi-circumference $d.a.b$), the ratio of the oval figure $a.z.g.d$ to the entire surface of the solar circle $a.b.d.g$ will be known. Likewise, in a lunar eclipse, its ratio to the surface of the lunar circle $a.b.g.z$ will be known, which was what was to be demonstrated.

**The Example of Ptolemy:**
The radius of the Sun $e.b$ is 15 minutes, 40 seconds, which he keeps constant. The visual radius of the Moon at the mean distance of the epicycle is 16 minutes, 40 seconds. Therefore, according to this ratio, when $b.d$ is 12 digits <note>A "digit" (digitus) is a traditional unit of eclipse magnitude, representing 1/12th of the diameter of the eclipsed body.</note>, $z.b$ will be 12 digits and approximately 20 minutes. Let us assume that $z.d$ is 3 digits; therefore $e.z$ will also be 3 digits, and $z.t$ is 6 digits and 10 minutes. Consequently, $e.t$ will be 9 digits and 10 minutes.

The square of $e.a$ is 36 square digits. The square of $t.a$ is approximately 58 and a fraction. The difference between these is 2 digits and 2 minutes. Divided by $e.t$ (that is, 9 digits and 10 minutes), the difference between $e.k$ and $k.t$ will be 13 minutes and 18 seconds. Thus, $e.k$ will be 4 digits and 28 minutes, and $k.t$ will be 4 digits and 42 minutes. From these, each of the lines $a.k$ and $k.g$ will be 4 digits. Therefore, triangle $a.e.g$ is 17 square digits and 52 minutes, and triangle $a.t.g$ is 18 digits and 48 minutes. Furthermore, from the ratio of $e.a$ to $a.k$, when $e.a$ is 60, $a.k$ will be 40; therefore arc $a.d$ is 41 degrees and 49 minutes, where the circumference of a circle has 360 degrees. Likewise, from the ratio of $t.a$ to $a.k$, which is 6 digits and 10 minutes to 4 digits, when $t.a$ is 60, $a.k$ will be 38 and 55 minutes; therefore arc $a.z$ is 40...

...[degrees] 26 minutes. Likewise, according to the proportion of 1 to 3 and 8 minutes 30 seconds, while the radius $e.a$ is 6 units, the circumference $a.b.g.d$ will be 37 <term>digits<note>In medieval astronomy, a "digit" is a unit of measure equal to 1/12th of the diameter of a celestial body.</note></term> and 42 minutes. And the area of the solar circle is 113 square digits and 6 minutes. By the same proportion, while the radius $r.a$ is 6 digits and 10 minutes, the circumference $a.z.g.b$ becomes 38 digits and 45 minutes. And the area of the lunar circle is 119 digits and 29 minutes. 

The proportion of the circumference $a.b.g.d$ to the arc $a.d.g$ is the same as the proportion of the area of the circle to the area of the sector $a.e.g$. But if the angle $e.a$ is 180 degrees, the arc $a.d$ is 41 degrees and 49 minutes. Therefore, the area of the sector $a.e.g$ is 26 square digits and approximately 7 minutes, 15 seconds. Similarly, the sector $a.t.g$ will be 26 digits and 51 minutes. 

However, since the area of the triangle $a.e.g$ was 17 digits and 52 minutes, the <term>circular segment<note>Original: "portio." Here it refers to the area of the circle cut off by the chord.</note></term> $a.d.g.k$ is 8 digits and 23 minutes. And since the area of the triangle $a.t.g$ was 18 digits and 48 minutes, the segment $a.z.g.k$ is 8 digits and 3 minutes. Therefore, the area of the oval $a.z.g.d$ is 16 superficial <note>i.e., square</note> digits and 26 minutes. 

Now, the surface area of the said circle $a.b.g.d$ was 113 digits and 6 minutes; if we set this total area to be represented as 12 digits <note>normalizing the total area to the standard 12-digit scale of an eclipse</note>, the oval $a.z.g.d$ will be approximately 1 digit and 45 minutes. This is what was intended to be shown.

### Proposition 28.

**To inquire into the magnitude of the angle resulting from the intersection of the ecliptic and the circle passing through both centers of the luminaries, or of the Moon and the shadow.**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment ab with points g and d marked along it. A vertical or slanted line segment ae originates from point a. A curved line (arc) connects points e and g or d. Points are labeled a, b, g, d, e.</image-desc>

These angles are only sought at the beginnings and ends of eclipses, and at the beginnings and ends of the <term>stay<note>Original: "mora." In eclipse terminology, this refers to the period of totality (for a lunar eclipse) or the time the Moon spends entirely within the Earth's shadow.</note></term> of the luminaries. Let it be, therefore, that in a lunar eclipse, at the beginning of the whole event, the center of the shadow is point $a$ on the ecliptic $b.a.z$, and let the portion of the Moon's inclined circle be $e.g$, which is treated as if it were parallel to the ecliptic because of the smallness of its arc. 

At the beginning of the eclipse, let the Moon be at point $e$; at the beginning of its stay in the shadow, at point $d$; and at the middle, at point $g$. Lines $a.e$, $a.d$, and $a.g$ are then drawn. The goal is to find the angle $b.a.e$ and also the angle $b.a.d$. 

Now, the angle at $g$ differs from a right angle by an imperceptible amount. Line $a.e$ is the sum of the semi-diameters of the Moon and the shadow. Line $a.d$ is the semi-diameter of the shadow minus the semi-diameter of the Moon. Line $a.g$ is the latitude of the Moon at the middle of the eclipse; these values are known. Therefore, in the triangle $e.a.g$, the proportion of sides $e.a$ and $a.g$ is known. Thus, as in a plane triangle, the angle $a.e.g$ will be known, which is equal to the desired angle $e.a.b$. Similarly, through triangle $d.a.g$, the angle $a.d.g$ will be known, which is equal to the desired angle $d.a.b$. 

At the middle of the eclipse, however, such an angle is a right angle. The same applies to a solar eclipse: $a.e$ will be the sum of the semi-diameters, and $a.g$ will be the distance between the two centers at the middle of the eclipse; from these, the angle $a.e.g$ will also become known. 

But it is better if you work at the beginning of the eclipse using the sum of the semi-diameters and the true or apparent latitude of the Moon. At the beginning of the stay, use the semi-diameter of the shadow minus the semi-diameter of the Moon and the true latitude of the Moon at the start of the stay; the work will then be more precise. Truly, if you wish to rely on total precision, perform the work through the science of spherical triangles. For <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Roman astronomer.</note></term> made a table of these angles, which is entered using the eclipse digits; he assumed the Moon to be at the mean distance of its <term>epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain the varying speeds and distances of planets.</note></term>. From the digits and the sum of the semi-diameters, he found the arc $a.g$, with which he worked as has been described.

### Proposition 29.

**To determine the direction to which the "bend" of the darkness will approach in an eclipse.**

<image-desc>A complex circular diagram depicting an eclipse sequence. Labeled points include a, b, c, d, e, g, i, k, l, m, n, o.</image-desc>

For the sake of clarity, let the circle of the shadow in a lunar eclipse be centered on point $a$ on the ecliptic $b.a.c$. Because of the angles that were to be assigned by the preceding teaching, let there be a circle $d.n.e$ whose pole is $a$. Thus, if the Moon at some earlier time of the eclipse was at $b$...

<header>Book Six</header>

<margin>
[Diagram 1: A central point 'a' representing the Sun or the center of the Earth's shadow. It is surrounded by points 'e' and 'c' on the left, and 'b' and 'd' on the right. Diagonal points 'k', 'n', 'l', and 'm' show the directions of the 'flex' or inclination of the shadow based on the Moon's latitude.]
</margin>

the inclination <note>Original: "flexus," referring to the orientation or "prosneusis" of the eclipse relative to the horizon</note> of its shadow will look toward the east at point $e$. Conversely, at some later time, if it is above $c$, the inclination of its shadows will look toward the west at point $d$. If, however, it has latitude at some time—for instance, if at the beginning of the eclipse or the period of totality <note>Original: "morae"</note> it is in a northern latitude, say at $f$—its shadows will incline toward point $k$ in the south-eastern part, according to the size of angle $b.a.f$ known from the preceding. But if it is in a southern latitude, say at $l$, its shadows will incline toward $o$ <note>Referring to the diagram points</note> to the north-eastern part. Conversely, if at the end of the eclipse or totality it should be in a northern latitude, say at $m$, the shadows will be inclined toward $n$ to the south-western part. And if it is in a southern latitude, say at $g$, the shadows will incline toward $h$ to the north-western part, according to the sizes of the angles found from the preceding. Understand the same for a solar eclipse, except that you take the Sun in place of the shadow, and understand the inclination of the shadows to occur in the opposite way. For at the beginning of the eclipse, if the Moon is above $b$, the inclination of the Sun’s shadows will be toward the west. And at the end, if the Moon is near $c$, the inclination of the Sun’s shadows will be toward the east. Thus, Ptolemy calculated the sizes of these angles for the beginnings and ends of solar eclipses, as was said before, and likewise for the beginnings and ends of lunar eclipses, and the beginnings and ends of totalities.

## Proposition XXX.

### To define more certainly the point of the horizon which the inclination of the shadows looks toward.

<margin>
[Diagram 2: A large circle representing the horizon with axes n-o and p-q. An inner arc d-b-a-c represents the ecliptic. Point 'a' is the center of the shadow, 'f' is the Moon's center. A complex series of spherical triangles is constructed using point 'r' (the zenith/pole of the horizon) to calculate the arc on the horizon.]
</margin>

¶ Let the horizon be $n.o.p.q$, where $n$ is the western point of the <term>equinoctial<note>The celestial equator.</note></term>, $o$ the eastern, $p$ the meridian, and $q$ the north. Let the half of the ecliptic above the horizon be $d.b.a.c$, where $d$ is the western point and $c$ the eastern. Points $d$ and $c$ will be given from the given time by what was set forth in the Second Book; likewise, the equal arcs $o.c$ and $n.d$ will be known from the same. Also, let $a$ be the center of the Sun or the shadow, and $f$ the center of the Moon. Let the latitude of the Moon be $f.b$. Let the great circle passing through the two centers be $l.f.a.b.p$; the task is to find the arc $o.b$ or its equal $n.l$. Let the pole of the horizon be $r$, from which the quadrant <note>Original: "quarta circuli," literally a quarter-circle or 90 degrees</note> descending through $a$ is $t.a.m$, and let the portion perpendicular to $l.k.a.b$ be $t.k$, and when continued to the horizon, let it become $k.t.g$. Because two sides of the spherical triangle $f.a.b$, namely $f.b$ and $f.a$, and the right angle $b$ are known, therefore angle $f.a.b$ is known. Moreover, angle $t.a.c$ will be known because of the known point $a$ and the given time from the 45th [proposition] of the Second Book. Therefore the remaining angle $t.a.b$ is known, and thus angle $t.a.k$ becomes known. Therefore, in the triangle $t.a.k$, two angles $a$ and $k$ are known, and side $t.a$ is known from the 43rd [proposition] of the Second Book; therefore $t.k$ is also known. But $g.t$ is a quadrant of an arc; therefore $g.t.k$—that is, the size of angle $g.h.k$—is known. Thus, in triangle $a.b.m$, angle $h$ is known. But $a.m$ is also known, because it is the complement of $t.a$, and angle $h.a.m$ is known because it is equal to angle $t.a.k$; wherefore arc $b.m$ will become known. But also in triangle $c.a.m$, side $c.a$ is known, angle $m$ is a right angle, and angle $m.a.c$ is known because it is equal to $t.a.b$; wherefore side $m.c$ will become known. Since $b.m$ was already known, arc $c.b$ will be established. Moreover, from the first [proposition] of the Second Book, $o.c$ is known; wherefore arc $o.b$ is known, which was sought.

<header>The Seventh [Book]</header>

# The Seventh Book explains the variability of the motion of the fixed stars, demonstrating it in both Longitude and Latitude.

->Proposition One<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring dense foliage and scrolling vine motifs in a square frame.</image-desc>
To show by manifold experiment that the fixed stars of the zodiac maintain an unchanging distance, not only among themselves but also in relation to those stars outside the zodiac.
¶ The testimony that can be brought to this matter is solely from the side of Hipparchus <note>Original: "Abrachis," a medieval Latinization of the Greek name Hipparchus</note>. For he himself found only a very few recorded observations of the fixed stars from before his time—specifically those of Aristyllus <note>Original: "Arsatilis"</note> and Timocharis—which were of such a nature that they could not be safely trusted. However, we see that the arrangements <note>Original: "Figuras"</note> of the stars relative to one another—both of those within the zodiac and of those compared to stars outside it—which Hipparchus himself identified and left in writing, have remained unchanged to this day. For he said that the star in the southern lip of Cancer <note>The Crab</note>, the bright star that precedes the head of Hydra <note>The Water Snake</note>, and the bright star in the preceding Dog <note>Canis Minor</note>, are almost in a straight line, except that the middle one of them deviates to the south by one and a half digits <note>A "digit" or "finger" was an ancient unit of angular measure, roughly 1/12th of a degree or sometimes used for 5 minutes of arc depending on the system</note>; and the distances between them are almost equal. Likewise, of the four stars in the head of Leo <note>The Lion</note>, the two eastern ones and the star before the head of Hydra are in a straight line. Likewise, the star on the tail of Leo and the one on the tail of the Bear <note>Ursa Major</note>—the extreme and bright one under the tail—are almost in a line, except that the middle and eastern ones are one digit from the line. Likewise, the line that passes straight from the star under the tail of the Bear to the star in the tail of Leo joins the two stars that are between them. He wrote of many such arrangements, which Ptolemy also saw remained the same in his own time. And since about 260 years passed between Hipparchus and him, and he perceived that the arrangements had changed not at all in such a long time, he concluded that they always remain unchanged. And so that posterity might know this even more firmly, he added other arrangements which he observed in his own time. For he said that of the three stars in the head of Aries <note>The Ram</note>, the two northern ones, the bright star in the southern knee of the one carrying the head of Algol <note>Perseus</note>, and the star called Capella <note>Original: "alhaioth," from the Arabic al-ʿAyyūq</note>, are on a straight line. Likewise, a straight line passing through Capella and Aldebaran <note>The bright eye of Taurus</note> passes through the star in the forward foot of the Charioteer <note>Original: "retinentis habenas," referring to the constellation Auriga</note>, so that there is only a small difference. Likewise, Capella, the star which is shared by the horn of Taurus and the foot of the Charioteer, and the star in the right shoulder of Orion, are on a straight line. He wrote of similar arrangements in other cases, which we also see have remained the same today, even though the interval of time from Ptolemy to us covers about one thousand three hundred and twenty years. By these things, we have enough evidence that there is always one and the same relationship of all the fixed stars to each other, and that their motion is the motion of a single heaven in which they are established.

->Proposition 2<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' entwined with floral scrolls and a stylized mask or face at the top center of the letter.</image-desc>
That the fixed stars are moved by a motion other than the daily motion, and that their motion tends toward the succession of the signs <note>This refers to the "order of the signs," meaning west-to-east motion, which we now call the precession of the equinoxes</note>.
¶ The argument for this matter is from this: that their distance in longitude from the solstitial and equinoctial points does not remain [constant].

<summary>This page introduces Book Seven, focusing on the fixed stars and proving that while they maintain fixed positions relative to each other, they move collectively over long periods. By comparing observations from Hipparchus, Ptolemy, and the author's own 15th-century era, it demonstrates the stability of constellations across 1,500 years.</summary>
<keywords>fixed stars, precession, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, constellations, stellar coordinates, longitude, latitude, history of astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 118 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the fixed stars' motion from the start of Book Seven. It transitions from general observations about the stars' relative positions to the specific evidence for "precession"—the slow shift of the stars' positions relative to the equinoxes and solstices. It focuses on comparing observations made by Timocharis (3rd century BCE), Hipparchus (2nd century BCE), and Ptolemy (2nd century CE).</meta>

[The distance between the stars remains] always the same: but it increases according to the <term>succession of the signs</term> <note>The eastward movement through the zodiacal signs: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc.</note> as it proceeds: so that the stars which in ancient times were before the <term>tropical and equinoctial points</term> <note>The points of the solstices and equinoxes</note> are now found after those same tropical and equinoctial points. And the greater the time that has passed between the observations of the ancients and our own, the further the stars are found to have moved from their ancient places following the succession of the signs. Take the example of <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>Original: "Abrachis," a common medieval Latin corruption of the Greek name Hipparchos</note>: before him, Timocharis, while observing, found the star <term>Spica</term> <note>Original: "azennech," from the Arabic 'al-simāk al-a‘zal', referring to Spica, the brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note>—which is the ear of grain in Virgo—to be almost 8 degrees before the point of the autumnal equinox. Yet Hipparchus himself found that same star to be only 6 degrees before the autumnal point. In other stars as well, Ptolemy later found a similar motion when comparing the locations of the stars he discovered to those which Hipparchus had left in writing. He found that these locations had also changed according to the succession of the signs. 

He brings forth this example from the second year of Antoninus, in the month of <term>Pharmuthi</term> <note>Original: "Bromathi," a transcription error for Pharmuthi, the eighth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note> (which is the eighth month of the Egyptians), on its ninth day: as the sun was setting in Alexandria, with the final part of Gemini at the <term>midheaven</term> <note>The point where the ecliptic crosses the local meridian</note>, five and a half equal hours after noon. He observed the sun and the moon using an <term>armillary instrument</term> <note>A model of the celestial sphere consisting of a spherical framework of rings, used for determining the coordinates of celestial bodies</note>. The sun was seen at 3 degrees of Pisces, and the distance of the moon from the sun was 92 and one-eighth degrees. However, in truth, the sun was at 3 degrees, 7 minutes, and 24 seconds of Pisces. For its <term>parallax</term> <note>The difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note> near the horizon is nearly 2 and a half minutes. Thus the moon was seen at 5 degrees and one-sixth of Gemini at the midheaven. By the armillary instrument, the distance of the star which is the <term>Heart of the Lion</term> <note>Regulus, the brightest star in Leo</note> was seen to be 57 and one-tenth degrees from the moon. 

But it was necessary for the moon to have moved about a fourth part of a sixth [of a degree] according to the succession of the signs during that half-hour, and for its parallax to be against the succession of the signs from its visible place by half of one-sixth. Therefore, the visible place of the moon half an hour after sunset was 5 and one-third degrees of Gemini. But between it and the said star there were 57 and one-tenth degrees; wherefore it was necessary for the star to be at almost 2 and a half degrees of Leo. Thus its distance from the <term>tropical point</term> <note>The summer solstice</note> was nearly 32 and a half degrees. Now, Hipparchus said that he had observed this star in the 50th year of the third cycle of Calippus (that is, the 196th year after the death of Alexander), and it was then distant from the tropical point by 29 degrees and a half and a third [29° 50']. Therefore, from the time of Hipparchus until this observation by Ptolemy, it moved 2 degrees and two-thirds. The time from the hour of Hipparchus’s observation until this observation of Ptolemy was 265 Egyptian years and a little more. From this, it is understood that they move by approximately one degree in any 100 years according to the succession of the signs. From this, it seems to have happened that Hipparchus said concerning the length of the year: that the tropical and equinoctial points change toward the direction of the succession of the signs by no less than one-hundredth of a degree in a year. Ptolemy also found a similar change in other fixed stars from the locations that Hipparchus had written. From these facts, the purpose of the proposition is sufficiently concluded.

### Proposition III.

## That the motion of the fixed stars occurs around the axis of the ecliptic and upon its poles.

For the latitudes of the stars that Timocharis wrote—and those who were before Hipparchus—were also found to be the same by Hipparchus; similarly, they were observed by Ptolemy. And if any difference was found between the latitudes of the stars that Hipparchus wrote and the latitudes noted by Ptolemy, it was nevertheless very slight, such that it could have occurred by reason of the instrument or the sight during the observation. But their <term>declinations</term> <note>The angular distance of a body north or south of the celestial equator</note> from the equinoctial [equator] are not found to be the same by them. Thus...

It concludes that while the stars' latitudes relative to the ecliptic remain constant, their longitudes and declinations change.</summary>

Having established that the stars move eastward relative to the equinoxes, the author now provides specific numerical data comparing observations from three distinct eras—those of Timocharis (c. 300 BCE), Hipparchus (c. 130 BCE), and Ptolemy (c. 140 CE)—to prove that stars shift their positions relative to the celestial equator.</meta>

# Seventh [Book]

...so that neither <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>Original: "Abraachis," a common medieval corruption of the Greek name Hipparchos</note> found the same coordinates that <term>Timocharis</term> <note>A Greek astronomer from the 3rd century BCE</note> and the men of his time left in writing; nor did <term>Ptolemy</term> find them in agreement with those which Hipparchus had noted. Indeed, regarding the stars in the half of the sphere that proceeds from the point of the <term>winter solstice</term> <note>Original: "tropici hiemalis"</note> to the point of the <term>summer solstice</term> <note>Original: "tropici estiualis"</note> by way of the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>Original: "punctū vernale"</note>: their southern <term>declinations</term> <note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator</note> were seen to decrease, while their northern declinations were seen to increase. Conversely, for the stars in the remaining half of the sphere, the northern declinations were seen to decrease, while the southern ones increased. The greatest difference in this variation was found in those stars near the <term>equinoctial points</term> <note>The points where the celestial equator and ecliptic intersect</note>, and the smallest in those near the <term>solstice points</term> <note>Original: "puncta tropica"</note>.

For instance, concerning the bright star in the <term>Flying Vulture</term> <note>The constellation Aquila; the star is Altair</note>, Timocharis wrote that it had a northern declination of 5 degrees and 1/4 of a degree. Hipparchus found the same. But Ptolemy found 5 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/3 <note>Totaling 5 degrees and 50 minutes (5 5/6°)</note>. The middle star of the <term>Pleiades</term> in the time of Timocharis was inclined toward the north by 14 degrees and 1/2. In the time of Hipparchus, it was 15 degrees and 1/2. But in the time of Ptolemy, it was 16 degrees and 1/4. <term>Aldebaran</term> <note>The bright red star in the eye of Taurus the Bull</note> in the time of Timocharis was inclined toward the north by 8 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/4. In the time of Hipparchus, it was 9 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/4. In the time of Ptolemy, it was nearly 11 degrees. <term>Capella</term> <note>Original: "Albaioth," from the Arabic 'al-ayyūq', the brightest star in Auriga</note>, which is the bright star of the one <term>holding the reins</term> <note>The constellation Auriga, the Charioteer</note>: in the time of <term>Aristyllus</term> <note>Original: "Arsatilis," a contemporary of Timocharis</note> it was inclined toward the north by 40 degrees. In the time of Hipparchus, 40 degrees and 1/5. In the time of Ptolemy, 41 degrees and 1/6. <term>Bellatrix</term>, which is in the left shoulder of <term>Orion</term>: in the time of Timocharis it had a northern declination of one degree and 2/5. In the time of Hipparchus, one degree and 4/5. In the time of Ptolemy, 2 degrees and 1/2. The star in the right shoulder of Orion <note>Betelgeuse</note>: in the time of Timocharis it had a northern declination of 3 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/3. In the time of Hipparchus, 4 degrees and 1/3. But in the time of Ptolemy, 5 degrees and 1/4. <term>Sirius</term> <note>Original: "Albabor," from the Arabic 'al-abūr'</note>, which is in the mouth of the <term>Dog</term> <note>Canis Major</note>: in the time of Timocharis it had a southern declination of 16 degrees and 1/3. In the time of Hipparchus, 16 degrees. In the time of Ptolemy, 15 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/4. In these stars, therefore, and in many others in this half of the sphere containing the vernal point, the declinations were found through the succession of time to have increased if northern and decreased if southern; the most variation was found in those near the vernal point, and the least in those near the solstice points.

Likewise, the star <term>Regulus</term> <note>Original: "cor leonis," the Heart of the Lion</note> was found by Timocharis to be declined toward the north by 21 degrees and 1/3. By Hipparchus, 20 degrees and 2/3. By Ptolemy, 19 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/3. <term>Spica</term> <note>Original: "Azimech," from the Arabic 'al-simāk'</note>, which is the ear of grain in <term>Virgo</term>, was found in northern declination by Timocharis at 1 degree and 2/5. By Hipparchus, 3/5 of one degree. But by Ptolemy it was found declined toward the south by 1/2 plus 1/6 <note>Totaling 2/3 of a degree south</note>. The star at the end of the tail of the <term>Great Bear</term> <note>Ursa Major</note> was found by Aristyllus to be inclined to the north by 61 degrees and 1/2. Hipparchus found 60 degrees and 1/2 plus 1/4. Ptolemy, 59 degrees and 2/3. <term>Arcturus</term> <note>Original: "Alramech," from the Arabic 'al-rāmih'</note>, Timocharis said was declined to the north by 31 degrees and 1/2. Hipparchus, 31 degrees. Ptolemy, 29 degrees and 1/2. The star above the <term>Heart of the Scorpion</term> <note>Antares</note>, Timocharis found inclined toward the south by 18 degrees and 1/3. Hipparchus, 19 degrees. Ptolemy, 24 degrees and 1/4. From these and other similar examples, the stars in this half of the sphere were seen to decrease their northern declinations and increase their southern ones. Such a variety of declinations cannot exist unless the fixed stars, in their own proper motion, revolve not around the axis of the world and its poles, but around the axis of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The path of the sun</note> and its poles. And since their motion and the aforementioned variations agree and harmonize with this position, it will not be improper to assert that this motion takes place upon the axis and poles of the ecliptic, which is what was proposed.

# To confirm the amount of the movement of the fixed stars according to the succession of the signs from the change of their declinations.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
¶ This is more easily perceived from the stars near the points of equality <note>The equinoxes, where the celestial equator and the ecliptic intersect</note>: because in those locations, the <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator</note> varies the most. <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>Original: "Abrachis," a medieval Latinization of the Greek name Hipparchos</note> found the middle of the <term>Pleiades</term> <note>A famous star cluster in the constellation Taurus</note> at a northern declination of 15 degrees and one-sixth. [Ptolemy] found it at 16 degrees and one-quarter. Thus, the variation of this declination occurred over 265 years, one-sixth of a year, and half of a sixth. But that is almost equal to the way the declinations of two degrees and two-thirds of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky</note> differ near the end of Aries. <term>Albaioth</term> <note>The star Capella in the constellation Auriga</note> in the time of Hipparchus was declined 40 degrees and two-fifths to the north. But in the time of Ptolemy, it was 41 degrees and one-fifth. Therefore, in 265 years, a declination [change] of one degree and four-fifths occurred. But to this difference of declinations, two degrees and two-thirds correspond near the middle of Taurus on the ecliptic. The <term>left shoulder of Orion</term> <note>Original: "Numerus sinister orionis," likely a typo for "Humerus," referring to the star Bellatrix</note> in the time of Hipparchus declined to the north 1 degree and 4 fifths. In the time of Ptolemy, [it was] 2 degrees and a half. Therefore, it became more northern by about two-thirds of a degree. To this difference of declinations, almost 2 degrees and 2 thirds of one [degree] of the ecliptic correspond near the end of Taurus. Similarly, regarding the stars in the other half of the sphere, it was found: Hipparchus found the declination of the star called <term>Azimech or Spica</term> <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> to be three-fifths of one degree to the north. Ptolemy, however, found it to the south by half a degree. Therefore, it became more southern by one degree and a tenth. To this difference of declination at the end of Virgo, 2 degrees and 2 thirds of the ecliptic correspond. The star at the tip of the <term>Great Bear's tail</term> <note>The star Alkaid (Benetnasch)</note> was found by Hipparchus to be declined 60 degrees, a half, and a quarter to the north. Ptolemy found it at 59 degrees and 2 thirds. Therefore, it became more southern by one degree and a twelfth. To this difference of declination at the beginning of Libra, two degrees and two-thirds of one correspond on the ecliptic. <term>Alramech</term> <note>The star Arcturus</note> in the time of Hipparchus had a declination of 31 degrees, but in the time of Ptolemy, [it was] 29 degrees, a half, and a third to the north. Therefore, it became more southern by 1 degree and a sixth. To this difference of declination at the beginning of Libra, two degrees and two-thirds correspond. From these and similar observations, it is sufficiently proven that, because of the changes of the stars in the time interval between Hipparchus and Ptolemy, the stars must have moved according to the succession of signs <note>That is, moving eastward/forward through the zodiac</note> by 2 degrees and two-thirds. When two degrees and two-thirds are divided by 265 years, it results that this motion reaches one degree in almost 100 years.

...north, 5 degrees, 35 minutes. ¶ Likewise, **Agrippa** <note>Original: "Agrias," a 1st-century Greek astronomer</note> in **Bithynia**, in the 12th year of **Domitian** (which is the 840th year of the era of **Nabonassar** <note>Original: "Nabucho." The position of the moon according to calculation was therefore 21 degrees and 21 minutes of **Virgo**, and its latitude toward the south was 1 degree and five-sixths. But its visible position was 22 degrees and 12 minutes of **Virgo**, and its latitude was nearly 2 degrees south.

¶ For the middle of **Cancer** was at the mid-heaven. Thus, the position of **Spica** was 21 degrees and one-third of **Virgo**, and its latitude to the south was 2 degrees. Similarly, in the 42nd year of the same cycle (the 466th year of **Nabonassar**), on the seventh and a half day of the month, or three and one-eighth equal hours [after midnight]. With the sun in the middle of **Scorpio** after the moon had risen, he saw **Spica** touching the northern side of the moon. Although he wrote that it was 3 and a half temporal hours after midnight, it must have been 2 and a half equal hours after midnight according to apparent time, but exactly two equal hours according to mean time. At that time, the mid-heaven would be 22 and a half degrees of **Gemini**, and the parts of **Virgo** around **Spica** would be rising. The true position of the moon was therefore 21 degrees and 30 minutes of **Virgo**, and its latitude toward the south was 2 and a half degrees. But the visible position was 22 and a half degrees, and the latitude was 2 and a quarter degrees. Therefore, the position of **Spica** had a latitude of 2 degrees to the south, and it was then in 22 and a half degrees of **Virgo**. In the 12 years that passed between these observations, **Spica** moved by one-sixth of a degree. Therefore, in six times this period—namely 72 years—the star would move by one degree. But because that time period was brief, it is not to be relied upon [as a final figure].

For at the end of the eleventh hour (namely five temporal hours after midnight), the moon appeared to have already left **Spica** behind by an amount less than the moon's diameter, equidistant from its two horns. This visible conjunction with respect to the meridian of the Romans was five equal hours after midnight...

Time measured by the sun's actual position</note>, and according to <term>mean time</term> <note>Original: "tempus mediocre." Time measured at a perfectly uniform rate</note>, six hours and a quarter of an hour, or slightly more. At that time, the moon in its true course was in 25 degrees, a half, and a quarter <note>25° 45'</note> of **Virgo**, having a southern <term>latitude</term> <note>Distance from the ecliptic</note> of one degree and a third part of one <note>1° 20'</note>. According to its appearance, it appeared in 26 degrees and a quarter of **Virgo**, at the same southern latitude of two degrees, since the fourth degree of **Libra** was at the <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>The point where the meridian meets the ecliptic</note>. This observation was in the 456th year from the beginning of the reign of **Nabonassar**, on the 16th day of the month of **Phaophi** <note>Original: "Baba," the second month of the Egyptian calendar</note> having passed, during the night followed by the 17th day, three <term>temporal hours</term> <note>Hours calculated by dividing the night into twelve equal parts</note> after midnight. In equal hours, this was three and two-fifths of one, since the sun was in the 26th degree of **Sagittarius**. This was according to apparent time; according to mean time, it was three hours and a sixth of an hour. At that time, the moon in its true course reached one degree and a quarter of a degree of **Scorpio**, having a northern latitude of one degree and a third <note>1° 20'</note>. Therefore, the position of this star was also in the second degree of **Scorpio**, and it had a latitude of 1 degree and a third <note>1° 20'</note> toward the north.

¶ Likewise, the geometer **Menelaus** observed a star in **Rome** in the first year of **Trajan**, while the moon, according to estimation, was <term>conjoined</term> <note>Appearing in the same longitudinal position</note> with it. For the southern horn of the moon appeared in a straight line with the middle star and the southern star of the three that are in the forehead of the **Scorpion**. Its center, moreover, was thought by conjecture to be as far from the middle star as that middle star is from the southern of the mentioned stars; and it was following the middle star according to the succession of the signs. This observation was in the 845th year of **Nabonassar**, after the 18th day of the month of **Mecheir** <note>Original: "Mesir," the sixth month of the Egyptian calendar</note> had passed, after the middle of the night followed by the 19th day, five temporal hours having passed—in equal hours, six and a sixth of one. In **Alexandria**, however, this observation would have needed to be seven equal hours and a half after midnight according to apparent time, and almost the same by mean time; while the moon in its true path had reached 5 degrees and 20 minutes of **Scorpio**, having a northern latitude of 2 degrees and 10 minutes; to the sight, however, it was estimated at 5 degrees and 55 minutes of **Scorpio**. Likewise in a northern latitude of one degree and 20 minutes, since the mid-heaven was the last degree of **Libra**. It is therefore established that at this time, the said star was in approximately the fifth degree and 55 minutes of **Scorpio**, having a northern latitude of 1 degree and 20 minutes. Therefore, in the span of 391 Egyptian years which occurred between the two observations, this star, while keeping its latitude, moved 3 degrees and 55 minutes. Wherefore in 100 years, just as above, one degree will correspond to the movement; which is what we have sought until now.

<header>Book Seven</header>

### To explain what others have thought about the motion of the fixed stars.

In the city of Raqqa <note>Original: "Aracta," a city in modern-day Syria</note>, the most diligent student of philosophy **Albategni** <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), an influential Arab astronomer whose measurements were more accurate than Ptolemy's</note>, in the year 1191 from the era of the "Two-Horned One" <note>Original: "Adhilcarnaz," a reference to the Seleucid era, often associated with Alexander the Great</note>—that is, 1626 years from the beginning of the reign of **Nebuchadnezzar** <note>Original: "Nabuchodo"</note>—observed the fixed stars and compared their positions with those seen in previous times. He distributed the difference in their positions over the intervening time to determine the quantity of a single movement.

For he himself found the northernmost star of the three located in the brow of **Scorpio** to be at 17 degrees and 50 minutes of **Scorpio**. This same star appeared to the geometer **Menelaus** <note>Original: "Mileo," a 1st-century Greek mathematician</note>, as has been recited, at 5 degrees and 55 minutes of **Scorpio**. It follows, therefore, that in the time between these two observations, the star moved through 12 degrees and 55 minutes. That interval of time is 782 Egyptian years, since Menelaus completed his observation in the 845th year from the beginning of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. If, therefore, we assign the proper portion of this intervening time to a single degree, the star will seem to move by one degree in approximately 66 solar years.

He did the same for other stars. For the "Heart of the Lion" <note>Regulus</note>, which **Ptolemy** observed at 2 degrees and 10 minutes of **Leo**, he found at 4 degrees and 50 minutes of the same. Some of the ancients, however, thought that the sphere of the fixed stars moved continuously toward the east until it described a path of 8 degrees, and then returned toward the west by the same amount; afterward, they affirmed it returned to its original motion. They assigned 80 years to a single degree. They were led to this partly because they found the greatest variation of the sun and the length of the solar years to be inconsistent, and they thus imagined a motion of <term>trepidation</term> <note>A historical (now debunked) theory that the equinoxes oscillate back and forth rather than moving in a slow, continuous circle</note> in the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The outer shell of the universe in the geocentric model, containing the fixed stars</note>.

Whether the uncertainty of instruments introduced this variation, or whether nature has endowed the fixed stars with some motion still hidden from us, it is and will be extremely difficult to determine the nature of this motion because of its slowness. For if our ancestors were deceived by their instruments, we are necessarily deceived as well, since our observations—unless compared with those of the ancients—will never teach us anything. But if we judge that this hidden motion exists in the stars, it will be advantageous to keep a constant eye on the fixed stars and to leave recorded observations for those who come after us.

---

### Proposition 7.

### To understand, by the ingenuity of an instrument, how far the fixed stars are distant from the beginning of Aries and from the ecliptic itself.

While you were seeking the location of the moon earlier, you aligned the <term>armillary instrument</term> <note>A model of the celestial sphere made of metal rings, used for sighting stars and planets</note> by the sun. Now, however, because the sun still remains above the horizon and does not allow the fixed stars to appear, you will adjust the instrument by the position of the moon, which has been accurately calculated and seen. You will then observe any of the stars until it shines through both holes of the sighting rule to the eye. For then, just as with the moon, both the longitude and latitude will be known.

---

### Proposition 8.

### When the distances between three fixed stars are known, and the positions of two of them on the ecliptic are known: to reveal the longitude and latitude of the one existing outside the ecliptic.

Understand "distance" to mean the arc of a great circle to the centers of the stars...

<meta>This page continues the technical demonstration of how to determine the positions of stars. <header>Book Seven</header>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a spherical triangle positioned in the left margin. The triangle is defined by vertices a, b, and c. From a pole labeled z at the top, an arc passes through vertex a to meet the base arc at point g.</image-desc>

<margin>a</margin>
...of those existing in the ecliptic <note>The sun’s apparent path across the sky</note> is terminated. ❡ Let there be an arc of the ecliptic, **b. g.**, on the convex of the sphere. Let point **b** be one star and **c** be another star existing on the ecliptic. Let **a** be a star existing outside the ecliptic. Arcs of the distances **a. b.** and **a. c.** having been drawn, let an arc **z. a. g.** be dropped from the pole of the ecliptic, **z**, passing through star **a** to the ecliptic. Now I say: arc **b. g.** will be known together with arc **a. g.**, which is the latitude <note>The distance of a star north or south of the ecliptic</note>. For the triangle **a. b. c.** consists of known arcs of great circles; therefore, by the science of spherical triangles <term>spherical trigonometry</term>, its angle **a. b. c.** will be known. And because angle **a. g. b.** is a right angle, arc **a. g.** (the latitude) will be known along with arc **b. g.** But the place of star **b** on the ecliptic is assumed to be known; therefore, the place of star **g** will become known, which was the goal. However, here and in what follows, one must look carefully at how the star whose place is sought relates to the others. For if you describe a circumference around pole **b** according to the length of arc **a. c.**, and likewise around pole **c** according to the length of arc **a. b.**, you will see their intersection at point **k**. Therefore, if the star were placed at **k**, the calculations would be identical for both stars **a** and **k**, even though they are situated in different places. It must therefore be noted whether the star whose place is being investigated follows the other two according to the succession of the signs <note>The order of the Zodiac: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc.</note> or the contrary, which the distances themselves will sufficiently show. For if **a** has equal distances to **b** and **c**, its place on the ecliptic will be exactly in the middle between **b** and **c**. If, however, they are unequal, they recede from the midpoint: its place is toward that star from which it is less distant. In this way you will also proceed in the following sections.

### Proposition .ix.

<image-desc>A second geometric diagram in the left margin, showing a more complex spherical arrangement. A circular boundary contains points a, b, and c forming a central triangle. Arcs are drawn from a pole z at the top, passing through vertices a and b to reach points l and g on a lower arc. Point c is situated on this lower arc.</image-desc>

<margin>b</margin>
**W**ith the distances of three stars known among themselves: of which one has a known place on the ecliptic; and the second of the two existing outside the ecliptic has its longitude and latitude known; to inquire how much the third is distant from the beginning of Aries <note>The zero-point for measuring celestial longitude</note> and from the ecliptic.

❡ Let the arc of the ecliptic be **g. l.**, in which point **c** signifies the star whose place is known. Let **b** be the star existing outside the ecliptic, whose place on the ecliptic is known along with its latitude. And let **a** be the star whose place we seek. Having connected the three points **a**, **b**, and **c** through arcs of great circles **a. b.**, **a. c.**, and **b. c.**, let two quadrants <note>Quarter-circles</note> of circumferences be produced from the pole **z** of the ecliptic through the two points **a** and **b**, which are **z. a. l.** and **z. b. g.** Because triangle **a. b. c.** has three known sides, its angle **a. b. c.** will be known from the science of spherical triangles. But also in triangle **b. g. c.**, side **b. c.** and side **b. g.** are known, and angle **g** is a right angle. Therefore, angle **c. b. g.** becomes known, and thus the whole angle **a. b. g.** is known, and its adjacent angle **a. b. z.** is found. You have therefore triangle **a. b. z.** whose angle **a. b. z.** is known and whose two sides **a. b.** and **b. z.** are known. From this, arc **a. z.** will be known. Therefore, its complement is also given: namely arc **a. l.**, which is the sought latitude of the star. Moreover, for the same reason stated before, angle **a. z. b.** will also be known. Its quantity is determined by arc **g. l.**, which is known for this reason. Since the place of star **b** on the ecliptic is known, the place of star **a** on the ecliptic will also be known, which was what was sought. Although the arrangements of stars can occur in various ways, each requiring its own diagram, if you practice with this single example by considering the science of spherical triangles, you will execute any proposed task at will.

<header>Seventh [Book]</header>

# If three fixed stars have known distances between them, and any two of them have known longitudes and latitudes, the longitude and latitude of the remaining star will not be unknown.

<image-desc>A spherical diagram illustrating celestial coordinate geometry. It depicts a segment of a sphere with arcs labeled with letters (z, b, c, g, l, m, a) representing a spherical triangle and its projections onto the ecliptic, corresponding to the mathematical proof in the text.</image-desc>

¶ Consider three arcs of the ecliptic <note>The sun’s apparent path across the sky</note> **g, l,** and **m**. Let point **b** be the location of a star whose longitude is assumed to be known, along with its latitude. Let **c** be the second star, known just like the previous one, and **a** be the star whose location is sought. Having formed the triangle **a-b-c** by drawing arcs **a-b**, **a-c**, and **b-c**, let three quadrants of great circles be dropped from the pole of the zodiac, **z**; let these be **z-b-g**, **z-a-l**, and **z-c-m**. I say that arc **g-l** becomes known, and because of this, the distance of the star from the beginning of Aries <note>The vernal equinox, which serves as the zero-point for measuring celestial longitude</note> is found. For arc **g-m** is known by hypothesis <note>original: "ex hypothesi"</note>; since it determines the size of angle **g-z-m**, that angle **g-z-m** is itself found. Moreover, since triangle **b-z-c** has all sides known and angle **z** is now known, its angle **c-b-z** will be known. Likewise, the hypothesis has rendered all sides of triangle **a-b-c** known, wherefore its angle **a-b-c** is also discovered. If you subtract this from the known angle **c-b-z**, the angle **a-b-z** will remain known. Now, two sides **a-b** and **b-z** are known; therefore angle **a-z-b** will be known, and arc **a-z** likewise. Thus, therefore, arc **g-l** is elicited, because it determines the size of angle **a-z-b**. Furthermore, the position of star **b** on the ecliptic is known by hypothesis, from which the position of star **a** will not be unknown. If you subtract the now-known arc **a-z** from a quadrant <note>A 90-degree arc</note>, you will have the remaining arc of latitude **a-l**, which is not unknown; this is what I intended to show. I omit other ways of configuration, since they are easy to understand because of what has been said. Finally, if you please, you may infer a great corollary. Corollary:

## If all stars have known distances between one another, and at least two are established in longitude and latitude, it is necessary that all the rest become known as to how far they are distant from the beginning of Aries and how far they are removed from the ecliptic toward either of the poles.

->Proposition One.<-

<image-desc>Large woodcut initial 'V' depicting a nude male figure (possibly representing a constellation like Orion) standing among grapevine-like foliage. This celestial band, varied in color and of unequal width, is known to our senses as the "Milky Way" because it mostly appears to mimic the color of milk. However, the star in the left front knee is seen in the middle of this path. The part which is around the hind feet is thicker or brighter, though it appears only slightly. ## Proposition .ij.

->To explain in what manner a solid sphere is to be fabricated.<-

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'S' containing a woodcut of two figures, one seated and one standing, in a landscape with a classical building in the distance.</image-desc>

Construct a sphere from metal or another durable material. If it is of sufficient size, apply a celestial color <note>likely a deep azure or blue</note>. And on its convex surface find two points diametrically opposite: which shall represent the poles of the zodiac. And upon one of them, mark out the circumference of a great circle on the sphere itself: which you shall divide in the common manner into 360 equal parts. And near it, write the names of the twelve signs of the zodiac in their proper order: giving 30 degrees to each. Then take a thin and flexible plate <note>a flexible ruler or metal strip</note>. On its surface, establish a straight line equal to the semi-circumference previously described, and divide it into 180 equal parts. Proceed by numbering these parts from the middle of this divided line through the ends, until

on both sides you will reach 90 and place it. For by the function of this plate, the <term>latitudes</term><note>The distance of a star north or south of the ecliptic plane.</note> of the stars are understood. At the two ends of the plate, and at two points in the axis of the sphere opposite each other, you should make holes: and connect the plate itself to the spherical body with two pins: so that it can be easily rotated around those pins. This being done: have the <term>fixed stars</term><note>Stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to each other, unlike "wandering" planets.</note> known in longitude and latitude, either through your own observations or through another verification. And when you wish to impress any of them on the sphere: rotate the end of the plate, which passes through the poles of the <term>zodiac</term><note>The belt of the heavens through which the sun and planets move.</note>, to the location of the star; set it on the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The sun's apparent path across the sky.</note>. And having counted the latitude to its proper part, fix a mark near its end: which hereafter will represent the place of this star.

Therefore, when all the stars of one image <note>original: "imaginis," referring here to a constellation</note> have been impressed according to this instruction: you should draw the lines bounding the image itself so that each star has its own place or limb. Similarly, you will be able to designate the <term>Milky Way</term> on the convex surface of the sphere, if you have previously identified the noteworthy stars located in it. Then, through the two poles of the ecliptic and the beginning of <term>Cancer</term><note>The summer solstice point in the zodiac.</note>, draw the circumference of a great circle: and in it find the two <term>poles of the world</term><note>The North and South celestial poles.</note> through the maximum declination of the sun. And upon one of them, describe the circumference of a great circle in place of the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note>. It will be useful to have divided this into 360 equal parts, just like the ecliptic.

In the poles you have found, make two round holes: for two pins will later be inserted into them, around which the sphere will turn. Thus you have a completed sphere. Afterward, you shall make a ring <note>original: "armillam"</note> of suitable size. On one of its surfaces, which must always be positioned as the <term>meridian</term><note>The circle passing through the poles and the observer's zenith.</note>, make the circumference of a circle: which you should likewise distribute into 360 equal parts. And extend the numbers of these parts from two diametrically opposite points each up to 90. In those two points, make two holes equal to the aforementioned ones: so that the sphere, placed under this ring, can rotate like the <term>first mover</term><note>original: "primi mobilis," the outermost sphere in ancient astronomy that drives the daily motion of the heavens</note> around the pins inserted into the holes. Finally, you will fit another ring, on whose surface you will again divide the circumference of the circle into 360 parts in the manner previously described. This will hold the place of the <term>horizon</term>. So that with respect to this, one of the poles of the world may be raised, and the whole sphere may be positioned according to the character of any region. There will also be a need for a fourth circumference divided into ninety equal parts. This shall be made from a thin plate and will be attached to the top of the meridian. Indeed, it will perform its duty by meeting nearly all parts of the horizon freely beneath it. For if you place the mark of a star at the number of the altitude above the horizon of that star in this fourth part: the sphere having first been arranged according to the elevation of one of the poles: you will see the spherical body established just like the <term>firmament</term><note>The heavens or the sky.</note>.

### Proposition III

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring floral patterns and scrolled leaves within a square border.</image-desc>
**V**arieties of the relationships which the fixed stars have to the Sun and Moon and the rest of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> to be declared.

The relationship of fixed stars to the <term>luminaries</term><note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> and the five retrograde stars <note>the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>: happens now through <term>conjunction</term>: now through <term>opposition</term>. Sometimes truly through a <term>trine aspect</term>: <term>sextile</term>: or <term>quartile</term><note>A "quartile" is a square aspect of 90 degrees.</note>. By conjunction indeed generally: while one of the great circles passing through the poles of the ecliptic encompasses the center of the fixed star and the center of the planet. Similarly through opposition. Through a trine aspect truly while the great circles drawn through the poles of the ecliptic—of which one contains the center of the fixed star and the other the center of the planet—are distant from each other by a third part of the zodiac <note>120 degrees</note>. Through a sextile aspect truly when the distance of those circles, of which we spoke, has a sixth part of the zodiac <note>60 degrees</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial positions, moving from the physical construction of a globe to the theoretical "habits" or relationships between stars, planets, and the horizon. -># Eighth Book <-

And by the fourth <term>aspect</term><note>An "aspect" refers to the angular distance between celestial bodies; a "fourth aspect" or quartile occurs when they are 90 degrees (a quadrant) apart.</note> when their distance is equal to a quadrant: relationships of this kind happen to each of the stars that the firmament holds. However, a more specific relationship is found between the planets and those stars which the planets encounter in their journey; namely when any of the five <term>retrograde</term><note>Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which occasionally appear to move backward in the sky from Earth's perspective.</note> planets reaches the straight line that extends from the center of the world to the fixed star. This relationship claims the name of <term>conjunction</term><note>When two celestial bodies appear in the same position in the sky.</note> most properly for itself. The same thing happens to them in respect to the <term>luminaries</term><note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. But there is more: for the Sun is faster in its course than the fixed stars; because of this, a star which was previously seen after sunset ceases to appear because of its proximity to the sun. They call this relationship the **evening setting**. Then the Sun proceeds toward a conjunction with the fixed star. Afterward, when the Sun has moved far enough away from the star so that what was previously not seen due to the Sun’s proximity begins to appear again before sunrise: the philosophers gave the name **morning rising** to this relationship. Finally, understand that these relationships are to be considered in respect to the Moon as well.

### Proposition III.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial V with floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
To begin explaining the various relationships the fixed stars take in respect to the <term>horizon</term><note>The line where the earth meets the sky, determining what is visible to an observer.</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial Q with floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
There are four relationships of this kind: namely, rising; <term>mid-heaven</term><note>Also known as "culmination," this is when a star crosses the meridian (the line running from North to South through the zenith).</note> above the earth; setting; and mid-heaven below the earth. For in a <term>right horizon</term><note>An observer's view from the Earth's equator, where the poles lie on the horizon line.</note>, every star rises and sets, since the poles of the primary motion are on the surface of the horizon; for this reason, the horizon cuts all circles parallel to the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note> through the middle. Whence also the star’s duration during the day will equal its duration at night. Also, every star will cross the mid-heaven twice: once above the earth and once below the earth. But where the poles of the world are the poles of the horizon <note>This refers to the Earth's North or South Pole.</note>, none of the stars rise or set. For the equinoctial is revolved on the surface of the horizon; and the remaining circles parallel to it will also be parallel to the horizon in their circuit. Therefore, the stars in the upper hemisphere do not set, and the stars of the lower hemisphere do not rise. However, each of them will cross the mid-heaven twice in one circuit—these above the earth, and those below the earth. But other horizons, toward which the equinoctial is inclined and for which one of the poles is elevated, will have this consideration. Two small circles <note>In modern terms, the circles of perpetual apparition and occultation.</note> must be understood, equal to each other and parallel to the equinoctial, each of which touches the circle of the horizon. One is near the elevated pole of the world, and the other near the depressed pole. Therefore, whatever stars are contained between one of the small circles and the elevated pole do not set. But whatever is contained between the depressed pole and the small circle will never rise nor set, but will always be hidden. However, each of these stars will reach the <term>meridian</term><note>The imaginary line passing through the poles and the observer's zenith.</note> twice in one circuit: this one above the earth, and that one below the earth. All the remaining stars, which the two said small circles enclose, both rise and set, and cross the mid-heaven once above the earth and another time below the earth. Furthermore, whether a star begins to move from the horizon or from the meridian, the times of their return will be judged equal to the senses. Also, the time in which a star is led from the part of the meridian above the earth to the part of the meridian below the earth, or vice versa, is equal to the time it returns to the beginning of its motion, since the meridian cuts all the <term>parallels</term><note>Circles of latitude on the celestial sphere.</note> in which we measure the journeys of the stars into equal parts. But the time that lies between rising and setting is unequal to the time in which the star returns from setting to rising below the earth. This indeed happens in every <term>oblique horizon</term><note>Any location on Earth between the equator and the poles.</note>, except however for those stars which are on the equinoctial circle, for which the equinoctial is cut through the middle by the horizon, making their stay above and below the earth equal.
