divided. Furthermore, the time that elapses from the rising of a star to its <term>culmination</term><note>original: "mediatione celi"; the moment a star reaches its highest point in the sky as it crosses the meridian.</note> above the earth is equal to the time that flows from its culmination to its setting. For the meridian divides all portions of the <term>parallels</term><note>The circular paths stars appear to follow as the Earth rotates.</note> which are above the horizon into equal parts. The same happens below the horizon. However, the time which flows from the culmination above the earth to the star's setting in a <term>right sphere</term><note>original: "sphera recta"; the celestial sphere as seen from the Earth's equator, where the poles lie on the horizon.</note> is equal to the time that passes from its setting to its culmination below the earth. But in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>original: "sphera obliqua"; the celestial sphere as seen from any latitude other than the equator, where the paths of the stars are tilted relative to the horizon.</note> it is always unequal, unless the star is on the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note>. Similarly, the time from the culmination below the earth to the rising is equal in a right sphere to the time from the rising to the culmination above the earth. But in an oblique sphere, it is not, unless you find the star on the equinoctial. Finally, it happens in a right sphere that all stars culminating at the same time also rise and set at the same time—excluding, however, their own motion, which creates an exception between them, although it happens to be very small. But in an oblique sphere, it is not so; rather, of the stars that culminate together, the one that is further north precedes the other in rising, but follows it in setting, etc.

### Proposition 5

->**To usefully combine the stated relationships of the stars.**<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the beginning of the section, depicting floral patterns and foliage in a woodcut style square frame.</image-desc>
We shall indeed combine these relationships by observing with which part of the <term>zodiac</term><note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, marking the path of the sun and planets.</note> each of the stars rises, sets, or culminates. We shall also consider with which of the fixed stars each of the planets either rises or sets, or whether it culminates. We shall, however, descend more specifically to those relationships which the stars have to the sun and the horizon. For we shall divide them into nine modes. ¶ The **first relationship** is the **morning rising**: specifically when the sun and the star itself are positioned in the eastern part of the horizon. There are three modes for this. One is when the star, existing under the rays of the sun, rises immediately after the sun has risen. Another is when the sun and the star rise at the same time. But neither of these two is perceived by the senses <note>Because the sun's brightness obscures the star.</note>. The third is when the star, emerging from the rays, rises before the sun. ¶ The **second relationship** is called the **morning culmination**: specifically when, with the sun being in the eastern part of the horizon, the star is in the middle of the sky. We distinguish three modes of this as well. One of which is when the star culminates immediately after the sun has risen. This relationship cannot be observed by sight. Another mode happens when the star culminates as the sun is rising; this mode also cannot be seen. The third mode: when the sun rises immediately after the star culminates; this can be noted by sight. ¶ The **third relationship**: when the sun is in the eastern part and the star is in the western part of the horizon; and it is called the **morning setting**. There are three modes of this. One is when the star sets immediately after the sun has risen. Another is when the sun and the star are positioned most precisely on the horizon—the former on the eastern side, the latter on the western side. But neither of these modes is distinguished by the senses. The third mode: when the sun rises immediately after the star sets; the senses can comprehend that one. The **fourth relationship** is called the **meridian rising**, which occurs when the sun is on the meridian and the star is in the eastern part of the horizon. we shall give two modes of this. One, while the sun is in the middle of the sky above the earth and the star rises, which shall be called "diurnal." The other, while the sun is in the middle of the sky below the earth and the star is at its rising, which shall be called "nocturnal." The senses will not be able to comprehend the first, but they will the second. ¶ The **fifth relationship** is the **meridian culmination**, which happens while the star culminates while the sun occupies the meridian. There are two diurnal modes of this. One, while the sun and the star are together in the meridian above the earth. Another, while the sun is in the meridian above the earth and the star is in the middle of the sky below the earth. And neither of these is known by the senses. There are also two nocturnal modes...

<header>Eighth</header>

...nocturnal. One occurs while the sun is at the <term>meridian</term><note>The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith; here referring to the sun being directly "underneath" the earth at midnight.</note> below the earth and the star is at the <term>mid-heaven</term><note>original: "medio celi"; the point where a celestial body crosses the meridian.</note> above the earth. Another occurs while the sun is likewise at the mid-heaven below the earth and the star is with it at the meridian below the earth. The first of these two can be perceived by the senses, but not the second.
¶ The sixth configuration is called the **meridional setting**: namely, while the sun is at the meridian and the star sets. There are two modes of this. One is diurnal: namely, when the sun is at the mid-heaven above the earth and the star sets; this is not seen. The other is while the sun is at the mid-heaven below the earth and the star sets; this mode is visible to the senses.
¶ The seventh configuration is named the **evening rising**: namely, while the sun occupies the western part of the horizon and the star occupies the eastern part. From this, we distinguish three modes. One is when the star rises immediately after the sun sets; and this can be seen. Another is when the star rises exactly as the sun sets; which is not seen. The third is when the sun sets immediately after the star has risen; but this mode does not enter into the senses either.
¶ The eighth configuration will be named **evening mid-heaven** <note>Also known as evening culmination.</note>. This occurs while we position the sun in the west and the star at the mid-heaven, either above the earth or below it. This has three modes. One of these is while the star reaches the mid-heaven immediately after the sun sets, whether above the earth or below the earth. Another is while the sun sets and the star reaches the mid-heaven at the same time. The third is when the sun sets after the star has reached the mid-heaven.
¶ The ninth configuration will be when the sun and the star are both contained in the western part of the horizon; it is called the **evening setting**. We divide this into three modes. One occurs when the star, existing under the rays of the sun, sets after the sun's setting. Another is when the sun and the star set together at the same time. The third is when the star is enveloped in the solar rays before the sun sets.

## Proposition VI.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram representing a celestial sphere, positioned to the right of the lower text block. The diagram contains several intersecting arcs and a vertical axis labeled with letters: a, b, c, d, e, g, h, k, l, m, n, r, t, z, s. The arcs represent the celestial equator (a-e-g) and the ecliptic (b-e-d), intersecting at point 'e'. Point 'z' marks the celestial pole at the top, and 's' is at the bottom. Point 'h' is the pole of the ecliptic. Point 't' represents a star's position, through which arcs 'h-t-k-l' and 'z-t-m-n' are drawn to illustrate the relationship between different coordinate systems.</image-desc>

To work out how much <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note> a fixed star has, provided its distance from the beginning of <term>Aries</term><note>The point of the vernal equinox.</note> and from one of the poles of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The sun's apparent path; the coordinate system based on the earth's orbit.</note> is known.
¶ For this reason, I shall draw the <term>colure</term><note>A great circle on the celestial sphere that passes through the celestial poles.</note> distinguishing the greatest declinations of the sun, which shall be circle **a.b.g.d.**; under which I shall describe the half of the equinoctial circle **a.e.g.** and the middle of the ecliptic **b.e.d.** Let point **c.** be the head of Aries or Libra. Let **h.** be the pole of the ecliptic, and **z.** indeed be the pole of the equinoctial. Therefore, let the star be placed as desired at point **t.** Arcs **h.t.k.l.** and **z.t.m.n.** having been drawn, we seek arc **t.n.** <note>The star's declination.</note> But because from point **a.** two arcs descend, **a.h.** and **a.n.**, from the ends of which two others, **b.l.** and **n.z.**, being reflected, cross each other at point **r.**, there will be, by the method of conjunction <note>original: "viam coniuctionis"; a reference to Menelaus's theorem regarding spherical triangles.</note>, a proportion of the <term>sine</term> of **h.a.** to the sine of arc **a.z.** composed of two others: namely, the proportion of the sine of arc **h.l.** to the sine of arc **l.t.**, and the proportion of the sine of arc **t.n.** to the sine of arc **n.z.** Five of these are known; therefore the sixth will also become known. For arc **a.h.** is known because **a.z.** is a quadrant <note>90 degrees</note>, and **z.h.** is equal to the maximum declination of the sun <note>The obliquity of the ecliptic, roughly 23.5 degrees.</note>. Thus arc **a.z.** is known. Likewise, let arc **h.l.** be known. For since arc **k.l.** is erected perpendicularly above the ecliptic, arc **e.k.** will be like the <term>right ascension</term><note>The distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator.</note> and arc **k.l.** like the declination responding to the end of the arc of the ecliptic whose right ascension this is estimated to be—namely, arc **e.k.** Therefore, establish arc **e.k.** as known by hypothesis as a right ascension; and from a table, elicit the arc of the ecliptic responding to it, for which you may find its declination; this will be arc **k.l.** However, arc **h.k.** is a quarter of a circle; therefore the whole arc **h.l.** will be known. Similarly, arc **l.t.** is known because of arc **t.k.** (the latitude known by hypothesis) and arc **l.k.** previously known. But arc **n.z.** is a quarter of a circle; therefore, etc.

<header>Book</header>

The ratio of the <term>sine</term><note>In this historical context, the "sine" refers to a line segment within a circle of a specific radius, rather than the modern trigonometric function alone.</note> of $b. l.$ to the sine of $l. t.$ is the same as the ratio of the sine of $h. a.$ to the sine of $t. n.$

¶ For if the <term>total sine</term><note>original: "sinus totus"; the radius of the celestial sphere used as a standard value in calculations, often 60,000 or 100,000 in this period.</note> is placed as a mean between the sine of $b. z.$ and the sine of $t. n.$, the ratio of the sine of $h. a.$ to the sine of $t. [n.]$ will be composed of two: namely, from the ratio of the sine of $h. a.$ to the total sine, and the ratio of the total sine to the sine of $t. n.$ But the first of these is itself composed of two: namely, the ratio of the sine of $h. l.$ to the sine of $l. t.$ and the ratio of the sine of $t. n.$ to the total sine. Therefore, the ratio of the sine of $h. a.$ to the sine of $t. n.$ is composed of three: namely, of the sine of $h. l.$ to the sine of $t. l.$, and the sine of $t. n.$ to the total sine, and the total sine to the sine of $t. n.$ But these last two create a <note>original: "proportionem equalitatis"</note> ratio of equality <note>A 1:1 ratio, which cancels out in the calculation.</note>. Thus, the corollary is more easily evident in this way: Because from the arc $l. h.$ two perpendiculars descend onto $l. g.$, namely $h. g.$ and $t. n.$, therefore the ratio of the sine of $l. h.$ to the sine of $h. g.$ is just as the ratio of the sine of $l. t.$ to the sine of $t. n.$ If you wish to conclude this otherwise through the <term>science of spherical triangles</term><note>Spherical trigonometry, the primary tool for astronomers to calculate positions on the curved surface of the sky.</note>, proceed thus: Triangle $k. e. l.$ has two known angles, $k. e. l.$ and $e. k. l.$ The first is known because of the known maximum <term>declination of the sun</term><note>The obliquity of the ecliptic, or the tilt of the Earth's axis, which was a fundamental known constant in ancient astronomy.</note>. The second is known because it is a right angle. The arc $k. e.$ is also known. Wherefore the arc $k. l.$ will be known through the science of spherical triangles, along with arc $l. e.$ and angle $k. l. e.$ In this way, the entire arc $l. t.$ will be known. But in triangle $l. t. n.$, the two angles $l. t. n.$ and $t. n. l.$ are known. Therefore, arc $t. n.$, which is the sought-after declination of the star, will become known. ¶ Whether that declination is <term>southern</term><note>original: "meridionalis"</note> or <term>northern</term><note>original: "septentrionalis"</note> is determined by judgment. If you place point $b$ as the northern pole of the ecliptic and the star's latitude is northern, the declination will be northern. If, however, the star's latitude is southern, but smaller than arc $k. l.$—which falls from the circle of latitude between the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The sun's annual path across the sky.</note> and the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note>—the declination will again be northern. If the latitude is equal to that arc, the star will have no declination. But if the latitude is greater than that arc, the star's declination will be southern. In this manner, you may resolve the matter in every position.

## Proposition .vij.

### To discern the point of the ecliptic with which the star
### reaches the mid-heaven.

<image-desc>
A mathematical diagram of the celestial sphere. Within a large circle, various arcs and lines are drawn and labeled with letters: 'a' at the top, 'b' and 'z' on the left, 'd' on the bottom right, 'e' on the right, 'g' and 's' at the bottom. ¶ In the previously established arrangement, look at the figure which has the arcs $a. h.$, $a. n.$, $h. l.$, and $n. z.$ For by the <term>way of disjunction</term><note>original: "viam disjunctionis"; referring to a specific case of Menelaus's Theorem used in spherical trigonometry.</note>, the ratio of $n. l.$ to $l. a.$ will be composed of two: namely, the ratio of $n. t.$ to $t. z.$ and the ratio of $h. z.$ to $h. a.$ (I wish you to understand these as ratios of sines). Wherefore also the ratio of $h. z.$ to $h. a.$ is composed of the ratio of $z. t.$ to $t. n.$ and the ratio of $n. l.$ to $l. a.$, which is established thus: For the ratio of $z. h.$ to $h. a.$ is what remains from the subtraction of the ratio of $n. t.$ to $t. z.$ from the ratio of $n. l.$ to $l. a.$ Therefore, from $t. z.$ into $n. l.$ let $p$ be produced; and from $n. t.$ into $l. a.$ let $q$ be produced. The ratio of $z. b.$ to $h. a.$ will be as $p$ to $q$. Moreover, $p$ is aggregated from two: namely, $t. z.$ to $n. t.$ and $n. l.$ to $l. a.$, as is taken from the method of adding ratios. Wherefore $z. b.$ to $h. a.$ is composed of two: namely, $t. z.$ to $t. n.$ and $n. l.$ to $l. a.$ But five of these are known. For the declination of the star is known along with its complement. Also, the arc $l. a.$ is known, since it is the complement of the previously known arc $e. l.$ From this, the arc $n. l.$ will come forth as known. When this is subtracted from the known arc $e. l.$, the known arc $e. n.$ will remain. Therefore, point $n$ will have a known distance from that point of the equinoctial from which you wish to begin the <term>right ascensions</term><note>The distance of a point east of the vernal equinox, measured along the celestial equator.</note>. Therefore, by those things said in the second book, the point of the ecliptic corresponding to these ascensions will be known. With that point, the star will reach the meridian by the <term>primary motion</term><note>The apparent daily rotation of the heavens from east to west.</note>, which was what was sought. ¶ If you desire the same result by another process, do as I shall say. From the preceding, the arc of declination $t. n.$ was known, along with the angle $t. l. n.$

### Proposition VIII.

<image-desc>A celestial diagram showing a sphere with intersecting arcs labeled with letters z, b, k, t, e, g, d. The arc b-e-d represents the horizon, and a-c-g represents the ecliptic.</image-desc>

**T**o find the point of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere; the zodiac belt.</note> which rises together with a star.
¶ Let the <term>meridian</term><note>The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith.</note> circle be $a. b. g. d.$, under which is half of the ecliptic $a. c. g.$, with half of the eastern <term>horizon</term> $b. e. d.$; let the star which is now rising be $h$. Let a <term>quadrant</term><note>A quarter of a circle, measuring 90 degrees.</note> of a circle be drawn from the southern pole of the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note> $z$ through point $h$, which shall be $z. h. t.$ Therefore, the point $t$ with which the star <term>mediates the heaven</term><note>original: "mediat celum"; reaches its highest point on the meridian (culmination).</note> is known from the preceding proposition. However, the star does not rise with that same point in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>A view of the sky where the celestial equator is tilted relative to the horizon, as seen from anywhere other than the Earth's equator.</note>, although this would happen in a <term>right sphere</term><note>A view of the sky from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator passes directly overhead and meets the horizon at right angles.</note>. Instead, it rises with point $e$ of the equinoctial. Therefore, once point $e$ is found—specifically, how far it is from the point where the <term>right ascensions</term><note>The distance measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note> begin—the point of the ecliptic corresponding to it at this horizon will be known, with which I say the star rises. Because, however, between the two arcs $a. e.$ and $a. z.$ two others intersect, which are $e. b.$ and $z. t.$, the ratio of $z. b.$ to $b. a.$ will be, by the method of division, composed of two: namely, the ratio of $z. h.$ to $h. t.$ and the ratio of $t. e.$ to $e. a.$ Understand these as being <term>right sines</term><note>In medieval trigonometry, sines were treated as lengths of lines within a circle of a fixed radius rather than modern unitless ratios.</note>. Since five of these are known, the sixth will therefore be known: namely the arc $t. e.$ Thus point $e$ will be known, along with the point of the ecliptic which rises with it and the star $h$. Likewise, through the science of triangles, the triangle $e. h. t.$ has the side $h. t.$ known. For the <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the star is known from the things stated above. But the angle $e. t. h.$ is a right angle, and the angle $h. e. t.$ is known on account of the inclination of the equinoctial, which is assumed to be known; and it is the arc $a. b.$ Therefore, arc $t. e.$ will become known, and the rest as before. Finally, from this proposition, you will know the <term>diurnal arc</term><note>The arc of the sky through which a celestial body moves from its rising to its setting.</note> of the star. For if you subtract arc $t. e.$ from a quadrant for stars having a southern declination, or if you add it to a quadrant for northern stars, the known <term>semidiurnal arc</term> will result. When this is doubled, the diurnal arc will be produced. If you subtract this from the whole circle, you will see the remaining <term>nocturnal arc</term>.

**T**o investigate with which point of the ecliptic a fixed star sets.
¶ In the preceding figure, set the arc $t. k.$ equal to the arc $t. e.$, proceeding in the opposite direction from arc $t. e.$ For then point $k$ of the equinoctial, with which the star sets, will be known. The point diametrically opposite to that in the ecliptic will be known, which was what was sought. ¶ To give confidence to this work: let there be an oblique horizon $s. l. b. h.$, above which is half of the equinoctial $k. a. e.$ and two portions of the <term>parallels</term> $l. h.$ and $s. o.$, which two stars describe above the horizon. Let one of these be southern, and the other northern. Let arcs $z. o. m., z. t. h., z. r. l.,$ and $z. s. n.$ be drawn from the pole of the world $z$ elevated above the horizon. It mediates the heaven, however, at point $r$, which is the same as point $t$. Therefore, $e$, which is the rising, follows point $t$ of the mediation of the heaven. Point $k$, however, which is...

And the two arcs $t. e.$ and $k. r.$ are equal: because the proportion of the <term>sine</term><note>A mathematical ratio used in trigonometry to calculate the sides and angles of triangles within a circle.</note> of the arc of angle $t. e. h.$ to the sine of arc $t. h.$ is as the proportion of the sine of the arc of angle $r. k. l.$ to the sine of arc $r. l.$ For the angle $t. e. h.$ is equal to angle $r. k. l.$ and arc $t. h.$ is equal to arc $r. l.$ But this proportion is as the total sine to the sine of both arcs $h. e.$ and $k. l.$ For each of the angles $e. t. h.$ and $l. r. k.$ is a right angle. ## Proposition X.

<image-desc>A circular diagram in the left margin illustrating Proposition X. It shows a circle representing a sphere with several intersecting arcs. Labeled points include a (top), g (bottom), b and z (left), h (bottom center), e (right), and k, l, m, n, t in the interior.</image-desc>

**Given** the <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of a star and the degree [of the ecliptic] with which it <term>mediates the heaven</term><note>Reaches the meridian.</note>: to distinguish its <term>latitude</term><note>In this context, celestial latitude: the distance of a star from the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> and its true place on the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path the Sun traces through the stars over the course of a year.</note>.
Let the figure of the seventh [proposition] of this book be repeated: in which the arcs $e. m.$ and $t. n.$ are given, and the goal is to find arcs $t. k.$ and $e. k.$ From arc $e. m.$, through the knowledge of declinations, $n. m.$ will be known; hence $m. z.$ and $m. t.$ are given. But the proportion of the sine of $m. z.$ to the sine of $z. b.$ is as the proportion of the sine of $t. m.$ to the sine of $t. k.$: therefore, the latitude of the star is known. Likewise, the proportion of $h. z.$ to $z. b.$ is composed of two others: namely, $h. t.$ to $t. k.$ and $k. m.$ to $m. b.$, five of which were already known. Therefore, $k. m.$ will become known; whereby $e. k.$—which was sought—is known.

## Proposition XI.

<image-desc>A circular diagram in the left margin illustrating Proposition XI. It depicts the intersection of circular arcs (likely representing the horizon and the ecliptic) within a larger circle. Points are labeled: a (top left), z (top), b (left), e (center arc), k (bottom center), g (bottom right), and l, t, h along an inner arc.</image-desc>

**Finally**, to consider the <term>appearances</term><note>Heliacal risings: when a star first becomes visible in the dawn before the Sun rises.</note> and <term>occultations</term><note>Heliacal settings: when a star disappears into the Sun's glare at dusk.</note> of the fixed stars.
The Sun brings a certain influence upon the fixed stars: so that those which are now hidden from sight (the proximity of the Sun causing this) may later appear when the Sun has moved far enough away from them. Certain stars, even if they are perceived by sight after the Sun's setting, soon begin to vanish as the Sun approaches them. The cause of these events was found to be the proximity of the Sun to the stars. But at what time and at what distance from the Sun this occurs was quite difficult to know. For if we take two stars of unequal <term>magnitude</term><note>Brightness; in ancient astronomy, stars were ranked from first (brightest) to sixth (faintest).</note> on the ecliptic, the arc of the ecliptic between the larger star first appearing and the Sun itself will be smaller than the arc of the ecliptic between the Sun and a smaller star at the beginning of its appearance. For the rays of a larger star, because they are stronger and more numerous, are [less] obscured by those nearby. Therefore, the distance of the Sun from a star on the ecliptic alone cannot indicate the beginning of its appearance. ¶ Furthermore, not every two equal stars having equal distances from the Sun will appear [at the same time]. For I shall place the eastern half of the <term>horizon</term> as $b. e. d.$ and the eastern half of the ecliptic as $a. e. g.$ And let the <term>pole of the horizon</term><note>The zenith, or the point directly above the observer.</note> be point $z$, from which the arc $z. t. h.$ is drawn through the center of the Sun at the beginning of the appearance of the star, which point $e$ designates. And let us erect the arc $k. l.$ <term>orthogonally</term><note>At a right angle (90 degrees).</note> to the ecliptic. # The Eighth Book

...into a northern latitude. $k. l.$ you have for equal stars at $e$ through the arc of the ecliptic. $k. h.$ will be at a distance from the sun at the beginning of its appearance. It is established, however, that arc $k. h.$ is smaller than arc $e. h.$ ¶ Furthermore, for stars of equal magnitude—whether they are on the ecliptic or outside it—having equal latitudes on the same side, the determination of their first appearance will not be the same. ¶ For as it becomes clear from the second book, the inclinations of the ecliptic to the horizon vary; let the angle of such an inclination, $d. e. g.$, be greater than the angle of inclination $m. o. n.$ Let $e$ be a star appearing first on the ecliptic, and let $b$ be the location of the sun. Let $o$ also be a star on the ecliptic equal to star $e$.
<margin>c</margin>
If, therefore, I place the sun below the horizon at $k$, with the arc $r. l. k.$ drawn so that arc $o. k.$ (that is, the distance of the star from the sun) is equal to arc $e. h.$, the arc $l. k.$ will be smaller than arc $t. h.$ For the proportion of the <term>sine</term><note>A trigonometric function representing the ratio of the side opposite an angle to the hypotenuse; used here to calculate celestial positions.</note> of arc $k. l.$ to the sine of the arc of angle $b. e. t.$ is smaller: because each of them is as the proportion of the sine of arc $e. h.$ to the <term>total sine</term><note>The sine of a 90-degree angle, used as a standard reference in ancient trigonometry.</note>, on account of arcs $e. h.$ and $o. k.$ being equal, and likewise the angles $t$ and $l$ being right angles. Wherefore, in the second figure, the sun will be closer to the surface of the horizon than in the first. And therefore its light is more strongly and more manifoldly diffused above the horizon. Therefore, the light of the star placed at $o$ is [obscured] more than the star at $e$. But the star at $e$ first appears. Therefore, the star at $o$, though equal to it, will not appear. It is necessary, therefore, if we wish for the star at $o$ to be appearing, that the sun be moved further away from it. This will happen when we imagine the sun at point $q$, and we establish the arc $p. q.$ as equal to arc $h. t.$ Therefore, to Ptolemy, subtly considering all these things, it seemed worthwhile to establish a single average for stars of one magnitude, by which the beginning of their appearance <note>Heliacal rising: the first day a star is visible in the dawn sky before the sun rises.</note> or <term>occultation</term><note>Heliacal setting: the last day a star is visible in the evening sky before it is lost in the sun's glare.</note> could be known for every horizon and for every place on the zodiac, whether the star has latitude or not. By this mean he found the arc of a great circle passing through the poles of the horizon and the sun—an arc, I say, falling between the sun and the horizon at the beginning of a star's appearance or occultation—which we shall call the **arc of vision**. But even that arc has variation due to different <term>climates</term><note>Latitudinal zones of the Earth; ancient astronomers noted that atmospheric thickness changed as one moved toward the poles.</note>. For in northern climates, because the air is thicker, that arc will be larger than in climates closer to the south. For that same reason, even in one climate, a variation—however slight—will be seen to happen due to the changeability of the air.

Therefore, through the knowledge of spherical triangles, angle $l.r.y$ will be known. Since angle $d.l.r$ was known from the previous process, the arc $d.l.y$ will be left known, as well as its opposite $k.l.e$. The rest follows as before for stars having southern latitude: by merely changing the diagram, you will easily solve it through the logic of spherical triangles.

# Proposition 14.

That if a star has **latitude**, the same conclusion follows.
¶ Look at the figure above <note>original: "Precedente aspice figuram"</note>: where the star is located at point $l$. Arc $l.r$ will be directly joined to arc $k.l$ when the star is at the beginning of **Cancer** or **Capricorn** <note>The summer and winter solstices.</note>. This arc $l.r$ is known, because it is the **complement of the declination** <term>Complement of declination: 90 degrees minus the star's angular distance from the celestial equator.</term> of the star, known from the things previously noted. Arc $d.r$ is also known, because it is the **elevation of the arctic pole** <note>The observer's geographic latitude.</note>. But since angle $l.d.r$ is a right angle, then by the science of **spherical triangles** <note>Geometry performed on the surface of a sphere, essential for navigation and astronomy.</note>, angle $d.l.r$ will be known, as will its vertically opposite angle $k.l.e$. But angle $k$ is a right angle, and arc $k.l$ of the **latitude** <term>Latitude: The distance of a star north or south of the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</term> is known; therefore, arc $e.k$ shall be given as known, and angle $k.e.l$ will be known. Thus, triangle $t.e.z$ has two known angles, $t.e.z$ and $e.t.z$ (which is a right angle), along with side $t.z$, which is the known **arc of vision** <note>The vertical distance the Sun must be below the horizon for a star to be visible.</note>. Therefore, its side $e.z$ will become known. If you subtract the known arc $e.k$ from this, the remaining arc $k.z$ is known, which is the distance of the Sun from the star when it first appears. ¶ But if the star is not at the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, proceed thus: Triangle $l.r.y$ has two known sides, $l.r$ and $r.y$; $l.r$ is the complement of the star’s declination, and $r.y$ is equal to the **maximum declination of the Sun** <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis, approximately 23.5 degrees.</note>. Likewise, its angle $l.r.y$ will be known. For the distance of the star's true place from the start of Cancer or Capricorn is assumed to be known; therefore, by the science of spherical triangles, angle $r.l.y$ shall be known. However, you will find angle $d.l.r$ just as before; if you subtract angle $r.l.y$ from it in this configuration, angle $d.l.y$ will remain known, as well as its opposite $k.l.e$. Then proceed as above.

# Proposition 15.

To calculate how great an arc of the **ecliptic** <term>Ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</term> removes the Sun from a star at the start of its **occultation** <term>Occultation: The moment a star disappears from view, either by setting or being obscured by the Sun's light.</term>.
¶ The beginning of occultation at the western part of the horizon happens just as the start of **appearance** <note>Rising in the morning (heliacal rising).</note> occurs in the east. The arc of vision that serves for appearance will also be useful for occultation. Therefore, nothing was required for the work of appearance that will not also serve for occultation, with this one exception: instead of the angle which the horizon makes with the ecliptic in the east, for occultations you must take the western angle contained by the horizon and the ecliptic.

# Book Nine: The Orders of the Celestial Spheres. The diversities of the planetary motions and their mean motions; it also investigates the whole theory of Mercury through observation.

## Proposition One.

To show in what order the celestial spheres are to be arranged.

Our ancestors held various opinions on this matter. However, they all agreed on one point: that the sphere of the **fixed stars** was higher than all the other orbits of the planets. Below this, they consistently ordered the sphere of **Saturn**, then the sphere of **Jupiter**, and below this the sphere of **Mars**. Likewise, they assigned the lowest place to the **Moon**—and wisely so, whether because it is said to be the cause of solar eclipses, or because it has a more clearly known **diversity of aspect** <term>Diversity of aspect: Also known as parallax; the apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations.</term> than all the other stars. 

Regarding the remaining three, however, there was controversy. The most ancient authors placed the **Sun** below Mars, **Venus** below the Sun, and **Mercury** above the Moon. Later authors <note>original: "Posteriores vero"</note>, who more frequently observed the conjunctions of the Sun with Venus and Mercury, since they never perceived a solar eclipse to have occurred by the intervention of Venus or Mercury, judged that they should be placed above the Sun. Alpetragius <note>Al-Bitruji (died c. 1204), an astronomer from Al-Andalus who proposed a system of homocentric spheres as an alternative to Ptolemy's epicycles.</note>, however, who thought that the diversities of motions and their apparent velocities happened by a certain **"shortening"** <note>original: "incurtatione"; a term referring to the decrease in speed or deviation in Al-Bitruji's physical theory of motion.</note>, placed Venus under Mars, the Sun under Venus, and then Mercury. For Venus "shortens" less from the first motion than the Sun, at least on the part of the **epicycle** <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets.</term>. Mercury, however, shortens more than the Sun. 

Of these opinions, that which the ancients followed has been accepted by the moderns. Nor is it surprising if the Sun is not eclipsed by Venus and Mercury, even though they are joined beneath it. For it is possible for one of them to be joined to the Sun according to the longitude of the **zodiac** <term>Zodiac: The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, following the path of the Sun (the ecliptic).</term> in such a way that a straight line connecting the centers of the Sun and the eye does not pass through the center of the planet, just as often happens in the conjunctions of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. Therefore, they will not then prevent the rays of the Sun from reaching the eye. 

¶ Furthermore, since their bodies appear quite small in comparison to the Sun—so much so that the ancients, according to **Albategni** <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a famous Arab astronomer and mathematician whose observations refined the parameters of the solar year and the obliquity of the ecliptic.</note>, set the visual diameter of Venus at one-tenth that of the Sun. Because of this, its surface presented to our sight (which appears flat to the senses) must be one-hundredth the surface of the Sun. If we placed the three centers of the Sun, Venus, and the eye in a single straight line, the amount that Venus would subtract from the surface of the Sun would be imperceptible to the sight. 

¶ Moreover, the maximum distance of the Moon from the center of the world contains the earth's semi-diameter <note>The radius of the Earth.</note> nearly 64 times. The minimum distance of the Sun from the center of the world, however, contains that same semi-diameter 1070 times or more. It follows, therefore, that the distance between the two luminaries when they are closest to each other contains nearly 1006 semi-diameters of the earth. Nature does not allow this space to be empty; therefore, some celestial body must necessarily occupy it. But that body will be made of the completeness of the orbits of the Sun and Moon; for in vain would such a great mass be permitted in the heavens. For this reason, that space for the two orbits of Venus and Mercury by a natural fitness...

is indicated. However, which of these is situated above the other cannot be detected with any certainty. For **Mercury** appears very rarely in most climates. And if it does appear, it happens when it is around the mean distances of the **epicycle** <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets.</term>. At that time, although it may have a **diversity of aspect** <term>Diversity of aspect: Parallax, or the apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations.</term>, it is much smaller than that which it would have if it were at the opposite of the apogee <note>original: "opposito augis"; the point furthest from the center of motion.</note> of the epicycle. Therefore, this kind of diversity of aspect cannot be elicited exactly, since we can have total precision neither in the instruments necessary for this task, nor in calculating the motions of Mercury. The same should be judged concerning **Venus**.

## Proposition .ii.

To express the way in which the diversities of motions were recognized.

¶ In the beginning, it clearly appeared in these five stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> that there was a motion according to the succession of the signs—that is, from west to east—in relation to the **fixed stars**. Then, the first philosophers noted that for a certain time, their locations did not perceptibly change, and afterwards, they moved against the succession of the signs <note>original: "contra successionem signorum"; this describes retrograde motion, where a planet appears to move backward in the sky.</note>. They also understood that this diversity of motion was linked to the **Sun**. For after the conjunction of any of the three **superior planets** <term>Superior planets: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which orbit further from the Sun than the Earth does.</term> with the Sun, they saw them move with a very fast motion, and that this speed gradually decreased until they appeared stationary, and afterwards retrograde. And when they halved the total time of retrogradation, they found the Sun was opposite them in the middle of this time. And because they saw the same thing return under one consistency through frequent observations, they concluded for certain that in every **mean conjunction** of the Sun with any of these three, this diversity of motion would return. Likewise in all their equal distances from the Sun. 

Afterwards, they considered them when they had equal distances from the mean place of the Sun from their conjunction with the Sun. They found their motions in these nearly equal times were not equal. They also did the same for the distances of the locations in which the stars appeared stationary after the conjunction; for they found those distances to be unequal. This could by no means happen unless either the motions of the spheres on their centers were irregular—which nature indeed abhors—or the centers of their spheres were different from the center of the world. And because they found two types of diversities, they were forced to posit two types of spheres to which these things likely happened. 

To that diversity which recurs at their conjunction with the Sun, they gave the **orbit of revolution** <note>original: "orbem reuolutionis"; this refers to the epicycle.</note>. For the time from the faster motion of the planet to the mean motion seemed greater than the time from the mean motion to the slower motion; this is most suited to the orbit of revolution, but least to the eccentric. Also, for accounting for <note>original: "saluandos"; literally "to save," meaning to provide a mathematical model that matches the observed appearances.</note> the motions of latitudes (about which more below), this sphere is more fitting. 

But they attributed an **eccentric** <term>Eccentric: A circular orbit whose center is shifted away from the Earth.</term> to the second diversity. For they found the time from the slower motion coming from this diversity to the mean motion to be greater than the time from the mean motion to the faster motion. ¶ Furthermore, two locations in which the fastest and slowest motions occur due to this diversity are found to move according to the motion of the fixed stars; this can only happen to an eccentric sphere. In **Venus** and **Mercury**, they likewise posited epicycles by which there would be an occasion for retrograde motions. When they considered the aggregate of the two distances from the mean place of the Sun—namely the evening and the morning <note>The maximum eastern and western elongations of the inner planets from the Sun.</note>—they found that in one place of the zodiac it was different in quantity from the aggregate of this kind that occurred in another place. It was therefore necessary for the epicycle to be closer to the Earth in one place than in the other. And so, they necessarily posited that the sphere in which the epicycle is fixed was eccentric.

### Proposition 3

->To enumerate why it is uncertain by what periods of time the mean motions of these stars should be measured.<-

**T**o enumerate why it is uncertain by what periods of time the mean motions of these stars should be measured.
¶ Because we intend to know the true locations of these stars at any given time, and since their true motions (as stated above) are irregular in their velocity, we must consider the mean <term>Mean motion: An idealized, perfectly uniform circular motion used as a mathematical baseline to calculate a planet's actual, irregular position.</term> by which such true locations are derived: namely, from a known time to which a known mean motion corresponds. However, this could not be achieved through the **stations** <term>Station: The point where a planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing direction (retrograde).</term> of the stars, as some of the ancients did; specifically, by saying that the arc traversed by a star in the time between two stations was the mean motion corresponding to that time. For that time cannot be grasped with sufficient precision, since the star appears to remain in almost one place for a notable amount of time. Furthermore, the arcs of this kind between the first two stations are not equal because of the **eccentric** <term>Eccentric: A circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center, explaining why seasons or planetary stages vary in length.</term>. Nor will the path be found through their **risings**. For when the stars first appear, they suddenly disappear <note>This refers to heliacal rising, when a planet first becomes visible in the dawn sky after being obscured by the Sun's glare.</note>, so that their locations cannot be grasped. Additionally, the atmosphere itself is the cause for them appearing now sooner, now later. ¶ Furthermore, nothing will be achieved through observations relative to the **fixed stars**. For although in a known time one of the planets, returning to a fixed star, will have described a known arc, yet because its motion around the center of the world is irregular, it may happen by chance that it describes this arc, or one equal to it, at another time that is longer or shorter. Therefore, the arc of mean motion will not have been grasped. Finally, no small amount of error is introduced by the fact that stars near the horizon and stars in the middle of the sky do not appear equally distant from one another <note>This refers to atmospheric refraction and perhaps the "Moon illusion," where objects near the horizon appear differently than those at the zenith.</note>.

### Proposition 4

->Now to choose which path must be followed.<-

**N**ow to choose which path must be followed.
¶ It must be observed that one of them <note>The planets.</note> has a certain distance from the **mean location of the Sun**, and is in a known part of the zodiac according to **longitude**. Then, one must wait until the planet returns to the same location, and alongside this, has that same distance from the mean location of the Sun which it had before. With this condition standing, it is certain that the previous **diversities** <term>Diversity: Here referring to the synodic anomaly, the variation in a planet's speed and direction caused by its motion on an epicycle.</term> have returned: in the **epicycle** indeed because of the same distance from the Sun's location, and in the **eccentric** because the center of the epicycle has returned to the place where it was before. Thus the time between the two observations will be known, and the number of revolutions in longitude and diversity will be known. For in the three **superior planets** <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, the number of full revolutions in diversity at a certain time is equal to the number of revolutions of the Sun in that same time <note>A fundamental rule in the Ptolemaic system where the synodic cycles of superior planets are tied to the solar year.</note>, as you will easily gather from what was said above. In **Venus** and **Mercury**, however, the number of revolutions of longitude equals the number of revolutions of the Sun. For these three <note>The Sun, Venus, and Mercury.</note> have equal mean motions, since Venus and Mercury never exceed certain limits from the Sun. Furthermore, the number of revolutions of Venus and Mercury in diversity will be easily obtained if we first consider the time of one such revolution near its true value. These returns, just as **Ptolemy** learned from **Abrachi** <note>original: "Abrachi"; a common medieval Latin corruption of the name Hipparchus, the great Greek astronomer.</note> and recounts, are in this order:

**Saturn** has 57 revolutions of diversity in 59 solar years, plus one day and approximately a half and a quarter <note>1 and 3/4 days.</note> of a day. He calls a "year" (according to his custom) the time in which the Sun returns to the point of the equinox or solstice. In the said time, Saturn has two revolutions of longitude, and beyond these, 1 degree, 7 minutes, and 2 thirds <note>original: "tertias"; a division of a degree smaller than a second.</note>, and half of a tenth of one degree.

**Jupiter** has 65 returns of diversity in 71 solar years, minus 4 days and approximately a half, a third, and a 15th part of a day. The revolutions of longitude are 6, minus 4 degrees and a half and a third of one degree.

**Mars** has 37 revolutions of diversity in 79 solar years, plus three days and a sixth of a day and a 10th part of a day.

<header>Movement</header>

...approximately. And it completes 42 revolutions of longitude, 3 degrees, and one-sixth of a degree. In these three <note>The three superior planets: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, the number of revolutions in longitude added to the number of revolutions in diversity <term>Diversity: Also called "anomaly," this refers to the planet's position on its epicycle, which explains its changing speed and retrograde motion relative to the Sun.</term> are together equal to the number of revolutions of the Sun. **Venus** has 5 revolutions of diversity in 8 solar years, minus approximately two days, a quarter of a day, and one-twentieth of a day. Its revolutions in longitude, however, are the same as the Sun's: namely 8, minus two degrees and a quarter of one degree. **Mercury** has 145 revolutions of diversity in 46 solar years, plus approximately one day and one-thirtieth part of a day. And its revolutions in longitude are 46, the same as the Sun, plus one degree.

# Proposition 5

### To derive the mean motions of the five wandering stars for individual dimensions of time.

**C**onvert the number of solar years to which their revolutions of diversity correspond into days; to these, add the days that remain beyond the whole years along with their fractions, if they are to be added, or subtract them, if they are to be subtracted. Also, multiply the number of revolutions for this time by 360 parts [degrees], and divide the product by the number of days already obtained with their fractions; the result will be the mean motion of diversity corresponding to one natural day. For the three superior planets, the difference between this and the mean motion of the Sun per day is the mean motion in longitude corresponding to one day. Thus, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose "Almagest" provided the foundation for this mathematical system.</note> found the quantities of the mean motions for these five planets, as you see in this table, from which it is easy to create tables of mean motions for any specific time.

...at the perigee <note>original: "proprio"</note>. With line $DE$ cut at point $Z$, I describe upon it, according to the quantity $AD$, circle $HTK$ equal to circle $ADG$. However, it does not move uniformly around that center, but rather around point $D$. The uniformity of this motion, however, is measured with respect to a point at the summit of the epicycle. This point exists on a line passing through point $D$ and the center of the epicycle. In this manner, the diversity <term>Diversity: The apparent irregularities or changes in speed and direction (retrograde) observed from Earth.</term> that is perceived by the senses will be seen to occur.

### Proposition 7.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop-cap letter 'A' depicting a figure (possibly a scholar or astronomer) within a decorative frame.</image-desc>

**A**s for properly observing the arrangements of the various motions of Mercury:
First, I will describe the circle $ABG$ upon whose center $D$ the motion of Mercury is established as uniform in longitude. Let a straight line $ADEG$ pass through center $D$, the center of the zodiac $E$; $A$ will be the apogee of this excentric, which is called the equant <term>Equant: A mathematical point from which the planet’s motion appears uniform, even if its actual speed varies.</term>, and $G$ will be the perigee. Then, from $DA$, I take $DZ$ equal to $DE$. Upon center $Z$, according to the quantity $ZD$, let a small circle be made, which is $DH$. It must then be understood that the center of the excentric circle—the deferent <term>Deferent: The large circle that carries the center of the epicycle around the Earth.</term> which carries the epicycle—moves against the succession of the signs, tracing the circumference of this small circle. 

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram in the lower left margin illustrating the motion of Mercury. It features a large outer circle (labeled a, k, g, l) and several inner circular paths. An epicycle (labeled m, k, r, l) is shown on the left side, connected by lines to various central points (z, d, e, h, 3). The diagram represents the interaction between the deferent and equant circles.</image-desc> 

Now, therefore, let the center of the carrying excentric be at point $H$, upon which the excentric deferent circle $TK$ is made, equal to the excentric equant circle $AG$. With line $ZHT$ drawn, let angle $AZT$ be made equal to $ADK$. Upon $K$, I shall describe the epicycle $LM$. Now once again, as with the other planets, let us suppose that line $EA$ moves according to the motion of the fixed stars, carrying with it the two points $D$ and $Z$, as well as points $A$ and $G$ (namely, the apogee and perigee of the equant). Let us imagine point $H$, the center of the circle carrying the epicycle, together with line $ZHT$, moving uniformly against the succession of the signs around center $Z$, making one revolution in a solar year. Similarly, let us estimate that the excentric $TK$ moves upon its own center $H$, carrying the center of the epicycle $K$ along with line $DKL$ according to the succession of the signs, also making one return in a solar year. The motion of the center of the epicycle will thus become uniform around center $D$. For this reason, the name "equant" is given to circle $AG$, of which $D$ is the center. From this it will be clear that line $DKL$, which contains the center of the epicycle, meets line $ZHT$, which contains the center of the carrying excentric, twice in a solar year: once upon line $DA$ and another time upon line $DG$. Whenever the center of the epicycle is at the apogee of the excentric, the center of the deferent will stand at the apogee of the small circle $DH$. 

Finally, let us suppose the epicycle moves around center $K$, carrying the body of Mercury: in the upper half according to the succession of the signs, and in the opposite direction in the lower half. The uniformity of the planet's motion in the epicycle is taken from a point marked at the summit of the epicycle, which is indicated by a line coming from the center of the equant through the center of the epicycle. This, then, is the observation of the motions in these five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" (planetae) are the five planets known to antiquity: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note>. Why they are arranged in this way will be opened up step-by-step in the following section.

## Proposition 8.

When the center of the epicycle is equally distant from either of the two lengths <note>original: "longitudinũ," referring to the apogee and perigee</note> of the eccentric: the angles of diversity <note>The "angle of diversity" refers to the planetary equation, the difference between a planet's actual position and its mean or average position.</note> which occur because of the eccentric, and those maximum angles at the center of the world which are subtended by the semidiameter of the epicycle, are equal. From this it will be clear that the maximum and opposite elongations <note>original: "longitudines," here meaning the angular distance or elongation of a planet from the Sun.</note> of Venus from the mean position of the sun are equal.

For this purpose, I draw the eccentric circle that carries the epicycle, $a.b.g.d.$, upon center $e$, whose diameter passing through the center of the world <term>Center of the world: In this geocentric model, the Earth.</term> $z$ is $a.e.z.g.$. In this diameter, let $e.h.$ be cut equal to $e.z.$, so that $h$ is the point at which the regularity of motion is observed <term>Equant: The point $h$, from which the planet's movement appears uniform.</term>. Let $a$ be the further distance <term>Apogee: The point furthest from Earth.</term> and $g$ the closer distance <term>Perigee: The point closest to Earth.</term>. Taking angles $a.h.b.$ and $a.h.d.$ to be equal, I establish two equal circles on centers $b$ and $d$, representing the epicycle in two positions. From the center of the world $z$, I draw two lines $z.b.$ and $z.d.$, and also two lines $z.l.$ and $z.m.$ tangent to the epicycle. Likewise, let the semidiameters of the epicycle be $b.l.$ and $d.m.$, and let Venus be at points $l$ and $m$. With these things so arranged, I say that angle $h.b.z.$ is equal to angle $h.d.z.$, and likewise angle $b.z.l.$ is equal to angle $d.z.m.$. For because angle $a.h.b.$ was set equal to angle $a.h.d.$, line $h.b.$ will be equal to $h.d.$. Then, with $h.z.$ being a shared side, by the fourth [proposition] of the first [book] of Euclid, $z.b.$ becomes equal to $z.d.$, and angle $h.b.z.$ equal to angle $h.d.z.$—which are the angles of diversity occurring because of the eccentric. Next, since angles $l$ and $m$ are right angles, and line $b.z.$ is equal to $d.z.$, and the line $b.l.$ is also equal to $d.m.$, it follows from the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Euclid I.47).</note> that $l.z.$ is equal to $z.m.$. Then, by the eighth [proposition] of the first [book], angle $b.z.l.$ is equal to angle $d.z.m.$. These are the maximum [angles] at this position of the epicycle $z$ which are subtended by the semidiameter of the epicycle; which were the things to be demonstrated. 

¶ As a corollary, let $z.q.$ and $z.p.$ be parallel to the two lines $h.b.$ and $h.d.$; these will certainly pass through the mean position of the sun and Venus. Thus the two angles $b.z.q.$ and $d.z.p.$ will be equal to each other because of their equal alternate angles. When these are subtracted from the equal angles $b.z.l.$ and $d.z.m.$, they leave $q.z.l.$ equal to $p.z.m.$. But these are the two maximum elongations of Venus from the mean position of the sun, and they are opposite at this position of the epicycle in the eccentric and the planet in the epicycle. They are called "maximum" because $z.l.$ and $z.m.$ are tangent to the epicycle, and "opposite" because one of them is the evening [appearance] and the other the morning [appearance]. Thus the proposition is clear.

## Proposition 9.

In Mercury also, the same thing undoubtedly happens.

On the straight line $a.n.$, let point $a$ be the center of the orbit [marked] with the sign $u$. Let $b$ be the center of regular motion <term>Equant</term>. Let $g$ be a point as far distant from point $b$ as $b$ is from $a$. Let it be the center of the small circle whose circumference the center of the eccentric carrying the epicycle describes <note>Mercury's model in Ptolemaic astronomy is unique because the center of its eccentric moves in a small circle, creating a "pulsing" effect on its distance from Earth.</note>. I shall place the epicycle in two positions upon centers $d$ and $e$ such that, when lines $d.b.$ and $e.b.$ are extended, $g.b.d.$ and $g.b.e.$ are made equal. For by this, the epicycle will have equal distances from the furthest distance <term>Apogee</term>. Then, from the center of the world, which is $a$, I draw two lines, one of which is $a.l.$ and the other $a.m.$, tangent to the epicycle at $l$ and $m$; in these points of contact let us imagine the star to be. From $a$ also let $a.e.$ and $a.d.$ be drawn, and let the two semidiameters of the epicycle be $d.l.$ and $e.m.$. Now I say that the two angles $a.d.b.$ and $a.e.b.$, and likewise the two $d.a.l.$ and $e.a.m.$, are equal to each other. For above point $g$, I establish angle $n.g.z.$ equal to angle $g.b.d.$

Therefore $d.t.$ will be equal to $e.k.$, whereby the whole $b.d.$ is equal to the whole $b.e.$; and with $b.a.$ made common to the two equal angles $d.b.a.$ and $e.b.a.$, $a.d.$ will become equal to $a.e.$, and angle $b.d.a.$ will be equal to angle $b.e.a.$, which are the angles of diversity <term>Angle of diversity: The "equation of center," which accounts for the difference between a planet's uniform motion and its observed position due to its eccentric orbit.</term> occurring because of the eccentric. Then, because angles $l$ and $m$ are right angles, and the two lines $a.d.$ and $d.l.$ are equal to the two $a.e.$ and $e.m.$, $a.l.$ will become equal to $a.m.$; hence angle $d.a.l.$ is equal to angle $e.a.m.$, which are the maximum angles which the semidiameters of the epicycle subtend at this position. From this, just as you will prove in the case of Venus, you will prove that the two maximum elongations <note>original: "longitudines," here meaning angular distance from the Sun.</note> of Mercury from the mean position of the sun are equal.

### Proposition 10.

### Preparing the way to understand the nature of Mercury's varying motion.

<image-desc>A complex circular diagram illustrating planetary motion. It features a large outer circle, an interior eccentric circle, and an epicycle in the upper left. Various radial lines originate from centers 'e' and 'z', intersecting chords and tangents. Points are labeled a, b, d, g, k, l, m, n, p, q, z, and the number 3 is used as a point label.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'A' with floral patterns.</image-desc>There was no way to understand the nature of Mercury's various motions unless the position of the furthest distance <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</term> or the nearest distance <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</term> was first established. This location, however, could only be found through two maximum elongations <note>original: "elongationes maximas"</note> from the mean position of the sun that were equal and opposite. For when two such elongations are found, and the distance between the mean positions of the sun is halved, the middle point will be the location of either the furthest or the nearest distance. ¶ Truly, it will not be enough to have found such maximum equal and opposite elongations in a general sense—that is, where one is in the evening and the other in the morning—but it is advantageous that they be of a specific and clear opposition; I mean to say: so that one has a clear increase and the other a clear decrease. And to make that clearer: in the figure let there be an eccentric circle $a.b.g.d.$ on center $e$ equal to the motion of the center of the epicycle, whose diameter $a.e.z.g.$ passes through the center of the world $z$. Let the line $b.d.$ cut the line $a.g.$ perpendicularly at point $z$; therefore $a$ will be the furthest distance of the equant <term>Equant: The mathematical point used to explain the observed speed changes in planetary orbits.</term>, and $g$ the nearest. But $b$ and $d$ are the middle distances. At the two points $a$ and $g$, there is no diversity <note>original: "diuersitas," referring to the equation of center.</note> that occurs because of the center. At $b$ and $d$, however, it becomes greatest; for in proceeding from $a$ to $b$, the angle of this diversity increases continuously; from point $b$ to $g$, it decreases continuously; but from $g$ to $d$ it increases again, and from point $d$ to $a$ it decreases. ¶ Furthermore, the diversity which is due to the epicycle is greatest when proceeding from $a$ to that place in which the epicycle is closest to the earth; it increases continuously, so that according to the greater approach to the earth, that diversity becomes greater, and according to the lesser approach, it becomes smaller. Let us therefore place the epicycle in arc $a.b.$ as circle $l.m.$ upon center $k$, with the tangents $z.l.$ and $z.m.$ drawn, along with lines $e.k.$, $k.l.$, $k.m.$, and $z.n.$ parallel to $e.k$.

### Ninth Book

...will be from what was mentioned above. $f.n.$ is the line of the mean motion of the sun, and angle $l.z.n.$ is the maximum morning elongation from the mean position of the sun at this position of the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one, used to explain the complex paths of planets.</term>. And angle $m.z.n.$ is the evening elongation. And in this way, throughout the entire arc $a.b.g.$, the maximum morning elongation will consist of the angle of diversity <term>Diversity: Also called 'equation'; the geometric difference caused by the planet moving on an eccentric or epicyclic path rather than a perfect circle centered on Earth.</term> of the eccentric and the angle of the maximum diversity of the epicycle. However, the maximum evening elongation will be the remainder left after subtracting the diversity of the eccentric from the maximum angle of diversity of the epicycle.

But the opposite of this will happen in the semicircle $g.d.a.$ As the epicycle proceeds toward $b$, the angle of each diversity increases, and therefore the morning elongation has a clear reason for its increase. Hence, the maximum morning elongation can easily be observed in this position. The evening elongation, however, will be of uncertain and doubtful increase, or at least not clear. For although angle $k.z.m.$ increases, angle $n.z.m.$ also increases along with it; this must indeed be taken away from angle $k.z.m.$ to leave the evening elongation. It will therefore happen in a specific place on arc $a.b.$ that as much as the decrease of angle $k.z.m.$ adds, the angle $k.z.n.$ will diminish by almost the same amount. It will therefore be uncertain when the planet has its maximum evening elongation in this position of the epicycle; indeed, in many nearby parts, it will be thought to have equal evening elongations. For this reason, among the maximum elongations that occur in arc $a.b.$, we consider that only the morning one should be observed by us.

In the arc $b.g.$, because the diversity of the eccentric decreases and the diversity of the epicycle increases until the epicycle reaches the point nearest to the earth, the morning elongation—which is then completed from these—will be of uncertain increase. For in a certain place of this arc, as much as the diversity of the epicycle increases, the diversity of the eccentric perhaps decreases by the same amount. The evening elongation, however—since it is then the remainder after the subtraction of the diversity of the eccentric from the maximum diversity of the epicycle—will have a double reason for its increase, as the diversity of the eccentric decreases while the other increases. Therefore, in this arc, only the evening elongation should be observed, and the morning elongation should be ignored.

In the arc $g.d.$, after the place of the maximum approach of the center of the epicycle to the earth, the diversity due to the epicycle will decrease, but the diversity of the eccentric will increase. Since the morning elongation is the remainder after the subtraction of the angle of the diversity of the eccentric from the angle of the diversity of the epicycle, the morning elongation will show a notable decrease, while the evening elongation will be uncertain and doubtful.

Finally, in arc $d.a.$, both diversities decrease, of which the evening elongation consists. Therefore, the evening elongation itself will show a manifest decrease, while the morning one will be uncertain. 

In summary, therefore, the morning elongations in arc $a.b.$ will rightly be called "contraries" <note>original: "contrarie" – meaning they represent the opposite geometric conditions.</note> to the evening elongations in arc $a.d.$ This is because the former show a manifest increase, while the latter show a manifest decrease. Likewise, the evening elongations in arc $b.g.$ (approaching the point where the epicycle's center is nearest the center of the earth) are contrary to the morning elongations in arc $g.d.$ (moving away from the point nearest the center of the earth); the former manifestly increase, while the latter manifestly decrease. 

None of the remaining elongations deserve to be called contrary to one another, as they are not at all contrary according to increase and decrease. However, those which we have rightly called contraries will be useful for our purpose. For once two such points are found, the middle point between the two mean positions of the sun will certainly be the location of either the farthest distance <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</term> or the nearest distance <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</term> of Mercury's eccentric. For these contrary elongations cannot happen to be equal unless what we desire is true: that the location of the farthest or nearest distance lies exactly in the middle.

### Ninth Book

To determine the apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion; here called "longitudo longior."</term> or the perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the center; here called "longitudo propior."</term> of Mercury, and in which part of the zodiac it is located.

¶ To achieve this, let us take two observations from Ptolemy in which the maximum elongations <term>Elongation: The angular distance between the Sun and a planet as seen from Earth.</term> of Mercury from the mean position of the sun were equal: namely, the morning and the evening elongations. The first of these was in the 16th year of Hadrian <note>Reigned 117–138 CE</note>, on the 16th day of the month of Phamenoth <note>The seventh month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, after the evening hour had passed. For Mercury was seen to have reached one degree of Pisces, with the instrument <note>likely an astrolabe or armillary sphere</note> aligned by the star Aldebaran <note>The "Eye of the Bull" in the constellation Taurus</note>. However, the sun, according to its mean motion, was at 9 degrees and three-quarters <note>original: "medietate ⁊ q̃rta," meaning one half plus one quarter</note> of Aquarius. Therefore, its evening elongation from the mean place of the sun was 21 degrees and 15 minutes. ¶ The other observation was in the 18th year of Hadrian, on the 18th day of the month of Athyr <note>The third month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, after the morning of the nineteenth day had begun. For then, with the instrument aligned by Aldebaran, it was seen at 18 degrees and three-quarters of Taurus. And the sun, by its mean motion, was at 10 degrees of Gemini. Therefore, the maximum morning elongation was 21 degrees and 15 minutes. The difference between the two mean motions of the sun was 120 degrees and 15 minutes. If we add half of this to 9 degrees and 45 minutes of Aquarius, the result is 10 degrees of Aries, minus one-eighth of a degree. For this reason, the diameter of the eccentric passing through the apogee cut the zodiac at 9 degrees and 53 minutes of Aries, which was the knowledge being sought. ¶ The same result will also emerge through two other observations of Ptolemy. The first of these was in the first year of Antoninus Pius <note>Reigned 138–161 CE</note>, when 20 days of the Egyptian month of Athyr had passed, the morning of which was the 21st day, during the evening hour. Having aligned the instrument by the star at the Heart of the Lion <note>Regulus</note>, he found Mercury at its maximum evening elongation at 7 degrees of Cancer, while the sun, according to its mean motion, was at 10 degrees and 10 minutes of Gemini. Thus, the maximum elongation of Mercury from the mean place of the sun was 26 degrees and 30 minutes. ¶ The other of these was in the fourth year of Antoninus, when 18 days of the month of Phamenoth had passed, in the morning of the nineteenth day. For then, having aligned the instrument by the star Antares <note>original: "Antares: que cor scorpionis dicitur," Antares: which is called the heart of the scorpion</note>, he found Mercury at 13 degrees and 30 minutes of Capricorn, while the sun, by its mean motion, was at 10 degrees of Aquarius. Thus, the elongation was 26 degrees and 30 minutes. The difference between the two mean places of the sun was 120 degrees and 30 minutes. When half of this is added to the mean place of the sun from the first observation, the result is 10 degrees and 15 minutes of Leo. It is therefore necessary to proceed through this place with the diameter of the eccentric passing through both elongations.

->Proposition XII.<-

The apogee and perigee of the eccentric move just as the fixed stars move.

Therefore, the greater morning elongation from the mean place of the sun was 25 degrees and one-third. To this elongation, Ptolemy selected a comparable one from the ancients out of two observations in this manner. In the aforementioned 23rd year, as Dionysius wrote, on the fourth day of the month of Thoth, in the first hour of the night, there was a line which passed over the two horns...

### Ninth Book

...of Taurus, decreased from the position of Mercury by a quantity of three diameters of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refers to the Sun and Moon; their apparent diameters were often used as a rough unit of measurement in ancient astronomy</note>. For this was in the 486th year of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabuchodo." refers to the Era of Nabonassar, beginning 747 BCE, commonly used by Ptolemy</note>, in the month of Phamenoth <note>The seventh month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, on the evening of its first day, with the Sun—according to its mean motion <term>Mean motion: The theoretical average speed of a celestial body, ignoring the speed changes caused by its elliptical orbit.</term>—being at 29 degrees and 30 minutes of Aries. Therefore, the evening elongation <term>Elongation: The angular distance between the Sun and a planet as seen from Earth.</term> of Mercury from the mean position of the Sun was 24 degrees and 10 minutes.

Likewise, as Dionysius wrote, in his 28th year, on the seventh day of the month of Gamelion <note>An Athenian month</note>, the star of Mercury was seen meeting the "heads" of Gemini <note>The stars Castor and Pollux</note>; it was indeed more southerly than the head of the following twin <note>Pollux</note> by an amount of a third part of the moon's diameter. And it appeared to be distant from that same head by a little less than double the distance that is between the two heads. And because the head of the following twin, according to Ptolemy's calculation, was then at 22 degrees and 40 minutes of Gemini, it was deduced that Mercury appeared at 29 degrees and 20 minutes of Gemini. And this observation was in the 491st year of Nabonassar, five days having passed in the month of Pharmouthi <note>The eighth month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, at the first hour of the night. The Sun, according to its mean motion, was at 2 degrees and 50 minutes of Gemini. Therefore, the evening elongation of Mercury from the mean position of the sun was 26 degrees and 30 minutes.

¶ Furthermore, the difference between the mean positions of the Sun in these two observations was 33 degrees and 20 minutes. But the difference of the evening elongations was 2 degrees and 20 minutes. Moreover, the difference in elongation—for which we seek a comparison—above the first elongation of these observations is 1 degree and 40 minutes. Therefore, a proportional part must be taken from the 33 degrees and 20 minutes, according to the ratio of 1 degree and 40 minutes to 2 degrees and 20 minutes. This comes to approximately 24 degrees, which must be added to the mean position of the sun of the first observation: namely, 29 degrees and 30 minutes of Aries; and the result will be 23 degrees and 30 minutes of Taurus. Indeed, when the Sun is in this position, the evening elongation of Mercury becomes a maximum of 25 degrees and 50 minutes.

Therefore, the comparable elongation to the first was found; in these, the difference of the mean positions of the Sun was 95 degrees and 20 minutes, half of which is 47 degrees and 40 minutes. When added to the Sun's position in the first observation—which was 18 degrees and 10 minutes of Aquarius—it produces 5 degrees and 50 minutes of Aries. Therefore, the line passing through the center of the world and the apogee <term>Apogee: The "longitudo longior," or the point in an orbit furthest from the center.</term> and perigee <term>Perigee: The "longitudo propior," or the point in an orbit closest to the center.</term> of Mercury's eccentric <term>Eccentric: A circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center.</term> was, at this time, at 6 degrees of Aries. By the aforementioned observations of Ptolemy, this line came to 10 degrees of Aries. And because between these observations of Dionysius and Ptolemy there were nearly 400 years, it is established that this line moved approximately 4 degrees in 400 years; therefore, in 100 years, it moved by approximately 1 degree. But in that same amount of time, the movement of the fixed stars in their place was just as much, as was proclaimed by Ptolemy; therefore, what we intended to show is clear.

This observation was made in the 512th year of the years of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabuchodo." refers to the Era of Nabonassar, starting 747 BCE</note>, when 9 days of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar</note> had passed: on the morning of the tenth day. Therefore, the morning elongation <term>Elongation: The angular distance between a planet and the Sun as seen from Earth.</term> from the mean position of the Sun was 21 degrees.

Likewise, in the 67th year of the Chaldeans, when 5 days of the first month of Lheus <note>A month in the Seleucid calendar</note> had passed: Mercury was seen near the eastern and northern star which is in the forehead of Scorpio <note>Likely the star Beta Scorpii, also known as Graffias or Acrab</note>. We have, therefore, two morning elongations. One of 21 degrees, with the Sun according to its mean motion being at 5 degrees and 10 minutes of Scorpio. The other of 22 degrees and 30 minutes, with the Sun according to its mean motion at 24 degrees and 50 minutes of Scorpio. We seek, therefore, at which position the mean motion of the Sun exists when the morning elongation is 21 degrees and 40 minutes <note>Ptolemy is looking for a specific value to match a corresponding evening elongation found elsewhere</note>. We do it in this way: The difference between the mean positions of the Sun is 19 degrees and 40 minutes. The difference between the stated morning elongations is 1 degree and 30 minutes. But the difference between the first morning elongation and the one whose position is sought is 40 minutes. Therefore, let a proportional part be taken from 19 degrees and 40 minutes, according to the proportion of 40 minutes to 1 degree and 30 minutes; this is almost 8 degrees and 45 minutes. For these—because the difference is small—Ptolemy took 9 degrees. When these are added to the mean position of the Sun for the first elongation, it results in 14 degrees and 10 minutes of Scorpio.
