This is equal to the evening elongation which occurs when the Sun, according to its mean motion, is at 27 degrees and 50 minutes of Leo. Between these mean positions of the Sun, the distance is 76 degrees and 20 minutes. Therefore, the midpoint between them is at 6 degrees of Libra. Thus, at this time, the line of the eccentric <term>Line of the eccentric: The axis running through the center of the planet's orbital circle and the Earth; it points toward the apogee (farthest point) and perigee (nearest point).</term> of Mercury passes through 6 degrees of Aries and 6 degrees of Libra. 

But in the time of Ptolemy, it was found to be at 10 degrees of Aries and Libra. There is no doubt, therefore, that in the intervening time—which is 400 years—it has moved 4 degrees; and it is established that the fixed stars move by exactly the same amount according to the opinion of Ptolemy. Therefore, by these and similar judgments regarding the other wandering stars <note>original: "stellis errantibus," referring to the planets</note>, we are compelled to estimate that the points of furthest and nearest distance <note>The apogee and perigee</note> are linked to the motion of the fixed stars <note>This refers to the phenomenon of precession, where the entire celestial coordinate system shifts slowly over centuries</note>.

# Ninth [Book]

...[the center] is closer in Libra than in Aries: because nothing else creates the difference in these types of elongations <term>Elongation: The angular distance between a planet and the Sun as seen from Earth.</term> from the Sun except for the rising of the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle; used to explain the varying speeds and directions of planets.</term> toward the center of the world. Indeed, the variation that usually occurs through the eccentric <term>Eccentric: A circular orbit where the Earth is not located exactly at the center.</term> is non-existent in these two observations.

->Proposition XV.<-

**To calculate the ratio of the radius of the epicycle to the line contained between the center of the epicycle at its greatest distance <note>original: "longitudine longiori," commonly called the apogee.</note> and the same center of the epicycle placed at the opposite distance.**

Let the straight line $a.g.$ pass through the greatest and nearest distance of the equant <term>Equant: A mathematical point used to account for the observed speed variations in planetary orbits.</term>. On this line, let point $b$ be the center of the world. Let $b.a.$ pass through 10 degrees of Libra, and $b.g.$ pass through 10 degrees of Aries. Upon the two points $a$ and $g$, let two circles be drawn to represent the epicycle. With lines $a.d.$ and $g.e.$ drawn tangent to the epicycles from $b.e.$ and $b.d.$, let us imagine the planet at its morning distance at point $d$ and at its evening distance at point $e$. Since angle $a.b.d.$ is known through the preceding [proposition] to be 19 degrees and 3 minutes, and angle $d$ is a right angle, the ratio of $d.a.$ to $a.b.$ will be known. Similarly, angle $e.b.g.$ is known through the premise to be 23 degrees and 15 minutes, and angle $e$ is a right angle; therefore the ratio of $e.g.$ to $g.b.$ also becomes known. Thus, the ratio of $d.a.$ to $a.g.$ which was sought will be known. So Ptolemy, while $a.b.$ is 120 parts, found $a.d.$ to be 39 parts and 9 minutes, and $b.g.$ to be 99 parts and 9 minutes. Therefore, the whole $a.g.$ is 219 parts and 9 minutes. Dividing $a.g.$ in half at point $z$, $a.z.$ will be 109 parts and 35 minutes. Therefore, $z.b.$ is 10 parts and 25 minutes.

->Proposition XVI.<-

**That the center of Mercury’s epicycle reaches its greatest proximity to the center of the world twice in a solar year. From which it will be clear that the eccentric carrier of the epicycle revolves around a center moving against the succession of the signs <note>This refers to retrograde motion, moving from east to west relative to the zodiac.</note>.**

One may take this from the observations of Ptolemy recounted above in the fourth [chapter] of this book. In those, the distance of the center of the epicycle on either side from the greatest distance was approximately four signs <note>A "sign" refers to 30 degrees of the zodiac.</note>. In the observation made in the 16th year of Hadrian <note>Hadrian ruled from 117 to 138 CE.</note>, with the Sun according to its mean motion being at approximately 10 degrees of Aquarius, the evening distance was 21 degrees and 15 minutes. Likewise, in the observation made in the fourth year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Hadrian's successor.</note>, with the Sun and Mercury again existing according to mean motion at 10 degrees of Aquarius, the morning distance was found to be 26 degrees and 30 minutes. Adding these two distances together results in 47 degrees and 45 minutes; the epicycle spans such an arc in this position, namely when it is distant from the greatest distance by 4 signs. You will elicit the same through other [observations] and for another position of the epicycle. For in the 18th year of Hadrian, with the Sun existing according to its mean motion at 10 degrees of Gemini, the morning distance was found to be 21 degrees and 15 minutes. In the first year of Antoninus, with the Sun again at 10 degrees of Gemini according to mean motion, the evening distance was found to be 26 degrees and 30 minutes. When these distances are collected, they also total 47 degrees and 45 minutes, and the epicycle spans such an arc in this position. Truly, the evening distance from the mean place of the Sun was found to be 23 degrees and 15 minutes at the nearest distance, and it is manifest that an equal morning distance occurs in the same place. Therefore, doubling 23 degrees and 15 minutes results in 46 degrees and 30 minutes, which the epicycle spans when existing at its nearest distance. It is therefore established that the epicycle is closer to the center of the world when it is distant from the greatest distance by four signs than when it is at the [greatest] distance...

...situated at the closer distance. For this reason, it occupies a larger arc of the heaven; therefore, in the figure above, point 3 was not the center of the eccentric, but was a point situated equally distant from the center of the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle; used to explain the varying speeds and directions of planets.</term> at the closer distance and its opposite. ### Proposition XVII.

**To determine the point with respect to which Mercury has a regular motion of longitude.** <note>The "regular motion of longitude" refers to the equant point, the theoretical spot in space where the planet's speed would appear perfectly uniform.</note>

We shall arrive at this through two observations of the greatest elongations <term>Elongation: The angular distance between a planet and the Sun as seen from Earth.</term>, both of which are in the same position relative to the farthest distance <note>original: "longitudine longiori," commonly called the apogee.</note>. To make the work easier, let the distance of the epicycle according to the mean motion in both elongations be three common signs from the farthest distance toward the same side. Let us take the first observation, which was in the 14th year of Hadrian, on the 18th day of the month of Mesre (the twelfth Egyptian month) <note>Mesre is the final month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, at the completion of the evening hour, with Theon observing Mercury distant from the beginning of Leo by 3 degrees and 50 minutes, just as Ptolemy reports, using Regulus <note>original: "cor leonis," the Heart of the Lion star.</note>. Therefore, Mercury, according to Ptolemy’s calculation, was at 6 degrees and 20 minutes of Leo, while the Sun, according to its mean motion, was at 10 degrees and 5 minutes of Cancer. Thus, the evening elongation remained as 26 degrees and 15 minutes. 

Another observation was Ptolemy's in the 20th year of Antoninus, on the 21st day of the month of Mesre, in the morning; in this, Mercury was seen through armillary spheres <term>Armillary sphere: A model of objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings, used for astronomical observations.</term> aligned by Aldebaran <note>A bright star in the constellation Taurus.</note> at 20 degrees and 5 minutes of Gemini, while the Sun, by its mean motion, was positioned at 10 degrees and 20 minutes of Cancer. Therefore, the elongation was 20 degrees and 15 minutes. Thus, the sum of both greatest elongations was 46 degrees and 30 minutes. 

Now, for the sake of the proposition: let the line *a.g.* pass through the farthest and nearest distances, in which point *b* is the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note> and point 3 is the center of the small circle. Let part *b.a.* of this line pass through 10 degrees of Libra, which is where the farthest distance is located, and *b.[g.]* through 10 degrees of Aries. Then, from point *b*, let a perpendicular *b.m.* be raised above *a.g.*, which will be the line of the Sun's mean motion in these two observations. Let the circle of the epicycle *k.l.* be described upon center *e*, which lines *b.k.* and *b.l.* touch at points *k* and *l*. With two radii *e.k.* and *e.l.* drawn, I drop a perpendicular *e.h.* from point *e* to line *a.g.*, and I will connect *e* with *b*. Line *e.b.* will thus contain point *h*, which we are seeking, since line *b.m.* is also assumed to be the mean motion of Mercury. Because the sum of the two greatest elongations is known, half of it will be known, and that is angle *e.b.l.* And the ratio of *e.l.* to *e.b.* will be known, since angle *l* is a right angle. Likewise, by subtracting the known morning elongation angle *e.b.m.* from angle *e.b.l.*, the known angle *e.b.m.* will remain, which equals angle *b.e.h.* because lines *h.e.* and *b.m.* are parallel. And since angle *h* is a right angle, the ratio of *e.b.* to *b.h.* will be known. But the ratio of *e.b.* to *b.l.* was already known, so the ratio of *e.l.* (the radius of the epicycle) to *b.h.* will also be known. But previously the ratio of *e.l.* to *3.b.* was known; therefore, the ratio of *3.b.* to *b.h.* will be known. Thus Ptolemy, in the parts by which he found *3.b.* to be 10 parts and 15 minutes, found *b.h.* to be 5 parts and 12 minutes. Therefore...

### Proposition XVIII.

To determine how large a radius the circle revolving the center of the eccentric should have.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a vertical line with points labeled from top to bottom: z, m, n, b, h, and s. To the right of this line is a point e. Keeping the previous configuration: from point **z**, let a perpendicular line be drawn toward the left to the line **a-g**, which shall be **z-n**, equal to line **z-a**, so that each of them consists of the radius of the eccentric and the radius of the small circle. Moreover, while the center of the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle upon which a planet moves, while the center of that small circle itself moves along a larger circle (the eccentric).</term> is at point **e**, because of the similarity of the motions and their contrary positions, the center of the eccentric will be on line **z-n**. Therefore, let point **m** be the center of the eccentric itself. 

The length of line **z-m** is sought in this way. Angle **m-z-h** is a right angle; and angle **e-z-b** differs little from a right angle. Therefore, the two lines **n-z** and **z-e** are joined to each other almost directly as a single line. From the 15th [proposition] of this book, **a-z** was made known with respect to the radius of the epicycle. For **a-z** was 109 parts and 35 minutes; and the radius of the epicycle was 39 parts and 9 minutes. Therefore, **z-n** is known. 

But from the preceding, **b-e** was known in the same respect, to which **z-e** is equal. Therefore, **n-z-e**, as a straight line, is known; and its half, **n-m** or **m-z-e**, is known. And this is the radius of the eccentric. Thus, by subtracting **m-n** from **n-z**, **m-z** remains known; and it is almost equal to line **z-h**, the knowledge of which was sought.

If you wish to strive for everything more precisely as in this figure: extend the straight lines **n-e** and **m-e**. And because from the preceding, line **b-h** was precisely found from its suppositions with respect to line **b-z**, line **b-z** also remained precisely known. But **e-h** will be known because of the known lines **e-b** and **b-h** and the right angle at **b**. 

Similarly, **e-z** will become known, and angle **e-z-b** will be known. From this, the whole angle **e-z-n** will become known. But in triangle **z-e-n**, the two sides **n-z** and **z-e** are already known, as is the angle they contain. Therefore, angle **z-n-e** will be known. This is equal to angle **m-e-n**, since each of the lines **n-m** and **m-e** is equal to the radius of the eccentric. Thus, the exterior angle **z-m-e** will be known. Therefore, triangle **z-m-e** has three known angles; thus the ratios of the sides will be known. But **z-e** was known with respect to the radius of the epicycle, or with respect to line **z-b**; therefore **m-z** will be known in the same respect, and so forth.

### Proposition XIX.

Therefore, the ratio of the radius of the epicycle in parts of the radius of the eccentric, set at will, will also be known. Likewise, from the 17th and the preceding: the ratio of the radius of the epicycle to line **b-h** and to the radius of the small circle is elicited. But also, the ratio of **b-h** to **b-z** was concluded as known. Now, however, the ratio of the radius of the eccentric to the radius of the epicycle is known. Therefore, the ratios will emerge...

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin illustrating the mathematical model for Mercury's orbit. It features an epicycle circle with center z and points k and t on its circumference. **To attest whether those things concluded concerning the motions of Mercury and the proportions of the lines agree with visual experiments.**

**E**arlier, in the fifteenth proposition of this book, we found through two observations of the greatest elongations <term>Greatest Elongation: The maximum angular distance Mercury appears to reach from the Sun as seen from Earth; because Mercury is so close to the Sun, this is the only time it is easily visible.</term> of **Mercury** that when it is distant by its mean motion from the eccentric apogee <note>The "longitudo longior" or the point where the planet is furthest from the Earth.</note> by a distance of 4 common signs <note>A "sign" in ancient astronomy is 30 degrees; 4 signs equal 120 degrees.</note>, the sum of the two greatest elongations—namely the morning and the evening—is approximately 47 degrees and 45 minutes. If, therefore, through calculation based on the propositions of the lines and other things concluded before this, we find the same result consistently, we shall have confidence in everything discovered thus far.

For the sake of this demonstration, let there be a line **a-e** passing through the perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the Earth; Latin: "longitudo propior".</term> of the eccentric. Let **a** be the apogee in the direction of Libra, and **e** be the perigee in the direction of Aries. On this line, let **d** be the center of the world <note>The Earth, in this geocentric model.</note>, **g** be the center of uniform motion <term>Equant: The "centrum motus equalis," a point off-center from which a planet's motion appears to move at a constant speed.</term>, and **b** be the center of the small circle.

Let angle **a-g-z** be four common signs, that is, 120 degrees (where four right angles are 360). On center **z**, I describe the circle of the epicycle **t-k**, having drawn two straight lines touching it—the tangent lines **d-t** and **d-k**. I will join the points of contact to the center of the epicycle via lines **t-z** and **k-z**. I will also connect the center of the epicycle with the center of the world by line **d-z**. Furthermore, I will make angle **a-b-h** equal to angle **a-g-z**, and make line **b-h** (the radius of the small circle) equal to **b-g**, connecting the two points **h** and **g** by line **h-g**. Then, from point **d** to line **g-z**, I will drop a perpendicular line **d-l**. With these things thus arranged, I will seek the angle **t-d-k**, which combines the two greatest elongations of Mercury.

In this position of the epicycle, because angle **a-b-h** is equal to angle **a-g-z** and line **b-h** is the radius of the small circle, point **h** will be the center of the eccentric due to the similarity of motions. Now, angle **h-b-g** is one-third of two right angles <note>60 degrees</note>, since angle **a-b-h** is two-thirds of two right angles <note>120 degrees</note>. Therefore, the two angles **h-b-g** and **b-g-h** are equal, and they amount to two-thirds of two right angles. For this reason, each of them will be one-third of two right angles <note>making them 60 degrees each</note>. Thus, triangle **b-g-h** will be equilateral and equiangular. Consequently, angle **b-g-h** is equal to angle **d-g-z**; therefore, the two lines **h-g** and **g-z** are joined directly to each other as a single line. Line **h-z** will therefore be the radius of the eccentric.

Next, because triangle **g-d-l** has known angles, line **d-l** will be known in relation to **d-g**, and similarly **g-l** in the same relation. From this, the entire line **h-l** is known, and the remainder of the eccentric radius, **l-z**, is known. And because line **d-l** is known, **d-z** will be known relative to the radius of the eccentric **h-z**. But in the same relation, **z-t** <note>the epicycle radius</note> is known, and angle **t** is a right angle. Therefore angle **z-d-t** is known, and angle **t-d-k** is double that.

Therefore, after a diligent calculation, angle **t-d-k** will come out to approximately 47 degrees and 45 minutes (where four right angles are 360 degrees). This same angle is also found by visual observation, which we have attested to this point. If you wish to amuse yourself by playing <note>A charming invitation to the reader to test the math themselves.</note> with the geometry, you can adapt your numbers to other locations where you have observed the greatest elongations, so that you may have greater certainty regarding the proportions of the lines found above. For if the number corresponds to the observation, there is no doubt that we have successfully found the causes for the variations in the motions of Mercury.

Ninth [Book]

## Proposition XXI.

To demonstrate geometrically that the epicycle's proximity to the Earth is greater when it is distant by four common signs from the furthest longitude than when it is at the closest longitude of the eccentric.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram is positioned to the right of the first block of text. It features a circle with a vertical diameter labeled 'a' at the top and 'e' at the bottom. Several points are marked along this vertical axis: 'f', 'b', 'g', and 'd'. From point 'g', a line extends to the left to a point '3' on the circumference of the circle. Another line connects point 'd' to point '3'. Near the center point 'b', there is an internal label 'h' and a line connecting it to 'b' and 'g'.
</image-desc>

To demonstrate geometrically that the proximity of the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; used to explain the retrograde motion of planets.</term> to the Earth is greater when it is four common signs <note>In the zodiac, "common signs" (Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces) are 30 degrees each. Four signs equal 120 degrees.</note> distant from the furthest longitude <term>Furthest longitude (Apogee): The point in an orbit where a celestial body is at its maximum distance from the Earth.</term> than when it is at the nearest longitude of the eccentric <term>Eccentric: A circular orbit that is not centered on the Earth.</term>. 

Let line **a-e** be passing through the furthest and nearest longitude of the equant <term>Equant: A mathematical point used to explain the observed speed changes in planetary orbits.</term>, on which point **d** is the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note>, **g** is the center of uniform motion, and **b** is the center of the small circle. Let **f** be the point where the center of the epicycle is located when it is at its furthest longitude. Now, let it describe a semicircle against the succession of the signs <note>original: "contra successionem signorũ"; meaning moving in the opposite direction of the zodiac's order.</note> so that it is at point **g**, over which, as the center, the circle **a-e** is described as the eccentric carrying the epicycle. 

Because of the similarity of the motions, the center of the epicycle will be at point **c**. Then, let the angle **a-g-3** be set at 120 degrees, so that four angles <note>The author likely means four segments of 90 degrees or a total circle.</note> are 360 degrees. On the line **g-3**, let point **3** be the center of the epicycle, distant from the furthest longitude by 120 degrees. Let an angle **a-b-h** be set equal to angle **a-g-3**, and let line **b-h** be equal to **b-g** or **b-f**. When line **g-h** is drawn, each of the angles **b-g-h** and **b-h-g** will be a third of two right angles <note>i.e., 60 degrees, as the sum of angles in a triangle is 180 degrees (two right angles).</note>, and the triangle **b-h-g** is equilateral, since the two sides **b-h** and **b-g** are equal and the angle **b-h-g** is a third of two right angles. 

But angle **d-g-3** is also a third of two right angles; therefore, the two lines **b-g** and **g-3** are joined directly to each other as one line. And because **b** is the center of the eccentric, and the center of the epicycle was placed at **3**, then **b-3** will be the semidiameter of the eccentric, equal indeed to **g-e**. However, when the equal parts **b-g** and **g-d** are taken away, **g-3** will remain equal to **d-e**. 

Likewise, from the 19th [proposition] of this book, the line **g-d** is 3 parts, and **g-b** is just as many, so that the whole **b-3** is 60 parts. Therefore, **g-3** will be 57 parts. Thus, angle **g-d-3** is greater than angle **g-3-d**. But these two said angles equal two-thirds of two right angles. Therefore, angle **g-d-3** is greater than a third of two right angles, and thus it will be greater than angle **d-g-3**. For this reason, line **g-3** is longer than line **d-3**. But **d-e** was equal to **g-3**; therefore **d-e** is longer than **d-3**. Each of these is the distance of the center of the epicycle from the center of the world: the line **d-3** when the center of the epicycle is distant from the furthest longitude by four common signs, and **d-e** when it is at the opposite of the eccentric’s peak <note>The perigee, or closest point.</note>. Thus, the proposition is established.

## Proposition XXII.

To make the mean motion of the argument of Mercury certain.

Previously, from the fourth and fifth [propositions] of this book, we derived this kind of mean motion <term>Mean Motion: The average speed of a celestial body, assuming a perfectly circular orbit at a constant speed.</term> for any amount of its time. And because the observations by which the numbers of the revolutions and times were perhaps found were rough and not sufficiently exact, their recording is held in doubtful faith. 

Therefore, to make this more certain, we shall proceed in this manner through one observation, as will be seen below. We shall consider the distance, if there be any, of the planet from the mean furthest longitude of the epicycle; and similarly through another observation. If we see that the difference between the positions of the planet in the epicycle, found by this skill, is equal to the mean motion of the argument <term>Argument: The angle used to determine a planet's position within its epicycle.</term> for the time mediating between the observations according to the tables already made, it is sufficient. 

If it is not, we shall distribute the excess throughout the days of that time, and we shall add a portion of one day to the mean motion found through the tables, if it is to be added. Or we shall subtract it, if it is to be subtracted. It will be added when the motion found through observations is greater than the motion found through the fourth and fifth [propositions] of this book. [It will be] subtracted [when...]

...if on the contrary. Through one such observation—which will serve our purpose—Ptolemy <term>Ptolemy: Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated science for over a millennium.</term> acted in the 20th year of Antoninus <note>original: "Antonij"; refers to the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius. The year is approx. 137 AD.</note>, on the evening of the second day of the eleventh month <note>original: "Achita"; likely refers to the Egyptian month Pachon.</note>, with the instrument rectified by the star of the Lion's Heart <term>Lion's Heart: The star Regulus (Alpha Leonis), used as a fixed reference point in ancient astronomy.</term>. Indeed, he found Mercury at 17 degrees and 30 minutes of Gemini, since its position was 1 degree and 10 minutes above the visible position of the Moon. Furthermore, this observation was made four and a half equal hours <note>Equal hours: Hours of fixed duration (60 minutes), as opposed to "temporal hours" which varied with the seasons.</note> before midnight in Alexandria, while the 12th degree of Virgo was at the midheaven, and the Sun was at its mean course <term>Mean course: The theoretical position of a celestial body if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle.</term> at 22 degrees and 34 minutes of Taurus.

In the figure, let there be a line passing through the furthest and nearest longitudes <term>Longitudes: Here meaning the apogee (furthest point) and perigee (nearest point).</term> of Mercury, **a-b-g-d-e**, in which **a** is the furthest longitude, **e** the nearest, **d** the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" in this geocentric model is the Earth.</note>, **g** the center of equal motion <term>Equant: The point "g" around which the planet's motion appears uniform.</term>, and **b** the center of the small circle. Let the epicycle be described upon center **z**, and I extend line **d-z** to point **k**, which is the true summit or apogee of the epicycle, and line **g-z** to point **t**, which they call the mean apogee of the epicycle. The planet itself, which in this observation fell at point **l**, shall be positioned there; I will connect it with the two points **d** and **z** by lines **l-d** and **l-z**. Having drawn the perpendicular **z-s**, I finally establish angle **b-h-g** equal to angle **d-g-z**, and line **b-h** equal to **b-g**, with two lines **h-g** and **h-z** being drawn. Now, the arc **t-l** must be sought, through which the planet is distant from the mean furthest longitude of the epicycle.

Because the angle **g-b-h** of triangle **g-b-h** is known (since it is equal to angle **d-g-z** on account of the known position of the furthest longitude and the mean position of the sun), and the two angles **b-g-h** and **b-h-g** are equal (due to the sides **b-g** and **b-h** being equal), each of them will therefore be known, and the ratio of line **h-g** to **b-g** will be known. Moreover, **b-g** is known in respect to the semi-diameter of the eccentric; therefore **h-g** is also known in the same respect. But because angle **b-g-h** is known, angle **h-g-z** of triangle **h-g-z** becomes known, and the ratio of **h-z** (the semi-diameter of the eccentric) to **h-g** is already known; hence the ratio of line **h-z** to **g-z** will be known, and therefore **g-z** is known. Thus, triangle **d-g-z** has two known sides, **d-g** and **g-z**, and a known angle **d-g-z**; from which line **d-z** will become known in respect to the others, and angle **d-g-z** is known. Its opposite angle **t-z-k** will also be known, and arc **t-k** known; similarly, angle **g-d-z** will be held as known.

Likewise, the true position of the planet was grasped by observation, and the position of the nearest longitude is known; thus angle **e-d-l** becomes known. But angle **e-d-z** is also known; therefore angle **z-d-l** remains known. Thus triangle **d-z-l** has two known sides, **d-z** and **z-l**, and the angle **z-d-l**; because of this, the angle [at l] becomes known. Moreover, angle **k-z-l** is equal to the two already known angles **z-d-l** and **z-l-d**; therefore it will be known itself, and the arc **k-l** which subtends it is calculated. If we then add to this the previously known arc **t-k**, we will finally assemble the entire known arc **t-l** which we were seeking.

Another observation for Mercury was in the 21st year, as Dionysius wrote (reported by Ptolemy), when 22 days of the month of Alatrabis <note>likely the month of Athyr</note> had passed. And that was in the year 486 of Nabonassar <note>original: "Nabuchodo"; a common medieval error substituting Nebuchadnezzar for Nabonassar, the era used by Ptolemy.</note>, when 18 days of the month of Thoth <note>original: "Thoch"</note> had passed, in the morning of the nineteenth day. For Mercury was seen shining, following the succession of the signs, removed from the line which passes through the northern star in the forehead of Scorpio and through the middle star which is in its forehead, by the quantity of the Moon's diameter. Moreover, Mercury was distant from the northern star in the forehead [of Scorpio] toward the north by the quantity of two diameters of the luminaries <note>Luminaries: The Sun and the Moon.</note>. Therefore, a firm conjecture will give that it was in 3 degrees and 20 minutes of Scorpio, with the Sun then existing by mean course in 20 degrees and 50 minutes of Scorpio. And Mercury was not then at its maximum longitude <term>Maximum longitude: The greatest elongation or distance from the Sun.</term> from the position of the Sun, because four days later—specifically on the 26th day of the month of Alatrabis—it was seen to be distant from the said line by the quantity of a diameter of the Moon and a half. In these four days, the mean motion of the Sun increased by nearly 4 degrees, and the motion of the planet by only half a diameter of the moon.

<header>Ninth [Book]</header>

Now let us derive its location on the epicycle. Let point **a** on line **a-e** be the furthest longitude <term>Furthest longitude: Also known as the apogee, the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</term>, and **e** the nearer longitude. Let **d** be the center of the world, **g** the center of uniform motion <term>Center of uniform motion: Often called the equant, this is the theoretical point from which the planet's speed appears constant.</term>, and **b** the center of the small circle. Let the epicycle be described around center **z**, with lines **z-d**, **z-g**, and **z-b** drawn. Let line **z-g** cut the circumference of the epicycle at its lower part at point **k**. Let the position of the planet on the epicycle, according <gloss>according</gloss> to that <gloss>which</gloss> was observed, be point **l**, which I will connect to the center of the epicycle and the center of the world by lines **l-z** and **l-d**. Next, I will establish angle **a-b-h** equal to angle **a-g-z**, and make line **b-h** equal to line **b-g**, extending lines **h-z** and **h-g**. Therefore, because angle **a-b-h** is known (since it is equal to angle **a-g-z** because of the mean position of the Sun and the known furthest longitude), and the two angles **b-h-g** and **b-g-h** are equal, each of them will be known, and line **h-g** will be known relative to **b-g**. But angle **a-g-z** is also known, so the entire angle **b-g-z** of triangle **h-g-z** is known. Since the two lines **h-g** and **h-z** are known, **g-z** becomes known relative to **h-z** and **b-z** (or **g-d**). Furthermore, angle **d-g-z** is known; therefore, line **z-d** will be known relative to **d-g** and thus relative to **h-z**. Angle **g-d-z** will also be known, along with angle **g-z-d**. And because angle **a-d-l** is known—due to the true position of the planet provided by observation and the known furthest longitude—the remaining angle **z-d-l** will be known. Moreover, the ratio of **d-z** to **z-l** is known, for each of them is known relative to **h-z**. Therefore, angle **d-z-l** will be known.

<margin><image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating planetary motion (likely Mercury) within an epicycle. It shows a circle with a central point z, intersected by several lines originating from a line containing points a, b, g, d, e. Points are labeled with letters: a, e, d, g, b, h, z, k, l.</image-desc></margin>

Previously, angle **g-z-d** was known; therefore, angle **k-z-l** remains known, as does arc **k-l** and its chord. This is indeed the distance of the planet from the mean nearer longitude of the epicycle. If you add a semicircle to this, you will complete its distance from the furthest longitude. Finally, you have two distances of the planet from the mean furthest longitude of the epicycle, which you may compare to each other, and recognize their difference, if any exists. If this difference is equal to the mean motion of the argument <term>Argument: In this context, the "argument of latitude" or "argument of anomaly," referring to the planet's position relative to its epicycle's apogee.</term> for the time between the mean observations as extracted from the tables, you shall have faith in those tables. If, however <gloss>however</gloss>, it is not equal to it, proceed as was instructed above.

->Proposition 22.<-

### To establish the roots of the mean motions of Mercury for a specific certain moment in time.

The mean motion in longitude takes for itself the root of the Sun. For the mean motion of the argument (or diversity), however, proceed as follows: From one of the observations described above, or from those made by yourself, derive the distance of the planet from the mean furthest longitude of the epicycle. Afterward, through the time that passes between your observation and the instant for which you wish to establish the root, learn the mean motion of diversity through its tables. Subtract this motion of the argument from the distance of the planet from the apogee of the epicycle that the observation provided, adjusting with full revolutions <note>original: "reuolutionibus"; full 360-degree cycles around the circle.</note> in the usual manner if necessary. You will do this if the moment of observation was later than the moment for which you are working out the root. If, however, it was earlier, add this mean motion of the argument to the said distance. Once any full revolutions that may have resulted are cast out, you will have the desired root.

## First Proposition.

### To determine at which points the diameter of Venus’s eccentric <note>original: "ecẽtrici"; an eccentric is an orbital circle whose center is offset from the Earth.</note>, passing through its furthest and nearest longitudes, intersects the ecliptic.

The investigation is conducted no differently than it was for Mercury. For we will consider two mean positions <note>The "mean position" is where the Sun or a planet would be if its motion were perfectly circular and uniform, rather than its actual, observed position.</note> of the Sun: specifically, when Venus has its maximum elongations <term>Elongation: The angular distance between the Sun and a planet as viewed from Earth.</term> from the mean position of the Sun, and these elongations are equal to each other but in opposite directions <note>One being an evening appearance and one a morning appearance.</note>. For the point midway between these two mean positions of the Sun, along with the point diametrically opposite to it, will be the points we seek.

In the 16th year of Hadrian <note>Hadrian was Roman Emperor from 117–138 CE. Astronomers like Ptolemy used regnal years for precise dating.</note>, on the 21st day of the month of Pharmouthi <note>original: "Phormuth"; the eighth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, as Theon <note>original: "Taion"; likely referring to Theon of Alexandria, a commentator and observer who provided data to Ptolemy.</note> reports—and as Ptolemy records—the star of Venus was observed already at its maximum evening elongation from the mean position of the Sun. It seemed to precede the middle of the Pleiades <note>A prominent star cluster in the constellation Taurus.</note> by the span of the Pleiades themselves. Thus, according to Ptolemy’s calculation, Venus was at 1 degree and 30 minutes of Taurus. The mean position of the Sun was then at 14 degrees and 15 minutes of Pisces. Therefore, the evening elongation was the greater <note>i.e., the maximum</note> value of 47 degrees and 15 minutes.

Then, in the 4th year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor 138–161 CE.</note>, on the 11th day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar.</note>, at the morning of the 12th day, Ptolemy observed the star of Venus distant from the fixed star in the left knee of the following Twin <note>This refers to the constellation Gemini; the "following twin" is Pollux.</note> by nearly a quarter of a degree toward the East and North. Therefore, the position of Venus was at 18 degrees and 30 minutes of Gemini. The mean position of the Sun was then at 5 degrees and 45 minutes of Leo. Consequently, the morning elongation was the maximum of 47 degrees and 15 minutes. 

When we bisect the arc intercepted between these two mean positions of the Sun, we reach the end of 25 degrees of Taurus. Therefore, the furthest and nearest longitudes <term>Furthest and nearest longitudes: Also known as the apogee and perigee, these are the points in an orbit farthest from and closest to the Earth.</term> will be at 25 degrees of Taurus and 25 degrees of Scorpio; this is what we set out to investigate.

We shall confirm the same through two other observations. The aforementioned Theon, in the 4th year of Hadrian, on the 19th day of the month of Athyr <note>original: "Atur"; the third month of the Egyptian calendar.</note>, on the morning of the 20th day, observed Venus at a distance from the fixed star at the tip of the southern wing of Virgo <note>Likely the star Spica or one nearby in the constellation Virgo.</note> by the span of the Pleiades—perhaps subtracting the arc subtended by the star of Venus itself. For Venus seemed to be distant toward the south from the said star by the width of the lunar diameter. And because, according to Ptolemy's calculation, this star in the 4th year of Hadrian was at 28 degrees and 5 minutes of Leo, if we add the span of the Pleiades (which is 1 degree and 30 minutes), the position of Venus comes to 20 minutes of the first degree of Virgo. The Sun in its mean course was at 17 degrees, 7 minutes, and 52 seconds of Libra. Therefore, the maximum morning elongation was 47 degrees and 32 minutes.

Then, in the 21st year of Hadrian, on the ninth day of the month of Mesori <note>original: "Mesoz"; the twelfth month of the Egyptian calendar.</note>, in the evening, Ptolemy observed Venus near the twenty-sixth star of Aquarius—namely, the northern star in the small quadrilateral near the first pouring of the water. It seemed to precede that star by two-fifths of one degree. Venus also appeared...

->Proposition II.<-

### To assign their own specific locations to the further and nearer longitudes of Venus.

It is now certain that one longitude is at 25 degrees of Taurus and the other at 25 degrees of Scorpio. But which is in which place? We shall be taught by two observations. One of these was made by Theon <note>original: "Taion"; referring to Theon of Alexandria, an astronomer who observed during the reign of Hadrian.</note>, as recounted by Ptolemy, in the 13th year of Hadrian, in the eleventh Egyptian month, Athyr <note>original: "Achita"</note>; specifically, after two days had passed, in the morning of the third day. At that time, Venus was seen to precede the straight line that passes through the foremost of the three stars in the head of Aries and through the star in its hind foot. I say it was seen to precede it by 1 degree and 24 minutes. And the distance of Venus from that star in the head of Aries was almost double the distance of Venus herself from the star in the hind foot. Now, the position of the star in the head of Aries was then in 6 degrees and 36 minutes of Aries, and its northern latitude was 7 degrees and 20 minutes according to Ptolemy's numbering. The position of the star in the hind foot was in 14 degrees and 45 minutes [of Aries], and its southern latitude was 5 degrees and 15 minutes. From this, it is concluded that Venus was in 10 degrees and 36 minutes of Aries, having a southern latitude of 1 degree and 30 minutes. The Sun, by its mean course, was in 25 degrees and 24 minutes of Taurus. Therefore, the greatest morning elongation was 44 degrees and 48 minutes.

Another observation was made by Ptolemy in the 21st year of Hadrian, after two days of the fifth month, Tybi <note>original: "Tobi"</note>, had passed, in the evening hour. For Venus was seen, in relation to the two stars in the two horns of Capricorn, to be in 12 degrees and 50 minutes of Capricorn. The Sun, in its mean course, was in 25 degrees and 30 minutes of Scorpio. Therefore, the greatest evening elongation was 47 degrees and 20 minutes. Because these greatest elongations with respect to the mean position of the Sun occur solely because of the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the eccentric).</term> while the planet is at the apogee or the opposite point of the eccentric, the variation caused by the eccentric is then nil. This kind of greatest elongation is found near 25 degrees of Scorpio and near 25 degrees of Taurus. It is clear how great the elongation was according to the preceding observation; thus, at this time, the further longitude of Venus's eccentric was in the 25th degree of Scorpio, and the nearer longitude is clearly in its opposite [Taurus], the knowledge of which was sought.

## Proposition V

**To find the mean distance of Venus from the further longitude of the epicycle.**

¶ To carry this out, we shall assume the position of the further longitude of the eccentric found above, as well as the ratios of the lines we have derived, and finally the true position of the planet as revealed through observation. Ptolemy observed Venus in the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor; the second year of his reign was approximately 139 AD.</note>, on the 29th day of the month of Tybi <note>Tybi was the fifth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar used by Ptolemy.</note>. It was then in a straight line which, to the eye, passed through the center of the Moon and the first star of Scorpio—specifically the one in the brow of the Scorpion that is further to the north <note>Likely the star Beta Scorpii, also known as Acrab.</note>. The distance of the Moon from Venus following the order of the zodiac signs was 6 degrees from the other distance of Venus from the aforementioned star. The northern latitude <term>Latitude: The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</term> of Venus appeared to Ptolemy to be 2 degrees and 30 minutes. That observation was made 4 equal hours and 45 minutes after midnight. For the Sun was at 23 degrees of Sagittarius, and the Mid-heaven <term>Mid-heaven: The point of the ecliptic that is highest in the sky at a given time.</term> was at 26 degrees of Virgo. The Sun, according to its mean motion, was at 22 degrees and 9 minutes of Sagittarius. ¶ With this established, let the diameter of the eccentric passing through the further and nearer longitude of the eccentric of Venus be

Therefore, since the ratio of **g b** to **g z** is known, **b z** will be known in relation to **g z**, and consequently in relation to **b d**. From this, **d z** will also be known, as well as the angle **b z d**, which is equal to **h z t**. Angle **b d z** also becomes known, as does its supplement **z d e**. Since the position of the planet has been discovered, the angle **e d k** will be known, and therefore the remaining angle **k d z** will be given. But the ratio of **d z** to **z k** is known, because both lines **d z** and **z k** have a known ratio to the line **g z**. Thus, angle **d k z** becomes known, and consequently the exterior angle **h z k**. If you subtract the known angle **h z t** from this:

->### Proposition VI<-

<margin>

We shall investigate this same distance again, from which we will establish the mean motion of the argument <term>Argument: In this context, the "argument" is the position or motion of a planet along its epicycle.</term> of Venus more certainly, if there be need. Timocharis <note>The text reads 'Limocaris,' a common Latin variant for the Greek astronomer Timocharis of Alexandria (c. 320–260 BCE).</note> observed—as Ptolemy relates—in the 52nd year after the death of Alexander <note>The era of Alexander's death began in 323 BCE; year 52 corresponds to roughly 272 BCE.</note>, on the 18th day of the last Egyptian month <note>The month of Mesori.</note>, the star of Venus; and he saw it joined to the star of the Virgin <note>Virgo</note>, namely the one following it which is at the tip of the southern wing of the Virgin <note>The star Spica.</note>. Thus, the position of Venus was in 4 degrees 10 minutes of Virgo. But at that time, the position of the perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the Earth; the Latin 'longitudo proprior' literally means 'the nearer longitude.'</term> of Venus was in 20 degrees 7 minutes 55 minutes of Scorpio, because of its motion with the fixed stars. However, in this observation, Venus was not at its greatest distance from the mean position of the sun, because three days later—namely on the 21st day of the said month, in the night which the 22nd day follows—it was already seen in 8 degrees 7 minutes 50 minutes. It was judged, therefore, that Venus was then in the upper half of the epicycle, and that this maximum morning elongation <term>Elongation: The angular distance between the Sun and a planet.</term> had already passed. In this observation, the sun in its mean course was at approximately 17 degrees 7 minutes 20 minutes of Libra; therefore, the distance of the position of Venus from the mean position of the sun was 43 degrees 7 minutes 10 minutes. In the second observation, however—namely after three days—the mean position of the sun was in 20 degrees and 59 minutes of Libra. And therefore the distance of Venus from the mean position of the sun was 42 degrees and 9 minutes. With these distances, I resume the previous figure without any variation, except that the epicycle is before the perigee of the eccentric, just as the observation itself compels. The angle **g b z** will be known because of the position of the perigee and the mean position of the sun. But the ratio of **b g** to **g z** is known; therefore **b z** is known in respect to **b g**, and consequently in respect to **b d**. From this, the line **d z** will also be given in this respect, and the two angles **b z d** and **b d z** will be given. Likewise, the two angles **h z t** and **z d e**. And because the observation made the position of the planet in the zodiac known, the angle **e d k** will be known. If you subtract from this the known angle **e d z**, the angle **k d z** will remain known. However, the ratio of **d z** to **k z** is known, since both have a known ratio to the line **g z**. Therefore angle **d k z** is known, and the exterior angle **b z k** is given, and finally the whole angle **k z t** is recognized. The arc **t h k** subtended by this will be known. When this is taken from the whole circle, the arc **t k** will remain known; and this is the distance of the planet from the mean apogee of the epicycle. We shall therefore have, from two such observations, two distances of the planet from the apogee of the epicycle. And from this the arc of the epicycle will be clear—if there be any—described after complete revolutions. If this is equal to the motion of the argument or diversity <term>Diversity: A term for the variation in a planet's speed caused by its motion on the epicycle.</term> for the mean time extracted through the tables, the tables are good. If, however, it is unequal, let the excess be divided by the days which are between the two observations; and let the result be added to the motion of the argument of one day found from the tables, if the arc of the epicycle extracted through the observations was greater than the arc which the tables gave. Or let it be subtracted from it, if it was less; and one will have the rectified mean motion of the argument in one day, which the corollary intended.

# Tenth Book

For the argument <term>Argument: In medieval astronomy, this refers to the position of a planet along its epicycle.</term> or diversity of motion in Venus, choose an observation in which you can place your trust. Through this observation—as shown in the previous section—determine the distance of the planet from the mean apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit furthest from the center; "longitudo longior" in Latin.</term> of the epicycle. Then, for the length of time between said observation and the first moment of time for which you wish to establish a root <term>Root: A "radix" or reference value for a planet's position at a specific epoch/date.</term>, collect the mean motion of the diversity from the tables. Thus, if the moment for which you seek the root precedes the moment of the observation, subtract the mean motion of the diversity corresponding to that time from the planet's distance from the mean apogee of the epicycle. Or, if it follows the observation, add it; you will then have what you seek. This is done with the exception that full rotations should be borrowed if necessary, or discarded, according to the requirements of the calculation.

### Proposition VIII.
->To show how the diversity in the motions of the three superior planets—namely Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—can be recognized.<-

<margin>
<image-desc>A circular diagram in the right margin illustrating the geometry of an eccentric orbit with an epicycle. Lines connect a central point to the center of the epicycle and to points on its circumference.</image-desc>
</margin>

At the beginning of all such work, it is necessary to find the location of the apogee and the perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the center; "longitudo propior" in Latin.</term>, along with the distance of the center of the eccentric from the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" refers to the Earth in this geocentric model.</note>. For then the quantity of the second diversity, of which the epicycle is the cause, can be obtained. But in these three planets, the clever method that led us to the locations of the apogees <note>original: "augium"</note> of Venus and Mercury does not apply. Those planets [Venus and Mercury] cannot exceed certain limits with respect to the Sun; therefore, at a certain hour, it is clear to us that they are on lines drawn from the center of the world touching the epicycle. In these [superior] planets, however, it is not so, because their motion in longitude has no such binding connection to the Sun. One must therefore consider by what means an easy path to this might be found. There is no better or more certain way than to find the true location of the center of the epicycle several times. Having this, we proceed almost as we did with the Moon according to the model of the eccentric. 

It seemed to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated medieval science.</note> that these three superior planets have the same arrangement in the centers of their orbits as Venus: namely, that the center of the eccentric carrying the epicycle <term>Deferent: The large circular path that carries the smaller epicycle.</term> was midway between the center of the world and the center of equal motion <term>Equant: The "center of equal motion" (punctum aequans); a point from which the planet's motion appears uniform.</term>. And he believed that the mean apogee of the epicycle always faced said center of equal motion, just as in Venus and Mercury. But what reasoning compelled him to this is not entirely clear, except that the experiment agrees with the hypothesis—or because in all other stars having two diversities, he found double points: one which would be the center of the eccentric carrying the epicycle, and another which would be the determinant of equal motion, whether in the epicycle alone (as in the Moon), or in both the epicycle and the eccentric (as in Venus and Mercury).

### Proposition IX.
->Any of the three superior planets, being at the true apogee of the epicycle or its opposite, will be proven to be in the line of the mean motion of the sun.<-

<margin>
<image-desc>A detailed geometric diagram in the lower right margin labeled with letters (a, b, g, d, e, z, h, t, k, l, m). </margin>

Let us now suppose, for the sake of easing the business, that all surfaces of the epicycles and eccentrics lie within the surface of the ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of the Earth's orbit.</term>. For whatever error their deviation from the ecliptic might introduce is imperceptible. Let the eccentric circle carrying the epicycle be **a b g** on center **d**, whose diameter **a g** indicates the apogee and the opposite of the apogee. In this diameter, let **e** be the center of the world and **z** the center of equal motion. Upon center **b**, I describe the circle of the epicycle **t k l**, with two lines drawn through the center of the epicycle: **z t** from the center of the equant, and **e h** from the center of the world. Thus, point **b** will be the true apogee...

Point $t$, however, is the mean apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion; here, "aux media" refers to the apogee as calculated by mean motion.</term>: with respect to which the motion of the argument <term>Argument: The position of a planet along its epicycle.</term> is regulated. And let $l$ be its opposite. And let the planet be either in point $k$ or in $h$. I say that the line $e-h$ will be the mean motion of the Sun, or a line directly joined to it. In this time, therefore, the planet has described the arc $t-k-h$ of the epicycle through the mean course of diversity <note>original: "medium cursum diuersitatis"; this refers to the planet's movement on the epicycle which accounts for its retrograde motion.</note>, and the center of the epicycle has described an angle $a-z-b$ around the center of equal motion <term>Equant: The "center of equal motion" ($z$ in the text) where the planet's speed appears uniform.</term>, which is equal to the two angles $b-e-z$ and $e-b-z$, or its opposite $t-b-h$. If we thus combine the motion of the planet in the epicycle with the motion of longitude <term>Longitude: The position of the epicycle's center along the main orbital circle.</term>, the result is the whole circle and the angle $a-e-b$. Now the angle $t-b-k$ will be the mean motion of the argument at this time. To this let us add the angle $a-z-b$ of the motion of longitude, or the two angles $e-b-z$ and $b-e-z$; there will result two right angles with the angle $b-e-z$. Let the line itself, therefore, be $e-m$, so that the angle $g-e-m$ is equal to the angle $b-e-z$. Because of this, the line $e-m$ will be directly joined to the line $e-b$. Therefore, the planet will be on the line of the mean motion of the Sun, continued as far as you like in either direction, which was what was proposed.

### Proposition X.

->A line drawn from the center of the epicycle to the center of<-
->the planet’s body, while it exists outside the apogee or its<-
->opposite, is parallel to the line of the mean motion of the Sun.<-

I resume the first illustration, noting this: that the planet is at point $n$, and the line of the mean motion of the Sun is $e-s$. Let the center of the epicycle and the line of the mean motion of the Sun have begun to move together from the apogee of the eccentric $a$, and the planet from the mean apogee of the epicycle. Therefore, the line of the mean motion of the Sun has described the angle $a-e-s$, and the planet in the epicycle has described the angle $t-b-n$, while the center of the epicycle has described the angle $a-z-b$, which is equivalent to the two angles $e-b-z$ and $b-e-z$. Therefore, the three angles $t-b-n$, $b-e-z$, and $e-b-z$ (which is equal to $h-b-t$) will be equal to the angle $a-e-s$. Thus, by subtracting the common angle $a-e-b$, there will remain the angle $b-e-s$ equal to the angle $h-b-n$. Wherefore the lines $e-s$ and $b-n$ are joined as parallels <note>original: "equidistantes"</note>, which was to be demonstrated.

### Proposition XI.

->For any of the three superior planets, when it is positioned on the line<-
->of the mean motion of the Sun (extended as far as you like), it will<-
->be proven to be at the true apogee of the epicycle or its opposite.<-
->From this it will be established that the center of the epicycle and the<-
->center of the planet’s body are found under one point of the heavens.<-

This is the converse of the ninth [proposition] of this book. For the planet will be at the true apogee of the epicycle when, according to its true course, it reaches the mean position of the Sun. But it will be at the opposite of the apogee when it is positioned opposite to the Sun. This I shall demonstrate as follows: If the planet were not at the apogee or its opposite, the center of the epicycle would not be on the line of the mean motion of the Sun (extended as far as you like), but outside of it. Therefore, let a line be drawn from the center of the planet to the center of the epicycle, which indeed, by the previous proposition, is parallel...

Consequently, two parallel lines would intersect, which is impossible. By refuting this impossibility <note>This is a "reductio ad absurdum," a common logical proof where you show an idea must be true because its opposite leads to a mathematical impossibility.</note>, our proposition is confirmed. The truth of the corollary is also clear. For a planet is never at the apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit farthest from the center of Earth.</term> of its epicycle or at its opposite point unless it lies on a line drawn from the center of the world through the center of the epicycle. Since, as has been proven, it must necessarily be at the true apogee of the epicycle or its opposite, the planet itself will also be on such a line drawn from the center of the world through the center of the epicycle. This line, if extended all the way to the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the distant sphere of fixed stars.</note>, will strike a single point under which both the planet and the center of the epicycle are positioned.

## Proposition XII.
### To investigate the true position of the Epicycle of any of the three superior planets.

<margin>
<image-desc>A faint geometrical diagram is visible in the right margin, consisting of a circle with several intersecting lines, possibly representing orbital paths or epicycles discussed in the text.</image-desc>
</margin>

**O**bserve the position of the planet with a reliable instrument: either in relation to the fixed stars, whose positions are known, so that you may recognize its true position. If you find it to be in opposition to the mean position of the Sun, the result will be the same as concluded in the previous proposition: it will be the true position of both the epicycle and the planet. Therefore, the position of the epicycle will have been found. You would also have the same result if you could detect the moment the planet aligns with the mean position of the Sun. However, this conjunction cannot be perceived, because the rays of the Sun act as a hindrance, preventing the planet from being seen. Therefore, in the oppositions to the Sun—which the ancients called "the conditions of the extremity of night" <note>original: "habitudines extremitatis noctis"; this refers to when a planet is visible for the entire night, being exactly opposite the Sun.</note>—it will be possible to find the true position of the epicycle. This, as will be seen below, will prove useful for finding the eccentricity <term>Eccentricity: The measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</term> and the position of the apogee of the eccentric.

## Proposition XIII.
### To set forth the necessary means for finding the position of the apogee of Mars.

**B**y using three states of the "extremity of the night," in which the three positions of the epicycle have been subtly explored, we shall achieve this; just as we worked with the moon according to the method of the eccentric when its three positions were known. ¶ There was one observation of Ptolemy regarding Mars in the 15th year of Hadrian <note>Hadrian was a Roman Emperor; astronomical records often used regnal years for dating.</note>, when 26 days of the month of Tybi <note>Tybi is the fifth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, used by Ptolemy for its consistency.</note> (the fifth month) had passed, in the night, specifically one hour after midnight. At that time, the star <note>Early astronomers often referred to planets as "wandering stars."</note> was seen at 21 degrees of Gemini. Thus, the true center of the epicycle was also at that same place. ¶ The second observation was in the 19th year of Hadrian, after the 6th day of the month of Pharmuth had passed, three equal hours before the middle of the night. And the star was seen at 28 degrees, 7 minutes, and 50 seconds of Leo. ¶ That most famous philosopher <note>Referring to Ptolemy.</note> made the third observation in the second year of Antoninus, on the 12th day of the month of Athyr (the eleventh month), two equal hours before the middle of the night; and the star of Mars appeared at 2 degrees and 33 minutes of Sagittarius. The interval of time that fell between the first and second observations was four Egyptian years, 96 days, and 7 hours and 20 minutes. The time between the second and third was 4 Egyptian years, 96 days, and one equal hour. In the first interval of time, the mean motion of the longitude of Mars was 81 parts or degrees and 44 minutes. In the second, 95 degrees and 28 minutes. The true motion of longitude in the first interval was 67 degrees and 50 minutes. In the second interval, it was 93 degrees and 44 minutes. Having recited these, let us first assume that which we also practiced with the moon, and which we premised near the beginning of the ninth book: computing all motions on the surface of the ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit.</term>, even if the moving bodies themselves are not always there.

be in the ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit.</term>: since the error arising from the inclination of the remaining circles above the ecliptic either does not occur at all, or is very slight; the ease of the operations invites us to this approach. Therefore, let three equal circles be described on the surface of the ecliptic. One is the eccentric carrier of the epicycle, $a.b.g$, centered on point $d$. Another is the equant <term>Equant: A mathematical point used to explain the observed speed changes of planets; the planet appears to move at a constant speed around this point rather than the center of its orbit.</term> circle, $e.z.h$, centered on point $t$. And finally, the circle $k.l.m$ centered on point $n$, which is the center of the world <note>original: "centrum mundi"; in this geocentric context, it refers to the center of the Earth.</note>. These three centers lie on the straight line $s.q.f.c$. Let the line $n.t$ be divided in the middle at point $d$, just as was established near the beginning of the ninth [book]. Now, on the eccentric carrier of the epicycle, let there be three points $a, b, g$, representing the three locations of the center of the epicycle in the said three observations. These points will be connected to the center $t$ of equal motion by the lines $t.a.e$, $t.b.z$, and $t.h.g$. Likewise, we shall draw the lines $n.k.a$, $n.l.b$, and $n.g.m$. Therefore, the arc $e.z$ of the equant circle, which the center of the epicycle described in the first interval of time, and $z.h$, the arc which it described in the second interval, are both known because the time intervals are known. Similarly, arc $k.l$, which the line of the true motion of the epicycle described in the first interval, is known; and arc $l.m$, which it traversed in the second interval, is also known. If, therefore, arc $k.l$ were subtended <note>Subtended: To be opposite to and extend under an angle or arc.</note> by the arc $e.z$ of the equant, and arc $l.m$ corresponded to arc $z.h$, it would not be necessary to have placed point $d$ in the middle between $n$ and $d$ by chance (so to speak), nor would we work otherwise than we did above regarding the Moon according to the path of the eccentric of the first inequality. But the known arc $k.l$ is subtended by the unknown arc $a.b$, and the known arc $l.m$ corresponds to the unknown arc $b.g$. It would be necessary, however, for both of these to be known. For if we draw lines $n.e, n.z,$ and $n.y$ cutting the circle $k.l.m$ at points $r.o.y$, then arc $n.o$ <note>The text likely means arc $r.o$ here based on context.</note> will be subtended by the known arc $e.z$, but it remains unknown. Likewise, the unknown arc $o.y$ will correspond to the known arc $z.h$. However, both must be known so that we might strive for our goal easily and precisely. Yet this cannot be done unless those small arcs $r.k$, $l.o$, and $y.m$ are known. For once these are added or subtracted—as the situation requires—the arcs $r.o$ and $o.y$ will emerge as known. But there is no way of knowing these small arcs unless the position of the apogee <term>Apogee: The "augis," or the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth.</term> of the eccentric is held; the one depends upon the other. Nevertheless, since the power to proceed directly and precisely does not exist, it will be easier and more certain to find these small arcs from the position of the apogee known by estimation, than to search for the position of the apogee by taking these small arcs by estimation—and then to attempt the rest, to see if they agree with the observations.

### Proposition XIV.

To investigate the distance of the eccentric equant from the center of the world by estimating near the truth.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin showing an arc of a circle with points a, b, and g. Below the arc is a point d, representing a center, with lines connecting it to a, b, and g. A horizontal line passes through point d, marked with s on the left and e on the right.</image-desc>

For it is not important to reach precision in the first steps; instead, we will first take, in the previously shown figure, the arcs $e.z$ and $z.h$ as known in truth, and the unknown arcs $r.o$ and $o.y$ as if they were known. These indeed differ only slightly from arcs $k.l$ and $l.m$. From them, we will find the position of the apogee and the eccentricity. Then, having divided the result, we will seek the small arcs $r.k, l.o,$ and $m.y$, and we will add them to the arcs previously known, or subtract them from them if the situation requires, so that the arcs we desire may emerge as known to us. We will then find the position of the apogee and the eccentricity once more, and likewise these small arcs again. We shall repeat this work until we arrive at sufficient precision. For this reason, I shall draw the eccentric circle, on whose center the motion of the planet in longitude is equal: let this be circle $a.b.g$. Let arc $a.b$ be that which the epicycle described by equal motion from the configuration of the first night's extreme to the second. ### Proposition 16.

To calculate the small arc of the first configuration.
¶ I repeat part of the thirteenth figure of this [book], and I intend to find the small arc $k.r$. However, I first continue the line $e.t$ so that two perpendiculars, $d.p$ and $n.h$, can fall upon it. Therefore, because angle $e.t.s$ was known from the preceding, angle $d.t.p$ will be known. And angle $p$ is a right angle; for which reason the ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of $d.t$—which is half of $n.t$—to $d.p$ will be known. Likewise, the ratio of the same $d.t$ to $p.t$ will be known. But $d.t$ was known with respect to $d.a$ or $t.e$; therefore, both lines $d.p$ and $p.t$ will also be known by that same respect. Whence line $a.p$ will be known. If we add $p.t$ (equal to $b.p$ <note>This likely refers to a segment in the diagram's construction.</note>) to this, the whole $a.h$ will come out as known. Furthermore, $n.h$ is double the known $d.p$. Therefore, because lines $n.h$ and $a.h$ are known and angle $h$ is a right angle, line $n.a$ will be known along with angle $n.a.h$. Likewise, $t.e$ is known, since it is the radius <note>term: "semidiameter"; the distance from the center to the edge of the circle.</note> of the equant circle <note>term: "circuli equantis"; a mathematical circle used to account for the observed non-uniform speeds of planets.</note> of the eccentric, and $t.h$ is known; therefore the whole $e.h$ may be known. This, together with the previously known $n.h$, will reveal line $e.n$, from which angle $n.e.h$ will also be known. When this is subtracted from the previously known angle $n.a.h$, it will leave the known angle $a.n.e$; for which reason the small arc $k.r$ which was sought will come out as known.

### Proposition 17.

To investigate the small arc of the second configuration.
¶ I wish to repeat the second part of the previous figure in which $a$ fell, and I will labor to find the arc $o.l$. Since angle $z.t.s$ is known, both lines $d.p$ and $p.t$ will be known with respect to $d.t$. And for that reason, with respect to $d.b$, the radius of the eccentric is known. Also, lines $p.h$ (equal to $p.t$) and $n.h$ (double $d.p$) will become known. Therefore, since angle $h$ is a right angle, line $n.b$ will become known along with angle $n.b.h$. Furthermore, line $z.h$ consists of two knowns: $z.t$, namely the radius of the equant, and $t.h$, known from elsewhere. From this and the known line $n.h$, line $n.z$ will be revealed, whence angle $n.z.b$ becomes known. If you take this from the known angle $n.b.h$, the known angle $b.n.z$ will remain, and therefore the arc $l$ which was requested is known.

### Proposition 18.

To comprehend the quantity of the small arc in the third configuration.
¶ I will cut from the said figure the part for this configuration, in which, because of the known angle $f.t.h$, the ratio of $d.t$ to $d.p$ will be known. Similarly, the ratio of the same $d.t$ to $p.t$ will be known. Whence the whole $r.t$ will become known. And therefore the remainder $h.x$ from $h.t$, the radius of the equant, will remain known; this, with $n.x$ (double the known $d.p$), will elicit the known line $n.h$. Whence also angle $n.h.x$ will be manifest. Then, because of the known radius of the eccentric $d.g$ and line $d.p$, line $d.g$ <note>Likely referring to a segment of the radius.</note> will become known. If you take from this the line $p.x$ (equal to $p.t$), it will leave $g.x$ known. This, with line $n.x$, will give the known line $n.g$ and the known angle $n.g.x$. When this is taken from the known angle $n.h.x$, the found angle $g.n.h$ will remain, and arc $y.m$ will be known. Therefore, having found those three small arcs, return to the first figure of the 13th [proposition] of this [book]. You have learned from the 15th [proposition] of this [book] that the apogee of the eccentric falls between the first two configurations.

## Propositio xix.

->To ingeniously examine whether the conclusions regarding eccentricity and the distances of the three configurations from the apogee agree with the experimental observations.<-

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a vertical axis with points f, h, d, z. Radiating lines from these points connect to an arc on the right containing points k, r, o, l, y, m. Points n, q, and g are also shown near the bottom of the arc construction.</image-desc>

It is clear from what was said above what the ratio of the eccentricity to the radius of the eccentric is, along with the distances of the three configurations from the apogee of the eccentric—distances, I say, calculated on the equant circle. Now, observations have shown the distances of the three configurations from each other with respect to the center of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "orbis signorum"; literally "the circle of signs."</note>. The path is now prepared to arrive at these distances through rational lines. If we find them to be as great as those found from the observations, we shall judge everything concluded so far to be established. 

Therefore, let the eccentric <note>original: "eccentricus epicycli delator"; the eccentric carrier of the epicycle.</note> of the epicycle be $a.e.z$ upon center $d$. In its diameter $c.z$, passing through the center of the world $n$, let there be point $t$, the center of uniform motion. Let the center $e$ of the epicycle in the first configuration be above point $a$, which I will connect with the three points $n$, $d$, and $t$ by three lines: $a.n$, $a.d$, and $a.t$. Having extended the line $a.t$ far enough, I will drop two perpendiculars, $d.p$ and $n.b$. By the last operation of the preceding [section], angle $a.t.e$ was known; for which reason the ratio of both lines $d.p$ and $p.t$ to line $d.t$ becomes known. But $d.a$, the radius of the eccentric, is known; therefore $a.p$ will also be known. If you add $p.b$ (equal to $p.t$) to this, the whole $a.b$ will be gathered as known. From this, and finally from line $n.b$, the line $a.n$ and angle $n.a.b$ will be known. Now, this angle $n.a.b$, when subtracted from angle $a.t.e$, will leave angle $e.n.a$ known, which is the distance of the first configuration from the apogee of the eccentric with respect to the center of the zodiac. 

In the second configuration, with the remaining parts arranged as before, I place the center of the epicycle at point $b$. Because angle $e.t.b$ is again known from the preceding, both lines $d.p$ and $p.t$ will become known with respect to the radius of the eccentric; therefore line $b.p$ will become known. ## Proposition 20.

Finally, to investigate the true location of the apogee of the eccentric, from which also the distance of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric and the distance of the planet from the apogee of the epicycle according to mean motions will be established.

¶ Choose any of the three mentioned configurations (or those observed by yourself) and find the distance of one of them from the apogee or its opposite using the method described above. If you count this distance from the known position of the star in this configuration according to the sequence of the signs—or against it, as the situation requires—you will be led to the location of the apogee. Following the example of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the astronomer whose work this text refines.</note>, who found the distance of the epicycle in the third configuration from the <term>perigee</term> <note>original: "longitudine propiori"; the point in the orbit closest to the center.</note> to be 52 degrees and 56 minutes. Now, the star’s position was at 2 degrees and 35 minutes of **Sagittarius**; to this location, he added 52 degrees and 56 minutes following the order of the signs, and he found the opposite of the apogee (that is, the perigee) at 25 degrees and 30 minutes of **Capricorn**. Consequently, the apogee opposite to it is at 25 degrees and 30 minutes of **Cancer**. But as a corollary, let the circle of the epicycle be $k.l.m$ around center $g$ in the third configuration. Angle $e.t.g$ was known from above, and this is the distance of the epicycle from the apogee according to the mean motion. Likewise, the location of the apogee is now known, and the location of the planet was known; angle $g.n.z$ is known. If you subtract the known angle $g.t.n$ from this, the angle $t.g.n$ will be left known, and arc $k.l$ will be found. Therefore, when that is subtracted from the semicircle, it leaves arc $m.k$ known, which is the mean distance of the planet from the apogee of the epicycle.

To discover in which part of the zodiac the apogee of the eccentric lies by another process.

If anything uncertain is mixed into a beautiful demonstration, the intellect will thereafter be repelled by it. But if you wish to avoid this, embrace this path. Yet perhaps this difficulty will cause no less trouble here than uncertainty does elsewhere. Four configurations...

## Proposition 22.

### To determine the ratio of the eccentricity to the radius of the eccentric.

<image-desc>Two circular geometric diagrams are positioned to the right of the main text. The top diagram features a circle with a center 'e' and points 'a', 'b', 'g', and 'd' on its circumference. Radial lines connect 'e' to these points. A vertical line 'z-h' passes through the center. Outside the circle, four points 't', 'k', 'l', and 'm' are marked along an outer arc.
