¶ For the execution of this, I set the eccentric circle that carries the epicycle <note>known as the "deferent" circle.</note> as $a, b, g$ on center $d$. On its circumference, let three points $a, b, g$ represent the center of the epicycle in three configurations. Let the line passing through the apogee and its opposite be $z-h$, upon which lies the center of the world, point $e$, and the center of uniform motion, $v$ <note>The "equant" point, from which the planet's motion appears regular.</note>. Let the line $z-h$ itself divide the arc $b-g$ in half. I shall then extend lines $a-e, b-e, g-e,$ and $g-e$, as well as lines $a-v, b-v,$ and $g-v$. I will also connect the three points $a, b, g$ to one another: $a-b, b-g,$ and $a-g$. Finally, I shall also extend the diameter of this eccentric, which is $b-d-l$. Since, therefore, the time between the second and third configuration is known, angle $b-v-g$ will be known, along with its half, $b-v-z$; from which angle $b-v-e$ is known. But because the location of the apogee is known from the preceding [proposition], and because the location of the second configuration is known, angle $b-e-v$ will be given. Thus, since triangle $b-v-e$ has known angles, its sides will be known relative to each other; therefore, $e-v$ will have a known ratio to $b-v$. But the angles of triangle $a-v-e$ will be known by similar means, since the location of the first configuration is given along with the location of the apogee. On account of this, angle $a-e-v$ will be known. But angle $a-v-z$ is also given, since $b-v-z$ is known, and $a-v-b$ is similarly known because of the time between the first and second configuration. Wherefore the ratio of $e-v$ to $a-v$ is known. Since, however, angle $a-v-b$ is given, the ratio of $a-v$ to $a-b$ will be known, and angle $a-b-v$ will also be known. Likewise, triangle $b-v-g$ has a known angle $b-v-g$. But angle $g-b-v$ is equal to angle $b-g-v$; therefore, each of them is known, and the ratio of $b-v$ to $b-g$ is given. Wherefore $b-g$ is also known with respect to $a-b$. Since angle $a-b-g$ consists of two angles already known (namely $a-b-v$ and $g-b-v$) and the two sides $a-b$ and $b-g$ are known relative to each other, angle $b-a-g$ will be known. Wherefore arc $b-g$ is also given, and its chord $b-g$ is known with respect to the radius of circle $a-b-g$. But $b-g$ was known with respect to $v-e$, just as all the remaining lines were. Therefore, line $v-e$ will also be known with respect to the radius of the eccentric; and this is the <term>eccentricity of the equant circle</term>. Then, because arc $b-g$ is known, the remainder $g-l$ will be known, and angle $g-b-l$ will be known. Once the known angle $g-b-v$ is subtracted, the known angle $v-b-l$ remains. But the ratio of $b-v$ to the radius of the eccentric $b-d$ is also known. Therefore, by the same respect, line $d-v$ becomes known. When this is subtracted from the total $e-v$, the remainder $d-e$ is known; and this is the <term>eccentricity of the deferent circle</term>. Thus, both eccentricities have been elicited. In this process, however, the centers of the equant and the deferent are assumed to be different. Whether this...

# Book [Tenth]

...Whether it happens thus or not, you will recognize it by this path. You have the known angle $g-b-v$, along with angle $g-b-l$. If these are different, you shall declare the centers to be different. However, if you find them coinciding, say that the <term>eccentrics</term> <note>Circles whose centers do not coincide with the center of the Earth.</note> share a center. All these things hold true by placing the center of the world [Earth] in a single straight line with the centers of the eccentrics. If it were otherwise, one would have to proceed in a different manner.

### Proposition 22.

**T**o compare the radius of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> to the radius of the eccentric of Mars according to a certain proportion.
The observations for this are more difficult to grasp: they are made near the configurations that they call the <term>extremities of night</term> <note>original: "extremitates noctis"; refers to a planet in opposition, when it is visible throughout the night.</note>. For here, the angle of diversity <note>The angle of parallax or anomaly.</note> which occurs because of the epicycle varies perceptibly. Ptolemy took one observation in the second year of Antoninus, on the third day after the third "extremity of night" mentioned above: specifically, on the 15th day of the eleventh month, <gloss>which is Athyr</gloss>, after it had passed, three hours before midnight. For he observed Mars through the instrument of <term>armillary spheres</term> <note>A model of objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings.</note> adjusted to the star Spica. It was seen at $1^\circ 36'$ of Sagittarius, while the sun by its mean motion was at $5^\circ 27'$ of Gemini. The <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>The point of the ecliptic that is highest in the sky.</note> was at the 20th part of Libra. The star of Mars also appeared according to the center of the moon then at $1^\circ 36'$. However, the moon had its visible place at the beginning of Sagittarius, whence the location of Mars was most certain.

Now I describe the eccentric circle that carries the epicycle, $a-b-g$, upon center $d$, whose diameter passing through its <term>apogee</term> and the opposite point is $a-d-g$. In this, let point $s$ be the center of equal motion <note>The equant point.</note>, and $e$ the center of the world. Let the epicycle $h-t-k$ have its center at point $b$, and let the planet be at point $n$. I draw the lines $s-b-h, d-b, e-b, e-n,$ and $b-n$, and the perpendicular lines $d-l$ and $d-m$ onto line $s-b$. [I draw] another perpendicular $b-s$ onto the continued line $e-n$. Now, the distance of the center of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric was known in the third configuration, and from that moment of observation until now a known time has flowed; therefore, the distance of the center of the epicycle from the apogee is now known. From this, angle $a-s-b$ is known, and angle $d-s-b$. Therefore, the proportion of $d-s$ to both $d-m$ and $s-m$ will be known. Wherefore, both of these will be known in respect to the radius of the eccentric, $d-b$. From this, $b-l$ will also be known. Furthermore, $l-m$ is equal to $m-s$, and $e-l$ is double $d-m$. Therefore, $b-l$ is known along with $e-l$, and thus line $e-b$ is calculated. Angle $e-b-l$ will also be found as known. Since the location of the previous longitude is known and the location of the star has been observed, the angle $g-e-s$ will be given. The angle $g-e-b$ is rendered known because of the two known angles $b-s-e$ and $e-b-s$. There remains, therefore, the known angle $b-e-s$. Whence $b-s$ will become known in respect to $b-e$. Likewise, the mean distance of the planet from the farthest longitude of the epicycle is known; wherefore angle $k-b-n$ is known. But angle $k-b-t$ was known; therefore the remaining angle $n-b-t$ will be known. These, with the known angle $b-e-n$, will reveal angle $b-n-s$, and thus the proportion of $b-n$ to $b-s$ will emerge as known. From this, the proportion of $b-e$ to $b-n$, the radius of the epicycle, will be manifest. But $b-e$ was known in respect to the radius of the eccentric; therefore $b-n$ will also be known by that same respect, which was what was to be shown. Ptolemy found the radius of the epicycle of Mars to be 39 parts and 30 minutes of one whole part, while he set the radius of the eccentric at 60 parts.

### Proposition 23.

**T**o apply effort toward correcting the mean motions of Mars.
In the 13th year of Dionysius—specifically the 52nd year from the death of Alexander, or the 476th from the beginning of the years of <term>Nabonassar</term> <note>original: "Nabucho."; referring to the Era of Nabonassar used by Ptolemy.</note>—as Ptolemy relates, on the 20th day of the third month, <gloss>which is Athyr</gloss>, as it passed, at the dawn of the 21st day, the star of Mars was seen to cover the fixed star which is in the northern side of the brow of Scorpio. In this observation, the sun according to its mean course was in $23^\circ 54'$ of Capricorn, and this fixed star was in $2^\circ 14'$ of Scorpio.

<header>Tenth [Book]</header>

The location of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth.</note> was at $21^\circ 25'$ of Cancer according to the calculation of Ptolemy; because between this observation and the first one of Antoninus there were nearly 409 <term>Egyptian years</term> <note>A year of exactly 365 days, used by ancient astronomers for ease of calculation.</note>, to which, by Ptolemy’s estimation, approximately $4^\circ 6'$ correspond. ¶ With this established, let there be an <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit whose center is shifted away from the Earth.</note> carrying an <term>epicycle</term> <note>A smaller circle carrying the planet, which itself moves along the larger eccentric circle.</note> *a-b-g* upon the center *d*. On its diameter, passing through the apogee and the point opposite it, let point *a* be the apogee and *g* its opposite. Let *e* be the center of the world [Earth] and *d* the center of equal motion <note>Known as the equant, the point from which the planet's speed appears uniform.</note>. Let the epicycle be *h-t* upon the center *b*, and let the planet itself be at point *t*. Let the line *e-l* represent the mean motion of the sun. Also, let lines *e-b*, *d-b*, *b-t*, and *b-n* be drawn perpendicular to the line *e-t*. Indeed, let the line *t-e* be extended beyond *e* until *d-m* can fall perpendicularly upon it. And let the line *d-s* be drawn parallel to the line *e-t*. Therefore, because the mean position of the sun is given, and the true position of the planet is established, the angle *t-e-l* is given. Angle *b-t-e* is equal to this: since from Proposition 10 of this book, the lines *b-t* and *e-l* are parallel. Therefore, triangle *b-t-n* is known by its angles; wherefore the proportion of the <term>semidiameter</term> <note>The radius.</note> of the epicycle *b-t* to *b-n* is known, and the line *b-n* is known with respect to the semidiameter of the eccentric. Then, because the angle *t-e-g*—or its opposite *d-e-m*—is known from the position of the planet and its distance from the apogee, and since angle *m* is a right angle: *d-m* will be known with respect to *d-e*. But *d-e* is known with respect to the semidiameter of the eccentric; therefore *d-m*, which is equal to *s-n*, will be known by that same respect. But *b-n* was already known in this regard; therefore the remaining part *b-s* will be given. From this, because the semidiameter *b-d* is known, *d-s* will be given, and angle *b-d-s* will be known. Furthermore, angle *s-d-e* is known, because it is equal to the given angle *t-e-g*. Therefore the whole angle *b-d-e* is known, as is its adjacent angle *b-d-z*. But also the proportion of the semidiameter *b-d* to *d-z* is now known. Wherefore angle *b-z-d* will become known along with angle *a-z-b*, which is the angle of the distance of the planet's mean position from the apogee of the eccentric. Moreover, the two angles *b-z-g* and *g-e-l* are equivalent to angle *h-b-t*; since these themselves are known, the angle *h-b-t* will be known, which shows the mean distance of the planet from the apogee of the epicycle. Thus we have the mean motion of the planet for this observation. Since this kind of motion was also known above in the third relation, the difference of those motions—if there be any—is known. But the time existing between the two observations is known, and the motion of longitude corresponding to this time can be extracted through the fourth and fifth [propositions] of the ninth book. If this is equal to the difference of the mean motions taken from the observations, the <term>tabulation</term> <note>The reference tables used for calculation.</note> of the mean motion is certain. If, however, it is unequal: you shall note the excess, and by the usual manner distribute it across the days of the mean time, so that <unclear>it may result</unclear> in the proportion of error for one day; this must be added to or subtracted from the motion of one day previously tabulated, just as the matter itself requires.

# Proposition 25.
## To adapt the roots of the mean motions of Mars to a specific time.

<image-desc>A second geometric diagram, very similar to the first, showing the arrangement of circles and lines for the calculation of the roots of the mean motions of Mars. It includes a large circle (eccentric) and a smaller circle (epicycle) with points 'a', 'b', 'd', 'e', 'g', 'h', and 't' marked, along with auxiliary perpendicular lines.</image-desc>

Now you have the mean motion in longitude. Therefore, count the time that is between the moment of the observation and the moment for which you have decided to establish the <term>root</term> <note>The "root" (radix) is the base position of a planet at a specific epoch or starting date.</note>. Subtract the mean motion collected from the rectified table for this time from the mean motion which the observation gave, if you want the root for a past time. Or add it, if you want it for a future time. And that which results will be the desired root. You shall act in a similar way for the root of <term>diversity</term> <note>diversity: "diuersitas," referring to the anomaly or the second inequality in planetary motion.</note>. Truly, since the distance—if there be any—between the two mean positions of the sun and the planet is always equal to the distance of the planet from the mean apogee of the epicycle, it will be sufficient to have established the root for the mean motion of the planet in longitude.

## The eleventh book clearly treats the Theory of Jupiter and Saturn: and it most aptly reveals how to derive the true motions of all the planets together.

### First Proposition.

<image-desc>A large square woodcut decorative initial 'A' featuring a central cherub or winged figure seated in an ornate basin or font, surrounded by symmetrical scrolling vine work and floral motifs.</image-desc>

¶ Regarding the investigation of this matter, there is no difference between Jupiter and Mars, except that the occurrences of the night <note>original: "extremitates noctis", referring to the specific times of observation during the night</note> fall differently; this, however, does not alter the quality of this type of science. We shall complete our purpose with three observations. One of these was made by Ptolemy in the 17th year of Hadrian: on the first day of the eleventh month, Athyr <note>OCR "Athica"; Athyr is the third month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, one equal hour before midnight. And Jupiter was seen through the instrument at $23^\circ 7'$ of Scorpio.

¶ The second observation was in the 21st year of Hadrian, on the 13th day of the second month, Phaophi <note>original: "Baba", the Coptic name for Phaophi</note>, two equal hours before midnight. And the star of Jupiter was seen at $7^\circ 54'$ of Pisces.

¶ The third, indeed, was in the first year of Antoninus, on the 20th day of the third month, Athyr <note>OCR "Athus"</note>, five equal hours before midnight. And the star was seen at $14^\circ 24'$ of Aries. Now, the time that flowed from the first observation to the second was three <term>Egyptian years</term> <note>A year of exactly 365 days used for astronomical calculations.</note>, three months, 16 days, and 23 equal hours. That which was between the second and the third was one Egyptian year, one month, seven days, and seven equal hours. The <term>true motion</term> <note>The actual observed position of the planet.</note> of Jupiter in the first interval of time was $104^\circ 7' 43''$. And the <term>mean motion</term> <note>The theoretical position if the planet moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle.</note> of longitude was $99^\circ 7' 55''$. In the second interval, however, the true motion of Jupiter was $36^\circ 7' 30''$, while the mean motion was $33^\circ 26'$.

Let the line *d-g* be drawn until it meets the circumference at point *e*. Likewise, from points *a* and *b*, let two lines *a-d* and *b-d* be extended, along with three chords *e-a*, *a-b*, and *e-b*, and three perpendiculars *a-t*, *b-h*, and *e-z*. Because angle *b-d-g* is known from the observations, the ratio of *d-e* to *e-h* will be known. Angle *b-e-g*, because of the arc *b-g*, is known; therefore the remaining angle *e-b-h* is known, and thus the ratio of *b-e* to *e-h* is known. Likewise, because angle *a-d-g* is known through the observations, angle *a-d-e* will also be known, and therefore the ratio of line *d-e* to *e-z* is manifest. ## Proposition 2.

->To work out the distances of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric in each of the three positions, along with the eccentricity, near to the truth.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circle representing the eccentric orbit. Points A, B, and G (gamma) are on the circumference. Line segments connect these to point D, the center of the world (Earth). Point K is the center of the eccentric circle. A vertical diameter line L-K-D-M passes through both centers.</image-desc>

Let the eccentric motion equaling the motion of Jupiter be ABG, in which chord EG is drawn, and let point D be the center of the world upon it. Outside the portion EBG, let the center of this circle be marked at point K, with its diameter LKDM drawn passing through the center of the world. Let L be the point of the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> and M be the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric. From the center K, let a perpendicular KZ be drawn to the line EG, which continues to point S on the circumference. Furthermore, let two lines DA and DB be drawn for the two remaining positions. Since, therefore, the two lines DG and DE are known from the preceding <note>Referring to the calculations in Proposition 1</note> with respect to the semidiameter of the eccentric, the product of one by the other will be known. This product is equal to the product of DM times DL; wherefore that is known. When this is subtracted from the square of the semidiameter KM, the square of line KD will remain known, whence the line itself is known: which is indeed the sought eccentricity <term>eccentricity: the distance between the center of the Earth and the center of the orbital circle</term>.

¶ Furthermore, line ZD becomes known, since it is the difference between the two known lines ZG and DG. Therefore triangle KDZ has known sides and a right angle Z; wherefore angle DKZ is known, and for that reason arc MS is known. But the whole arc SG is given, since it is half of the known arc ESG. Therefore, by subtracting arc SM, arc MG remains known, which is the distance of the third position from the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric. If we subtract this from the known arc BG, arc BM will remain known, by which the second position precedes the opposite of the apogee. And if we add the known arc AB to this arc BM, arc AM will result, which is the distance of the first position from the opposite of the apogee. ¶ If it is desired to find the distances of these positions from the apogee, subtract each of the aforesaid distances from the opposite of the apogee from a semicircle; and the distances of these positions from the apogee of the eccentric, which we proposed to find, will remain.

## Proposition 3.

->To calculate the small arcs which we need for a more precise finding of the apogee.<-

...ta. <note>original: "ta" is the suffix of a word continued from the previous page, likely "connotata" or "terminata"</note> But from the radius of the eccentric $a.d.$ and the now known line $d.h.$, the line $a.h.$ <note>OCR reads 'a.b.', but geometric logic suggests 'a.h.' as the segment on the axis</note> will be established. If you add line $h.k.$ (which is equal to $h.z.$) to it, the whole line $a.t.$ becomes known; from this and line $e.t.$ (which is double $d.h.$), line $a.e.$ will be made known, and therefore angle $e.a.t.$ will be discovered. Similarly, from the radius of the equant <term>equant: an imaginary circle used to account for the observed non-uniform speed of planetary motion</term> $z.s.$ and the known line $z.k.$, the whole line $s.k.$ is produced. This, together with $e.t.$, makes line $s.e.$ known, from which angle $e.s.t.$ will be understood. When this is subtracted from angle $e.a.t.$, the known angle $a.e.s.$ remains. We shall add the arc of this angle to the position of the epicycle in the first observation <note>original: "prima habitudine"</note> and use the resulting sum in the new calculation.

¶ For the second observation, let us arrange the layout similar to the previous one, except that point $b$ is closer to the opposite of the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth; its opposite is the perigee</term>. From angle $n.z.b.$, following the preceding rule, the ratio of $z.d.$ to both lines $d.h.$ and $h.z.$ will be known; thus each of them will be known in respect to the radius of the equant. Therefore, having subtracted $t.z.$ (which is double $h.z.$) from line $s.z.$, the known line $s.t.$ remains. This, with line $e.k.$ (double $d.h.$), will identify line $s.e.$, from which angle $e.s.k.$ will be known. Likewise, from the radius of the eccentric $d.b.$ and the known $d.h.$, line $b.h.$ will be established. If you subtract line $t.b.$ from it, known line $b.t.$ remains, from which and line $t.e.$ (double $d.h.$), line $b.e.$ will become known. Therefore, angle $e.b.t.$ will also be known; we shall subtract this from angle $e.s.t.$ so that the known angle $b.e.s.$ remains. We subtract the arc of this angle from the true place of the epicycle in the second observation and work with the remainder in the new calculation, just as was done in the case of Mars.

¶ Finally, in the third observation, let us not change the labels of the figure. However, let us place the mark for this observation after the opposite of the apogee. Since angle $g.z.d.$ was known, both lines $d.h.$ and $h.z.$ will be known in respect to $d.z.$. After subtracting $z.t.$ (which is double $h.z.$) from the radius of the equant $z.s.$, $t.s.$ remains known. From this and line $e.t.$, line $e.s.$ is returned, from which angle $e.s.t.$ will also become known. Likewise, from the knowns $d.g.$ and $d.h.$, line $h.g.$ will be manifest. From that, by removing line $h.t.$, known line $t.g.$ will remain, from which finally and $e.t.$, $e.g.$ and angle $e.g.t.$ are found. If we subtract this from angle $e.s.t.$, it leaves the known angle $g.e.s.$. Let us add the arc of this angle to the true place of the epicycle in the third observation and use the sum in the new calculation.

Now let us use these true motions, having been found, in place of those we received through observations. By their differences, and retaining the mean motions found earlier, let us extract once more the eccentricity and the distance of each observation from the apogee of the eccentric or from its opposite. Again, let us seek small arcs of this kind and proceed as before until we have achieved good certainty. The indicator of this will be when these small arcs found in one operation are equal to the arcs found in the following one. The most excellent Ptolemy found this distance of the centers, when compared to a radius of the eccentric of 60 parts, to be 5 parts and 30 minutes.

Therefore, we shall be satisfied with those things concluded above regarding eccentricity and other matters.

### Proposition 5

-> To investigate in which part of the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note> Jupiter <-
-> has the apogee of its eccentric. <-

The preceding demonstration elicited the distance of the third observation from the perigee. But the location of this observation in the circle of signs is also known from observation; therefore, the location of the perigee will be known, and consequently, the location of the apogee. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Almagest" this text explains</note> found the location of the apogee at 11 degrees of Virgo. For the location of the third observation was at 14 degrees and 23 minutes of Aries. Its distance from the perigee following the succession of the signs was 33 degrees and 23 minutes. If we subtract this from 14 degrees and 23 minutes of Aries—adjusting by one full revolution—the perigee results at 11 degrees of Pisces. It is established that the apogee is at the diametrically opposite point <note>11 degrees of Virgo</note>.

## Proposition 7.
### To demonstrate the ratio of the radius of the epicycle to the radius of the eccentric.

<image-desc>A large, detailed geometric diagram is situated on the left side of the text block. it depicts a large circle (eccentric) with a smaller circle (epicycle) interior to it. Various lines connect the center points (labeled e, d, z) to points on the circumferences (labeled a, g, h, t, k, b). Several perpendicular lines are drawn (labeled m, l, n). Below this primary diagram is a second, much fainter and sketchier version of a similar circular geometry.</image-desc>

In the second year of Antoninus <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius, c. 139 AD</note>, on the 26th day of the month of Mesore <note>the last month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, nearly five equal hours before sunrise after midnight, Ptolemy, using armillary spheres <term>armillary sphere: an astronomical instrument with rings representing the great circles of the heavens</term> aligned to the star Aldebaran, found the true position of Jupiter at 15 degrees and 45 minutes of Gemini. For Jupiter appeared entirely conjunct <term>conjunction: when two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky</term> with the Moon, except that the Moon was slightly inclined toward the south. And the position of the Moon, according to Ptolemy's calculation at that same time, was likewise seen to be at 15 degrees and 45 minutes of Gemini. In this observation, the Sun's mean motion was at 16 degrees and 11 minutes of Cancer, and the "midheaven" <term>midheaven: the point of the ecliptic that is highest in the sky</term> was at 2 degrees of Aries.

Having stated this, I describe the eccentric circle that carries the epicycle, centered at **d**, which shall be **a-b-g**. On its diameter **a-g**, which passes through the apogee and its opposite point <note>the perigee</note>, let point **z** be the center of uniform motion <term>equant: the point around which a planet moves at a constant speed</term>, and let **e** be the center of the world <note>the Earth</note>. Then, at point **b**, beyond the perigee, just as the observation requires, I describe the epicycle **h-t-k**, and let the planet be at point **k**.

Finally, I will draw lines **z-b-h**, **d-b**, **e-b-t**, **e-k**, and **b-k**, as well as two perpendicular lines **d-m** and **e-l** falling on line **z-b**, and the perpendicular **b-n**. Now, because the time elapsed between this observation and the one for which we learned the planet's mean position in the preceding text is known, the mean motion of the planet corresponding to this time will also be known. Although this [motion] is not yet sufficiently corrected, it will introduce no error here. Since the mean position in that [earlier] observation was known, it will now also be given. From the position of the perigee <note>original: "opposito augis"</note> and the already known mean position of the planet, angle **b-z-g** will be known, and the ratio of each of the lines **d-m** and **m-z** to line **d-z** will be known; therefore, each of them will be known in relation to **d-z**. From the radius **d-b** and the known line **d-m**, line **b-m** will be found, as will the remaining segment **l-b**, after **l-m** (which is equal to **m-z**) is subtracted. From this, and from **e-l** (which is double **d-m**), line **b-e** will be recognized, for which reason angle **e-b-l** will also be known.

Because angles **e-z-b** and **e-b-z** are known, angle **g-e-b** will be known—that is, the distance of the epicycle's center from the perigee of the eccentric. Next, just as the mean position of the planet was found, so its distance from the mean apogee of the epicycle—namely, arc **h-k**—will be found. Earlier, angle **e-b-z** was known, to which angle **h-b-t** is vertically opposite; thus arc **h-t** is known. When this is subtracted from arc **h-k**, arc **t-k**—the true argument of the planet <term>argument: the angle representing the planet's position on its epicycle</term>—remains, and angle **t-b-k** will be known.

From the position of the planet known through observation and from the position of the perigee, angle **g-e-k** will be known. Angle **g-e-b** was known previously, so the known angle **b-e-k** will remain. Finally, when this is subtracted from angle **t-b-k**, it leaves angle **b-k-e** as known. And since angle **n** is a right angle, the ratio of both lines **e-b** and **b-k** with respect to **b-n** is known; therefore, the radius of the epicycle **b-k** will be known in relation to **e-b**. But since **e-b** was known in relation to the radius of the eccentric, then **b-k** will also be given in relation to the same, which is what was to be demonstrated. Ptolemy found the radius of the epicycle to be 11 parts and 30 minutes, where the radius of the eccentric contains 60 such parts.

### How the discovered mean motions of Jupiter are made more certain through industrious effort.

Just as we proceeded in our attempt regarding Mars, so here...

<header>Eleventh</header>

We shall proceed by choosing one observation that teaches us the position of Jupiter most certainly in the year 45, according to the time of Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Alexandria, an astronomer whose calendar was used by Ptolemy</note>. On the tenth day of the month named Ju-uenū <note>likely the Egyptian month Epiphi</note>, as Ptolemy recounts, the star of Jupiter was seen to cover the fixed star of Cancer, which is named the Southern Ass <note>Latin: *Asinus meridianus*; modern: Delta Cancri</note>. This observation occurred in the year 83 from the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, 323 BC</note>, on the 17th day of the month of Athyr <note>Latin: *Athica*</note>, specifically when the 11th hour had passed: in the morning of the 18th day, while the Sun in its mean course was in 9 degrees, 7 minutes, and 56 seconds of Virgo.

The position of this fixed star in the first year of the Emperor Antoninus was 11 degrees, 7 minutes, and 20 seconds of Cancer. However, this earlier observation preceded that time by nearly 378 years; according to Ptolemy’s calculation, the motion of the eighth sphere <term>eighth sphere: the sphere of fixed stars, which shifts slowly due to the precession of the equinoxes</term> corresponds to 3 degrees, 7 minutes, and 47 seconds across that interval. Therefore, at the time of the observation, the position of the fixed star—which was also the position of Jupiter—was 7 degrees, 7 minutes, and 33 seconds of Cancer. Similarly, because the position of Jupiter’s apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth</term> in Ptolemy’s time was in 11 degrees of Virgo, it must have been in 7 degrees, 7 minutes, and 13 seconds of that same sign during this earlier observation.

Now the way is prepared for our proposal. Let us draw an eccentric circle <note>an off-center circular orbit</note> **a-b-g** upon center **d**. On its diameter **a-g**, which passes through the apogee and its opposite point <note>perigee</note>, let point **e** be the center of the world <note>Earth</note> and **z** be the center of equal motion <term>equant: the point from which a planet's motion appears uniform</term>. Let an epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term> be described upon point **b**, and on its circumference, let point **t** represent the planet in this observation. Having drawn lines **z-b-h**, **d-b**, **e-b**, **e-t**, and **b-t**, let a perpendicular line **d-n** be dropped from point **d** onto line **e-t**. Let this be continued until it meets line **d-s**, which is equidistant to **e-n**, so that angle **s** becomes a right angle. Furthermore, let two perpendiculars, **d-m** and **b-b**, be drawn with **b-f** and **d-e** with respect to lines **e-t** and **d-b**. 

Let the line of the Sun’s mean motion in this observation be **e-l**. Therefore, because the position of the apogee is known, along with the Sun's mean position and the planet's true position, angle **l-e-t** will be known, as will its alternate angle **b-t-e**. Since angle **n** is a right angle, side **b-n** of triangle **t-b-n** will be known relative to **b-t**. Likewise, because of the known position of the apogee and the given position of the planet, angle **b-t-e** will be known. Since angle **m** is a right angle, **d-m** is known relative to **d-e**. Indeed, **s-n** is equal to this, and thus the whole **b-s** is known relative to the radius of the eccentric **d-b**. Since **b-f** and **d-e** are known relative to it, two sides of the right-angled triangle **b-d-s** are known; therefore all its angles are given along with the remaining side. 

From this, the whole angle **a-d-b** will be known, from which **z-k** and **k-d** will be known relative to **d-z**, the radius of the eccentric. Thus **k-b** remains known, from which line **z-k** and line **z-b** will become clear along with angle **z-b-k**. Thus the two angles **z-d-b** and **z-b-d** are known, and therefore the exterior angle **a-z-b** will be noted, which is the mean distance of the epicycle from the apogee. But angle **a-e-l**, the mean distance of the Sun from the apogee of Jupiter's eccentric, was already known. These two angles, from what was declared above, are equal to angle **h-b-t**. For point **h** is the mean apogee of the epicycle; therefore angle **h-b-t** is known, and arc **h-t** is known. 

We have thus concluded the distance of the planet from the apogee of the eccentric according to its mean course of longitude. The position of the apogee is known, and therefore the mean position of the planet is given. We taught a similar thing in the sixth [proposition] of this [book]. Thus, the difference between the two positions will be clear, if there is any. If the mean motion extracted through the tables is equal to this difference, we shall believe the tables to be good. If not, we shall divide the excess among all the days between the two observations; that which results we shall add to the motion of one day taken from the tables, if it must be added. Or we shall subtract it, if it must be subtracted, and the corrected motion of one day will result. From this, finally, we shall manufacture new tables, just as was done in the other cases. Similarly, we could correct the mean motion of diversity <term>motion of diversity: also known as the anomaly, representing the planet's movement on its epicycle</term>. However, since the mean motion of diversity depends on the mean motions of the Sun and any of the three superior planets, it will be sufficient to have corrected the mean motion of longitude.

## To establish the root for the mean motion of Jupiter in longitude at a set time.

From the preceding section, you have the mean motion <term>mean motion: the average speed of a planet, as if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant rate</term> of Jupiter at a specific time. Therefore, take from the newly updated tables the mean motion corresponding to the difference between two times: namely, the time for which you derived the preceding mean motion, and the other time to which you have decided to adapt the root <term>root: a base value or "epoch" used as a starting point for astronomical calculations</term>. 

Subtract this motion from the one you derived by observation if you desire the root for a past time; or add it to the same if you desire it for a future time, and you will have the desired root. Furthermore, two roots will provide the root for the mean motion of diversity <term>motion of diversity: often referring to the anomaly or the planet's movement relative to its epicycle</term>: specifically, the root of the mean motion of the Sun and the root of the mean motion of the planet, after one is subtracted from the other.

## Proposition 10

### To finally observe the diversity of the motions of Saturn in a rational manner.

In the beginning, we shall strive to find the location of the apogee <term>apogee: the point in a planet's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth; Latin: *aux*</term>; for without it—which is the gateway to the rest—we shall achieve nothing in Saturn, just as we could not in Mars or Jupiter. We shall be taught from three observations in which part of the zodiac its apogee was located. 

Ptolemy made the first of these in the second year of Hadrian. For while he watched Saturn on two successive nights, he found on the first night that it had not yet reached the state of the "end of the night" <note>This refers to the acronychal rising, or opposition, when a planet is directly opposite the sun and visible all night</note>. On the second night, however, he found that it had passed this state. By balancing the data, he deduced that it had been in this state after noon on the seventh day of the month of <term>Machur</term> <note>The Egyptian month Mechir</note>, after six equal hours. Thus, its true position was in 1 degree and 13 minutes of Libra, because the Sun in its mean course was in 1 degree and 13 minutes of Aries. 

In the second observation—which was in the 17th year of Hadrian, four equal hours having passed after noon on the 18th day of the month of <term>Athica</term> <note>The Egyptian month Athyr</note> (specifically the eleventh month)—Saturn was at the opposite point to the mean position of the sun, in 9 degrees, 7 minutes, and 40 seconds of Sagittarius. 

In the 20th year of Hadrian, Saturn was in this state of the "end of the night" at noon on the 24th day of the month of <term>Mesre</term> <note>The Egyptian month Mesore</note> (the last month), and its true position was in 14 degrees and 14 minutes of Capricorn. 

Therefore, the time that flowed from the first state to the second was six Egyptian years, 70 days, and 22 equal hours. In this time, the mean motion of Saturn was 75 parts (or degrees), 7 minutes, and 43 seconds. The time from the second state to the third was three Egyptian years, 35 days, and 20 equal hours. And the mean motion of Saturn in that time was 37 degrees, 7 minutes, and 52 seconds. Its true motion <term>true motion: the actual observed position of the planet, which varies due to its elliptical-like path and distance</term> in the first interval of time was 68 degrees and 27 minutes. In the second interval, it was 34 degrees, 7 minutes, and 34 seconds.

Since, therefore, both **d.e.** and **b.e.** have a known proportion with respect to **e.h.**, then **b.e.** will be known with respect to **d.e.** Similarly, from angle **a.d.e.** (because angle **a.d.g.** is known), **z.e.** will be known with respect to **d.e.** 

Moreover, angle **a.e.d.** is known because arc **a.b.g.** is known; for which reason the remainder **e.a.d.** is discovered. And therefore, the proportion of **a.e.** to **e.z.** is found. Consequently, the proportion of **a.e.** to **d.e.** will become known. Thus, the two lines **a.e.** and **b.e.** have a manifest quantity with respect to line **d.e.**; therefore, they will be known in relation to each other. Furthermore, when angle **a.e.b.** is known from arc **a.b.**, each of the lines **a.t.** and **t.e.** will be known with respect to **a.e.**; from which also the remainder **t.b.** is found. From that, **a.b.** will also be made known. However, **a.b.** is [known] with respect to the diameter...

->Proposition 11.<-

### To determine for each of the three observations how far it stands from the apogee of the eccentric or its opposite, and how far the center of the eccentric is removed from the center of the world.

With the eccentric described around point $k$ as its center, let chord $ge$ be placed in it, where point $g$ is the known point of the third observation mentioned above. On its circumference, let there be two points, $a$ and $b$, for the remaining observations. Let center $k$ be within this portion $eabg$. Let the diameter of the eccentric, which passes through its center and the center of the world, be $lkdm$; let $d$ be the center of the world <term>center of the world: in this geocentric model, the Earth</term>, and $l$ be the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth; original: "aux"</term> of the eccentric. Finally, let the perpendicular line $kz$ be drawn to chord $ge$, continuing to point $s$ on the circumference. The preceding proof makes the two lines $ed$ and $dg$ known in relation to the radius of the eccentric. Therefore, by subtracting the product of one from the other from the square of the radius, the square of line $kd$ will remain known. Consequently, the line itself is known, which is the distance between the two centers. Furthermore, $ez$, the half of chord $eg$, is known. Thus $zd$ will be known. Since angle $z$ is a right angle, angle $dkz$ will be discovered, and arc $gm$ will be known. But arc $gs$ is also known, because it is half of the known arc $gse$. Therefore, by adding the two arcs $gs$ and $sm$, the entire arc $gsm$ is made known. If we subtract this from a semicircle, arc $lg$ will remain known, which is the distance of the third observation from the apogee of the eccentric. Likewise, arc $bg$ was known; when it is subtracted from $lg$, arc $lb$ will remain known as the distance of the second observation from the apogee. Finally, when this is removed from arc $ab$, arc $al$ will remain known, which is the distance of the first observation from the apogee—which is what we intended to show.

## Proposition 13.

**T**o find the arcs described by a star <note>The "star" refers to the planet Saturn</note> in its true course across two intervals of time from those things which have been concluded. From this, it will be clear that the eccentricities and other matters have been well-established.

Angle $bel$ will be known: namely the distance of the second observation from the apogee. From which angle $gel$ you should subtract angle $bel$. And if the remainder is equal to the arc which the star described through its true motion in the second interval of time, it is now certain that all things have been well-found. Since they clearly agree with the observations, therefore, etc.

### Proposition XVI.

To work out the proportions of the two semidiameters of the eccentric and the epicycle.
A very certain consideration is needed for this purpose. Our Ptolemy, in the second year of Antoninus, on the sixth day of the month of Mesir <note>An Egyptian month, roughly equivalent to late January/February</note>—specifically when the sixth day had passed—four equal hours before midnight, detected the position of Saturn using his instrument rectified by the star Aldebaran and in relation to the moon. He found it at 9 degrees, 7 minutes, and 4 seconds of Aquarius, while the Midheaven <term>Midheaven|The point of the zodiac that is at its highest altitude on the meridian at a given time</term> indicated by the instrument in Alexandria was the last degree of Aries. At that time, the sun in its mean course was at 28 degrees, 7 minutes, and 41 seconds of Sagittarius. He estimated, however, that according to the visual appearance at that time, Saturn fell 30 minutes following the order of the signs from the northern horn <note>Likely the 'Northern Horn' of Taurus, the star Elnath</note>. But the visible position of the moon then, according to Ptolemy’s calculation, was at 8 degrees, 7 minutes, and 34 seconds of Aquarius, from which the position of Saturn was certain. And because the time intervening between this observation and the third observation mentioned above was known, the mean motion of Saturn’s longitude during this time was also known. Even if this motion is not yet fully rectified, it cannot introduce any sensible error into this work. The mean position of Saturn in that third observation was also known; therefore, the mean motion of Saturn in this consideration will not be unknown. By a similar method, the mean distance of the moon from the apogee of the epicycle in this consideration became known. ### Proposition XVII.

# To make the mean motions of Saturn very certain.

The path that is open for Mars and Jupiter will lead us to our goal, if we first accept the true location of Saturn through observation. Thus, in the 802nd year of the Chaldeans <note>The Seleucid era, used by Hellenistic and Babylonian astronomers</note>, in their month named Lhestendefin <note>likely a Latinization of a Babylonian month name like Shebat</note>, on the fifth day, around the beginning of the night, Saturn was seen below the southern shoulder of Virgo <term>Virgo|The zodiac constellation of the Maiden</term> by two digits <term>digit|An ancient unit of angular measure, roughly 1/12th of a degree</term>. This observation was in the 519th year from the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosaris"</note>, on the 14th day of the month of Tybi <note>original: "Tobi," the fifth month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, which had passed, around the beginning of the night, while the sun in its mean course had reached 6 degrees and 10 minutes of Pisces. According to the numbering of Ptolemy, the location of this fixed star in the first year of Antoninus <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius, r. 138–161 AD</note> was at 15 degrees and 10 minutes of Virgo. But between this ancient observation and the first year of Antoninus, there were nearly 366 Egyptian years, to which approximately 3 degrees and 40 minutes correspond for the motion of the fixed stars <term>precession|The slow movement of the stars over time due to the Earth's wobbling axis</term>. If we subtract these from 15 degrees and 10 minutes, the location of this star will remain at approximately 9 degrees and 20 minutes of Virgo. Similarly, the apogee of Saturn, which in the time of Ptolemy was at 23 degrees of Scorpio, was then at approximately 9 degrees and 20 minutes of Scorpio.

### Finally, to establish the epochs for the mean motions of Saturn.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the right margin depicting an eccentric circle with points labeled a, b, d, e, z. An epicycle is centered at point b, with a line segment extending to point k. For the time that exists between the observation in which the mean motion of the planet was known and the moment for which you intend to establish the epoch <note>original: "radicem", literally 'root', the starting point for astronomical calculations</note>: extract the mean motion through the now-corrected tables. Then, subtract that from the mean motion of the planet if you wish to establish the epoch for a past time, or add it to the same if for a future time; and you will have the desired epoch. If you wish for a specific epoch for the motion of diversity, act similarly. Truly, since that motion depends upon the mean motions of the sun and the planet, its epoch will undoubtedly take its origin from their mean motions as well.

Because of this and line *e-n*, line *e-b* will be known; from this, angle *e-b-n* will be recognized. ¶ Furthermore, he assumes the mean argument: namely, arc *t-k*. Wherefore, because angle *l* is a right angle, both of the lines *k-l* and *l-a* will have a known proportion to line *k-b*, which is the radius <note>original: "semidiametrum"</note> of the epicycle <term>epicycle|A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent); used to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward</term>. But the radius of the epicycle is known with respect to the radius of the eccentric. Whence, in this respect, the aforementioned lines will be known. But line *e-b* was known; let us add line *b-l* to it, and the whole *e-l* will become known. From this and line *k-l*, line *e-k* will be known; hence the angle *k-e-l* will come to be known. Moreover, when we have subtracted the previously known angle *e-b-s* from angle *a-s-b*, the angles *a-e-b* and *b-e-k* remain, from which the entire angle *a-e-k* is obtained, which is the **true distance of the planet from the apogee** <note>original: "auge," meaning the highest point or furthest distance</note> **of the eccentric**. Since the location of the apogee <note>original: "augis"</note> relative to the start of **Aries** <note>The first sign of the zodiac, used as a reference point for celestial longitude</note> is evident, the true distance of the planet from the start of Aries will be known; this is what they call the **true motion**, which was the demonstration expected.

¶ Lest the frequent multiplication and division of numbers, or the extraction of roots, or any other operation should cause weariness to the calculator, our ancestors created tables for the practitioners, in which they industriously arranged these types of angles necessary for discovery. Indeed, if you wish to listen, I will provide the way these tables are constructed. One way will suffice for the three superior planets [Mars, Jupiter, Saturn] and for Venus. For the **mean center** <term>mean center|The angular distance of the center of a planet's epicycle from the apogee, calculated as if it moved at a constant speed</term>—to use modern terms—if it is less than a **quadrant** <note>90 degrees or a quarter-circle</note>: seek the right sine <note>original: "sinum rectum"</note> and the sine of its complement <note>The cosine</note>. Multiply both of these by the eccentricity, and divide the product by the total sine <note>The "total sine" is the maximum value in a sine table, representing the radius of the calculating circle</note>. That which results from the sine of the mean center, multiply it by itself and subtract it from the square of the radius of the eccentric. Take the square root of the remainder. To that root, add that which resulted from the sine of the complement. Multiply this sum by itself and add the square of double that which came from the sine of the mean center. The square root of the sum will be the distance of the center of the epicycle from the center of the world at this mean center; keep this value. Then, take double the value that came from the sine of the mean center and extend it by the total sine. Divide the product by the value you saved. The result will be the sine of the **equation of the center** <term>equation of the center|The angular difference between the planet's actual position and its hypothetical uniform 'mean' position</term>, the arc of which is the equation of the center itself. This, if it pleases you, you will place in the table directly across from the mean center, so that whenever there is need for it, you may have it ready without a long operation such as has just been shown.

¶ If, however, the mean center is more than a quadrant, subtract it from a semicircle [180°]; and take the first sine—to put it briefly—as well as the second sine, or the sine of its complement. Multiply both by the eccentricity, and divide each of the products by the total sine. Keep the results. Subtract the square of the result from the first sine from the square of the radius, and from the square root of the remainder, subtract the result from the second sine. Multiply what remains by itself, and join it to the square of double what came from the first sine. The square root of the sum will be the distance of the center of the epicycle from the center of the world; keep this value. Then, multiply double the value from the first sine by the total sine, and divide the product by the saved root. The arc of the result will be the sought-after equation of the center.

¶ But if the mean center is a quarter of a circle [90°], cast away the square of the eccentricity from the square of the radius. To the remainder, add the square of double the eccentricity. The square root of the sum is the line of the distance of the epicycle's center from the center of the world; keep it. Finally, extend double the eccentricity by the total sine. Divide the product by the saved root. For the sine of the resulting arc is the sought equation of the center.

# Eleventh [Chapter]

It is now clear how all the **equations of the center** <note>The "equation of the center" is the mathematical correction needed to account for a planet's elliptical-like motion around an eccentric center rather than a perfect circle around the Earth.</note> can be known through the semicircle. As for the equations of the remaining semicircle: because they are found in a similar way and are equal in quantity to the previous ones, I shall pass over them. Indeed, when the center of the epicycle <term>epicycle|A small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of this small circle itself moves around a larger circle (the deferent).</term> is at an equal distance from the mean **apogee** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> on either side, the resulting equations of the center are equal.

Finally, so that the **equations of the arguments** <note>The "equation of the argument" or "anomaly" corrects for the planet's position on its own small epicycle circle.</note> may become known, the procedure requires the planet's **true argument**: 

If it is less than a quadrant <note>90 degrees</note>, take its first sine and its second sine <note>In modern terms, the sine and cosine.</note>; multiply both of them by the number for the radius of the epicycle relative to the radius of the eccentric (which was calculated above). Divide each product by the **total sine** <term>total sine|The radius of the standard mathematical circle used for these calculations, often set at 60,000 or 100,000 in medieval trigonometry.</term>. 

Add the result from the second sine to the distance of the epicycle’s center from the center of the world. Then, take this sum and square it; add that to the square of the result from the first sine. The **square root** of this total will give the distance of the planet's body from the center of the world; keep this value aside. Next, multiply the result from the first sine by the total sine, and divide that product by the square root you saved. The result will be a sine, and the arc corresponding to it is the sought-after equation of the argument.

¶ If, however, the **equated argument** is more than a quadrant, subtract it from a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>, and find the first and second sines of the remainder from your tables. Multiply both by the radius of the epicycle. Divide both products by the total sine. Subtract the result of the second sine from the distance of the epicycle’s center from the center of the world. Square the remainder and add it to the square of the result from the first sine. The square root of this sum will predict the distance of the planet's body from the center of the world; save this value. Then multiply the result from the first sine by the total sine, and divide that product by the saved root. What results is the right sine, the arc of which will be the desired equation of the argument.

¶ And if you set this true argument to be exactly equal to a quadrant, add the square of the epicycle's radius to the square of the line that measures the distance of the epicycle from the center of the world. Call the square root of this sum the distance of the planet from the center of the world. Then multiply the radius of the epicycle by the total sine and divide the product by the saved root. The arc of the resulting value will be the sought-after equation of the argument.

Thus, you will not be ignorant of the equations of the arguments through the semicircle. The other semicircle has equations equal to the first, so I will let that pass for now. Place these two equations opposite their numbers in a table, as they are usually sought there if you wish to have composed tables. 

Now, if the center of the epicycle always maintained an equal distance from the center of the world in its motion, these two equations would suffice to equalize the movements. However, that is not the case. Therefore, so that the movements may be equated without the tables becoming too numerous, one must consider **proportional minutes** <term>proportional minutes|A correction factor used to adjust astronomical tables when a planet's distance from Earth varies.</term> and the variations in diameter, just as we do for the **Moon**. However, the equations of the arguments will be found here at the position where the epicycle is at the "mean distance" of the eccentric. Because of this, double proportional minutes will be needed. Indeed, the excesses of the equations corresponding to the arguments at the apogee and its opposite are so great that if you were to use simple proportional minutes (as with the Moon), you would certainly deviate from the truth. Regarding these, consult what has been stated concerning the Moon.

¶ Finally, we shall work on how the **equations of Mercury** may be understood. First, we come to the equations of the center. If the mean center is less than 60 degrees, subtract it from a semicircle and multiply the **chord** of the remainder by the eccentricity. Divide the product by the total sine and save the result. Then, add half of the mean center to the center itself; find the first and second sines of this sum and multiply both of them by the previously saved value. Divide both products by the total sine. The result from the first sine, multiplied by itself...

# Book Twelve: Broader Investigations Concerning the Various Conditions of the Planets: specifically, Direct Motion, Station, and Retrograde Motion. It most clearly distinguishes some variations in longitude occurring due to the motion of the epicycles.

## First Proposition.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating planetary motion models. It shows a large circle (the concentrum) with center 'z' and an eccentric circle with center 'n'. A point 'b' on the concentric circle serves as the center for a smaller epicycle. Lines connect 'z' to several points ('a', 'b', 's', 'o') and 'n' to point 'o'. If you posit a single **variation** <note>original: "diversitatem"; refers to the irregularity in a planet's observed speed or path.</note> for the **higher planets** <note>The planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>: an epicycle on a concentric circle, or an **eccentric** <term>eccentric|A circular orbit whose center is offset from the center of the Earth.</term> circle without an epicycle, will be a sufficient cause for it.

¶ Understand this regarding the variation which is linked to the Sun. Let us assume, therefore, that the motion of the epicycle on the concentric circle and the motion of the planet in the epicycle, when combined, equal the **mean motion** <note>The average or "smoothed out" movement of a celestial body.</note> of the Sun, just as the demonstrations shown above require. Furthermore, let the center of the eccentric move according to the **succession of the signs** <note>The normal west-to-east order of the zodiac (Aries to Taurus, etc.).</note> at the same speed as the Sun; and let the planet itself proceed with the same speed as the epicycle on the concentric. Let a line drawn from the center of the world, parallel to the line going out from the center of the eccentric through the center of the planet, determine its middle position. ¶ Let there be, therefore, a circle concentric to the world, **a. b. g.**, upon the center **z**, and let point **a** be where the center of the epicycle was while the planet was at the apogee of the epicycle—specifically, point **o**—and while the Sun was joined to the planet in its mean course; and let point **h** be the center of the eccentric. Now, however, let the epicycle be upon point **b**, and the planet in the epicycle be upon point **o**. Thus, with lines **z. b. d.**, **b. o.**, **n. o.**, **z. o.**, and **z. s.** having been drawn, the angle **a. z. b.** will be the mean motion, and angle **d. b. o.** will be the variation, or the mean motion of the argument. Let the angle **a. z. s.** be the mean motion of the Sun. Hence, on line **z. s.** will be the center of the eccentric, which we call **n**. Let us therefore first assume the concentric and eccentric to be equal, and the ratio of the semi-diameter of the concentric to the semi-diameter of the epicycle to be equal to the ratio of the semi-diameter of the eccentric to the distance between the centers. Therefore, line **z. h.** (or **z. n.**) will be equal to **b. o.** Since, however, the two angles **a. z. b.** and **d. b. o.** equal the angle **a. z. s.**, once the common angle **a. z. b.** is subtracted, the angle **b. z. s.** will be equal to angle **d. b. o.**; for which reason **z. b.** and **n. o.** are equal and parallel to each other. And because they are equal, the two lines **z. n.** and **b. o.** will be parallel. Whence, upon center **n**, a circle described/

And because line *z.b.* is set as the **mean motion** <term>mean motion|The idealized, uniform circular motion of a planet, as if it traveled at a constant speed.</term> of the planet—which is indeed parallel to line *n.o.* drawn from the center of the eccentric—the planet will be on line *n.o.* and for this reason at point *o*. ->Proposition 2.<-
->In Venus and Mercury, the same must be seen.<-

Let us assume the motion of the epicycle on the concentric is as fast as the mean motion of the Sun, and let the motion of the argument for each planet be its own. Truly, let the motion of the center of the eccentric proceed according to the **succession of the signs** <note>Direct motion through the zodiac, from West to East.</note> at a rate equal to the combined sum of the mean motion of the Sun and the mean motion of the argument. Thus, repeating the former figure in which angle *a.z.b.* is the mean motion of the Sun: angle *b.z.s.* will be equal to angle *d.b.o.* of the motion of the argument. Therefore line *z.n.* will be parallel to line *o.b.*, and the rest follows as before. From these things it clearly follows that, according to the model of the epicycle and concentric, whatever happens concerning **station** <term>station|A point where a planet appears to stop moving against the background of stars.</term> and **retrogradation** <term>retrogradation|When a planet appears to move backward through the zodiac.</term> also happens to it according to the model of the eccentric, even though both the center of the eccentric and the line of the planet’s mean motion move only in the succession of the signs. Indeed, that will occur in proportional places: I mean to say, if at a certain distance of the planet from the **apogee** <note>The highest or farthest point in an orbit.</note> of the epicycle the planet appears stationary, it will likewise appear stationary at an equal distance from the apogee of the eccentric. Now, if the planet had only a single variation of its motion, as **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – 190 BC), a Greek geometer famous for his work on conic sections and planetary theory.</note> and other ancients thought, it would be enough to have shown the cause of station or retrogradation by way of the epicycle. But since we concluded above a double variation—namely, because of both the eccentric and the epicycle—we would labor in vain to determine the points of stations in the eccentric alone, or the epicycle and concentric; therefore, I set these matters aside. Let us come, then, to the matter itself; so that we may follow it more clearly, let us hear certain preliminaries.

->Proposition 3.<-
->If the base of a rectilinear triangle be cut into two portions,<-
->one of which is not smaller than the side connected to it,<-
->the ratio of that portion to the remaining portion of the base will be greater<-
->than the ratio of the angles which are above the base in permuted order.<-

Let the base *b.g.* of triangle *a.b.g.* be divided into two portions *b.d.* and *d.g.*, of which one—namely *g.d.*—is not smaller than side *a.g.* I say that the ratio of line *g.d.* to line *d.b.* is greater than the ratio of angle *a.b.g.* to angle *a.g.d.* For let *g.d.* first be equal to *a.g.* With the dividing line *a.d.* extended, I draw a line from point *g* parallel to it, until it meets the continuation of *a.b.* at point *z*. Also, I shall produce a line parallel to *g.d.*, which is *a.e.* Thus there will be two sides of the **parallelogram** *a.d.g.e.*, *a.e.* and *d.g.*, which are equal; likewise, *a.d.* and *e.g.* are equal to each other. Therefore, having described an arc of the circumference of a circle according to the size of *a.g.*, it will pass through point *e*. Let the arc be *g.e.h.* Therefore, the ratio of triangle *z.a.e.* to triangle *a.e.g.* is greater than the ratio of **sector** <term>sector|A portion of a circle enclosed by two radii and an arc.</term> *h.a.e.* to triangle *a.e.g.*, since sector *h.a.e.* is a part of the triangle...

-> Proposition 4. <-

### To discern for which stars station or retrogradation occurs, and for which it does not.

<margin>
<image-desc>An astronomical diagram representing an epicycle (circle labeled a, b, g, t) with center d. An observer or Earth is at point e. Lines connect point e to the epicycle's center and various points on its circumference (a, g, t, l). Point a is marked as the apogee and g as the perigee.</image-desc>
</margin>

A star having a single motion according to the **succession of the signs** <term>succession of signs|The standard forward movement of planets through the zodiac, from West to East (e.g., from Aries to Taurus).</term> and a regular one around the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note> is never seen to **retrograde** <term>retrograde|The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky, where it seems to move from East to West against the background stars.</term>. But one that has a double motion—either on account of an **epicycle** <term>epicycle|A small circular path whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</term> and a concentric, or an **eccentric** <term>eccentric|An orbital circle whose center is not the Earth, but a point offset from it.</term> alone whose center is mobile—undergoes retrogradation; provided, however, that its motion, by which it is moved separately, tends against the succession of the signs. To make this clearer: let the circle of the epicycle be *a. b. g.* upon center *d.*, and the center of the world be *e.*, from which a line *e. d. a.* is drawn through the center of the epicycle; and let *a.* be the **apogee** <term>apogee|The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth; called 'aux' in the original Latin.</term> of the epicycle, and *g.* the **perigee** <term>perigee|The point in an orbit closest to the Earth; called 'oppositum augis' or 'opposite of the apogee' in the original Latin.</term>. I say, therefore, generally: if the ratio of line *d. g.* to line *e. g.* is not greater than the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle's motion to the velocity of the star in the epicycle, it is not possible for the star to appear to retrograde. For if this were possible, it would most likely happen at point *g.*, for there the motion of diversity <note>The apparent change in speed caused by the epicycle's rotation.</note> subtracts the most from the motion of longitude <note>The mean forward motion along the zodiac.</note>; but what was said does not happen there. For let us take a very small arc *g. t.*, with line *e. t.* and line *d. t.* drawn. Because, therefore, the base of triangle *d. t. e.* is divided into two portions *d. g.* and *g. e.*, and one of them—namely *d. g.*—is not smaller than side *d. t.*, it will be, by the preceding proposition, that the ratio of line *d. g.* to *g. e.* is greater than the ratio of angle *d. e. t.* to angle *e. d. t.* And thus the ratio of angle *d. e. t.* to angle *e. d. t.* is less than that of line *d. g.* to *g. e.* But the ratio of *d. g.* to *e. g.* was set as not greater than the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet in the epicycle. Therefore, the ratio of angle *d. e. t.* to angle *e. d. t.* is much less than the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the star. But the velocity of the star is now determined by angle *g. d. t.*; therefore, the angle of the epicycle's velocity is greater than angle *g. e. t.* Let that angle be *g. e. l.* Therefore, in the time in which the star describes the arc of the epicycle *t. g.*, it is seen to have described angle *l. e. g.* around the center of the world against the succession of signs—if, while the center of the epicycle were at rest, the star *l.* were moved only in the epicycle. But also in that time, the epicycle described around the center of the world an angle greater than angle *t. e. g.* according to the succession of signs. Thus, the star appeared to move in the succession of signs according to the quantity of the difference of these angles, namely according to the quantity of angle *l. e. t.* In no way therefore...

...it has undergone <term>retrogradation</term><note>Retrogradation is the apparent "backward" motion of a planet in the sky against the background of the stars.</note>. ¶ The same will be proved if we take arc *g.z* after drawing lines *e.z* and *d.z*. For again, angle *g.e.z* will be smaller than the angle of the velocity of the epicycle's motion. Therefore, let that angle be *g.e.m*. While the <term>planeta</term><note>Original: "planeta." In this context, it refers to any "wandering star," including the Sun and Moon in ancient systems.</note> describes angle *g.d.z* around the center of the <term>epicycle</term><note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note>, it appears from the <term>center of the world</term><note>The center of the world refers to the Earth in this geocentric model.</note> *e* to have described angle *d.e.z* against the succession of the zodiac signs because of the epicycle. But in that same time, the center of the epicycle described angle *m.e.d* according to the succession of the signs. Since this angle exceeds angle *d.e.z* when the two motions are combined, the planet will be seen *not* to retrograde, but to move according to the succession of the signs. From this it follows that retrogradation happens neither to the Sun nor to the Moon. For the Sun has the same velocity along the path of the epicycle as the epicycle has around the center of the world. Moreover, the ratio of the semidiameter (radius) of the epicycle to the part of the concentric semidiameter that is outside the epicycle is much smaller than this ratio of equality. Indeed, according to the numbers of <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work formed the basis of medieval astronomy.</note>, it is roughly as 1 to 23. You shall judge similarly regarding the Moon. ¶ In the remaining five <term>erraticis</term><note>Original: "erraticis," referring to the five planets known since antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> (planets), something else appears. For the ratio of line *g.d* to line *e.g* is greater than the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the star. It is possible, therefore, to draw a line from point *e* intersecting the epicycle such that the ratio of half of that part which is within the epicycle to the part of the line drawn outside is as the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the star. For by moving away to either side from the position of line *e.a*, the partial lines that fall within the epicycle gradually decrease, while those outside the epicycle increase. Therefore, having marked two such lines, *e.t.k* and *e.z.h*, so that the ratio of half of line *t.k* to line *e.t* is as the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the star; and likewise, let the ratio of half of line *z.h* to line *e.z* be the same. I say that the planet, being at either point *t* or *z*, will appear <term>stationarius</term><note>Stationary: the moment a planet appears to stop moving before changing direction from direct to retrograde motion, or vice versa.</note>. and through the whole arc *t.g.z* it will appear retrograde. In the entire remaining arc of the epicycle, however, it will appear <term>directus</term><note>Direct motion: the standard West-to-East movement of a planet across the sky.</note>, as will be demonstrated below.

## Proposition V.
### To determine the stationary point of a star in the epicycle.

Let the circle of the epicycle be *a.b.g* upon center *c*. And let the center of the world be *z*, from which line *z.e.a* is drawn through the center of the epicycle. And let the ratio of *e.g* to *g.z* be greater than the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the star. Otherwise, neither station nor retrogradation would happen to the star, as the preceding section showed. And let there be another line *z.b* intersecting the epicycle at two points *b* and *h*, such that the ratio of half of *b.h* to line *h.z* is as the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the star—which is indeed possible, as was touched upon before. I say that this line determines the point of station. For the star being at *b* will appear stationary. For however large an arc is taken from *b* toward the <term>augem</term><note>The "auge" (apogee) is the point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note>, in that place the planet will appear direct. But in the arc extended from *h* toward the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle, however small it may be, the star will appear retrograde; wherefore it will necessarily appear stationary at point *b*. ¶ Hear the demonstration of this matter. First, let arc *b.k* be taken toward the apogee of the epicycle, with line *z.k.l* and line *b.k* drawn. Likewise, let two radii of the epicycle, *e.h* and *e.k*, be extended. Because the base *b.z* of triangle *b.k.z* is divided into two portions *b.h* and *h.z*, and *h.z* is greater than side *b.k*, the ratio of line *b.h* to *h.z* will be (by the third [proposition] of this [book]) greater than the ratio of angle *b.z.k* to angle *k.b.z*, and therefore greater than the ratio...

...of the angle *b.z.k* to double the angle *k.b.z*. Therefore, the ratio of half the line *b.h* to the line *b.z* is greater than the ratio of angle *b.z.k* to double the angle *k.b.z*, that is, to the angle *h.e.k*. But the ratio of half of *b.h* to *b.z* was established as the ratio of the <term>velocity</term><note>In this context, velocity refers to the angular speed of the celestial bodies.</note> of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet. Wherefore, the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet—namely, the angle *h.e.k*—is greater than the ratio of angle *b.z.k* to that same angle *h.e.k*. Therefore, the angle of the epicycle’s velocity corresponding to angle *h.e.k* of the planet’s velocity is greater than angle *b.z.k*.

Let the angle *b.z.n*, therefore, be equal to the angle of the epicycle's velocity. While the planet describes the angle *h.e.k* within the <term>epicycle</term><note>A smaller circle that carries the planet, while the center of this circle moves along a larger path called the deferent.</note>, it appears from the <term>center of the world</term><note>The Earth, in this geocentric model of the universe.</note> to have moved against the succession of the signs by the amount of angle *b.z.k* due to the epicycle's internal rotation. But in that same time, the center of the epicycle describes the arc *h.n.z*, and thus the entire epicycle is moved according to the succession of the signs through the angle *b.z.n*. Therefore, the epicycle moves forward more than the star moves backward due to its motion within the epicycle, specifically by the angle *k.z.n*; and by that much, the star appears to move according to the succession of the signs. For this reason, throughout the entire arc *h.k*, the planet appears <term>direct</term><note>Moving forward in the sky from west to east.</note>.

However, if we take the arc *h.m*—no matter how small—from point *b* at the <term>opposite of the apogee</term><note>Original: "oppositum augis." The point on the epicycle closest to the Earth, often called the perigee.</note> of the epicycle, the planet will appear <term>retrograde</term><note>Moving "backward" in the sky, from east to west.</note> throughout this entire arc. For when the lines *z.m*, *b.m*, and *e.m* are drawn, according to the third proposition of this book, the ratio of *z.h* to *h.b* will be greater than the ratio of angle *m.b.z* to angle *b.z.m*. For the base of the triangle *b.z.m* is divided into two portions, *z.h* and *h.b*, one of which (namely *z.h*) is greater than the side of the triangle *z.m*. Consequently, the ratio of *b.h* to *h.z* is conversely smaller than the ratio of angle *b.z.m* to angle *m.b.z*. And therefore, it is smaller than the ratio of double the angle *b.z.m* to double the angle *m.b.z*. From this, the ratio of half the line *b.h* to the line *h.z* will also be smaller than the ratio of angle *b.z.m* to double the angle *m.b.z*—that is, to the angle *h.e.m*.

But the ratio of half the line *b.h* to the line *h.z* was as the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet. Therefore, the ratio of the angle of the epicycle's velocity to the angle of the planet's velocity is smaller than the ratio of angle *b.z.m* to angle *h.e.m*. Since angle *h.e.m* is the velocity of the planet in the epicycle, the angle of the epicycle's velocity will be smaller than angle *b.z.m*. Let that angle be *b.z.t*. Thus, while the planet describes arc *h.m* and angle *h.e.m* in the epicycle, it appears from the center of the world to have described angle *b.z.m* against the succession of the signs. But in that same time, the center of the epicycle has moved according to the succession of the signs through angle *b.z.t*. Therefore, the planet's backward motion around the center of the world (due to its motion in the epicycle) is greater than its forward motion (due to the motion of the whole epicycle) by the angle *m.z.t*. Wherefore, while the star moves through arc *h.m*, it will appear to have moved backward through angle *t.z.m*. 

Since, therefore, the star is direct throughout the entire arc *h.k*, and retrograde throughout the entire arc *h.m*, it is necessary that point *h* be the end of direct motion and the beginning of retrogradation. And for that reason, it will be the <term>stationary point</term><note>The point where the planet appears to stand still in the sky before reversing its direction.</note>, which was to be demonstrated. The same will be shown similarly in all respects if the planet is placed after the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle, just as it has now been placed before such an opposite.

Given the ratio of two lines: if the rectangle contained beneath them is known, each of them becomes known.
