## Proposition VII.

**Once the distance of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric is known: to derive the velocities of the epicycle and the planet corresponding to a proposed mean motion.**

For example, if the distance of the center of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of this circle moves around a larger circle (the deferent).</note> from the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit that is furthest from the Earth.</note> was 10 degrees, and I wish to know how much it moves in reality with respect to the center of the world while the center of the epicycle moves by one degree in its <term>mean motion</term><note>The theoretical uniform speed of a celestial body, before corrections for its specific orbital position are applied.</note>, and how much the planet moves in the epicycle, I shall proceed in this way. With the mean center—which is the mean distance of the epicycle from the apogee of the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth.</note>—I take the <term>equation of the center</term><note>A correction factor used in ancient astronomy to account for the difference between a planet's mean position and its true position due to the eccentricity of its orbit.</note>, which I save. Then, to the mean center I have already used, I add the arc of the proposed mean motion. With this combined total, I find the equation of the center again in the usual way. I subtract the difference of these two equations, if there be any, from the arc of the proposed mean motion if the epicycle was between the two mean passages toward the apogee of the eccentric. Or, I add it to the same if it was toward the opposite of the apogee. This rule holds as long as the epicycle remains on the same side with respect to the apogee or its opposite. I mean to say: if the given mean center placed the epicycle before the apogee, the sum of the mean center and the proposed arc of mean motion should likewise place the epicycle before the apogee; or if one placed it after the apogee, the other should do so as well. If, however, one of them placed the epicycle before the apogee and the other after the apogee, it is necessary to join the two equations and subtract the sum from the arc of the proposed mean motion. For if one of them placed the epicycle before the opposite of the apogee and the other after, the sum of these equations of the center must be added to the proposed mean motion. For the velocity of the planet in the epicycle, let the mean <term>argument</term><note>In astronomy, the "argument" refers to the position of a body along its path, usually the epicycle.</note> corresponding to the proposed mean motion be taken; this is easily done if it is known what time that proposed mean motion corresponds to. Then, to this mean argument, add or subtract that which you added or subtracted above to obtain the velocity of the epicycle. The reason for this type of operation will be clearly evident from those things given above regarding the angles of diversity resulting from the eccentric, if you apply your mind to it.

## Proposition VIII.

**To determine how far a planet is from the true apogee of the epicycle at the beginning of retrogradation or direct motion.**

Let there be the circle of the epicycle *d.e.z.b* upon the center *a*, having a known distance from the apogee of the eccentric, and because of this (from the previous proposition), its velocity with respect to the velocity [of the planet] is known. Let a straight line be drawn from the center of the world, which is *g*, cutting the epicycle in two points *e* and *z*, such that the ratio of half of the line *e.z* (namely, the line *t.z*) to the line *z.g* is as the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet in the epicycle. Before this, however, lines *a.t* (perpendicular to *e.z*) and *a.z* (the radius of the epicycle) are drawn, with the line *g.b.d* indicating the apogee *d* of the epicycle and its opposite *g* <note>original: "indicantibus"</note>. The arc *d.e.z* is sought. For by the fifth proposition of this book, point *z* is in the place in which the planet is <term>stationary</term><note>A "stationary point" occurs when a planet's forward motion in its epicycle perfectly balances its backward motion relative to Earth, making it appear to stand still before it begins retrograde motion.</note>...

### Proposition IX.

->**To calculate the mean motion of diversity for the time of half the**<-
->**retrogradation.**<-

<image-desc>An astronomical diagram demonstrating the geometry of planetary retrogradation. Two circles represent an epicycle at different points in its orbit. The upper circle is marked with points d, e, s, and t, with lines showing the center of the world (e) and the center of mean motion (t). The lower circle shows the epicycle positioned between the apogee and the center of the eccentric. A primary vertical axis d-e-z is shown, along with lines of sight from point e to various points on the epicycle circumference.</image-desc>

This motion which we seek is described on the circumference of the epicycle by the planet in its mean course of <term>diversity</term><note>Often called 'anomaly'; the position of a planet on its small circle (epicycle) relative to its farthest point from Earth.</note> from the beginning of retrogradation to its middle. This middle, however: as we now suppose: is the instant in which the planet is at the opposite of the true apogee of the epicycle: that is, opposite the mean place of the sun. Because if the opposite of the true apogee of the epicycle did not vary with respect to the opposite of the mean apogee of the epicycle: the preceding would have sufficiently taught the sought-after arc. But it is not so: rather, that point is always varying. ¶ For, so that it may be more easily known: let line *z.e* be drawn in the figure through the apogee of the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular orbit that is not centered on the Earth.</note> *z* and the center of the world *e*. On which let the center of uniform motion be *t*. Let the epicycle be placed between the apogee and the mean distance of the eccentric: which is the circle *a.b.g* described upon the center *d*. Line *e.d.a* is drawn to the true apogee of the epicycle: which is *a*. But the opposite of the true apogee is point *g*. But let the opposite of the mean apogee of the epicycle be point *h*: with line *t.h.d* being drawn. Now let the planet beginning to move in retrograde be at point *b*. Therefore, we shall have the known arc *b.g* from the preceding. However, the planet does not describe [this arc] precisely from the beginning of retrogradation until its middle. For as the planet approaches the opposite of the epicycle's apogee: that epicycle recedes further from the apogee of the eccentric. Therefore, the angle of diversity *e.d.t* will for that reason be greater in the middle of retrogradation than in its beginning. And thence the opposite of the true apogee of the epicycle will be more distant from the opposite of the mean apogee. Therefore, in the middle of the retrogradation, let the opposite of the true apogee of the epicycle be point *m*. Therefore, the planet will describe the arc of the epicycle *b.m* from the beginning of retrogradation to its middle. At the end of the retrogradation, however, the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle will be changed by an arc almost equal to arc *g.m*. Let it be estimated, therefore, to have come to point *n*, so that from the middle to the end of the retrogradation [it travels] an arc of the epicycle almost...

<margin>3</margin>
[The calculator] manages to describe [an arc] equal to arc *b.m*. We seek, therefore, arc *b.m*, which would indeed be found immediately if arc *g.m* were known. But this arc cannot be known unless the angles of diversity <note>original: "anguli diversitatis"; referring to the difference between the mean and true positions</note> arising from the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular orbit where the Earth is slightly offset from the center of the circle.</note> are known; one of which occurs at the beginning of the <term>retrogradation</term><note>The apparent backward motion of a planet through the zodiac.</note>, and the other at its midpoint. For the difference of these angles would reveal arc *g.m*, if the beginning and middle of the retrogradation happened to fall before or after the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of the Earth.</note>. But if one occurred before and the other after the apogee (or its opposite), the collected angles of diversity would achieve the same result. Therefore, let us take pains to extract these angles of diversity as close to the truth as possible. Arc *b.g* is known, because the ratio of the velocity of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> to the velocity of the planet is known. Therefore, since arc *b.g* measures the velocity of the planet on the epicycle, the arc which the epicycle describes correspondingly will be known. Take, therefore, the <term>equation of the center</term><note>The mathematical correction used to find the true position of a planet based on its eccentric orbit.</note> with the mean center, which you used previously while you were seeking arc *z.h*, and save it. Then, to this mean center, add the arc of the velocity of the epicycle which you have most recently extracted, and having collected them, seek the equation of the center again. Note the difference between this equation and the previous one; for it will be nearly equal in the proposed case to arc *g.m*. Subtract it, therefore, from the previously known arc *b.g*, and the sought arc *b.m* will remain, provided the epicycle was moving toward the apogee between the two mean lengths of the eccentric. Or add it to the same, if it was positioned in the remaining part of the eccentric. Indeed, you shall observe this while the beginning and the middle of the retrogradation fall in the same part of the apogee or its opposite. For if they occur in different parts, join the equations of the center and work with the sum as before. Once this arc is found, if you double it, you will have nearly the entire arc of retrogradation. Finally, the time responding to this arc will be easily established if you consult the tables of mean motions. If you wish to make this work more precise, inquire after the finding of the arc of diversity for the corresponding mean motion of longitude, and use it consequently in place of the arc which I extracted above through the proportion of the velocities of motion.

### Proposition X

![Decorative initial A] To determine the arc of half of the retrogradation.
¶ I shall take up again the previous figure, which gave the known angle *a.g.t*, through which the planet would indeed move backward in the time of half the retrogradation, if in this time the epicycle did not move according to the motion of the eccentric. But in the meantime, [the epicycle] itself moves according to the sequence of the signs <note>original: "secundum signorum sequentiam"; meaning direct or prograde motion.</note>. It will therefore be necessary for the angle—which the line of the true motion of the epicycle describes in this time of half the retrogradation—to be subtracted from angle *a.t.g*. For the remainder will indicate how much the planet will retrograde in this time. Furthermore, from the preceding, the time of half the retrogradation is known, for which the tables of its mean motion of longitude will give a known value. Thus, the distance of the epicycle from the apogee of the eccentric is known at the beginning of the retrogradation by supposition, and at the middle of the retrogradation by the addition of this mean motion which corresponds to the time of half the retrogradation. Therefore, through the tables of equations, the arc which the epicycle describes by its own true motion in the time of half the retrogradation will be known. This arc, therefore, having been taken away from angle *a.g.t*, leaves the sought arc of retrocession. If you double this, you will have nearly the true arc described by the planet against the sequence of the signs during the time of the whole retrogradation.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary motion from Book Twelve. The previous page dealt with finding the arc of diversity and the equation of the center to determine the beginning and midpoint of retrogradation. This page focuses on Proposition XII, evaluating Ptolemy's method for calculating the "stations"—the points where a planet appears to stand still before changing direction—at different points in its orbit.</meta>

<header>Twelfth [Book]</header>

operation <note>original: "operationem"</note>: which the ninth [proposition] of this book taught. Once the stations have been found for this triple position, he proceeds as follows. He establishes the first number as the difference between the maximum distance of the center of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle called the deferent.</note> from the center of the world and its average distance. For the second number, he takes the difference between this distance at the specific position where he proposes to find the station and the average distance. Likewise, he takes as the third number the excess [difference] between the two stations, one of which occurs at the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth; original: "auge".</note> and the other at the mean distance.

¶ He then multiplies the second by the third, and divides the product by the first. The resulting fourth value he subtracts from the station value given by the mean distance of the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular orbit where the Earth is offset from the geometric center.</note>, or adds it to the same, just as the calculation requires. He operates in no different a manner for those positions of the epicycle that are enclosed between the mean distance of the eccentric and the opposite of the apogee <note>The perigee, or closest point to the Earth.</note>. In this way, he seems to have extracted the stations of the planets for every position of the epicycle on the eccentric. However, he assumes this one thing: that as much as the epicycle either approaches or recedes from the center of the world when moving away from the mean distance of the eccentric, these stations will increase or decrease proportionally. Indeed, this assumption is not a matter of necessity.

¶ For I shall demonstrate in this manner that the same first stations are found at various distances of the epicycle from the center of the world. Let there be a circle of an epicycle *a. b. g.* on center *d*, and let the center of the world be *c*, which is connected to the center of the epicycle by line *c. d.* and extended to the apogee of the epicycle *a*. Let a line *e. b.* be drawn from a point *e* <note>Point *e* here acts as an auxiliary point for the observer's perspective.</note> through the center of the world, cutting the epicycle and determining the point of the station *g*. Let line *b. z.* be parallel to *a. e.*, and let line *b. t.* cut through point *g*, falling wherever it may at point *l*. Therefore, there will be two triangles, *b. l. g.* and *e. g. t.*, which are equiangular <note>Having the same angles; similar triangles.</note>. Because of this, the ratio of line *b. g.* to line *g. l.* is as the ratio of line *b. g.* to *g. t.* Therefore, by permutation, *b. g.* is to *g. e.* as *g. l.* is to *g. t.*, wherefore the ratio of line *b. g.* to *g. t.* is greater than the ratio of *b. g.* to *g. e.*, and thus the ratio of half of line *b. g.* to line *g. e.* is also greater.

Let us therefore place the station point *g* at the mean distance of the eccentric: namely, when the center of the epicycle is distant from the center of the world by line *d. e.* Then imagine the epicycle receding from this position toward the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric until the distance of its center from the center of the world is as line *d. t.* Now, because of this retreat from the mean distance of the eccentric, the ratio of half of line *b. g.* to line *g. t.* becomes greater than the ratio of half of line *b. g.* to line *g. e.*, as was shown. Similarly, the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet for distance *d. t.* becomes greater than the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet at distance *d. e.* Since the motion of longitude is rendered that much greater as the epicycle approaches the opposite of the apogee.

If it is possible, therefore, that as much as the ratio of half of line *b. g.* to line *g. t.* exceeds the ratio of half of line *b. g.* to *g. e.*, so much does the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet at the distance of the epicycle *d. t.* exceed the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet at distance *d. e.*, then the ratio of half of line *b. g.* to line *g. t.* is as the ratio of the velocity of the epicycle to the velocity of the planet. Therefore, point *g* will then be the location of the station while the epicycle is distant from the center of the world by line *d. t.*—which was the same point *g* that was the location of the station before, while the epicycle was at the mean distance. Therefore, although the distance of the center of the epicycle from the center of the world has varied, the location of the station remained unchanged, which is what I intended [to show]. However, the neglect of this precision will introduce no sensible error; wherefore I judge that Ptolemy's procedure, which although not perfectly refined is nonetheless convenient enough, should be followed.

# Given a proposed position for Venus in the circle of the signs: to inquire how great its maximum evening elongation from the sun can be at that location.

¶ Contemplate the figure placed before your eyes. In this diagram, let the line *a-b-e* pass through the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth; original: "augem".</note> of the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth; original: "ecentrici".</note> and its opposite point. Of this line, let one end—namely, *a*—be the apogee, and the other end, *e*, be the opposite of the apogee <note>The perigee, or the point closest to Earth.</note>. On that same line, let point *d* be the center of the world <note>The Earth.</note>, *g* be the center of the eccentric, and *b* be the center of the uniform motion of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A smaller circle carrying the planet, which itself moves along the larger eccentric circle.</note>. Next, let a circle *h-t* be described around center *z*. Let the line *d-t* touch <note>original: "contingat", meaning it is tangent to the circle.</note> this circle at point *t*. Its center *z* should also be connected to the three points *b*, *g*, and *t* by the lines *z-b*, *z-g*, and *z-t*. Let line *b-z* be extended to *h*, the mean apogee of the epicycle. Finally, let perpendicular lines be drawn: *b-m* to *g-z*, and *g-k* to *d-t*, and likewise *g-l* <note>original: "g-z", but the geometry suggests "g-l" based on the subsequent mention of point l</note> to *z-t*. 

¶ We seek, therefore, while Venus is on line *d-t* at its furthest distance from the position of the sun, how great its <term>evening elongation</term><note>The angular distance of a planet from the sun when it appears as an "evening star" after sunset; original: "longitudo veſpertina".</note> is. In the previous steps, the position of the apogee of Venus's eccentric was given as known, and now the position of this star is assumed to be known; therefore, angle *a-d-t* will be found to be known. From this, the ratio of the eccentricity *g-d* to the line *g-k* (which is equal to *l-t*) will not be unknown. Both lines *d-g* and *z-t* were known with respect to the radius of the eccentric; therefore, *l-t* will become known in that same respect. The remaining part *z-l* will also be measured relative to line *g-z*, the radius of the eccentric. Thus, two sides of the triangle *z-l-g* (namely *z-g* and *z-l*) are known, and angle *l* is a right angle. Therefore, its angle *z-g-l* will be known. Now, the whole angle *d-g-z* consists of three angles: namely, *z-g-l*, which is already known; the right angle *l-g-k*; and angle *d-g-k*, which is known because angle *g-d-k* was previously known and *k* is a right angle. Thus, angle *d-g-z* itself will become known.

The remaining angle—namely, *b-g-z*—will be known from the two right angles <note>The sum of angles on a straight line is 180 degrees or two right angles.</note>, and because of this, both lines *b-m* and *m-g* will be proportional to line *b-g*. Indeed, line *b-g* is known with respect to the radius of the eccentric *g-z*. Thus, the remaining line *m-z* together with line *b-z* will be given as known. From this, angle *b-z-m* will not be unknown. This angle, together with the known angle *b-g-z*, is equivalent to angle *a-b-z*. Therefore, angle *a-b-z* will be known, and thus the distance of the true position of Venus (which is also common to the sun's position) from the apogee of the eccentric will be established. Consequently, that mean position will by no means be hidden. Through those things which were discussed in the third book, the true position of the sun will come forth as known from its mean position. Since the position of Venus is placed as desired and the true position of the sun is clear, the interval that falls between their true positions will be known. And this was what was desired.

## Proposition 14.

# To determine the maximum elongations of Mercury from the sun, given its true position in the zodiac.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle (epicycle) with center point e. A line gh originates from point g and is tangent to the circle at point h. Another line passes from g through the center e to a point s. Various other points a, b, and d are marked on associated radii and projections.</image-desc>
</margin>

In the line *a-b-g*, let point *a* be the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in the orbit furthest from Earth; original: "aux".</note> of the <term>eccentric</term><note>A circular orbit whose center is not the Earth; original: "ecentrici".</note>. Let *g* be the center of the world <note>The Earth</note>, *b* the center of uniform motion <note>The equant point, where the planet's speed appears steady</note>, and *t* the center of the small circle which the center of the eccentric describes. Let the circle of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A smaller circle carrying the planet around the larger orbit; original: "epicycli".</note> *z-b* be established upon center *e*, which the line *g-h* touches at point *h*. Let its center *e* be connected to the three points *b*, *g*, and *h* by their respective lines. Let the position of the planet, which the line *g-h* indicates in the <term>zodiac</term><note>The "circle of signs"; original: "orbe signorum".</note>, be known. The goal is to find the maximum <term>elongation</term><note>The angular distance between a planet and the Sun; original: "longitudinem".</note> of Mercury from the true position of the sun. We cannot achieve this by the same spark of ingenuity we relied upon for Venus. For although the angle *a-g-h* is known, the distance of the center of the epicycle from any of the three points *g*, *b*, and *t* is not known, and knowledge of this is necessary for the task. We must, therefore, think of another way to obtain the means of reaching our purpose. We are certain of this: if the angle *a-b-e*—that is, the motion of the mean longitude—is known, then the "angle of diversity" *b-e-g* along with angle *b-g-e* can be known through the principles demonstrated above. Therefore, the line *e-g* will also be known in relation to the semi-diameter of the eccentric; and in that same relation, the semi-diameter of the epicycle will also be known. From this, angle *e-g-h* and consequently the whole angle *a-g-h* will be known. Thus, from an assumed mean position of the planet, the door is opened to calculating its true position.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a larger circle with a horizontal diameter marked with points c, a, and b. Point c is at the far left, a is at the far right, and point b is located on the lower right curve of the circumference.</image-desc>
</margin>

¶ Moreover, if the mean position of the sun is given, who would not know how to strive for its true position? Therefore, by assuming at will a mean position for either the sun or Mercury—since this mean motion is common to both—we will easily recognize the maximum elongation of Mercury, whether it be in the morning or the evening.

¶ Now let us proceed happily to the matter itself. To make it more pleasant to understand, I shall use an example in my discourse. Suppose I wish to be taught, when Mercury is established according to its true course at the beginning of Aries, how great its maximum elongation from the true position of the sun can be—whether I prefer the morning or the evening distance. I set by chance—though based on a reasonable estimate—a mean position of the sun (or Mercury) such that, after completing the work I just mentioned, the true position of Mercury falls at the beginning of Aries, or very near it. If the true position of Mercury reaches the beginning of Aries, I will be certain that for Mercury located at the start of Aries, such a maximum elongation from the sun can occur as the work itself has shown.

¶ If, however, the true position of Mercury falls outside the beginning of Aries, consider the zodiac *b-a-c*, in which point *a* is the beginning of Aries and point *b* is the true position of Mercury. Finally, I shall choose another mean position, so that the true motion of Mercury at its maximum elongation is forced to fall beyond the beginning of Aries—for instance, falling at point *c* in the figure. I will thus have two maximum elongations of Mercury: one occurring when Mercury is at point *b*, and the other when it is at point *c*. Through these, I shall find its maximum elongation at point *a* by this clever method: from the difference between the two maximum elongations occurring at the two locations *b* and *c*, I take a proportional part according to the ratio of the known arc *a-b* to the whole known arc *b-c*. I shall then add this proportional part to the maximum elongation reaching point *b* (if the other elongation was larger), or subtract it from it (if the other was smaller). I will then have the maximum elongation from the true position of the sun that occurs when Mercury is at the beginning of Aries, which was my intent. You shall work no differently for the other locations of the zodiac. Therefore, where there is no power to succeed with a simple attempt due to a lack of intermediate data, do not let your own sluggishness deter you from reaching the goal through a double effort.

<header>Book Thirteen</header>

# The Thirteenth Book of Theoretical Investigation: The final part, namely on the motion of the planets in latitude; it measures their considerations most clearly.

->Proposition 1.<-

<image-desc>To the left of the main text block are two faint geometric diagrams. The top diagram shows a large circle (the eccentric) with a smaller circle (the epicycle) attached to its rim, with several intersecting lines passing through the centers, illustrating the inclination of the orbits. The bottom diagram is a circle divided by a horizontal diameter with arcs above and below it, likely representing the nodes. In the center of the page is a large, ornate square woodcut initial "L" decorated with white foliate and scroll patterns on a black background.</image-desc>

**To open the way of investigation into the latitudes of the three superior planets.**

Through frequent observations in his own time, Ptolemy conjectured that the greatest <term>latitudes</term><note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic (the Sun's path); original: "latitudinibus".</note> occur for Saturn and Jupiter when they are located at the beginning of the sign of Libra or near it. For Mars, however, they occur around the end of Cancer, perhaps when the planet is placed at the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth; original: "auge".</note> of the <term>eccentric</term><note>The main circular path of the planet, which is off-center from the Earth; original: "eccentrici".</note>—I mean northern latitudes. In the diametrically opposite parts of the zodiac, however, he observed the greatest southern latitudes. Having explored this sufficiently, Ptolemy began to observe the planets, each one at the limit of its maximum latitude: sometimes indeed when the planet was at the true apogee of its <term>epicycle</term><note>A smaller circle that carries the planet, which itself moves along the larger eccentric orbit; original: "epicycli".</note> or near it (since at the apogee of the epicycle a planet hardly or never appears clearly to the eye because the solar rays interfere), and at other times at the opposite point of the apogee <note>The perigee, or the point closest to Earth.</note>. 

He noted, moreover, that a planet existing at the point opposite the apogee of the epicycle is removed from the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky, used as the reference plane for planetary latitude; original: "eclyptica".</note> by a greater latitude than when it is in the apogee itself, both in the northern and southern parts of the eccentric. Both of these latitudes—those belonging to the true apogee of the epicycle and its opposite point—were seen to be northern when the planet was in the northern half of the eccentric, and both were discerned as southern when it was in the southern half. This situation indicated that the entire diameter of the epicycle was moved away from the ecliptic toward the north, or entirely toward the south. This could not happen unless the center of the epicycle and that part of the surface of the eccentric in which the center of the epicycle is placed were to decline toward that same direction. 

Therefore, our Ptolemy concluded that the surface of the eccentric is inclined to the surface of the ecliptic. He called the two boundary points of this intersection <term>nodes</term><note>Original: "nodos".</note>, just as he did with the Moon. By the same reasoning, the surface of the epicycle is also proven to be inclined to the surface of the eccentric. For unless that were certain, you would by no means see latitudes of different quantities occurring when the planet is at the apogee of the epicycle compared to when it is at the opposite point. 

Then, with no less diligence, he awaited the arrival of the center of the epicycle at one of the nodes, so that he understood it to be a <term>quadrant's</term><note>A distance of 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle.</note> distance from the northern limit. He also chose a position for the body of the planet at a quadrant's distance from the true apogee of the epicycle. Whenever he saw these two conditions coincide, he did not detect any latitude in the star. He found the same thing even when the planet existed in other parts of the epicycle, provided the epicycle itself remained at the node. By this judgment, he conjectured that the entire surface of the epicycle in this position never crosses the surface of the ecliptic. 

To conclude, therefore, following in Ptolemy's footsteps, we shall assert that for these three superior planets, the surface of the eccentric is inclined to the surface of the ecliptic with a fixed inclination, and the surface of the epicycle is inclined to the surface of the eccentric, yet not with a fixed inclination. This is so that the part of the epicycle's longitude closer to the eccentric moves away from it toward the same direction as that part of the eccentric in which the epicycle is placed. However, the diameter of the epicycle passing through the mean longitudes, just as it is known to lie in the surface of the ecliptic, the epi[cycle]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word.</note>

### Proposition 2.

->Finally, to resolve certain preliminaries regarding the<-
->latitudes of Venus and Mercury.<-

While Ptolemy was diligently observing what variations Venus and Mercury had in their latitudes, he understood that when the center of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one (the eccentric); original: "epicycli".</note> was positioned at the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth; original: "auge".</note> of the <term>eccentric</term><note>The main orbital circle, centered on a point other than the Earth; original: "eccentrici".</note>, the planet would have the same latitude when it was at the true apogee of the epicycle as it had when at the opposite point. He found a similar result when the center of the epicycle remained at the opposite point of the eccentric's apogee. However, this latitude for Venus was northern at both of the mentioned positions of the epicycle; for Mercury, it was southern. From this, it was clear that the entire <term>diameter</term><note>The straight line passing through the center of the epicycle; original: "diameter".</note> of the epicycle passing through its apogee and its opposite—and therefore also the center of the epicycle—would tend toward the north in the case of Venus, but toward the south in the case of Mercury. This cannot happen unless that part of the eccentric which then contains the epicycle tilts in that direction. Afterward, he sought to observe other positions of the planet in the epicycle, while the epicycle remained at the apogee of the eccentric. He judged it especially important to note the greatest <term>elongations</term><note>The maximum angular distance a planet reaches from the Sun as seen from Earth; original: "longitudines".</note> of the planet from the Sun, both in the morning and in the evening. He found, therefore, that with the epicycle of Venus positioned at the apogee of the eccentric, the evening elongation had more of a northern tilt than the morning elongation. He experienced the opposite of this at the point opposite the eccentric's apogee. For there, he noted that the morning elongation tended more toward the north than the evening one. But in the case of Mercury, it was otherwise. For at the apogee of the eccentric, he found its evening elongation tilted more toward the south than the morning elongation. At the opposite of the eccentric's apogee, the contrary was true. He was no less diligent in gathering data when the center of the epicycle was situated at either of the nodes. For he considered that when the planet was at a distance of a quarter of a circle on either side of the epicycle's apogee, it would have no latitude from the ecliptic. At the apogee and its opposite, however, it would not lack latitude, and indeed it varied. For he saw that the nearer distance of Venus's epicycle on the left side of the eccentric—where the motion of elongation is diminished—was tilted more toward the south than its further distance. The opposite occurred at the other node, where the elongation of the epicycle was tilted more toward the north. He found these latitudes in Mercury to be contrary in every respect. For at the node on the left half of the eccentric, the nearer distance of the epicycle was tilted more toward the north than the further distance. The opposite occurred at the other node. In summary, therefore, we understand for both of these two planets that the eccentric undergoes a tilt from the ecliptic—not a fixed one, but a varied one—the change of which follows the true course of the epicycle. For when the epicycle is at the apogee of the eccentric or its opposite, this type of <term>deviation</term><note>The specific tilting motion of the orbital plane; original: "deuiatio".</note> is at its maximum. As it moves away from this position, it is gradually diminished until it becomes nothing, but the entire surface of the eccentric is situated within the surface of the ecliptic; this occurs when the center of the epicycle is at either of the nodes. Moving away from there, the deviation of the eccentric begins to grow again. In Venus, as was said, it is always toward the north; in Mercury, however, it is toward the south. The epicycle, however, has this variation at the nodes: its diameter passing through the apogee and its opposite is not in the surface of the <term>deferent</term><note>The main circular path that "carries" the epicycle; original: "deferentis".</note>, but is inclined toward it. At the apogee of the eccentric and its opposite, that entire diameter is situated in the surface of the eccentric. But the diameter of the epicycle perpendicular to the said diameter in that position—namely at the apogee of the eccentric or its opposite—is not in the surface of the eccentric, but is away from...

## Proposition 2.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' showing a figure (possibly a scholar or deity) in a classical landscape or architectural setting.</image-desc>

Now to learn how great the total latitudes of Venus and Mercury are, from which the inclinations of each of the surfaces to the others will clearly be established.
¶ Venus, remaining at the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth; original: "auge".</note> of its <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle; original: "epicycli".</note> or its opposite, is found to have a latitude of 10 minutes, whether the epicycle itself is positioned at the apogee of the eccentric or at its opposite. ¶ Mercury [is found to have] 45 minutes. Therefore, such will be the deviation or declination of the eccentric of each of them toward the surface of the ecliptic. Nor should one wonder how there is the power of observing this, since both of them, remaining at the apogee of the epicycle or its opposite, do not appear to the observer, as the solar ray brings an impediment <note>The "solar ray" refers to the Sun's glare, which hides these planets when they are close to it; original: "radius solaris impedimentum afferat".</note>. Indeed, I say the planet was not observed in these two positions, but in places very near them. Thus, you may conjecture that such a latitude occurs when the planet is in the apogee of the epicycle or its opposite. ¶ Furthermore, in the mentioned locations of the eccentric, the <term>reflections</term><note>A term for the specific "bending" or shifting of the orbital planes to account for observed north-south movement; original: "reflexiones".</note> were found to differ by 5 degrees. In Venus, this occurs without sensible diversity at the apogee and its opposite. In Mercury, however, the difference of the reflections occurring at the opposite of the eccentric's apogee adds half a degree over those which occur at the apogee of the eccentric. Thus, if you weigh the average difference between the extremes of the reflections, you will assign five degrees for Mercury, just as for Venus. From this it is drawn out: that the maximum reflection of either half of the epicycle from the surface of the eccentric is almost two and a half degrees. For this reflection, doubled, completes five degrees. We shall draw out the angle of inclination of the epicycle's surface to the eccentric's surface a little further below. Finally, when the epicycle of Venus is positioned at either of the nodes, the star itself, being at the apogee of the epicycle, is seen to have had a latitude of one degree on either side of the ecliptic; and at the opposite of the epicycle's apogee, six degrees and one-third of a degree. From this, it is concluded that the angle of inclination of the epicycle's surface to the eccentric's surface in this position contains two and a half degrees. For if you draw a straight line from the <term>center of the world</term><note>In this geocentric model, the Earth is the center of the world; original: "centro mundi".</note> through the center of the epicycle in this position, which cuts the convex surface of the epicycle at two points; and if you count 2.5 degrees from the highest of these in whichever direction you wish, two lines connecting the ends of such an arc will contain an angle of one degree at the center of the world (where four right angles are 360 degrees). But if you count the same amount from the lowest point and understand the lines converging at the center of the world in the manner mentioned, the angle contained in them will be almost 6 degrees and 20 minutes. This angle of inclination will be used later for drawing out individual latitudes. The latitude of Mercury, however, being at the apogee of the epicycle, comprises 1 degree and 45 minutes <note>original: "vno g. 7. 45. m." - likely a transcription or typesetting error for 1° 45', a standard value in this context.</note>. At the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle, it is almost 4 degrees. Thus, the inclination of the epicycle's surface to the eccentric's surface seems to demand for itself six degrees and a quarter of one degree.

### Proposition 5.

**To reveal how great the inclinations of its circles are through the maximum latitudes of Mars.**

We know one thing common to **Venus** and **Mercury**: that although the star itself undergoes many different latitudes, while one of them is usually found to be at its maximum, the other is zero. Thus, one yields to the other, so that the astronomer can see how great each is individually. However, in **Mars**, and finally in **Saturn** and **Jupiter**, it happens far differently. For the maximum latitude which each of them usually has depends partly on the epicycle and partly on the eccentric. Thus, it does not allow one to be known clearly and separately from the other. Therefore, to carry out our purpose, we shall proceed by another path. **Mars**, having its seat at the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle while the epicycle itself is placed at the apogee of the eccentric, is seen to cross the <term>solar path</term><note>The ecliptic or the path of the Sun; original: "phebeum iter".</note> by a space of 4 degrees and one quarter of a degree [4° 15']. But at the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric [at its closest point to Earth], it is separated by a quantity of 7 degrees. Let us therefore draw a figure in which two lines, **a. b.** and **g. d.**, are the common intersections of a surface perpendicular to the ecliptic and falling from the center with those intersected surfaces. Let **a. b.** lie in the ecliptic, while **g. d.** never exceeds the surface of the eccentric. Finally, upon the two centers **g** and **d**, let us describe two circles representing the epicycle, which shall be **h. t. k.** and **m. n. s.** And let the diameter of the epicycle **h. g. k.** be inclined to the diameter of the eccentric, and similarly **m. d. s.** over the same, with lines **e. h.**, **e. k.**, **e. m.**, and **e. s.** drawn from the center of the world, **e**, to the four points **b**, **k**, **m**, and **s**. Therefore, the star being at the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle, with the epicycle placed at the apogee of the eccentric, it is seen to have a latitude according to the size of angle **a. e. k.** But at the opposite of the apogee of the eccentric, it is separated from the ecliptic by angle **b. e. s.** These two angles are known, as was seen above. Yet neither of the angles **g. e. k.** nor **d. e. s.** is held as known. However, the difference by which one exceeds the other has been found. For it is the difference of the two given angles **a. e. k.** and **b. e. s.**, since the angles **a. e. g.** and **b. e. d.**, being opposite to each other, must be equal. If, therefore, someone were to give the known ratio of angle **g. e. k.** to angle **d. e. s.**, both would soon be discovered. In order, therefore, that this ratio may be known close to the truth, let us imagine a straight line passing through the center of the world and the center of the epicycle in two understood positions. Let us note the points of intersection of this line with the convex surface of the epicycle on the side opposite the apogee of the epicycle. However many equal arcs of the circumference of the epicycle we count from either of these points, and connect their ends to the center of the world, all the angles which the said lines contain with the line drawn through the center of the epicycle and the center of the world will be equal to one another. The same happens in the remaining position of the epicycle. Moreover, from those things which [were discussed] in the eleventh book...

...the angles of divergence <note>Also called 'angles of diversity' or parallaxes; these represent the apparent displacement of a planet as seen from Earth due to its position on its epicycle; original: "angulos diuersitatum".</note> depending on the <term>epicycle</term> have been explained: if we count a certain arc from the opposite of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion; original: "augis".</note> of the epicycle, it will be easily established by how great an angle it is subtended at the <term>center of the world</term> <note>The Earth, positioned at the center of the universe in this geocentric model.</note>. Indeed, this is no more difficult at the opposite of the apogee of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit whose center is not the Earth; original: "eccentrici".</note> than at the apogee itself. Therefore, let us take such equal arcs from the circumference of the epicycle, understood to be at the apogee of the eccentric and at its opposite. However, we investigate from the part of the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle and the <term>equant</term> <note>A mathematical point used to account for the observed speed changes in planetary motion; original: "equãtis".</note>, because they are subtended by angles at the center of the world. For if we compare these two angles with one another, we will have a proportion close to the truth that our angles of latitude now have. That proportion will serve our purpose in this way: Let one of those angles be **p** and the other **q**; let **p** be the greater and **q** the smaller. Let their difference be **r**. Since the proportion of **p** to **q** is as the angle **d.e.s.** to the angle **g.e.k.**, the proportion of **r** to **q** by division will be as the difference of the two angles **d.e.s.** and **g.e.k.** to the angle **g.e.k.** But the angles **r** and **q** are known, along with the aforementioned difference of the angles. Therefore, the angle **g.e.k.** will not be unknown. If you add the often-mentioned difference to it, the angle **d.e.s.** will result as known. Therefore, in the triangle **g.e.k.**, whose two sides **g.e.** and **g.k.** are known, with angle **g.e.k.**, the angle **e.g.k.** will become known through the science of plane triangles. And this is the angle of <term>inclination</term> of the epicycle to the surface of the eccentric. Which <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the astronomer whose work formed the basis of this text.</note> concluded to have two degrees and a quarter of a degree ($2.25^\circ$). He learned that the angle **a.e.g.**—namely the inclination of the eccentric to the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky, used as the reference plane for planetary latitudes; original: "eclypticā".</note>—is contained within one single degree ($1^\circ$). If the desire to render this kind of work more precisely should take hold, you may use the arc **t.k.** or the angle **e.g.k.** to extract the terms of the proportion mentioned above. Then, proceed through all steps as before.

### Proposition VI.

Saturn and Jupiter finally require the inclinations 
of their circles to be known to the astronomer.
Although these two share many characteristics in their movements with Mars, they are seen to differ from it in this one respect: the latitudes of Mars occurring at the apogee of the eccentric and its opposite have perceptible differences when the relative latitudes are compared to one another. However, the difference between the latitudes of Saturn and Jupiter—occurring when they are at the opposites of the apogees of their epicycles and at the limits of their greatest latitudes—is not apparent to the senses. For this reason, another means will reveal the goal of our proposition. Turn your eyes to the figure of the preceding [proposition]. But do not look at any circle of the epicycle except the one situated at the apogee of the eccentric upon center **g**. Now, the latitude of Saturn was found when it was positioned at the apogee of the epicycle (while the epicycle remained at its northern limit) through conjecture which could be obtained from its appearances and disappearances <note>Referring to the heliacal rising and setting of the planet; original: "apparitionibus atqz occultationib⁹".</note> to be nearly 2 degrees. But at the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle, it was 3 degrees. For Jupiter, at the apogee of the epicycle, it was 1 degree; but at the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle, 2 degrees. Therefore, in this figure, the angle **h.e.k.** comes forth as known. For it is the difference between the two latitudes. And if the proportion of angle **h.e.g.** to angle **g.e.k.** were known, who would be ignorant of either of them? Likewise, if the arc **h.z.** or **t.k.** (which would be equal to it) were known, both of the two angles **h.e.g.** and **g.e.k.** would immediately be held, since the proportion of line **e.g.** to line **g.h.** or **g.k.** is also known. But these arcs are not known. Let us therefore take two equal arcs—of whatever size—yet close by estimation to the arcs **h.z.** and **t.k.** which are still unknown. This we shall do through the tables of divergences, by joining the two angles of divergence corresponding to the equal arcs at the apogee and the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle...

...until we find the sum <note>The "aggregatum" refers to the total of the calculated angles.</note> to be equal to the known angle H-E-K. We have established how great the angles are by which they [the arcs] are subtended at the <term>center of the world</term> <note>The Earth, at the center of the geocentric system.</note> through those things concluded near the end of the eleventh book. For the proportion of those angles will be nearly equal to the proportion of angle H-E-G to angle G-E-K. And let one of them be **p** and the other **q**, where **p** is indeed the greater and **q** the smaller. Therefore, if the proportion of **p** to **q** is as angle K-E-G to angle G-E-H, then by addition <note>A mathematical operation on proportions where (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d; original: "coniunctim".</note>, the proportion of **p** and **q** together to **q** will be as the whole known angle H-E-K to angle H-E-G. Thus, from three known quantities, the fourth will become known: namely, angle H-E-G. When this is added to angle A-E-H—the angle of minimum latitude—the whole angle A-E-G will be known; this is the angle of inclination of the <term>eccentric</term> to the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun, used as the reference plane for planetary latitudes.</note>. Finally, the proportion of line E-G to the radius of the <term>epicycle</term> G-B is known because the position of the epicycle is known, along with angle G-E-B; therefore, through the science of plane triangles, angle E-G-B is recognized. When this is subtracted from two right angles <note>180 degrees.</note>, angle H-G-Z will remain known; it measures the inclination of the epicycle to the surface of the eccentric. But if you wish to strive for greater precision, use arc H-Z now (since angle H-G-Z is known) in place of the one through which you previously elicited the proportion necessary for this matter. Carry out the rest as before, and repeat this type of work until you arrive at a good precision for angle G-E-H. 

Ptolemy, moreover, set the proportion he used for Saturn as 18 to 23, and for Jupiter as 29 to 43. He concluded that the angle of inclination of the eccentric to the ecliptic in Saturn is 2 degrees and 26 minutes; in Jupiter, however, it is 1 degree and 24 minutes. But persuaded by the ease of operation, for Saturn he took two and a half degrees for the inclination of the eccentric. In Jupiter, however, one and a half degrees. Moreover, he measured the inclination of the epicycle to the eccentric as 4 and a half degrees in Saturn, and 2 and a half degrees in Jupiter.

->Proposition 7<-

To elaborate through geometry what the previous proposition taught.

This adds a new element to the preceding: by what method, from line G-K being known relative to line G-E and angle H-E-K, both angles B-E-G and G-E-K can be known, and from there the sought-after angles of inclination. Therefore, from the preceding figure, I will cut out triangle H-E-K, which has a circumscribed circle H-L-K with center O. Let E-G be continued to point L on the circumference. From this center, let three radii proceed—namely O-P, O-K, and O-R—one of which cuts line L-E at point R, and another cuts line K-H through the middle and perpendicularly at point D. Finally, let line E-G-L be drawn through point G. Thus, from the given angle H-E-K and the proportion of E-G to G-K, we seek our objective. Since, therefore, angle H-E-K is assumed to be known, the chord H-K will be known relative to the diameter of the circle, as will its half, G-K. The square of G-K subtracted from the square of the radius will leave the square of line G-O known, from which the line G-O itself will be given as known. Likewise, line G-E has a known proportion to line G-K (the radius of the epicycle); therefore, line G-E, when related to the diameter of the circle, will become a quantity not unknown. From this line and line L-G, a product is made as great as that from H-G times G-K, or G-K times itself <note>This refers to the Power of a Point theorem, where the product of the segments of two intersecting chords are equal ($EG \times GL = HG \times GK$).</note>. Thus L-G will be known in this respect, and therefore the whole L-E and its half L-R. If you subtract line L-G from this, the residue G-R will be known. Thus, two sides O-G and G-R of the right triangle O-G-R are known; therefore, its acute angle G-O-R will be known, and thus arc P-R. If you subtract this from half of arc E-R-L (which is known because of its chord L-E), arc L-P will remain known. Finally, when this is taken from arc H-P, arc H-L will be left as known, and therefore angle H-E-L will not be unknown. Likewise, [combine] arc L-P with arc P-K...

### Proposition 8.
### To determine how much latitude either Venus or Mercury
### possesses at any distance from the apogee of its epicycle.

The same process and the same diagram will serve for both Venus and Mercury. Therefore, let the epicycle E-T-D be established at one of the <term>nodes</term> <note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the ecliptic.</note>, and let a flat surface perpendicular to the ecliptic pass through the center of the epicycle **B**. Let the common section of this surface with the epicycle be the line D-E. Now, let the common section of this intersecting surface with the ecliptic be the line A-B, so that **B** represents the center of the epicycle as it passes through the middle of the eccentric; let another diameter H-Z cut the diameter of the epicycle D-E perpendicularly, and let the entire surface of the epicycle meet the said intersecting surface at right angles. By this arrangement, every line on the surface of the epicycle perpendicular to line D-E is parallel to the surface of the ecliptic, with only one line H-Z excepted, which lies in the very surface of the ecliptic. Let the planet, therefore, be at point **T**, having a known distance from the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> of the epicycle or its opposite. From this point **T**, let a perpendicular T-M be dropped to the surface of the ecliptic. Let the two points **T** and **M** be joined to the <term>center of the world</term> <note>The Earth, considered the center of the universe in this geocentric model.</note> by lines A-M and A-T. We seek, therefore, the size of angle T-A-M from certain known things: namely, the angle A-B-E, the proportion of lines A-B and B-E, and the distance of point **T** from either of the two points **D** and **E**. We will carry out this execution if we extend an orthogonal line from point **T** to line D-E, which shall be T-K. Likewise, [extend] a perpendicular L-K to the surface of the ecliptic, with two lines T-B and L-M being produced, from which it follows that the quadrilateral T-K-L-M has parallel sides and right angles. Now you may rely on a logical deduction: Since angle E-B-T is assumed to be known, and angle **K** is a right angle, each of the two lines T-K and K-B will be known in relation to the radius of the epicycle B-T. From this, line L-M is given. Likewise, in triangle K-B-L, the angle K-B-L is known through the fifth [proposition] of this book, and angle **L** is a right angle; therefore K-L will be known in relation to K-B, or equal to T-M; and line L-B will also be known. Thus, all [lines] become known in relation to line B-T, and consequently in relation to line A-B, from which if you subtract line B-L, A-L will remain not unknown. This [line], together with line L-M, because of the right angle **L**, will produce the known line A-M and the recognized angle L-A-M. This is indeed the angle of diversity in longitude. From the now known line A-M and the line T-M elicited above, the line A-T will be established, along with angle T-A-M, which is the sought-after angle of latitude.

### Proposition 9.
### The inclination of the epicycle introduces no
### sensible error into the motion of longitude.

In the beginning of the ninth book, while we were explaining the conditions of the celestial spheres, we assumed that the surface of the eccentric nowhere recedes from the surface of the ecliptic, and that the surface of the epicycle lies within the surface of the eccentric. We also did this while we were striving, through many considerations, to determine the causes of the various motions, treating the surfaces as if they [were uniform] to one another...

¶ Let there be, therefore, the circle of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> D-T about the center B, imagined on the surface of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun; the reference plane for celestial measurements.</note>. ## Proposition 10.

<image-desc>A complex geometrical diagram in the right margin depicting astronomical calculations. It includes a large circle representing an orbit or the ecliptic and a smaller epicycle circle. **To measure the entire latitudes of the three superior planets.**

¶ For these three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>: since the inclinations of the epicycles are mixed with the inclinations of the <term>eccentrics</term> <note>Orbits whose centers are offset from the Earth.</note>, we must proceed by another way. Let there be, therefore, a flat surface erected above the ecliptic cutting the epicycle. Let the common intersection of this and the ecliptic be the line A-B. Let the common difference of it with the surface of the epicycle be the line D-G-E. Let point A be the center of the zodiac <note>original: "orbis signorum."</note>, and point G be the center of the orbit of revolution <note>The epicycle's center.</note>, around which the epicycle D-E-Z-H is drawn. Let its diameter B-Z be extended, cutting diameter D-E at right angles. Let the surface of the epicycle be positioned such that every line drawn perpendicularly upon line D-E in the surface of the epicycle is equidistant from the surface of the ecliptic. 

Let the arc E-T be given: namely, the distance of the planet from the opposite of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The perigee, or the point in the epicycle closest to the Earth.</note> of the epicycle. From this point, I draw a perpendicular. But from the two points T and K, I drop two perpendiculars to the surface of the ecliptic, which are T-L and K-B, joining the two points B and L. Having extended the two lines A-T and A-L, we intend [to find] from the angles of inclination of the eccentric and epicycle—and the proportion of line A-G to G-E—the angle B-A-L from the position of the planet in the epicycle (that is, the diversity in the motion of longitude) and the angle T-A-L of latitude. 

But first, I will drop the perpendicular K-M to the line A-G, having also extended the two lines G-T and A-K. From the right-angled triangle G-K-T, whose angle T-G-K is assumed to be known, each of the lines T-K and K-G will have a known quantity in relation to G-T, the radius of the epicycle. But the angle K-G-M of the epicycle's inclination is known, and angle M is a right angle. Therefore, the two lines K-M and M-G will become known in relation to K-G, and therefore in relation to G-T. Since the position of the epicycle is assumed to be known, the proportion of line A-G to line G-T will be recognized. Therefore, all lines K-T, K-G, K-M, and M-G will become known in relation to line A-G. 

Subtracting the now-known M-G from A-G, the remainder A-M is not unknown. From this, together with the known line K-M, the line A-K will become known because angle M is a right angle. From this, the angle M-A-K is also known. Furthermore, the angle G-A-B of the eccentric's inclination was known; therefore, the whole angle K-A-B will be known. And angle B is a right angle; therefore, each of the lines K-B and A-B will be given as known in relation to the previously known A-K. Likewise, line B-L is known, since it is equal to the previously known K-T. For the quadrilateral T-K-B-L consists of parallel sides and known angles; therefore, from lines A-B and B-L with the right angle B, the line A-L will be given as known. And thus the angle B-A-L is known, which is the angle of diversity of the longitudinal motion. Furthermore, from the now-known line A-L, and line T-L equal to the previously known K-B, and the right angle A-L-T, there is produced...

### Proposition 11.

<image-desc>A complex geometrical diagram illustrating the maximum reflection of latitude. It features an epicycle circle (d-e-z-h) at the top with point 'b' as its center. A vertex 'a' at the bottom of the image has lines radiating towards the circle, including a tangent line a-e. Several perpendicular lines are drawn from points on the epicycle (d, e, z) down to a base line and a radial line, forming a series of right-angled triangles labeled with points m, n, s, t, k, l. This visualizes the trigonometric relationships discussed in the text.</image-desc>

That the maximum latitude of reflection occurs at the point of contact <note>The point where a line from Earth is tangent to the epicycle.</note>.
¶ For the sake of ease, let us place the center of the epicycle in the surface of the <term>zodiacal circle</term> <note>original: "orbis signorum"; the ecliptic plane.</note>. Let it be $b$, around which the epicycle $d-e-z-h$ is described. Let a line be drawn from the center of the world through the center of the epicycle itself, which shall be $a-b-g$. Let another line be drawn touching [tangent to] the epicycle, $a-e$. Let another also cut the epicycle in two points, $d$ and $z$. From the points $d, e,$ and $z$, let perpendicular lines be extended. One set indeed to the surface of the zodiacal circle, namely $d-m, e-n,$ and $z-s$. The others, $d-t, e-k,$ and $z-l$, to the line $a-d$. Let the ends of these perpendiculars be joined by the lines $t-m, k-n,$ and $s-l$. Let line $a-n$ be drawn, as well as line $a-s-m$. For it is necessary that these three points $a, s,$ and $m$ be in one straight line: since they are in the common section of the surface cutting the ecliptic at right angles and passing through the line $a-d$. With these things thus arranged, it must be shown that the greatest latitude of reflection usually happens for a planet existing at point $e$. For there are three equiangular triangles: $d-t-m, e-k-n,$ and $z-l-s$, since each has a right angle. The remaining angles are also equal, since the two lines containing them are parallel to each other. Therefore, the ratio of $e-k$ to $e-n$ will be as $d-t$ is to $d-m$, and as $z-l$ is to $z-s$. But the ratio of $e-k$ to $e-a$ is greater than $d-t$ to $d-a$, and likewise greater than $z-l$ to $z-s$. If, therefore, from the ratio of $k-e$ to $e-a$ (which is greater than the ratio of $d-t$ to $d-a$), you subtract the ratio $k-e$ to $e-n$ (equal to the ratio $d-t$ to $d-m$), and similarly you remove the ratio $d-t$ to $d-m$ from the ratio $d-t$ to $d-a$, there will remain the ratio $n-e$ to $e-a$ as greater than the ratio $d-m$ to $d-a$. And the ratio $n-e$ to $n-a$ itself is greater than the ratio $z-s$ to $z-a$ by a similar middle ratio. Since the three angles $a-n-e, a-m-d,$ and $a-s-z$ are right angles, the angle $e-a-n$ will be greater than the angles $d-a-m$ and $z-a-s$. By a similar path, you will prove this for the remaining positions of the planet in the semicircle $g-e-h$; all, clearly, as they proceed toward point $e$.

With the epicycle remaining at the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The large off-center circle that carries the epicycle.</note> or its opposite [the perigee], to derive how great the inclination of its surface is to the surface of the eccentric.
¶ Venus and Mercury adopt one and the same arrangement in this matter. In which the surface of the epicycle is the circle $g-d-e$ upon center $b$, inclined to the surface of the eccentric. From the center of the world, let a line $a-d$ come forth, tangent to the epicycle at point $d$, and another line $a-e-d$ passing through the center of the epicycle, cutting the circumference of the epicycle in two points, $g$ and $e$. Then, from point $d$, let three lines be produced: $d-b$ (the radius of the epicycle), $d-z$ (perpendicular to line $g-e$), and $d-h$ (perpendicular to the surface of the eccentric). Also, let point $b$ be joined with the two points $a$ and $z$...

Therefore, from the angle of reflection $d-a-b$, which the preceding demonstration showed to be at its maximum in this position of the planet, we seek the angle $d-z-h$ which determines the required inclination. In the case of Mercury <note>original: "mercurio"</note>, however, it is seven degrees. Do not be troubled by the fact that in the third proposition we summed these <term>latitudes of reflection</term> <note>The component of planetary latitude caused by the tilting or "reflection" of the epicycle's plane.</note> considered with respect to the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun through the sky; the reference plane for astronomical measurements.</note>, and applied half of that sum to the present purpose. Even though the center of the epicycle in these considerations was not located on the surface of the ecliptic, the inclination of the center to the ecliptic is so small that no sensible error can occur here.

## Proposition 13.

**That the maximum angle of true diversity is found at the point of contact.**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circle (epicycle) representing an astronomical model. A vertical diameter 'g-h' and a chord 'e-b' are shown. A point 'a' (the observer's position) is located significantly below the circle, with radiating lines connecting to points 'g', 'e', 'f', 'b', 'k', 'l', 'h' on the circle. Point 'k' represents the point of tangency (contact). Internal points are labeled 'm', 'n', '3'. The diagram is used to prove that the angle of parallax is greatest when the line of sight is tangent to the epicycle.</image-desc>

It is advisable to understand the terms we will use. I call the "angle of <term>diversity</term> <note>original: "diuersitatis"; also known as the equation of the argument or parallax, it is the angular difference between a planet's mean position and its actual position as seen from Earth.</note> estimated in longitude" that which would result if the surface of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle upon which a planet moves, while the center of the epicycle itself moves along a larger circle (the deferent).</note> lay within the surface of the ecliptic, just as we assumed at the end of the eleventh proposition. 

You will not be able to imagine the "true angle of diversity" unless you erect two flat surfaces perpendicularly to the surface of the ecliptic. One of these should include the center of the epicycle; the other should pass through any given point on the circumference of the epicycle. For the angle contained by the two sections where these surfaces meet the ecliptic will be called—and is—the true angle of diversity in longitude, which falls between two places: namely, the true positions of the epicycle and the planet on the ecliptic. However, for the present purpose, and persuaded by the ease of the operation, we will consider this true angle of diversity on the surface of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth.</note>. For the inclination of the eccentric to the ecliptic is of such a magnitude <note>original: "tanta"; implies a magnitude small enough in this context to be negligible for the following proof.</note> that it does not introduce a sensible variation.

Therefore, repeating the figure from the eleventh proposition, it must be shown that angle $n-a-k$ is greater than all the angles of diversity occurring in the semicircle $g-e-h$. For in that eleventh proposition, it was shown that the ratio of line $e-n$ to $e-a$ is greater than the ratio of line $d-m$ to line $d-a$. Conversely, the ratio of $e-a$ to $e-n$ is smaller than the ratio of $d-a$ to $d-m$; therefore, the ratio of the square of $e-a$ to the square of $e-n$ will be smaller than the ratio of the square of $d-a$ to the square of $d-m$. 

Because the angle $e-n-a$ is a right angle, the square of $e-a$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $e-n$ and $n-a$. Similarly, the square of $d-a$ is equivalent to the two squares of lines $d-m$ and $m-a$. Thus, the ratio of the two squares $n-a$ and $n-e$ to the square $n-e$ becomes smaller than the ratio of the two squares $m-a$ and $m-d$ to the square $m-d$. From this, by division, the ratio of the square of $n-a$ to the square of $n-e$ is smaller than the ratio of the square of $m-a$ to the square of $m-d$. Therefore, the ratio of line $n-a$ to line $n-e$ will also be smaller than line $m-a$ to $m-d$. Moreover, the ratio of line $e-n$ to $n-k$ is just as $d-m$ is...

Therefore, the <term>angle of diversity</term> <note>Also known as the angle of parallax, this is the difference between a planet's "true" position seen from the center of the orbit and its "apparent" position seen from Earth.</note> $n-a-k$ is greater than the angle of diversity $m-a-t$. ## Proposition 14.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram of an epicycle and its relationship to a distant center. The diagram features a circle at the top labeled with points d, l, t, m, b, n, r, e, x, f, k, h. A series of lines radiate from the circle's points and converge at two distant points below: 'a' and 'p'. The lines form a long, narrow triangle, representing calculations of angular diversity (parallax) in planetary motion. Chords and perpendiculars are drawn within the circle to facilitate the geometric proof.</image-desc>

The greatest difference between the angles of diversity—where one is the estimated angle and the other the true—occurs at the <note>original: "punctum contactus"</note> point of contact.
I said "at the point of contact" <note>In geometry, this is the point where a line from the observer (Earth) is tangent to the circle of the epicycle.</note>. For you will not always find the maximum difference of this kind at that very point, except in the case of <term>Mercury</term>. In the case of <term>Venus</term>, however, this maximum difference is often found elsewhere, as will be explained a little further below. I will now follow Ptolemy by placing the circle of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one (the deferent), used to explain the complex paths of planets.</note> $g-e-b$ upon center $b$. The <term>center of the world</term> <note>In the geocentric model, this is the Earth.</note> is understood to be point $a$, from which will come the line $a-g-p$ through the center of the epicycle, and line $e-a$ touching (tangent to) the epicycle at point $e$. Let there be another point of the epicycle marked anywhere, $d$, which I will likewise connect to the center of the world by line $d-a$. Then, from the two points $e$ and $d$, I will draw two sets of perpendiculars. One set shall be to the surface of the eccentric, which are $d-m$ and $e-n$. The other set shall be to the diameter of the epicycle, namely $d-t$ and $e-k$. I will connect the ends of these perpendiculars with lines $m-t$ and $n-k$. Furthermore, I will connect the two points $m$ and $n$ to the center of the world by lines $m-a$ and $n-a$. 

It must therefore be shown, according to the manner of Ptolemy, that the difference between the two angles $e-a-k$ and $n-a-k$ is greater than the difference between the two angles $d-a-t$ and $m-a-t$. Since the angle $n$ of the triangle $e-k-n$ is a right angle, the side $e-k$ will be longer than the side $k-n$. Therefore, let a segment equal to $k-n$ be cut from $e-k$, which shall be $k-r$. Having drawn line $r-a$, let $t-l$ similarly be equal to $t-m$. Let point $l$ be connected with the center of the world $a$. Therefore, the angle $e-a-r$ will be the difference between the two angles $e-a-k$ and $n-a-k$. For the angle $r-a-k$ is equal to the angle $n-a-k$ because the two sides $r-k$ and $k-a$ are equal to the two sides $n-k$ and $k-a$, and the angles $a-k-r$ and $a-k-n$ are right angles. Similarly, the angle $d-a-l$ is the difference between the two angles $d-a-t$ and $m-a-t$. 

If, therefore, the excess of angle $e-a-r$ over angle $d-a-l$ followed from the excess of the ratio of line $e-r$ to line $d-l$ compared to line $d-a$, as Ptolemy supposed, our intention would proceed in this way: Line $a-d$ will necessarily intersect line $e-k$; let it intersect at $x$. From point $e$, let a line be drawn parallel to line $a-r$, which must necessarily meet with $k-a$ if it is extended far enough. For the two angles at $k$ and $c$ are less than two right angles. Let it meet, then, at point $p$. Now $e-p$ will be longer than $e-a$ because it is opposite the larger angle of triangle $e-a-p$. Wherefore the ratio of $k-e$ to $e-a$ is greater than the ratio of that same $k-e$ to $e-p$. However, $k-e$ to $e-p$ is as $k-r$ to $r-a$, or $d-t$ to $d-a$. Therefore, the ratio of $k-e$ to $e-a$ is greater than $d-t$ to $d-a$, which he also assumed as certain in the eleventh proposition of this book. But the ratio of $e-k$ to $k-r$ is as $d-t$ to $d-l$, since $k-r$ was cut equal to $k-n$, and $l-t$ equal to $t-m$. By conversion, therefore, the ratio of $e-k$ to $e-r$ is as the ratio of $d-t$ to $d-l$. But the ratio of $e-k$ to $e-a$ consists of two ratios: namely, the ratio of $e-k$ to $e-r$ and the ratio of $e-r$ to $e-a$. The ratio of $d-t$ to $d-a$ is similar. Therefore, by subtracting equals from unequals—specifically, one ratio from both sides—there will remain the ratio of $e-r$ to $e-a$, which is greater than the ratio of $d-l$ to $d-a$. If Ptolemy’s conclusion were correct, it would follow immediately that angle $e-a-r$ exceeds angle $d-a-l$, which was to be demonstrated.

### Proposition 15.

That the greatest difference of such angles for **Mercury** occurs infallibly at the point of contact.
¶ For the sake of removing confusion: I will separate the two triangles $e-a-k$ and $d-a-t$ which were combined in the preceding figure. I will do so on this condition: that they coincide at point $a$. Therefore, since in the case of Mercury the angle $e-a-k$ is less than half of a right angle <note>45 degrees</note>—for its greatest angle of diversity, which depends on the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain planetary motion.</note>, is 24 degrees, as 360 degrees constitutes four right angles—it does not exceed this. The angle $d-a-t$ will be much less than half of a right angle, since it is less than angle $e-a-k$. From this, angle $a-e-k$ will be greater than angle $a-d-t$, since both angles $k$ and $t$ are right angles. Therefore, let angle $d-f-l$ be equal to angle $a-e-k$. With lines $d-f$ and $l-f$ drawn, the two triangles $a-e-k$ and $f-d-t$ will be equiangular; therefore, the ratio of $a-e$ to $e-k$ will be as the ratio of $f-d$ to $d-t$. But the ratio of $e-k$ to $e-x$ is as the ratio of $f-d$ to $d-l$, as was established in the preceding section. Therefore, by equal proportionality, it is concluded that the ratio of $a-e$ to $e-x$ is equal to the ratio of $f-d$ to $d-l$. But angle $f-d-l$ was set equal to $a-e-x$. Therefore, the two triangles $a-e-x$ and $f-d-l$ will be equiangular, and angle $a-x-e$ will be equal to angle $d-l-f$; likewise, angle $e-a-x$ will be equal to angle $d-f-l$. Now, angle $a-x-e$ is worth a right angle along with angle $k-a-x$, which is less than half a right angle; wherefore angle $f-d-l$ is worth the same. Likewise, angle $d-a-t$ is less than half a right angle. Hence, the two angles $d-l-f$ and $d-a-t$ are less than two right angles. Therefore, the circumference of the circle circumscribing triangle $d-l-f$ will cut the line $l-a$. For this circumference cannot pass through point $a$; for then the two opposite angles $d-l-f$ and $d-a-f$ of the quadrilateral $d-l-f-a$ inscribed in the circle would be less than two right angles. If, indeed, it passed within $a$, they would again be much less than two right angles, which is contrary to the twenty-first proposition of the third book of **Euclid** <note>original: "vicesimeprime tertij Euclidis"; Euclid's Elements III.21 states that angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.</note>. Therefore, let the said circumference cut line $l-a$ at point $q$, with line $d-q$ and line $q-f$ extended. Thus, the two angles $d-f-l$ and $d-q-l$ consisting in the circumference and falling into one arc will be equal to each other. But angle $d-q-l$, being external to angle $d-a-q$, is greater than it; wherefore angle $d-f-l$ is also greater than angle $d-a-l$. But angle $d-f-l$ was equal to angle $e-a-x$; therefore, angle $e-a-x$ is greater than angle $d-a-l$, which was the demonstration sought.
