### Proposition 16.

However, to find the greatest difference of such angles, it is often necessary to look outside the point of contact.
¶ I resume the preceding figure, changing nothing at all. Now, angle $k-a-x$, when the center of the epicycle is located at the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "auge"; the point in the orbit furthest from the Earth</note> of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The large orbital circle whose center is offset from the Earth.</note>, is less than half a right angle, as is handed down from the second [proposition] of the tenth [book]. For there that angle is concluded to be 4 degrees, 7 minutes, and 48 full seconds. Then, therefore, as in Mercury, the greatest difference of such angles is found at the point of contact. While, however, angle $k-a-e$ is greater than half a right angle—which indeed happens in many positions of the epicycle—it is possible to give a point on the circumference of the epicycle in which the difference of the said angles is greater than that which usually occurs at the point of contact. For let each of the two angles $k-a-x$ and $k-a-e$ be greater than half a right angle, which is certainly possible. Now let angle $d-a-t$ be half a right angle. Relying therefore on the means assumed in the preceding, I shall conclude that angle $d-l-f$ is equal to angle $a-x-e$. But angle $a-x-e$ is greater than a right angle and half...

...rightness. For it is equivalent to two angles: namely, $k$, which is a right angle, and $k-a-r$, which by hypothesis is greater than half of a right angle <note>Greater than 45 degrees</note>. And because the angle $d-a-t$ was assumed to be half of a right angle, the two angles $d-l-f$ and $d-a-f$ will be greater than two right angles. Therefore, the circumference of the circle circumscribing triangle $d-l-f$ will not intersect the line $l-a$. For if it did intersect it, let it be at point $q$; with lines $f-q$ and $d-q$ extended, as in the preceding figure, the two angles $d-l-f$ and $d-q-f$ would be equal to two right angles. But those same angles $d-l-f$ with angle $d-a-f$ will be greater than two right angles; for which reason, angle $d-q-f$ is less than angle $d-a-f$, which is impossible by the **twenty-first proposition of the first book of Euclid** <note>This Euclidean theorem states that if two lines are drawn from the ends of one side of a triangle to a point inside the triangle, the lines will be shorter than the other two sides of the triangle but contain a greater angle.</note>. Nor will it pass through $a$, for then the same thing would be greater than itself. Let it therefore pass below $a$, and let $l-a$ be continued until it meets this imaginary circumference at point $s$. With lines $f-s$ and $d-s$ drawn, angle $d-s-l$ will be equal to angle $d-f-l$, since, standing on the circumference, they fall upon the same arc. But angle $d-a-l$ is greater than angle $d-s-l$, being an exterior angle compared to an interior one; therefore, it is also greater than angle $d-f-l$, which was equal to angle $e-a-r$. If, therefore, of two lines proceeding from the center of the world <note>The Earth, in this geocentric model</note>, one passes through the center of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> and the other cuts the epicycle, containing half of a right angle: it results that at both points of intersection, the difference of the said angles is greater than at the point of contact itself. Thus, the greatest difference of these angles will not always occur at the point of contact, but sometimes outside of it; which was to be demonstrated. ¶ If you were to set angle $d-a-t$ as less than half of a right angle, yet equal to angle $a-r-k$ (which is also less than half a right angle), while the rest remains as before, the circumference of the circle circumscribing triangle $d-l-f$ will pass through point $a$, and finally angle $e-a-r$ will be equal to angle $d-a-l$. You should strive for the deduction of this yourself, for it is similar to the previous ones.

### Proposition XVIII.

To conclude how great the maximum difference of such angles can be found. From which it will be clear that the reflection of the epicycle introduces no sensible variation to the motion in longitude.

¶ When we previously labored in the ninth and tenth propositions to find the causes of the diverse motions of **Venus** and **Mercury**, we assumed that the surface of the epicycle was contained within the surface of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere; the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note>. However, this is not the case, as we have shown in this book. We must therefore investigate the maximum difference of the angles of longitude: one of which would occur if we placed the epicycle in the plane of the ecliptic, and the other if we gave it an inclination. We do this so that we may know how to refute the criticisms of those opposing this divine study, who suspect that the assumed foundations are weak. For they will grant pardon if that error which they impute to the astronomer is found to be imperceptible. In this matter, one must rest satisfied, since in this art it is not within our power to reach a "geometric point" or absolute precision, given that instruments are what produce the results. Now, although the greatest difference of such angles does not always occur at the point of contact, we shall stand with the most illustrious **Ptolemy**, persuaded by the ease of the operation, as if that difference were greatest at the point of contact. ¶ Let us therefore resume the configuration of the twelfth proposition of this book. In which, on account of the right angle $a-d-b$ and the two lines $a-b$ and $b-d$ being known to each other, line $a-d$ will be known; and the angle of diversity $b-a-d$—calculated as if the surface of the epicycle were in the plane of the ecliptic—will become known. Furthermore, the ratio of $b-a$ to $a-d$ is as $b-d$ to $d-z$. Therefore, from three knowns, the fourth, namely $d-z$, shall not be unknown. From angle $d-a-b$ (that of the maximum latitude) and the right angle $b$, each line will also become known...

From this, the angle $z, a, b$ will also be known. If you compare this to the previously known angle $b, a, d$, you will find a difference of one minute for **Venus**, as **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose "Almagest" is the basis for this work.</note> recounts, and six minutes for **Mercury**. ## Proposition 18.

<image-desc>A large geometric diagram on the right side of the page depicting an astronomical model. It consists of a large circle representing an epicycle tilted at an angle. A point 'a' (representing the observer or center) is located at the bottom left, with multiple lines (ad, az, ab, ah, ae) radiating from it to intersect various points on and around the epicycle. Points labeled include a, b, d, e, z, h. The diagram illustrates the calculation of the angle of latitude (reflexion) for planets relative to the eccentric and epicycle.</image-desc>

**To investigate whether the values determined for the inclination of the surface of the epicycle to the surface of the eccentric correspond to sensory observations.**

In seeking the angle of inclination—from which the <term>latitude of reflection</term> <note>A component of a planet's northern or southern deviation from the ecliptic caused by the tilting of the epicycle.</note> is derived—we previously placed the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one (the deferent), used to explain retrograde motion.</note> at the mean longitude of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The main orbital circle of a planet, which is slightly off-center from the Earth.</note>. Now, however, keeping that same angle of inclination, we shall place the epicycle first at the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "auge" — the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> of the eccentric, and then at its opposite <note>The perigee, or the point closest to Earth.</note>. Through numerical calculation, we will investigate how much the maximum reflection can be in either place due to this kind of inclination of the epicycle. If we find the maximum latitudes of reflection to be equal to those we have detected through sensory observation, we shall, not without merit, praise and approve the discovery of the said inclination. From this same inclination, we will derive the latitudes of reflection for any other positions of the planet.

Resuming the figure we used for the twelfth proposition of this book: from the known lines $a, b$ and $b, d$, with the angle $a, d, b$ being a right angle, we will know the line $a, d$. For whether we place the epicycle at the apogee of the eccentric or at the opposite of the apogee, we will see that the line $a, b$ is known with respect to the radius of the epicycle, according to what was explained in the ninth and tenth books. Since the proportion of $a, b$ to $a, d$ is the same as $b, d$ to $d, z$, the line $d, z$ will be known because of the other three known values. From the twelfth proposition of this book, we have made known the angle $d, z, b$. Therefore, since angle $d, b, z$ is a right angle, $d, b$ will be known in respect to $d, z$, and thus in respect to $d, a$. But angle $a, b, d$ is a right angle; therefore, the angle $d, a, b$ will be known, which is the required angle of reflection.

By calculation, Ptolemy learned that for Venus, the angle $d, a, b$ is 2 degrees and 27 minutes at the apogee of the eccentric, but 2 degrees and 34 minutes at the opposite of the apogee. Thus, through this operation, the reflection at the apogee of the eccentric is found to be three minutes less than that which we claimed for the mean longitude; at the opposite of the apogee, it is four minutes greater. But we cannot perceive three or four minutes with our senses; therefore, the business of **Venus** stands well. **Mercury**, however, at the apogee of the eccentric—if we believe Ptolemy’s numbers—has a reflection of 2 degrees and 17 minutes. At the opposite of the apogee, it is 2 degrees and 46 minutes. Behold: here the reflection is thirteen minutes less, and there sixteen minutes greater than what we set for the mean longitude. This decrease and increase happens to be nearly a quarter of a degree, which corresponds sufficiently to the experiments of the instruments. The matter regarding **Mercury** therefore holds up well, which is what we have long desired.

## Proposition 19.

**The greatest angle of variation in longitude to the greatest angle of latitude holds nearly the same proportion as any other angle of longitude to its corresponding angle of latitude.**

The diagram from our eleventh proposition will serve our purpose here. ...the angle of latitude corresponding to it. For let it be understood that two circles are circumscribed around the two triangles $e, a, k$ and $e, a, n$. It is established that these two circles are equal, since they share one diameter, namely the line $e, a$, because the angles $a, k, e$ and $a, n, e$ are right angles. Similarly, let us circumscribe two circles around the two triangles $d, a, t$ and $d, a, m$, which by the same reasoning will be proven equal to each other. Furthermore, the proportion of line $k, e$ to line $e, n$ is as the proportion of $t, d$ to $d, m$. But the proportion of $k, e$ to $e, n$ is almost exactly as the proportion of their arcs. Likewise, the proportion of the chords $t, d$ and $d, m$ is nearly the same as the proportion of their arcs, because of their extreme smallness. Therefore, the arc subtended by line $k, e$ compared to the arc subtended by $e, n$ is as the proportion of the two arcs subtended by $t, d$ and $d, m$. Now, the proportion of these arcs is as the angles standing on the circumference at point $a$ and falling into those arcs, since the circles involved are equal. Hence, the angle $e, a, k$ will have nearly the same proportion to angle $e, a, n$ as angle $d, a, t$ has to angle $d, a, m$, which was the point to be concluded. From this, it is manifest that once the two angles $e, a, k$ and $e, a, n$ are known, along with the individual angles of the differences in longitude, the individual latitudes of <term>reflection</term> <note>Reflexio: a specific component of planetary latitude in the Ptolemaic model, particularly for Venus and Mercury, related to the tilt of the epicycle's diameter.</note> will be known—it was for the sake of this that the present theorem was forged.

->Proposition 20<-

**G**iven the distance of a planet from the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the epicycle furthest from the Earth; original Latin: "aux".</note> of the epicycle, to measure its angle of reflection.
Let the line $a, g$—passing through the center of the world $a$ and the center of the epicycle $b$—intersect the circle of the epicycle $g, d, e$. And let the planet be at point $d$, having a known distance from point $g$, which is the apogee of the epicycle. After drawing perpendiculars—specifically $d, t$ to the diameter of the epicycle and $d, m$ to the surface of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>The larger circular path upon which the center of the epicycle moves.</note>—let the lines $a, d$, $a, m$, and $t, m$ be extended together with the semidiameter of the epicycle $b, d$. Therefore, from the known angle $g, b, d$ and the right angle $t$, the length of line $d, t$ will be found in relation to the semidiameter of the epicycle, along with the length of line $t, b$. From this, the whole line $a, t$ will also be known in this respect. These, together with line $d, t$, will establish the known length of line $a, d$. Likewise, from the known angle $d, t, m$ (which is the inclination of the epicycle) and the right angle $d, m, t$, the line $d, m$ will be known in relation to $d, t$, and therefore in relation to $a, d$. Consequently, since the angle $a, m, d$ is a right angle, the calculated angle of latitude $d, a, m$ will be found. You will work in a similar fashion for the other positions of the planet. Therefore, if you dread the uncertainty that the preceding proposition presented, consult this present one, which admits no ambiguity.

->Proposition 21<-

**T**o adapt the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>Correction factors (minuta proportionalia) used to calculate a planet's actual latitude when it is at an intermediate point between its maximum northern/southern deviation and the nodes.</note> of the latitudes.
Everything given above concerning latitudes assumed the epicycle to be positioned either at the points of maximum latitude or at the <term>nodes</term> <note>The two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the ecliptic.</note>. However, nothing has been established for the intermediate locations. If, therefore, we wish to determine the individual latitudes for these intermediate places, it is necessary to know beforehand the angle of inclination of the epicycle to the surface of the eccentric; for that angle of inclination does not remain unchanged, as it was at the northern limit, the southern limit, or at the nodes. But to find inclinations of this sort for every single position of the epicycle on the eccentric is no small labor. Therefore, another means had to be devised by which the latitudes for the other positions of the epicycle might easily be learned, coming close to the truth. This intermediate method had to possess this condition: just as the maximum latitudes decrease because of the motion of the epicycle in other positions, so this method also makes adjustments proportionally. By this means, once the decrease of this intermediate factor is known, it becomes clear how much the latitudes themselves have decreased.

To make this matter easier to understand, we shall use an example position. Let...

<header>Thirteenth Book</header>

Therefore, let the circle of the ecliptic <note>original: "ecluptice circulus," the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> be $a, b, g, d$, upon which the inclined circle of Saturn is tilted; let these share a common center of the world, $c$. Let the pole of the ecliptic be point $z$, from which two quarters of great circles are dropped. One, $z, a$, passes through the point of maximum latitude—reaching, that is, the northern limit—by intersecting the circumference of the inclined circle at point $c$. The other, $z, h$, intersects the inclined circle at point $f$. Thus, just as any latitude of Saturn—occurring while the epicycle is placed at $e$—gradually decreases as the epicycle moves from $e$ toward the node <note>original: "nodum," the point where the planet's path crosses the ecliptic</note> at $b$, until it becomes zero while remaining there; so the arc of the circle passing through the pole of the ecliptic—which is intercepted between the ecliptic and the northern limit—is gradually diminished until none is found at point $b$. Therefore, the said arcs and the latitudes themselves seem to have a certain proportional connection; so that by as much as that arc decreases, the latitude itself is considered to have decreased by a proportional amount. Therefore, those arcs, when compared to the arc $e, a$, will become suitable means for estimating how much any given latitude has been diminished; and they shall be called, not without reason, proportional minutes <note>original: "minuta proportionalia," a scaling factor used to adjust maximum latitude values for different positions in an orbit</note>.

If you wish to know this doctrine in more convenient numbers for calculation, listen to this teaching: From the arc $e, a$, the arc $f, h$ will become known, just as was done in the specific latitudes of the Moon. Therefore, set the arc $e, a$ to 60 minutes, and learn how many such minutes are found in arc $f, h$. For these will be the proportional minutes for the position of the epicycle at point $f$. By as much as they decrease from the total proportional minutes (that is, 60), by that much also does any latitude of the planet reaching that point proportionally decrease from its correlated height, which the epicycle provides when positioned at point $e$. Ptolemy, however—who had a genius not only for discovering things, but also for using discoveries with subtlety—took all the latitudes of the Moon already calculated, and just as he multiplied the total latitude of five degrees by 12 so that the total proportional minutes would come out to 60, so he repeated all the remaining latitudes twelvefold individually, so that he might fashion his proportional minutes for the other locations. We are accustomed to using these proportional minutes for all the latitudes of the remaining positions, just as the explainers of the tables <note>referring to compilers of astronomical almanacs</note> instruct. Wherefore, etc.

## Proposition 22.

->Finally, to observe the appearances and <term>occultations</term> <note>the disappearance of a celestial body behind another, or its disappearance into the Sun's glare</note> of the planets.<-

Not without reason did Ptolemy claim the final place for the appearances and occultations of the planets, namely after the latitudes had already been explained. If these are bypassed, this science of appearances and occultations cannot be attained. Whatever, therefore, we said more extensively at the end of the eighth book regarding the appearance and occultation of the fixed stars, we wish to be repeated in this place. For just as those stars, now appearing in the evening after sunset, sometimes begin to disappear as the Sun approaches them, and then remain hidden for some time, and afterwards, as the Sun recedes from them, they begin to appear again in the morning; so also do the five wandering stars <note>the planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury</note>, though in a different manner. For in the case of the fixed stars, the approach of the Sun to them, or its recession from them, is the only occasion for occultation or appearance; which is also common to the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>. But in Mercury and Venus, the occasion for appearance or occultation is more complex. For they have these phases not only because of the Sun approaching or receding from them, but because they themselves, by approaching or fleeing the Sun, bring this kind of phase upon themselves. Thus it happens that, just as those phases occur simply for the fixed stars, so they do for the three superior ones; but for Venus and Mercury, they are doubled. For the three superior ones undergo an evening occultation and a morning appearance, just like the fixed stars. But Venus and Mercury [undergo] appearance not only in the morning...

<header>Book Thirteen</header>

...morning and evening occultation <note>original: "occultatione," the period when a planet is hidden by the Sun's glare</note>: and likewise they are found to undergo a double visibility. So that the astronomer might learn to prefigure the times for these phenomena—which are most pleasant to know—before they even occur, it was necessary to seek a single common medium whose foreknowledge would reveal to us the times of these appearances and disappearances. 

This medium could not simply be the arc of the ecliptic <note>the Sun's path</note> lying between the Sun and the star at its first appearance. This is because a single arc cannot apply to all five wandering stars <note>the planets</note>; we know that a larger, brighter star is seen at a shorter distance from the Sun than a smaller, dimmer star during its first appearance or occultation. Furthermore, variation is found even within the study of a single star. For the same star—sometimes being exactly on the ecliptic and at other times having a latitude <note>distance north or south of the Sun's path</note>—will have a different distance from the Sun at the start of its appearance. The distance also varies if the star has a northern latitude versus a southern one. A star appearing for the first time is distant from the Sun by a smaller arc if it has a northern latitude than if it were positioned directly on the ecliptic or to the south. 

Moreover, even if a star had no latitude at all, or if its latitude were constant, different horizons <note>different locations on Earth</note> create different distances between the Sun and the appearing star. Finally, no one doubts that in a single horizon, the same variation occurs due to the changing angle of the ecliptic over that horizon. 

However, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note> found one medium that does not suffer from these variations, except according to the brightness of the stars themselves. This is the arc of a great circle passing through the poles of the horizon and the Sun at the moment of appearance or occultation. I speak of the arc that is enclosed between the Sun (while it is below the horizon) and the horizon itself. This arc, in accordance with its function—as we also called it above in the eighth book—we shall name the **arc of vision** <note>original: "arcum visionis"</note>. Exactly how large this arc should be for each planet, and how it serves our purpose, will be explained below.

## Proposition 22.

<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap 'A' containing foliage and architectural patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

### To investigate the Arc of Vision studiously.

Observe any of the planets at the beginning of its appearance or its occultation: specifically, how far it is removed from the Sun according to the longitude of the zodiac. And if it has any latitude, learn its measurement and whether it exists to the north or the south. 

I shall praise observations of this kind even more if they are made near the sign of Cancer; indeed, they are most conveniently gathered at the very beginning of Cancer. For when the Sun is in that location, the air achieves a moderate serenity <note>likely referring to the clear summer skies of the Mediterranean where Ptolemy observed</note>. 

Once you have found the distance between the Sun and the star at its first appearance, repeat those figures that served the twelfth proposition of the eighth book: the first figure if the planet lacks latitude, and the second if it has latitude. To be brief: you should go directly to that twelfth proposition. There you will see whatever needs to be done. 

Ptolemy found the most ancient observations of the Chaldeans <note>ancient Babylonian astronomers</note> regarding this matter, which he admits were recorded in Syria. From these it is drawn that:
*   **Saturn**, at the beginning of its appearance while staying at the start of Cancer, is distant from the Sun by 14 degrees.
*   **Jupiter**, first appearing in that location, is 12 degrees and three-quarters of a degree from the Sun.
*   **Mars** is 14 and a half degrees distant.
*   **Venus**, rising in the evening, is removed from the Sun by 5 degrees and two-thirds of a degree.
*   **Mercury**, when distant from the Sun by 11 degrees and two-thirds at that point in the zodiac, has its evening appearance.

From these distances, he elicited the specific **arc of vision** for each of the planets: 
*   For **Saturn**: 11 degrees. 
*   For **Jupiter**: 10 degrees. 
*   For **Mars**: 11 and a half degrees. 
*   For **Venus**: 5 degrees. 
*   For **Mercury**: 10 degrees. 

It is established from these values that the arc of vision for Venus is smaller than its maximum latitude (which is found to be 6 degrees and 20 minutes when it is at the opposite point of its epicycle's apogee). Because of this, Venus sometimes appears in the morning before sunrise even when it has not yet reached that opposite point. For this reason, its position must be "deeper" <note>further below the horizon</note>; yet in the ecliptic, it is more distant from the start of Aries than the Sun's position is. You will surely marvel at this, unless you have inspected the unique behavior <note>original: "singulare accidens," an unusual astronomical occurrence</note> of Venus already mentioned. For the remaining planets...

...this is not found to be common among the planets. For each of them, a greater arc of vision <note>the distance the Sun must be below the horizon for a star to be seen</note> is required than their maximum latitude <note>the distance north or south of the Sun's path</note>. Therefore, they will by no means appear in the morning unless the Sun is deep enough within the zodiac <note>far enough below the horizon</note> when any one of them is found there.

## Proposition 24.

To investigate how great an arc of the ecliptic <note>the Sun's apparent path through the stars</note> lies between the Sun and a planet at its first appearance or disappearance, whether it has a latitude away from the ecliptic or not.

## Proposition 25.

To measure the time that passes from the evening setting <note>the moment a planet is lost in the Sun's glare</note> to the morning rising <note>when it emerges on the other side</note> of any of the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>.
¶ For the investigation of this matter, let the circle of the ecliptic be **a. b. g.** around center **d**. Let the position of the planet when it first disappears in the evening be **b**, and the position of the Sun be **a**. Therefore, from the known point **b**, using the preceding proposition, you have the known arc **a. b.**—which is how far the planet itself is distant from the Sun. From this arc, it will finally be known in how much time the Sun will travel across arc **a. b.** Meanwhile, however, the planet will not remain still; let it be moved to point **c**. When the Sun reaches point **c**, the planet will be at point **c**. From their distance—namely the arc **b. c.**—you will find the time in which the Sun travels arc **b. c.** Once that is traveled, the planet will be at point **h** because of its own motion during that time. You proceed in this way until they are seen to be joined <note>the moment of "conjunction" when the Sun and planet share the same longitudinal degree</note>. For example, let the Sun and planet now be joined at point **h**. From the moment of occultation <note>original: "occultationis," the period of hiding</note> until the moment of conjunction <note>original: "coniunctionis"</note>, the Sun has traveled the known arc **a. h.** and the planet the known arc **b. h.** The time in which these arcs are traveled will become known through what was already said above. By doubling this, you will have nearly the total time from the start of the occultation to the start of its reappearance. ¶ If you wish to have that time more precisely, set arc **k. h.** equal to arc **b. h.** Therefore, at the start of its reappearance, the planet will be either at point **k** or at an imperceptible distance from it. 
<margin>§</margin>Using the previous rule, find the distance between the Sun and the planet at the start of its appearance, with the planet being at point **k**. Let that distance be **k. g.** When the three arcs **a. b.**, **b. k.**, and **k. g.**—which are now known—are added together, the total arc **b. g.** will result. You will know how long it takes the Sun to travel this arc if you have sufficiently studied the third book of this work. That time will be the duration from the start of the occultation to the start of the appearance, which we were seeking. However, you will calculate all of this more easily if you subtract the planet's true motion in one day from the Sun's motion in one day, and then divide arc **a. b.** by the remainder. The result will be the time contained between the start of the occultation and the moment of conjunction. Doubling this will complete the time of the total occultation. ¶ Or, if you want the time of the total occultation even more precisely, find the planet's true motion (represented here by arc **b. h.**) for the time between the start of the occultation and the conjunction. Double that to find the planet's position at the start of its appearance. From that, investigate its distance from the Sun as before. Divide that distance by the Sun's "overtaking" speed <note>the difference in daily speed between the Sun and planet</note> in one day; this will give the time between the moment of conjunction and the moment of appearance. Join these two times together, and you will have your answer.

## Proposition 26.

**F**rom the morning setting <note>when the planet disappears into the dawn light</note> of Venus or Mercury until the evening rising <note>when it reappears after sunset</note>: to investigate how much time must pass.
¶ Neither the diagram for this proposition nor its execution differs in any way from the previous one, except where you previously placed the Sun, you now place Venus or Mercury. Where, in the previous proposition, you gave the planet's place, you will now place the Sun itself. For just as the Sun, by approaching the three superior planets, causes them to set, so Venus and Mercury, following the Sun, are the cause of their own disappearance. It is clear that the same happens regarding their rising. But here we count the time that flows from the morning setting until the evening rising. The previous proposition, however, taught how to measure the time lying between the evening setting and the morning rising. This by no means alters the nature of the process or the operation; therefore, you have what was proposed.

## Proposition 27.

**T**o explain how much time must pass from the evening setting of Venus or Mercury until the morning rising.
¶ The two preceding propositions taught the times in which it is established that the planets are always moving direct <note>original: "directos"; moving forward through the zodiac</note>. But in the time which the present proposition proposes to calculate, each planet is found to be retrograde <note>original: "retrogradus"; appearing to move backward against the background of stars</note>. Therefore, the matter itself requires another method of working. In this and the previous two propositions, we have spoken as if Mercury always has four times of appearances and disappearances, just like Venus. This, however, does not always happen, as will be determined below.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating a proposition from spherical astronomy or planetary motion. It consists of a circle representing the ecliptic or a planetary orbit. A horizontal diameter is labeled with 'g' at the left end, 'd' at the center, and 'a' at the right end. Along the upper arc of the circle, three points are marked: 'h', 'c', and 'b' (reading from left to right). Dotted lines drop vertically from points 'b' and 'c' toward the diameter line.</image-desc>

¶ For the sake of demonstrating the proposition, let the circle of the ecliptic <note>the Sun's apparent path</note> be **a. b. g.** around center **d**. In this circle, let point **b** signify the place of the star <note>meaning the planet Venus or Mercury</note> when it first disappears in the evening, measured from the true place of the Sun. Therefore, through the twenty-fourth proposition of this book, let the arc **a. b.** be found, which is how far the star is distant from the Sun. And because it is clear that the planet is retrograde in this position: let it be that from the instant of occultation <note>disappearance</note> until the instant of its conjunction <note>alignment</note> with the Sun, it has described arc **b. c.** against the succession of signs <note>moving backward</note>, so that the planet itself and the Sun are joined at point **c**. Therefore, the Sun and the planet together have described the whole arc **a. b.** And for that reason, add the motion of the planet in one day to the motion of the Sun in one day, and divide the arc **a. b.** by that total. For the time that will pass between the beginning of the disappearance and the instant of conjunction will result. When this is doubled—to make the work shorter—the total time that lies between the evening setting and the morning rising will be gathered. 

Or, if you wish to work more precisely, learn the length of arc **b. c.** from the time that falls between the evening setting and the conjunction. Once this is known, set arc **c. h.** equal to it, moving against the succession of signs. For **h** will be near the true place of the star appearing in the morning. Again, its distance from point **g** (which is the place of the Sun) will be made known by the twenty-fourth proposition of this book. Because the entire arc **h. g.**—which is now known—is traversed by both the Sun and the planet together from the instant of conjunction until the instant of the morning appearance, you should divide it by the combined daily motion of the planet and the Sun, just as before. This will give the time that falls between the conjunction and the morning appearance. Therefore, these two times added together will complete the total time between the evening occultation and the morning appearance. This is indeed what we set out to accomplish in this theorem.

## Proposition 28.

->To demonstrate that what we have asserted regarding the appearances and<-
->disappearances of Venus is consistent with visual observations.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>When Venus is near the beginning of Pisces and is located at the opposite of the apogee of its epicycle <note>the point in the planet's small orbital circle that is closest to the Earth, known as the perigee</note>: while she has a northern latitude of 6 degrees and 20 minutes, she is found to be hidden under the solar rays for only two days. Thus, only two days intervene between her evening setting and her morning rising. This happens near the opposition <note>specifically the inferior conjunction, when the planet passes between the Earth and the Sun</note> and seems remarkable unless you perceive the cause of the matter. For, as has been found, when she is near the beginning of Virgo at the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle—while she has a southern latitude of 6 degrees and 20 minutes—she does not appear at all for a space of sixteen days, which pass from her evening setting until her morning rising. 

¶ Therefore, if you wish to investigate whether the things determined about these disappearances and appearances correspond to observations <note>original: "experimentis"</note>: proceed as follows. For the start of the disappearance, determine the planet's distance from the sun through the twenty-fourth proposition of this book; do the same for the start of the appearance. From these, you will easily calculate the time that lies between the evening setting and the morning rising by the preceding proposition. Or, if you prefer: find the distance of the planet from the sun at the evening setting, which is like the "angle of diversity" <note>original: "angulus diuersitatis"; a technical term for the difference in position caused by the planet's movement on its epicycle</note> corresponding to a certain distance of Venus from the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle. For the center of the epicycle and the sun itself are situated in almost the same place in the zodiac according to longitude. 

Finally, learn how much of an arc at the opposite of the apogee of the epicycle corresponds to this angle of diversity. For the planet must traverse such an arc from its evening setting until its conjunction with the sun. Find this same kind of epicyclic arc for the start of the appearance, or double the one previously found. You will then have the total arc of the epicycle's circumference that the planet describes from its evening setting until its morning rising. From this, you will finally extract the sought-after time very easily. Thus, by calculating, Ptolemy found an arc of this kind—with Venus being at the beginning of Pisces—of one degree and a quarter part of one degree, to which approximately two days correspond. However, at the beginning of Virgo, he found an arc of this kind to be 10 degrees, to which 16 days of time are due. Thus, the things explained above correspond well with observations, which is what we wished to declare.

## Proposition 29.

->Finally, to attempt the same regarding Mercury.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C with foliate patterns and a central flower.</image-desc>It has been discovered that for Mercury, when it is at the beginning of Scorpio and has the maximum distance from the sun that it can have in that location, an evening rising does not occur. Furthermore, while at the beginning of Taurus, it is accustomed not to have a morning rising, even though it may be at its maximum elongation <note>the greatest angular distance from the sun as seen from Earth</note>. Therefore, if the conclusions we have so far adapted to appearances and disappearances harmonize with these observations, they will certainly be worthy of our trust. Therefore, through the twenty-fourth proposition of this book—to speak as briefly as possible—let the arc of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note> be found which must lie between the sun and Mercury when it is near the beginning of Scorpio, so that the star may truly rise. In that place also, let the maximum elongation be calculated that Mercury can have from the sun in that position, through those things explained at the end of the twelfth book. But if this maximum elongation of Mercury from the sun should be less...

...the distance which the evening appearance requires: we will hold as certain that Mercury, situated in that place in the evening, cannot rise <note>that is, it cannot be seen appearing in the sky</note>. For it is unable to move far enough away from the solar rays for its own light to strike the eye. And if that cannot happen for Mercury even when it is at its maximum distance from the sun, it will happen much less when it is less distant from the sun. ¶ Regarding the morning rising, I shall argue in exactly the same way. Ptolemy, therefore, for Mercury existing at the beginning of Scorpio, calculated the arc of its appearance <note>the "arc of vision" is the required vertical distance between the sun and a planet for the planet to become visible</note> as approximately 22 degrees. Yet the furthest it can be from the sun in that position is only 20 degrees and 52 minutes; therefore, Mercury cannot reach the required limit for its appearance. Finally, at the beginning of Taurus, he extracted the arc of its morning appearance as 22 degrees and 16 minutes. But its maximum elongation <note>distance</note> from the sun in that location is 22 degrees and 13 minutes. Because this remains less than the limit for a morning appearance, it does not allow Mercury to escape the solar rays so as to be visible to the sight. Therefore, the common wonder among us shall cease. For reason proves why for Venus, when setting in the evening, a sudden rising now almost occurs, and yet at another time a slow one; and why Mercury, at one time rises and sets in both the evening and the morning, but at other times is not seen at all, even though it stands at its furthest distance from the sun. We have decided to investigate this last point in this theorem, and so set a limit to the labor we have undertaken.

<margin>Proposition 8 of the first book <note>Likely referencing Ptolemy's *Almagest*, Book 1, Chapter 10, which contains this specific lemma for calculating chords</note></margin>
Of unequal arcs in a semicircle, the ratio of the greater arc to the lesser is greater than the ratio of the chord of the greater to the chord of the lesser.
